Global markets start week on negative note
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:27:27 UTC
15:27:27 KST

Global markets start a busy week with a sell-off trend, driven by US growth and inflation data, the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium and Nvidia's balance sheet.
Investors entered the week nervously as uncertainties regarding a cease-fire in the Middle East continued to complicate pricing, testing macroeconomics, monetary policy and the artificial intelligence theme simultaneously.
As negotiations between the US and Iran yielded no concrete results, the mutual defiance of the parties spreading to the economic field rather than remaining limited to the military front increased current uncertainties.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce new economic sanctions against Iran on Monday.
Oil prices maintained their high levels as geopolitical uncertainty persisted over the Strait of Hormuz, which plays an important role in energy supply, keeping concerns about inflationary pressures alive on a global scale.
Analysts said current pricing in money markets indicated the Fed could raise interest rates once by the end of the year, while these expectations could change depending on announced economic data and geopolitical developments in the Middle East.
The lack of clarity over the Fed's policy steps, in addition to ongoing uncertainties, turned attention to statements Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will make at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium on Friday.
US growth data and the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, an inflation indicator, remained among the important topics in investors' focus.
The data is expected to guide expectations regarding the Fed's interest rate path through the strength of economic activity and the course of inflation.
Financial results to be announced by Nvidia also remained among the important items to follow this week to gauge whether the artificial intelligence theme will continue, in addition to these developments.
Analysts said Nvidia's profitability and growth expectations and its forecasts for the future of the semiconductor sector could increase volatility in the markets.
The tariff issue between the US and Canada was also among the developments occupying the agenda.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the US proposed "economically unviable and unfair" conditions in ongoing trade negotiations, adding that Canada will respond in kind to Washington's new tariffs to protect workers, farmers, families and businesses.
Selling pressure eased in the bond market for a while after the US Treasury Department doubled its long-term bond buyback operations.
The 10-year US bond yield, which ended the week at 4.74% with a three-basis-point increase on Friday, started the new week at 4.71%.
The two-year US bond yield also dropped to 4.23%, a decrease of two basis points.
Expectations that the US Treasury Department could increase its interventions in the bond market continued to put pressure on the dollar.
The US dollar index started the new week flat at 98.8.
Finding support from the weakening dollar and the curbing of the rise in bond yields, an ounce of gold hit a nearly 14-week high, rising to $4,657 at the start of the new day.
The price of Brent crude oil for October delivery hovered at $93 per barrel, down 1.5%.
US index futures also started the week on a negative note.
Index futures in European derivatives markets started the week on a mixed course amid uncertainties regarding geopolitical developments in the Middle East.
Markets considered it certain that the European Central Bank (ECB) will raise interest rates next month as concerns continued that high oil prices in the region will increase energy costs.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for July in the Eurozone came in line with expectations last week, increasing 0.2% monthly and 2.9% annually.
Inflation remaining above the ECB's 2% target was among the factors supporting expectations of monetary policy tightening by the bank.
Investors will follow growth and the economic confidence index in Germany, European Central Bank (ECB) meeting minutes on Thursday, the unemployment rate in Germany on Friday and the consumer confidence index in the Eurozone this week.
Markets will also closely monitor messages regarding monetary policy at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in the US.
Asian stock markets started the week on a negative note in light of current developments.
Developments in the Middle East and messages at the Jackson Hole meeting are expected to affect the direction of regional markets.
The rise in US-Canada trade tensions brought concerns that a new tariff agenda toward the region could emerge.
Shares of China's leading e-commerce and technology company Alibaba fell 9.8% on reports that the company planned to sell $10.2 billion in shares to finance its investments in artificial intelligence.
South Korea-based electronics company Samsung Electronics announced it would transfer 90 trillion to 110 trillion won, around $65 billion to $80 billion, to shareholders this year.
Samsung shares lost 8% in value because the record $80 billion shareholder return plan did not meet expectations.
With these developments, Japan's Nikkei 225 index dropped 0.5%, South Korea's Kospi index 2.9%, China's Shanghai Composite Index 0.9% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index 2% near the close.
Following a buying-heavy course on Friday, the BIST 100 index on Borsa Istanbul ended the day up 0.82% at 14,514.82 points.
The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) decided to restart one-week repo auctions, which were suspended on March 1, 2026.

Typhoon signal in Hong Kong unlikely in next 2 days but expect unsettled weather
Observatory revises earlier prediction that typhoon signal could be issued on Tuesday or Wednesday, but residents can still expect thunderstorms
The likelihood that Hong Kong’s weather forecaster will issue a typhoon signal in the next two days is “relatively low”, although multiple tropical cyclones are set to bring unsettled weather to the city later this week.
The Observatory said at noon on Monday that Tropical Storm Narra was expected to skirt the coast of the Leizhou Peninsula in western Guangdong province in the coming days while “maintaining some distance from Hong Kong”.
Narra, a name provided by the Philippines, means Burmese rosewood.
On Monday, the Observatory said Hong Kong could expect showers and squally thunderstorms in the middle of the week under the influence of a southerly airstream, with occasionally strong winds offshore and on high ground.
Another cyclone located near Taiwan on Monday, Tropical Depression Gaenari – named after a type of native Korean flowering bush – had a relatively weak intensity and small circulation.

Türkiye boosts commercial integration with Islamic countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:25:15 UTC
15:25:15 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Türkiye's exports to Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) member countries reached $41.5 billion in the first seven months of 2026, increasing by $345.7 million on a yearly basis, the Turkish Trade Ministry announced on Monday.
The OIC was established in 1969 to strengthen cooperation and solidarity among Islamic countries and protect common rights and interests, representing approximately a quarter of the world's population and one-tenth of global income with its 57 member states, the ministry said.
In this context, the ministry's Strategy for Developing Exports with OIC Members effectively supports the activities of exporters toward Islamic countries that hold an important place in the global economy.
Under the strategy, which is also included in the 2026-2028 Medium Term Program, the share of Islamic countries in total exports, currently at 27%, is targeted to rise to 30% by 2028.
Within the scope of the strategy, 21 countries whose economic and commercial data were analyzed in detail were designated as first-phase focus countries, namely Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, the UAE, Algeria, Indonesia, Morocco, Ivory Coast, Qatar, Kuwait, Libya, Malaysia, Egypt, Nigeria, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Senegal, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Jordan and Oman.
Türkiye's foreign trade volume with OIC countries stood at $87.6 billion in 2013, increasing approximately 1.4 times to reach $119.1 billion as of 2025.
Last year, the countries with which Türkiye carried out the most trade among OIC countries were the UAE with approximately $19 billion, Iraq with $14.3 billion, Egypt with $7.9 billion and Kazakhstan with $7.9 billion.
Trade with OIC countries continued to increase in the first seven months of this year. In the January-July period, Türkiye's foreign trade volume with OIC countries increased by 2.2% compared to the same period last year, reaching $69.2 billion.
In the same period, Türkiye's exports to OIC countries stood at $41.5 billion, an increase of $345.7 million, or 0.8%, compared to the same period of the previous year.
In the January-July period of this year, the OIC countries where exports increased the most in value terms were Egypt, reaching a total of $2.8 billion with an increase of $522.2 million; Libya, reaching a total of $2.2 billion with an increase of $438.5 million; Syria, reaching a total of $2.1 billion with an increase of $296.8 million; and Jordan, reaching a total of $1.3 billion with an increase of $227.5 million.

Thai PM meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in three southern provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:24:38 UTC
15:24:38 KST

As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.
Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, already facing a flood crisis in the country’s north, held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to coordinated violence overnight in three southern provinces where a small-scale Muslim insurgency is active.
The meeting, held shortly before Anutin flew north to inspect the badly flooded province of Nan, followed 51 incidents on Saturday night in the southernmost provinces of Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala.
The attackers did not engage with military or police forces. Only three civilians were known to have been wounded and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday.
The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage. The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani.
A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men stalking outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire.
A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-haul services. It was not clear when they would be restored due to the uncertain security situation.
As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.
However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani (BRN). It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organisational means and support to stage such an action.
It is also the group with which the Thai government has been holding intermittent peace talks.
The three southernmost provinces are the only ones with Muslim majorities in predominantly Buddhist Thailand and the BRN has said that it is seeking self-rule for them.
Muslim residents have long complained of being treated like second-class citizens in Thailand, and separatist movements have been periodically active for decades.
Insurgent violence escalated sharply in 2004 and was met with heavy-handed crackdowns, further fuelling discontent.
According to Deep South Watch, a think tank based at the Prince of Songkla University’s campus in Pattani, 7,837 people have died in the violence in the past 22 years.
The last major flare-up came in July, when about 10 attackers opened fire and threw pipe bombs at soldiers at a security checkpoint in Narathiwat. Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians were wounded, including a 10-year-old boy.
Don Pathan, an independent security analyst, says the BRN carries out attacks largely for leverage as it negotiates with the Thai government.
“From the ground, BRN combatants are turned off by the boasting of military officials and wanted to use the spike in violence to demonstrate their capabilities," said Pathan.
"Many of the targets in these latest incidents were civilians, but BRN combatants were not after body counts. They want to send a stern message to the Thais of what they are capable of doing.”

Unknown Publisher

Japanese lawmakers travel to Beijing, seeking to mend ties after Takaichi’s Taiwan remark fallout
TOKYO (AP) — A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers, including one from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s governing party, headed to Beijing on Monday to meet with Chinese officials for the first time since ties between the two Asian rivals deteriorated after Takaichi’s comment on Taiwan angered China.
Japan seeks a chance to mend its strained ties with China as tensions have spilled over into the economy.
The group, which includes Gaku Hashimoto, a lawmaker of Takaichi’s governing Liberal Democratic Party and a former health and welfare vice minister, and a lawmaker each from two opposition parties Komeito and the Centrist Reform Alliance, is to meet with Chinese Communist Party officials during their visit through Thursday.
“Communication has been severed in all areas and we are beginning to see their impact in many areas,” Shinichi Isa, a top spokesperson for the CRA party, told reporters before leaving Tokyo’s Haneda airport. “I hope we can somehow find a clue to restart a dialogue.”
Isa, who has served as a diplomat at the Japanese Embassy in China, wrote on X earlier this month that bilateral ties have sunk to their worst since the 1972 normalization of relations. He wrote that officials had always remained in communication even during previous lows: “Now all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”
The situation is not in the national interest of either side, Isa said at the time, and the Chinese side accepted a request from Japanese lawmakers for a “window for dialogue.”
Soon after taking office, Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan that would justify the use of force, enraging Beijing.
The remark crossed what China considers a red line in its relations with other countries about Taiwan, which is a self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.
Takaichi has not retracted her comment, but when marking Japan’s World War II surrender on Aug. 15, she prayed remotely instead of visiting the controversial Yasukuni Shrine, seen by China and South Korea as lacking remorse for Japan’s wartime militarism and atrocities.

High earners buy nearly half of Dutch electric cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:21:11 UTC
15:21:11 KST

High earners buy nearly half of Dutch electric cars
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands’ shift to electric cars is being driven overwhelmingly by its wealthiest households, while lower earners buy up the country’s oldest and most polluting vehicles, new figures from national statistics office CBS show.
Of the roughly 259,000 fully electric cars and plug-in hybrids bought or changed hands in 2025, the highest-earning 10% of households took almost 75,000 – more than a quarter of the total. Add the next bracket down and the top fifth of earners account for close to half of every plug-in car sold.
At the other end, the lowest-earning 10% bought around 6,000, about 2% of the total. What they did buy skewed old and diesel: two-thirds of the cars bought by the poorest fifth were more than 10 years old, and diesel’s share was highest among the lowest earners.
The split reflects what people can afford. Most cars that change hands in the Netherlands are second-hand – of 1.7 million bought or transferred in 2025, only 148,000 were new – and the used market remains overwhelmingly petrol, with nearly 1.4 million of the total running on it.
The figures come as the government prepares to step in. From the last quarter of 2026, a scheme aimed at lower and middle incomes will let households scrap an old petrol or diesel car and claim a subsidy towards a second-hand fully electric one. The cabinet has set aside €52 million over three years for the measures.
The scheme is a direct answer to a long-standing criticism – that state support for electric driving has mostly reached the wealthy – that these figures now bear out.

Vietnam records nearly 100,000 HFMD cases in over 8 months
China
Unknown Publisher

14:18:48 CST
15:18:48 KST

HANOI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has recorded nearly 100,000 cases of hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) in the first eight and a half months of the year, more than 2.5 times the number reported during the same period last year, local daily Ha Noi Moi reported Monday, citing the Ministry of Health.
Over 3,000 new cases have been reported nationwide each week over the past four weeks, with infections concentrated in southern Vietnam, according to the ministry's Vietnam Administration of Disease Prevention.
Vo Hai Son, the administration's deputy director, said the surge coincides with the start of the new school year, when children have more frequent contact and interaction in group settings.
He warned of a high risk of outbreaks and wider transmission if personal hygiene and environmental disinfection measures are not strictly followed and cases are not detected early.
The administration has urged parents, caregivers and educational institutions to strictly follow the "three clean" principle, which includes clean food and water, a clean living environment and clean hands, the report said. ■

Vietnam tightens regulation on overseas jobs for contract workers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:18:41 CST
15:18:41 KST

HANOI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam on Monday tightened its regulations on overseas jobs for contract workers as the National Assembly passed a revised law, local media Tuoi Tre reported.
The revised law prohibits Vietnamese workers from taking overseas jobs that violate national security, social order and safety, or social morality, or endanger the health of workers and the community, as well as jobs not permitted by the receiving country.
It bans organizing overseas employment or recruiting, preparing and sending Vietnamese workers to areas affected by armed conflict or areas that competent authorities have advised people not to visit or to limit travel to.
The law also bans Vietnamese workers under contract from taking massage jobs abroad and organizations from sending workers overseas for such work.
The revised law will take effect on March 1, 2027, the government portal reported. ■

New Zealand moves to ban under-16s from social media
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:18:34 CST
15:18:34 KST

WELLINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's government moved ahead with plans to ban children under 16 from using social media, with legislation set to be introduced to parliament on Monday.
The Online Safety Bill would require high-risk social media platforms, including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, to take reasonable steps to verify that users are over the age of 16, using methods such as existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal identification, said a government statement.
The legislation would also require platforms used by children to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how those risks are being identified and reduced, it said.
Companies that fail to meet their obligations could face penalties of up to 10 percent of a platform's global revenue. The bill would also bring emerging technologies, including AI companion platforms, within the regulatory framework.
An online safety regulator would be established within the Department of Internal Affairs to independently monitor compliance, investigate platforms and enforce the law, the statement said.
"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said while making the announcement.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said the bill would bring New Zealand into line with other countries, placing greater responsibility on technology companies to protect children online.
"The bill places legal obligations on platforms. No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.
Winston Peters, leader of New Zealand First, a partner in the governing coalition, said his party shared concerns about children's online safety but would not support the ban, warning that enforcement could come at the expense of parental rights, individual freedoms and privacy.
Cassandra Mudgway, a senior law lecturer at New Zealand's University of Canterbury, welcomed the proposed online safety regulator and stronger platform accountability but questioned whether a ban on social media for under-16s would achieve the government's aims.
Mudgway warned that age verification could carry significant privacy costs, saying a ban would not necessarily make the online environment safer. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Chinese green technology powers Brazil's sustainable development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:18:33 CST
15:18:33 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- As China and Brazil deepen green cooperation, Chinese companies are bringing cutting-edge technologies to the South American country, helping diversify its energy supply and accelerate its push for sustainable development, according to industry insiders.
"China and Brazil share a high degree of consensus on building an ecological civilization," Zhou Zhiwei, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told Xinhua. Zhou cited Brazil's "New Industry" policy as an example, saying it is highly compatible with China's green development approach.
The industrial policy initiative, launched by the Brazilian government for the 2024-2026 period, aims to re-industrialize the country by boosting productivity, sustainability and innovation. Energy transition is one of the policy's key priorities.
The focus is similar to China's own development approach. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) prioritizes accelerating the comprehensive green transition of economic and social development, calling for faster progress in shaping green modes of production and day-to-day life.
The two countries' strategic priorities, including green development, energy transition and re-industrialization, are highly consistent, Zhou said, adding that as they deepen green cooperation, China's experience in areas ranging from infrastructure development to industrial modernization and technological innovation can offer a "valuable benchmark."
In a landmark move set to reshape Brazil's green energy infrastructure, State Grid Corporation of China has recently broken ground on a 1,468-kilometer ultra-high voltage (UHV) power transmission project, marking the largest investment in an electricity transmission franchise project in the South American country's history.
Leveraging China's mature UHV technology, the megaproject is scheduled to begin operation in 2029. It will serve as a vital energy artery, channeling wind, solar and hydropower from Brazil's resource-rich northeast to major load centers in the central and eastern regions. Once fully operational, the project is expected to deliver more than 20 billion kWh of clean energy annually, equivalent to a reduction of 6.84 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
Previously, State Grid had launched the Belo Monte UHV direct current Phase I and Phase II projects, which transmit large amounts of hydroelectric power generated in the Amazon basin in northern Brazil directly to the country's metropolitan southeast.
Such projects, powered by China's advanced clean energy technology, have helped Brazil optimize its energy resource allocation and accelerate the green and low-carbon transformation of its energy structure, according to an official statement from State Grid.
In addition to state-led infrastructure projects, private Chinese companies are also playing an increasingly active role in Brazil's green transition, bringing market-oriented solutions in areas such as clean energy, electric mobility and sustainable manufacturing.
A case in point is CHINT Group Co., Ltd., a smart energy solutions provider headquartered in east China's Zhejiang Province. The company has been operating in the Brazilian market for more than 20 years, with a localized ecosystem spanning operations, manufacturing, delivery, as well as research and development.
One of the latest milestones in the company's expansion in Brazil came in 2025, when it inaugurated a smart meter factory in the northwestern city of Manaus, mainly manufacturing electronic and smart energy meters. The entire production process is localized.
Nearly a year later, the factory has focused on creating local jobs and supporting the development of power technologies across Latin America. "By bringing our expertise in electricity and new energy to Brazil, we are deepening energy cooperation between the two countries and supporting the low-carbon transition of Brazil's power industry," said Shan Hao, country manager for Brazil at CHINT Global.
Likewise, EP Equipment, a Chinese manufacturer and service provider specializing in electric and autonomous forklifts, has also been exploring the Brazilian market for years.
To adapt to Brazil's operating conditions, including its tropical climate and muddy terrain, EP Equipment has enhanced the durability of its products and developed models, which feature long endurance and quick-swap batteries, to better meet the needs of the Brazilian market, said Zhao Hailiang, general manager of Zhejiang EP Equipment Imp. & Exp. Co., Ltd.
Commenting on the prospects for China-Brazil cooperation in the clean energy transition, Jose Medeiros da Silva, professor and director of the Brazil Studies Center at Zhejiang International Studies University, said that as two of the world's largest developing economies, the two countries can play a decisive role in exploring ways to integrate economic growth, social inclusion and environmental protection.
To provide further financial support for such cooperation, the Brazilian Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China have set up a 1-billion-U.S.-dollar investment fund, with the goal of expanding capacity cooperation in sustainable development. The fund focuses on supporting projects in areas such as climate change, new energy and infrastructure.
Looking ahead, analysts note that China-Brazil green cooperation not only complements the two countries' respective strengths, but also offers a valuable reference for cooperation between major Global South economies.
"China has capital, technology and manufacturing scale, while Brazil has abundant natural resources and a pressing need for sustainable industrialization," Zhou said, adding that such cooperation is not about one side aiding the other, but about promoting mutual benefit.
"More importantly, this cooperation model demonstrates that the transition to a green economy can be a driver of growth, rather than a drag on it," Zhou said. ■

"We will try to balance striving for good results at the Asian Games and preparing for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics," he added.
China will face Qatar in Doha on Aug. 27 before hosting Lebanon in Zhuji, east China's Zhejiang Province, on Aug. 31 in the fourth window of the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers.
Han Xu and Li Yueru, who are competing in the WNBA, are expected to join the national team for the FIBA Women's World Cup scheduled for Sept. 4 to 13 in Berlin.
The men's basketball competition at the Asian Games will begin on Sept. 10, while the women's competition starts on Sept. 17, both before the official opening of the Games on Sept. 19.
"With a long-term focus on building a sustainable talent pipeline, the Chinese men's and women's basketball teams are working to maintain their current strength while actively giving young players experience in international competitions, testing different lineups and developing talent reserves for future FIBA competitions and the Olympic Games," the official said. ■

Everybody's Home said that someone earning 70,000 Australian dollars in Sydney would spend 69 percent of their income on the median weekly unit rent in the city, the highest proportion of any capital. (1 Australian dollar equals 0.72 U.S. dollars) ■

Interview: U.S. military expansion in LatAm an "escalation of imperialism," says Brazilian analyst

RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Washington's recent expansion of ground military operations in Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and other Latin American countries represents an "escalation of imperialism" in the region, a Brazilian political observer has warned.
Noting that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the expansion earlier this month during his visit to Panama, Jose Luiz Niemeyer, an international relations professor at Brazil's Ibmec university, said the move marks a qualitative leap in Washington's interventionist policy, extending to ground operations the same approach it has used to strike boats in the Caribbean and Pacific.
"It is an extremely concerning move and, unfortunately, is in keeping with the U.S. historical approach to our region," Niemeyer said in an interview with Xinhua.
The United States is using the fight against drug trafficking not only to justify expanding its military presence, but also to impose "its security agenda without any regard for the sovereignty of Latin American countries," he said.
"The attacks on vessels in the Caribbean and the Pacific were already a unilateral action with serious human rights violations, resulting in more than 200 deaths and little presented evidence. Now, by applying that same logic to ground operations in countries like Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala, the United States is creating a highly dangerous precedent for direct interventions in our territory," he said.
Niemeyer questioned Washington's narrative about striking agreements with allied countries, saying they ignore popular will and national laws.
"What we are seeing is pressure from Washington on governments that are mostly ideologically aligned or in a position of political and economic vulnerability," he added.
From the Monroe Doctrine to the Roosevelt Corollary to the recent "Donroe Doctrine," Latin American countries "are faced with the same logic of domination that reinvents itself throughout the centuries," Niemeyer said, describing the latter two as extension and revival of the Monroe Doctrine as Washington's guiding policy for the Western Hemisphere.
By reviving that rhetoric with a play on the name of U.S. President Donald Trump, Washington "is saying out loud that the United States feels entitled to intervene wherever it wants in the region to 'defend its hemisphere,'" he said.
"What concerns me is that this rhetoric is being accompanied by concrete actions, with training, intelligence gathering and joint operations," he said. "In the long term, this creates a military dependency that makes us hostages to Washington's volatile and aggressive foreign policy."
Recalling the history of U.S. military intervention in the region, which is "full of troubling examples," the expert urged Latin American countries to stay alert.
"The history of our region is full of examples of what happens when the United States decides to 'help' us with its armed forces: dictatorships, human rights violations, dirty wars and stunted development. Brazil, with its tradition of non-intervention, must raise its voice against this escalation that threatens the entire continent," he said. ■

S. Korea's wage worker growth hits 2-year high in Q1

15:18:16 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's wage worker growth hit a two-year high in the first quarter due to strong recovery in the service sector that offset shrinking youth employment, statistical ministry data showed Monday.
The number of wage and salary worker jobs totaled 20,828,000 in the January-March quarter, up 292,000 compared to the same quarter last year, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
It marked the largest increase since the first quarter of 2024, when the country added 314,000 wage-paying jobs.
After hitting a record-low expansion of 15,000 in the first quarter of 2025, the job market showed a steady upward trajectory from 111,000 in the second quarter to 139,000 in the third quarter and 221,000 in the fourth quarter.
Jobs in health and social welfare, accommodation and food services, and science and technology sectors advanced 127,000, 59,000 and 37,000 each.
The construction industry continued to struggle, shedding 52,000 jobs on year in the first quarter.
The number of paid workers for those aged 20 and under decreased by 76,000, marking the 14th consecutive quarter of reduction since the fourth quarter of 2022.
The prolonged slump in youth employment was attributed to young individuals delaying their entry into the workforce to build resumes, combined with a corporate preference for experienced workers.
The wage-paying jobs for those in their 40s also shrank by 19,000, driven by a population decline in the age bracket.
Those aged 60 and older saw the biggest growth, adding 233,000 jobs, with employment for those in their 30s and 50s swelling by 115,000 and 40,000, respectively.
Job growth for the 30s cohort broke its previous record of 99,000 in the previous quarter as the traditional age for entering the labor market increasingly shifted from the 20s to the 30s. ■

====================================================================================================

The Belgrade tightrope: How Serbia’s president balances friendship with Moscow and support for Zelensky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:18:09 UTC
15:18:09 KST

Volodymyr Zelensky’s visit to Serbia in early August to see his counterpart Aleksandar Vučić proved a success for the Ukrainian president: Belgrade confirmed its commitment to Ukraine’s territorial integrity and may even help with ammunition production, even if only through intermediaries. Judging by the intensity of the subsequent Russian propaganda campaign, Moscow resented the Zelensky-Vučić talks, which showed that Belgrade is no longer Moscow’s exclusive partner. By hosting Zelensky, Vučić also sent a signal to his Western counterparts about his geopolitical usefulness in wartime. Belgrade still may not be willing to join the international sanctions regime levied against Moscow, but ties between the friendly capitals are nevertheless weakening. Vučić is focused on relations with the U.S. and China, while his political opponents, should they come to power, will seek to accelerate Serbia’s EU integration.
Until recently, Aleksandar Vučić was more than welcome in the Kremlin. However, the Serbian president clearly no longer believes Russia will score a decisive enough victory to force him to sever contacts with Kyiv. Had he thought otherwise, Volodymyr Zelensky would not have found himself in Belgrade earlier this month for a round of closed-door talks with his Serbian counterpart. In their public statements, both leaders confirmed their mutual recognition of one another’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, and they signaled that they are also contemplating the post-war future of their relationship.
The two sides left the key question of military cooperation unanswered, though reports did emerge on the eve of the meeting about a possible Serbian-Ukrainian drone development project, potentially funded by the UAE. Indirect military cooperation between Belgrade and Kyiv has been a focus of media scrutiny in recent years. According to the Financial Times, by mid-2024 the total value of Serbian weapons and ammunition that had found its way to Ukraine was around €800 million — even if in May 2025 Vučić denied the reports of military supplies after Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service accused Serbia’s defense industry of “trying to shoot Russia in the back.”
For some analysts, it is clear that Zelensky’s visit to Belgrade would not have taken place had Washington and other Western countries not believed Ukraine had reached a turning point in the war. Russian authorities, for their part, sought to minimize the significance of the Serbian-Ukrainian summit through their propaganda media. Officially, however, Moscow shifted the focus away from the meeting itself to a controversial remark by Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung journalist Michael Martens. At a press conference in Belgrade, Martens asked Zelensky how Europeans can “help kill more Russians” — a remark that, predictably, drew an angry rebuke from the Russian embassy in Germany.
Who did the “Nazi grandchild” help?
The FAZ editorial team quickly distanced itself from the “ambiguous phrasing,” stating that the question did not reflect the outlet’s editorial policy. But in the days that followed, the scandal only grew. The Russian embassy in Germany threatened Martens with prosecution through German and Russian law enforcement agencies. And indeed, on Aug. 15, criminal proceedings were opened against Martens in Russia on charges of incitement of hatred or enmity, which carry a sentence of up to six years in prison.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova also condemned the world’s “vaunted human rights activists and humanists” over their deafening silence in response to Martens’s words. “For the so-called civilized world,” Zakharova said, “this Nazi grandchild said exactly what they all think — he just didn’t call it ‘inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia,’ but literally ‘killing Russians.’”
The Moscow press picked up on the tone set by Zakharova and did its best to minimize the significance of Zelensky’s visit. The business outlet Kommersant, for instance, described the trip as an event “of a pre-electoral nature,” crowned only by the signing of a memorandum of understanding on agriculture.
The picture was rounded out by fringe Serbian politicians with negligible ratings, who told Russian state media that “the West is waging war against Russia,” that Serbs can only join the EU “as a humiliated nation,” and that the Ukrainian leader’s visit to Belgrade had “shaken” Vučić’s position ahead of a snap parliamentary vote coming up in October.
In short, Moscow signaled its lack of intention to make an original diplomatic move. The Russian Foreign Ministry had already made clear its attitude toward senior Kyiv officials being received in Serbia a month earlier, following the visit to Belgrade by Ukrainian parliament speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk.
At the time, Moscow complained that “hostile anti-Russian escapades had not received an appropriate response from the Serbian hosts.” It follows that by receiving Zelensky shortly afterwards, the “Serbian hosts” chose to ignore their Russian partners’ displeasure.
Not just an election stunt
Moscow is not in a position to derail such contacts, but the Kremlin and the Russian Foreign Ministry almost certainly understand that excessive pressure on Belgrade would push it further toward Kyiv and the West. In this sense, the scandal around the German journalist came at just the right moment, as it allowed Russian diplomacy to signal displeasure without directly attacking Vučić.
Despite Belgrade’s refusal to impose sanctions on Russia, the Kremlin has failed to halt the development of Serbia’s ties to Ukraine, let alone to make it an anti-Ukrainian ally. Zelensky’s visit, accompanied by constant reminders in the Western press about the indirect military cooperation between Belgrade and Kyiv, is a rather vivid illustration of this fact.
Despite Belgrade’s refusal to impose sanctions on Russia, the Kremlin has failed to turn Serbia into an anti-Ukrainian ally
Contrary to some assessments, the warm reception given to Zelensky in Belgrade is not a simple “election stunt” aimed at reassuring Brussels and pro-European voters. The visit was planned long in advance and with considerable care — not to mention that Serbia’s official election campaign had not yet begun.
Absent any election, political contacts between Belgrade and Kyiv have been intensifying in recent years. These have included meetings between Vučić and Zelensky on the sidelines of international summits, visits by senior Ukrainian officials — among them Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba — and two trips by Vučić to Ukraine in just over a year.
It became clear that an official meeting with Zelensky was in the works during the visit of Deputy Prime Minister Taras Kachka to Belgrade in May, when Serbia’s leadership confirmed its readiness to accelerate work on a free trade agreement. Incidentally, the visit was timed with the first-ever NATO-Serbia military exercises on Serbian soil. Notably, Serbia has not conducted military exercises with Russia since 2022.
Avoiding a choice between Kyiv and Moscow
Although Zelensky’s visit does not fundamentally alter Serbia’s foreign policy, it has been one of the diplomatic highlights in the Balkans in recent years. The visit confirmed that Serbia, despite its traditional ties to Russia — both at the political level and via the energy sector — is willing to maintain a dialogue with Ukraine.
The Serbian authorities have no intention of making a distinct choice between Kyiv and Moscow. They are prepared to maintain humanitarian assistance and closed-door contacts with Ukraine while refraining from joining the West’s sanctions campaign against Russia, which remains Serbia’s chief supplier of natural gas.
Vučić’s critics characterize this stance as contradictory and duplicitous. Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić recently accused the Serbian leader of double standards, posing a question to him on social media: “How is it that Serbia is one of the most important sources of weapons and ammunition for Ukraine, while sending one signal to Russia and a different one to Europe?”
For Vučić himself — the central figure in all key decision-making — this is not a contradiction but a convenient balancing act. He seeks to develop relations with competing powers while avoiding commitments that would foreclose other options. And in fact, Zelensky’s visit will help Belgrade expand its room for maneuver, preserving elements of its policy toward both Western countries and Russia.
For Vučić, cooperation with both Moscow and Kyiv is not a contradiction but a convenient balancing act
Vučić is demonstrating his usefulness to the EU and the U.S. during the war in Ukraine, all while stopping short of instituting a formal break with Russia. Some analysts see this as an attempt to win over the Trump administration by proving Serbia’s strategic value to Washington — an effort that has become increasingly visible with the launch of a U.S.-Serbia strategic dialogue in recent months.
Vučić’s view of the war and the world
In the past few years, Serbia’s foreign policy has been perceived as broadly pro-Russian — a perception that will persist even after Zelensky’s visit. A study by the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy found that the narrative portraying Ukraine as a puppet in a war between Russia and the West dominated Serbia’s pro-government press from early 2022 to mid-2025.
Echoing Kremlin rhetoric, Serbian government-controlled outlets portrayed Zelensky as an illegitimate president and Ukraine as a country subordinate to NATO and the West. Local tabloids amplified corruption scandals involving Zelensky’s entourage, writing that the entirety of Ukraine’s leadership was thoroughly compromised.
Many other facts about the Belgrade-Kyiv relationship were thus overshadowed — for example, the facts that Serbia has supported UN resolutions affirming Ukraine’s sovereignty, has taken in Ukrainian refugees, and has provided financial, humanitarian, and energy assistance that Serbian authorities estimate to be worth €60 million.
Following Zelensky’s visit, Vučić stated that Serbia had “lost nothing” by receiving the Ukrainian leader, and that “Ukraine has never been a hostile nation,” albeit while adding that Serbia “is not destroying its friendly relations with Russia.” Vučić reserves the key roles in the world for the United States and China, regarding the EU and Russia as less significant centers of power. Indeed, it is the strengthening of ties with Beijing and Washington that has been the main focus of official Belgrade’s efforts in recent years.
Vučić reserves the key roles in the world for the U.S. and China, regarding the EU and Russia as less significant centers of power
For Ukraine, whose main partners are in the European Union, Belgrade’s ambiguous geopolitical orientation presents no serious problems. Still, if Serbia’s pro-EU political opposition were to come to power in Belgrade, that would certainly represent a more favorable outcome for Kyiv.
For Russia, which claims serious influence in the Balkans and close ties with Serbia, the situation is more complicated. Belgrade’s rapprochement with Beijing and the rapid growth of Chinese investment have once again highlighted Russia’s limited capabilities, particularly during wartime. Beijing — which, unlike the Kremlin, does not demand a rejection of EU integration — has in effect replaced Moscow as Serbia’s key partner in the East.
Equally painful for Russia is Belgrade’s rapprochement with the United States and its bet on a strategic dialogue. All the more so since Washington’s new, more pragmatic strategy in the Balkans is aimed at displacing Russia from the region.

Victorian Environment Minister Jaclyn Symes told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that the vaccinated penguins will be caught again in three to four weeks for their second dose.
"We know that bird flu is here, we know we can't stop it, but we want to put the penguin colony in the best possible place to ensure that they are protected as much as possible," she said.
A 2025 report from the state's environment department estimated that an H5N1 outbreak among Phillip Island's little penguins could have a mortality rate of up to 40 percent.
Australia's first H5N1 case in a little penguin was confirmed on Phillip Island on Aug. 15. ■

Gadi Eisenkot is currently the leading contender in Israel’s race for prime minister. He is also walking around armed.
The former IDF chief of staff carries a gun as his campaign presses for stronger security amid threats against him, while the Shin Bet maintains that he does not meet the criteria for protection by Unit 730, the agency’s elite VIP security detail. Eisenkot is exposed to the public almost every day, moving through crowds, meeting voters and allowing people to approach him directly. His aides say threats have included references to the assassination of former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, including messages invoking the phrase “Rabin is looking for a friend.”
His camp also points to the possibility of threats from Iran, given Eisenkot’s years at the highest levels of Israel’s military and security establishment and Tehran’s interest in retaliating against senior Israeli figures following operations targeting Iranian officials. Yet despite the concern, Eisenkot has not been assigned a Shin Bet protection detail.
Several months ago, according to Eisenkot’s campaign, his headquarters hired a private security company. The company asked police for authorization to arm the guards but was refused. Weeks later, Eisenkot’s staff submitted another request to the police and Shin Bet, this time accompanied by information about specific threats. His aides say police did not respond. After the request became public, police said an answer would be provided, but Eisenkot’s camp says none has arrived.
The Shin Bet also promised to coordinate security arrangements, according to the campaign, but aides say that coordination did not initially materialize. Shin Bet chief David Zini later spoke directly with Eisenkot and, according to his camp, said authorization would be arranged for the private guards to carry weapons and that a contact person would be designated in the Shin Bet operations room. The campaign says neither happened immediately.
On Sunday, a representative from Unit 730 contacted Eisenkot’s Yashar party headquarters and said he would serve as the point of contact. Eisenkot’s aides regarded the move as insufficient and questioned why the matter was still being handled largely through telephone conversations rather than formal written decisions. They also asked why Zini had consulted Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee, and why Eisenkot was being denied full protection when, after the Oct. 28 election, he could hold a position that automatically comes with state security, whether as prime minister, defense minister or opposition leader.
Until a solution is found, Eisenkot is taking his own precautions. He carries a gun and recently completed a shooting-range test, where his performance was described as more than adequate.
Shin Bet: He does not meet the threshold
The Shin Bet presents a different picture. According to the agency, the request from Eisenkot’s headquarters was delayed because of a technical malfunction. Zini apologized to Eisenkot personally, and once the request was received, the agency carried out a security assessment.
The conclusion of the Shin Bet’s protection division was that Eisenkot does not require Unit 730 protection. Officials argued that there is no precedent for assigning such a detail to a candidate who does not already hold one of the positions classified as a symbol of government. Naftali Bennett is protected because he is a former prime minister, while Yair Lapid receives protection as opposition leader and former prime minister.
The claim that Benny Gantz received the same level of protection solely because he was a candidate was examined and, according to the Shin Bet, found to be incorrect, though there remains disagreement over the arrangements provided to Gantz during one of his election campaigns.
Zini nevertheless sought alternatives. He consulted Sohlberg, according to the Shin Bet, but did not ask the judge to make the decision for him. The agency then reviewed the intelligence again and its professional assessment remained unchanged: Eisenkot neither requires nor qualifies for a Unit 730 security detail under the existing criteria.
Zini spoke with Eisenkot on Thursday and explained the decision. Eisenkot himself appears to accept that, while the Shin Bet’s approach may be rigid and bureaucratic, it is consistent with existing rules and precedent. Zini also told him that permission for his private security guards to carry weapons should be granted within days. The guards are veterans of a specialized IDF security unit.
The political question
The dispute also reaches Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In political terms, Netanyahu and Zini both have strong reasons to ensure Eisenkot is adequately protected. Any attack on a leading prime ministerial candidate would immediately raise questions about whether the state had done enough to safeguard him.
The issue also highlights the role of the ministerial committee responsible for the protection of public figures. The committee previously approved Shin Bet protection for Netanyahu’s sons, Yair and Avner, but has not convened to discuss Eisenkot’s case despite a request being submitted. Its secretary, retired Col. Ronen Cohen, is a political appointee. Eisenkot’s camp has questioned why the committee has not met, though no evidence has been presented establishing that political considerations were behind the delay.
The broader question is whether the Shin Bet should bend established criteria when a candidate faces unusual threats, or whether doing so would open the door to political pressure over decisions that should remain strictly professional.
For now, the result is stark: Israel’s leading contender for prime minister is regularly moving through crowds, his aides say he faces specific threats, and the Shin Bet has decided that he does not warrant its full protection detail.
So Eisenkot carries his own gun.

French couple Jacques and Jessica Moretti have been the focus of intense scrutiny since the fire ripped though their bar Le Constellation, in the Crans-Montana ski resort in the early hours of 1 January.

Russia's Ozon says four logistics hubs targeted by Ukrainian drones
Aug 24 - Four logistics hubs owned by Russia's second-largest online retailer Ozon in southern Russia were targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks, the company said on Monday, bringing the number of targeted facilities to six since August 22.
Ozon said its logistics hub in Makhachkala, Dagestan, was on fire after a drone attack, while workers at warehouses in Adygeysk, in the Adygeya region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, had been evacuated.

Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on news of the attack, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.
Ozon has become Russia's second e-commerce giant, after rival Wildberries, to be targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks. Work at a logistics centre in the Samara region was halted after the first Ukrainian strike on the company's facilities on August 22. REUTERS

Here is a roundup of the main developments related to Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, August 24, 2026:
Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa have arrived in Kyiv.
Burnham is on his first international visit since becoming prime minister.
He was welcomed by Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, at the train station.

Ukraine stepping up attacks on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon
Ukraine has struck warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon on three consecutive days, with the company reporting another logistics center on fire.

Why is Ukraine struggling to defend itself against Russian air attacks?
In recent weeks and months, Russia has intensified its airstrikes on Ukraine, regularly firing dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, often at civilian targets.
To defend itself, Ukraine relies on advanced, foreign-made weapons systems — most importantly, US Patriot missiles.
The US war with Iran has depleted its own stockpiles, and Washington has resisted providing Kyiv with large numbers of missiles, leaving Ukraine more exposed to Russian bombs.
Even before the war with Iran, US support for Ukraine had wavered after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Trump, who had an angry public spat with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House, has sought to mend ties with Russia's Vladimir Putin, and ordered a pause of US military aid to Kyiv.
Over the weekend, Zelenskyy revealed that deliveries of Patriot interceptors had dropped by 50% since 2023.
"Over the entire year of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 — 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," he said. "For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264."
Debris from Ukrainian drone kills two children in southern Russia: governor
Falling debris from a Ukrainian drone attack landed on a childcare facility in Krasnodar, southern Russia, killing two children, the regional governor said early on Monday.
Seven other children and two adults were wounded in the attack, Veniamin Kondratyev said on Telegram. He added that a fire started at a warehouse after a drone fell on it.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, said there was a "major fire" at one of its logistics centers in Krasnodar as a result of a drone attack.
Another Ozon logistics complex in Dagestan was also hit, sparking a massive fire, Ukrainian monitor Exilenova+ reported. If confirmed, it would be the third Ozon facility to be struck on Monday.
Ukraine has also hit warehouses belonging to Russia's other major e-commerce website, Wildberries, in recent weeks.
While Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure, it has also struck commercial hubs and warehouses, which are easier targets and less heavily defended than military or energy sites. The attacks have inflicted losses worth billions of dollars.
Russian strike on Kharkiv kills 3
At least three people were killed after a Russian attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv, the local governor said on Telegram.
Oleh Syniehuhov said eight people were rescued by the emergency services, which were still working to identify other potential casualties.
Kharkiv is Ukraine's second-largest city, and lies around 30 kilometers (about 18 miles) from the border with Russia.

Ex-Ukrainian minister didn't call for elections until dismissed from government, lawmaker tells DW
Dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for elections earlier this week, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy comes under unprecedented pressure domestically.

EU pledges 'as much support as necessary'
The European Union has pledged its continued backing for Ukraine as the country celebrates its 35th Independence Day on Monday.
"We will continue to provide as much support as necessary, for as long as necessary — during the war, in peace negotiations and in reconstruction," EU Council President Antonio Costa said, according to an EU statement.
Costa added that EU sanctions on Russia were impacting its war coffers, and pledged to "intensify the pressure" until Moscow ends its war of aggression.
He also reiterated the bloc's position that Ukraine will one day become an EU member.
"Ukraine’s future in the European Union is the best guarantee of security and long-term democratic stability — for Ukraine and for Europe as a whole."
Costa will personally attend the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.
UK PM Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv in first trip abroad
The United Kingdom's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is visiting Ukraine on Monday, on his first international trip since taking office.
Burnham, who will co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine's foreign backers, is also set to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Several other world leaders, including co-chairs German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, as well as European Council President Antonio Costa and leaders from the Nordic and Baltic countries, will take part in the meeting, some of them in person and others remotely via video conference.
The meeting comes as Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union (USSR).
During his visit, Burnham will confirm that the UK has agreed to allow European weapons manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on British parts of the SCALP long-range missile to set up assembly lines in Ukraine, Downing Street said in a statement.
"On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes," Burnham said in a statement.
"Our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security," the British leader added.
The UK has been one of Ukraine's strongest international backers since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Britain has pledged more than 25 billion pounds ($34 billion, €29 billion) in military and civilian support so far and was the first nation to provide long-range strike weapons to Ukraine for defensive purposes in 2023, Downing Street said.
Burnham's trip to Kyiv comes after Zelenskyy traveled to the UK last month as the new prime minister's first foreign guest.

"The IRGC's surveillance and intelligence dominance cannot be limited only to the radars the enemy knows," he told Mehr News Agency.
He said Iranian forces used satellite-based and other monitoring methods that the United States might not yet be able to detect. "If the Islamic Republic did not have a seeing eye for monitoring maritime movements, how could it strike specific targets in sensitive points of vessels?" Mohebbi asked.
"When a missile hits the sensitive point of a ship or its engine room and the vessel stops moving, this demonstrates intelligence dominance and precise target identification capability," he said.
The IRGC spokesman said Iran had in fact "blinded the enemy's eyes" by striking its radars and surveillance network. Any U.S. assumption that destroying a number of known Iranian radars had eliminated Iran's monitoring capability was far from reality, he added.
"In the vast expanse of the Persian Gulf, even in the darkness of the night, when a missile hits its target with precision, it is clear that intelligence and operational dominance stands behind the operation," he said. "How Iran monitors its targets is not something the enemy can fully discern; the results and accuracy of the strikes demonstrate the level of Iran's intelligence superiority."
MNA

Can the EU fight underwater threats? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:00:55 UTC
15:00:55 KST

Underwater sabotage and hybrid threats are challenging Europe's security. In June, the Commission proposed €325 billion for five defence projects, including one on maritime and seabed surveillance. But what is the EU’s strategy to ramp up maritme defence? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
Maritime security is no longer just about guarding ports and shipping lanes. It’s about protecting what's invisible: the cables and energy pipelines on the seabed.
Underwater networks carry 99 percent of the world’s data, enable communication and trillions of financial transactions, and power entire nations’ energy supplies. A single cable cut or damage caused by drones, cyberattacks, or traditional military attacks can disrupt the security and economic stability of entire continents.
Europe faced multiple undersea infrastructure incidents, such as the Nord Stream explosion in 2022 and Balticconnector sabotage in 2023. Concerns grew after damage to underwater cables between Finland and Germany, Sweden and Lithuania in November 2024, and Finland and Estonia in December 2025.
The EU updated its Maritime Security Strategy in 2023 to tackle growing threats to its undersea infrastructure, including those linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It combines innovation, industrial cooperation, joint capability development, and data-sharing to combat physical and cyber threats.
In March 2026, the EU launched the Industrial Maritime Strategy to boost the competitiveness, resilience, and sustainability of its waterborne sector, including shipbuilding, shipping, and ports. The new Counter-Drone Action Plan advances maritime defence by focusing on unmanned naval drones and counter-drone systems against aerial, surface, and underwater threats.
The EU invests in detection and surveillance tech, including the 2025 Cable Security Action Plan to prevent and detect attacks, €92 million OceanEye for maritime awareness, and €6 million SOUND2 project using AI for threat detection through underwater acoustics.
Do you want to know more about Europe's maritime security strategy? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot!

How can I convince NHS pensions that I am not dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:00:54 UTC
15:00:54 KST

I stopped receiving my NHS pension in May and, when I rang to ask why, I was informed that I was deceased.
I have repeatedly called to no avail and my emails have received auto-generated responses.
The same thing happened last December and I was without my pension for four months, during which I had to borrow from my brother. That time, I was told that someone had changed my account details and my pension had been paid to the wrong person.
The problem was sorted out after I sent identity verification, and now here I am again, only this time I’m apparently dead.
My husband and I are under severe financial distress because of this error and are in dread of the end-of-month bills.
IM, Cape Town
Your plight has echoes of the Teachers’ Pensions fiasco in which retired teachers had their income stopped after they were declared dead by the system.
You worked in the NHS for 11 years before retiring to your native South Africa in 2015.
The blunder has left you in such dire straits that you can no longer afford the international calls to the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), which administers the pension scheme, and you mention that you have had to live with a broken tooth for a month because you can’t cover the dentist’s fee.
Last month you flew to the UK with money borrowed from a friend, to try to resolve the problem in person. It got you no further forward. Promised call-backs did not happen and you were told, two months after your first complaint, that your “death” needed to be referred to the fraud department.
Days after your arrival in the UK, an email informed you that because of a system upgrade, NHSBSA would only be able to assist with general queries for eight days.
A further week passed and you were informed that an investigation into your case was required and you would hear back within 30 days.
It seems nothing had been done to resolve the problem during the months you had been kept waiting, and no action was taken to escalate it when you flew over. In the meantime, you are stuck indefinitely in the UK, apart from your elderly husband and sleeping on a friend’s sofa while you try to get answers.
Three weeks after I contacted NHSBSA, it finally paid the arrears – by now three months’ worth – into your account and apologised for the distress and hardship you have been caused.
An NHSBSA spokesperson said: “While we cannot go into the specific details of the case, an error was made in the records, which we have now corrected. We take our responsibility to members extremely seriously, and this case has shown us where we need to do better.”
As for compensation, not least for the expenses you have been caused, it said it would discuss this with you.

Fairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets faster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

Fairphone’s top Android for 2026 is a little faster with more memory while maintaining full compatibility with its previous phone, including its repairable and ethical chops.
The Fairphone 6+ continues the Dutch cooperative’s mission to make consumer electronics longer lasting and more sustainable, containing 51% either recycled or ethically sourced materials while being fully repairable at home with just the one screwdriver included in the box.
It is also the first model to expand beyond Europe, going on sale in the US directly from Fairphone. But the new Android costs £70 (€50) more than the launch price of its predecessor, available from £569 (€649/$650), competing directly with Google’s £499 Pixel 10a and Apple’s £599 iPhone 17e.
The 6+ is an almost exact clone of the Fairphone 6, with the same plastic body, 120Hz OLED screen and fingerprint scanner in the power button. It also supports the same excellent modular accessories that simply screw into the back of the phone to add a lanyard, handle or wallet.
The new model is 2g heavier, but the biggest difference for the 6+ is an upgraded chip to the newer Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and an additional 4GB of memory for 12GB in total.
The Gen 4 chip is about six to 10% faster in testing, which places it firmly in the mid-range category alongside the likes of the Nothing Phone 4a Pro with the same chip. It won’t win any performance awards and is significantly slower than chips used in Apple, Samsung or Google’s latest smartphones, but it feels snappy enough in use and can be used for light gaming without issue.
The battery life is very similar to the phone’s predecessor, lasting about a day and a half between charges with the screen actively used for about five hours across 5G and wifi, for messaging, note-taking, photos and browsing. Most will need to charge it nightly, which is a bit behind the curve. A full charge takes about 80 minutes using a 30W power adaptor (not included), hitting 50% in under half an hour.
The 6+ also has the same dual-camera system as its predecessor with a 50-megapixel main and 13MP ultra-wide camera. It has improved since its debut last year through software updates, which have fixed a few of the issues and inconsistencies. It can shoot pretty good photos with a bit of work and manages a reasonable 2x zoom. It isn’t the best in lower light conditions, though its new Super Night AI feature helps.
Specifications
- 
  Screen: 6.31in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (431ppi)
- 
  Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4
- 
  RAM: 12GB
- 
  Storage: 256GB + microSD
- 
  Operating system: Android 16
- 
  Camera: 50MP + 13MP, 32MP selfie
- 
  Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4 and GNSS
- 
  Water resistance: IP55 (splash/rain)
- 
  Dimensions: 156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mm
- 
  Weight: 193g
Google’s Android 16 or e/OS
The 6+ ships with last year’s Android 16, not the latest Android 17, but will be supported with updates until 2033 at least, which is roughly the same as mainstream rivals.
Fairphone’s software is generally clean and uncluttered with only an additional gallery app and the My Fairphone app for repair and diagnostics from the standard Android app loadout. It has Google’s Gemini in various bits, but no other AI additions to get in the way. It also features Fairphone’s “Moments” minimalist interface, activated by the big yellow switch on the side, for a less distracting smartphone experience.
But for those who want an alternative to Google’s Android, the phone is available with the privacy-focused, open-source version of Android, without Google services, called /e/OS.
Sustainability
The battery will maintain at least 80% of its original capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles and it can be replaced at home using a single screwdriver along with the rest of the 12 modular components. Batteries cost £34.20, screens £77.00 and the main camera £59.88. The phone was awarded 10 out of 10 for repairability by specialists iFixit.
The handset is made with 51% recycled or fair materials, while Fairphone publishes life cycle reports for its products.
Price
The Fairphone Gen 6+ costs £569 (€649/$649.99) with Google Android or £598.63 (€699.99/$699.99) with e/OS.
For comparison, the Google Pixel 10a costs £499, the Apple iPhone 17e costs £599 and the Nothing Phone 4a Pro costs £519.
Verdict
The Fairphone 6+ continues to demonstrate that good, solid Android phones can be made fully repairable at home without specialist tools.
It is only a small spec bump on the original Fairphone 6, which helps keep up with mainstream rivals without sacrificing parts compatibility, sustainability or ethical credentials. It is also available directly in the US for the first time. But that also means the 6+ shares the same flaws as its predecessor.
The camera, battery life, performance and screen are all decent, if far from the best you can get for the money. However, those looking for a high-end smartphone experience best look elsewhere as the Fairphone can’t match a recent iPhone, Pixel or Galaxy S with similar levels of software support.
That makes it hard to recommend to everyone. But for those who prioritise repairability and ethical ethos, this is the phone for you.
 Pros: choice of Android operating systems, modular accessories, repairable-at-home design, recycled and fair materials, microSD card slot, good screen, five-year warranty, software support to 2033
Cons: mid-range performance, average battery life, fingerprint scanner can be tricky to press, average camera, cannot be submerged in water, no Android 17 yet.

On Donetsk’s ‘life or death’ highway with the Khyzhak brigade – photo essay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

“Holy yeah! Yeaaaah! Done!”
Booooooom.
“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!” Dzhango from the Khyzhak brigade shouts in English. He has just shot down a Russian FPV drone.
A small moving target that wants to kill you is a challenge with an asterisk.
I don’t manage to photograph the drone above us, but I’m glad that Dzhango shoots more accurately. The normal rule is for everyone else is to stay under cover and not stick your head out.
The tasks of Dzhango’s mobile fire group are different – to stand watch and shoot down Russian drones.
The H20 highway runs from the frontline city of Kramatorsk to the battlefield in Kostyantynivka in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The last road always becomes either the “road of life” or the “road of death”. Drone warfare is deadly simple – everything flies toward the road; any movement is a target. Us too.
The road is covered with scars: FPV drones, cluster munitions, artillery, glide bombs – a map of modern war. Pears on the ground are entangled with fibre-optic cable – this harvest will not be gathered. Anti-drone nets fall on to a highway strewn with burned-out ground robots, pickup trucks, and armoured vehicles. Donetsk is crumbling before my eyes.
The fighters of the Khyzhak brigade are police patrol officers who joined up. The five of them share a dugout with Zhuzha, a dog that came to them in search of food and cuddles. A shower, a washbasin, a kitchen, even a plasma TV playing Michael Jackson’s They Don’t Care About Us – a parallel universe built underground. The peace sign on Jackson’s T-shirt contrasts with the sound of loading magazines.
Above, the kill zone, which lives by its own rules: food and water are delivered by ground robots, via electric scooters, or through the sky while Ukrainian Vampire drones carry supply packages above.
“We try as much as possible to shoot down whatever is flying toward us. We understand that it’s someone’s ground robot, or someone’s car, or even – someone’s life,” Dzhango tells me. He is 31, from Chernivtsi, which is more than 1,000km away.
In the morning he talks to his family on a video call – on the screen there’s a beach, white sand, colourful umbrellas, his son – a parallel world. “What I miss most is my family, my child … living through the coolest moments of his childhood from a distance. His first baby teeth fell out! And I wanted to pull them out with a string, as my father did.”
His son knows exactly what Dzhango’s job looks like and asks: “Bring me an FPV!”
Dzhango does not bring FPVs home.
His son’s birthday is tattooed on his right arm. On the left – a long scar and a tattoo: “Jump off the cliff and wings will grow.” It is a reminder of his father’s advice and of a police shift in Chernivtsi, when he was wounded – three bullets – and his 22-year-old colleague, Taisiia Tataryn, was killed. After a long rehabilitation, he joined the combat unit.
Every morning we walk the same streets and tree lines, but the landscape changes – fresh craters, fallen trees, smoke on the horizon. The remains of drones and munitions form a map of the area – here a Molniya, a Russian kamikaze drone, is stuck in a tree.
Here – since the beginning of July – a dead civilian has been lying under a black plastic bag. A little further on – a soldier from a neighbouring unit, his body will be evacuated in a couple of days. In the tree line – a burned scooter, an FPV strike; a fighter from another unit was evacuated, but the soldiers will say that he died in hospital that night.
“Something’s flying!” – within seconds the guys start shooting.
Dzhango’s comrade, 41-year-old Young, associates every successful shoot-down with adrenaline and a rush. He served almost eight years in the police and almost two years in the Khyzhak brigade.
On his very first combat mission, two small fragments entered his body; he calls it luck. On the next one – an FPV drone hit the side window of his armoured vehicle – the shaped charge flew inside. “A flash behind me – out of the corner of my eye I see that something exploded inside. Sparks, smoke, you can’t see anything, it’s impossible to breathe,” he recalls.
One of his brothers-in-arms died instantly; a second was seriously wounded: “I guess the shaped charge passed through him, and then hit the floor where another fighter was sitting … And it exploded between his legs.”
Now his task is to make sure another FPV does not reach his comrades’ vehicle.
The only intact building among the erased skeletons of houses is the church.
A blue eye looks out. Some of the saints are on the floor, others remain by the altar. Dzhango lights a candle – according to tradition, a candle is lit either for the health of the living or for the repose of those no longer here. Half an hour later, the artillery shelling will begin, and the church will come under fire. A week later I receive a short message: “The church burned down.”
While waiting for the rotation out, we sit along the highway on scattered chairs and stools under the dense cover of the trees.
Dzhango plays Madonna’s Music from his phone, then Justin Timberlake’s Mirrors, and dances a little. From time to time he pauses – to stop and listen whether something is flying.
Then he turns the music back on and sings along again.
Even in abnormal circumstances, inside war – at least you can always choose the soundtrack.
The next day Dzhango will write saying that they shot down another nine drones.
And then – send a video of how another morning in the dugout began with “Good Morning, good morning to you” from the musical Singin’ in the Rain.
“Easy peasy lemon squeezy!”, he said.
