Co-living “micro-apartments” becoming a top choice for international students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:49:15 UTC
14:49:15 KST

As the new academic year approaches, the student rental market gains momentum every year, with the number of homes available for rent traditionally increasing by around 15%. International tenants account for a significant share of the rental segment: nearly 12,000 mobile students were registered last year, most of whom look for accommodation in the capital.
International students are also becoming more demanding when it comes to their temporary homes. While in the past they typically opted for dormitories or a room in a shared apartment, a new generation of co-living is now gaining ground — small, fully equipped private apartments combined with shared work, leisure and household facilities.
The growing demand for comfort and privacy is also making co-living properties attractive to local investors, who may potentially recover their initial investment in less than ten years, according to the latest Housing Buyer Confidence Index published by real estate agency Latio.
Housing Buyer Confidence Index data for July
- 47 days — the average time required to sell a property at market price (49 in June, 48 in May, 48 in April, 50 in March, 47 in February and 48 in January);
- 17% of homes were sold within one month of being listed (18% in June, 19% in May, 20% in April, 18% in March, 20% in February and 20% in January);
- 20% of sellers asked prices that were disproportionately high compared with market conditions (22% in June, 21% in May, 21% in April, 20% in March, 17% in February and 17% in January);
- 2% of buyers offered more than the advertised asking price (1% in June, 1% in May, 1% in April, 1% in March, 2% in February and 2% in January).
In July, approximately 3,350 apartments were available for purchase in Riga, 15% fewer than during the same period last year. In Riga’s residential neighbourhoods, average transaction prices for apartments in new developments reached €2,630/m², compared with €3,650/m² in the city centre.
A total of 2,260 apartments were available on the primary market in July. In renovated buildings, average transaction prices exceeded €3,000/m², representing a 12% increase year-on-year. On the secondary market for newer developments, average transaction prices were around €2,280/m² in Riga’s neighbourhoods and exceeded €3,200/m² in the city centre.
The seasonal increase in supply was less pronounced in the rental segment. Approximately 2,570 rental apartments were available in July, almost the same number as in June. Around 65% of these were located in central Riga, including pre-war buildings, renovated properties and new developments. The city centre remains popular not only among local residents but also among students.
Mobile students — a growing rental audience
International mobility is having an increasing impact on Latvia’s student rental market. According to data from the Central Statistical Bureau of Latvia, one in six students in Latvia comes from abroad. During the 2025/2026 academic year, there were 11,900 mobile students studying in Latvia, an increase of 7.5% over the year. Around 4,000 mobile students began their studies at Latvian higher education institutions last year.
This group is concentrated primarily in Riga and particularly at two universities: Rīga Stradiņš University (RSU), with 3,103 mobile students, and Riga Technical University (RTU), with 2,578.
Students have a range of temporary accommodation options, from university dormitories to privately rented apartments or homes shared with other students. RSU and RTU both provide several student residences, but capacity is limited, meaning some students have to seek alternatives on the private rental market.
As overall living standards have risen, students’ expectations have also changed. Historically, one of the most common models involved several tenants sharing an apartment, with each person renting a separate bedroom while sharing the kitchen and bathroom. Although this reduced accommodation costs, it also required compromises in terms of privacy and comfort.
The market response — the modern co-living concept
Modern co-living developments are now expanding rapidly, combining compact private living spaces with shared infrastructure and services.
One example in central Riga is Youston Co-Living on Krišjāņa Valdemāra Street. The project comprises 174 fully equipped investment apartments ranging from approximately 12 to 27 m². Each has its own kitchen, bathroom and furniture, while residents also have access to a gym, steam room, cinema and gaming rooms, co-working facilities, a shared kitchen and dining area.
Prices for apartments currently available for sale start at around €46,000, with the smallest units measuring approximately 11–12 m². According to Latio, around 93% of the apartments in the project are currently rented out.
“The concept of co-living is nothing new, but it has acquired an entirely new meaning in the real estate market. In the past, it immediately brought to mind several people living together in one apartment. Today, co-living means modern and functional individual apartments in buildings equipped with shared infrastructure. Tenants no longer have to sacrifice privacy in order to experience a sense of community and benefit from shared services,” explains Ksenija Ijevleva, market analyst at Latio.
Latio emphasises that the actual return on any investment property must be assessed individually, taking into account management costs, potential vacancy periods, taxes and other expenses.
Gross returns can reach 11% annually
Mobile students are one of the most visible target groups for co-living, as they typically need fully furnished accommodation for a defined period of study and often have little interest in buying furniture or entering into complicated long-term rental arrangements.
However, the potential tenant base is much broader. Such apartments may also appeal to local students, young professionals, people relocating to Riga for work, and foreign specialists who need accommodation for a limited period.
Student budgets also vary considerably. On the traditional rental market, a one-room apartment in a standard Soviet-era building in Riga’s most popular residential neighbourhoods currently rents for around €250–340 per month, while a one-room apartment in a new development can cost approximately €340–530 per month.
With co-living, tenants pay not only for the private apartment itself but also for the location, furniture and shared facilities. As a result, the product competes not only with renting a room in a shared student apartment, but also with high-quality small apartments in central Riga.
The investment potential is another reason why co-living is attracting attention from property buyers. The value of a compact apartment is determined not only by its size, but also by its ability to appeal to several different groups of tenants.
“For an investor, the key question is not whether the apartment will specifically be occupied by an international student, but how much demand there would be from other tenant groups if student numbers declined. If a compact apartment is centrally located, fully equipped and suitable for a student, a young professional or someone staying in Riga temporarily, its potential uses are much broader. This is why co-living can also be attractive to local investors looking for a small property with an established rental model,” says Ksenija Ijevleva.
For example, purchasing a co-living property for €46,000 and generating average rental income of €430 per month would result in annual gross rental income of €5,160, equivalent to approximately 11.2% of the purchase price.
If rental income remained at this level, the initial investment would theoretically be recovered in less than nine years. After that period, the investor would still own the property itself — an asset whose future value could either increase or decrease depending on market conditions.
Experts stress, however, that this calculation does not include taxes, property management, maintenance or other ownership-related expenses. Investment decisions should therefore not be based solely on a low purchase price or headline yield. Investors should also consider the location, management costs, rental agreement terms, potential vacancy periods, future demand and the property’s liquidity when it eventually comes to resale.
*To keep the public better informed about current developments in the real estate market, Latio publishes its Housing Buyer Confidence Index every month, compiling five key indicators that characterise market conditions during the previous month.

Waking up to see the golden walls of the Old City of Jerusalem is something the Jewish people have dreamed about for generations. Luckily, I was fortunate enough to be able to do so at the City of David guest resorts last week.

However, City of David has now expanded its reach in the area to offer more than just fascinating historical tours. There is a hanging bridge, plenty of nearby parks, a light show, and Israel’s longest zip line.
I was able to go zip lining with a companion of mine, and found it to be magical. We began at Trotner Park, and walked along the Armon Hanatziv Promenade until we reached Mitzpe David.
We were fitted for harnesses and helmets, and waited a few short minutes before our ride of a lifetime.
Soaring above the pine forests, you can see the entire Jerusalem skyline laid out at your feet. If I’d kept my phone on me, I certainly would have taken pictures of the breathtaking views.
I’d recommend the Mitzpe David Zip Line for families with children with boundless energy, or any thrill-seekers in general. It was 731 meters of pure fun!
Facilities were well maintained, comfortable, and spacious
After all of that adventure, my companion and I were excited to take a breather in our room at the City of David Guest Resort.
The overall facilities were well maintained, comfortable, and spacious. It’s perfect for families with young children or couples who just want a little bit of extra space.
My room was great. I found that it was tastefully decorated with touches that felt biblical and modern at the same time. I also enjoyed the pristine bathroom, which featured a spacious shower with excellent water pressure. The room also had comfortable furniture, a mini fridge, tea and coffee service, and a great view of the courtyard and the ancient walls beyond.
The gated courtyard in the facility was gorgeous and featured well-maintained landscaping. I thought that the trailing grapevines and the fig and olive trees scattered around the property gave it an authentic touch. The courtyard made me feel like I could slow down, sit back, and just enjoy all of the beauty the Holy City has to offer.
After a bit of a rest, my companion and I enjoyed a short bus ride to dinner and drinks near Shuk Mahaneh Yehuda. We wandered around the area, trying several places that were new to us, and enjoyed being tourists in our own country.
After all of that, I ended my day of adventures in Jerusalem in a comfortable, spacious bed with luxurious sheets.
The premier location in terms of Old City access
It cannot be emphasized enough that this resort does one thing better than any other hotel in Jerusalem: its access to the Old City.
Not only is the resort directly next to the archaeological wonders of the ancient City of David tour, but it is also just minutes away from the Dung Gate entrance to the Old City.
The next morning, my companion and I were able to start our second day of adventures without the hassle of navigating public transportation.
We got an early start to the day and left the resort at around 10 a.m., just as several tour groups began flooding into the property to see the archaeological sites. The resort’s proximity to the heart of Jerusalem let us take our time to walk through the Old City unhurried, happy, and well-rested.
If you’re looking to take a step back in time while still enjoying all of the comforts of the modern day, the City of David Guest Resort is the place for you.■

The Thursday staff strike at Ben-Gurion Airport was the result of serious management failures and insufficient preparation for summer staffing shortages, former Israel Airports Authority chairman Maj.-Gen. (res.) Eliezer "Chiney" Marom told 103FM on Sunday.
"I don't want to point an accusing finger, but there is a management failure here. When you reach the summer without enough workers, and things deteriorate to the point where workers are collapsing from exhaustion, then there is a problem," Marom, who also served as Israel’s Navy commander, said.
"There is a major shortage of workers. It shows that preparations for the summer were inadequate."
Marom also addressed earlier warnings from workers' committee chairman Pinchas Idan about the labor shortage and the Airports Authority's failure to prepare for the summer months.
"There is a serious management problem here. There was a failure to prepare, and you can see it. There were warning after warning, and the situation kept getting worse and worse, but no preparations were made. This was not a surprise."
'A wildcat and unjustified strike'
According to the former chairman, when he returned from abroad earlier this month, he waited over two hours for his suitcase and was told there were not enough workers at the airport to move passengers’ luggage in a timely fashion.
"The matter is simple. Ultimately, this should not have happened. This was a wildcat and unjustified strike, even though Pinchas does not call it a strike," Marom said.
He noted that while he respected Pinchas and the two had worked well together, what happened at the airport was “completely unacceptable.”
"You don't stop work on the busiest day of the year, with tens of thousands of people," he stressed.
An exceptionally long tenure as chairman
Marom was also asked about Idan's exceptionally long tenure as chairman of the Airports Authority workers' committee.
"Ultimately, these are elections that are held regularly, and the man is simply elected time after time," he said. "One can ask whether the term should be limited, as, for example, with the prime minister's term. That is a very, very good question."
When asked about the employment of relatives at Ben-Gurion Airport and the subject of nepotism, Marom explained that the issue wasn’t always regulated in Israel
“A friend would bring in a family member, and so on. It wasn't only at the Airports Authority; it happened everywhere. At a certain point, the issue was regulated, and ultimately the Civil Service Commissioner established certain percentages of employees who may be hired despite being relatives, and so on. The Airports Authority complies with that,” he explained.
"The State Comptroller examines it from time to time. It stopped many years ago. But this is really history, and many family members came in. Not only Pinchas's, by the way. Family members worked at the railway, the ports, and elsewhere. That no longer exists."

Board overseeing PKK disarmament to hold first meeting

14:46:38 KST

A board established to monitor implementation of the legal framework for the PKK’s disarmament and dissolution is set to hold its first meeting on Aug. 24 under the chairmanship of Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz.
The meeting will focus on the body’s working procedures and the formation of subcommittees based on the needs of the disarmament and dissolution process. Matters requiring coordination among state institutions may also be discussed.
The board was created under the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration, published in the Official Gazette on Aug. 18 as part of the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative.
Alongside Yılmaz, it comprises the ministers of justice, foreign affairs, interior and defense, the presidential secretary-general, the head of the National Intelligence Organization and the secretary-general of the National Security Council.
Under the law, security institutions are responsible for determining whether the PKK and affiliated groups have ended their de facto existence and surrendered all weapons and ammunition under their control. The finding must then be confirmed by a National Security Council decision published in the Official Gazette.
The board will monitor and assess implementation of the law.
Following the council’s decision, it may periodically review whether the organization has been fully dismantled, drawing on observation reports, and request further judicial, administrative or legislative measures.
It will also review decisions to defer investigations, prosecutions and sentence enforcement.
Once the legal conditions are met, the board may ask the relevant courts to lift restrictions on rights arising from such proceedings or convictions.

New Zealand proposes social media ban for under-16s
August 24, 2026
New Zealand's government is set to introduce legislation Monday banning children under the age of 16 from social media, following the lead of several countries across the world, including neighbor Australia.
What does New Zealand's social media ban entail?
The Online Safety Bill would require platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook to verify users are 16 or older using tools such as facial age estimation and digital ID, with fines of up to 10% of global revenue for non-compliance.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the harm to children is too great to ignore.
"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," he said, citing effects on mental health, sleep and education. Education Minister Erica Stanford said penalties would apply only to platforms, not families.
When will the bill be introduced?
The bill's future is uncertain, as coalition partners NZ First and ACT have both voiced opposition, questioning the law's effectiveness. Australia's similar ban took effect last year, though a June study found little evidence it reduced teen social media use, AFP reported.

====================================================================================================

Tallinn Fringe Festival at 10: How do you Fringe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:45:00 UTC
14:45:00 KST

Tallinn Fringe Festival at 10: How do you Fringe?
Tallinn's Fringe Festival marks its 10th anniversary this year, and writer Todd Williams explains how to make the most of the month-long event taking place around the Estonian capital until September 18, and why there's something for everyone.
I was recently talking to Dan Renwick, owner and operator of Heldeke! theater-bar here in Tallinn, and he asked me an interesting question.
"How do you Fringe?" It's a good one, and, coming from the man behind the beating heart of the international celebration of all things creative, one that I've taken quite a bit of time answering.
The Tallinn Fringe Festival begins last week, and whether you're into stand-up comedy, burlesque cabaret, experimental theatre, or just stumbling into a wine tasting that turns into a concert, it's got something for you. So I guess my ultimate answer to "how do you fringe?" would be "it depends on who you are, or, perhaps, where you are."
When people arrive at a Fringe Festival, sometimes they don't know that they're even in it. They may even wander into Heldeke!, order a drink, and find themselves face-to-face with a burlesque performer mid-routine, wondering if this is just a Tuesday in Tallinn or something they should be buying a ticket for. (It's both.)
That's the thing about Fringe that took me a full year of living in this city to understand: Tallinn doesn't announce itself. It's a city that reveals itself in layers, with cobblestones that turn an ankle if you're not paying attention, a medieval wall that gives way to a Soviet-era block that gives way to a converted power station full of art. Fringe just turns the volume up on something that was already happening. For one month, the city stops pretending it's subtle.
Dan's answer to his own question, when I turned it back on him, was simple: "you show up." No ticket required for much of the calendar. No dress code, unless you count "willingness to be surprised." Heldeke! itself, tucked into Kalamaja, Tallinn's shabby-chic answer to Williamsburg or Shoreditch, depending on your reference points, is ground zero for this philosophy. It's not a venue so much as an artistic dream with a bar: cabaret one night, a wine tasting that turns feral by the second glass the next, a magician performing card tricks for children on a Sunday afternoon before the room resets itself for something considerably less family-friendly by nightfall.
Case in point, on opening night, the venue hosted Love is a Lube, a genre-blurring set from Lebo Sibul, d'Argento, and Cvm Unity that splits the difference between cabaret, music, and spoken word, the kind of show that resists a clean elevator pitch, which is precisely the point. Ask three people what they saw and you'll get three different shows. That's not a bug in the Fringe model. That's the whole model.
The same night, a few doors down in the same building, Ana Falcon ran "Please the People: Comedy Challenge Show", free, English-language, and built entirely around audience whim. You show up not knowing what the show is going to be, and neither, really, does Ana. That's a genuine tightrope act, performed nightly, for free, by someone who clearly doesn't need the safety net. It's the kind of thing that could only exist in a festival built on the honor system, with no gatekeepers and no curators, just an artist and a venue owner shaking hands and agreeing to see what happens.
But here's the part that surprised me most once I actually looked into how this festival works: no one person runs it on a show-to-show level. There's no central booking office, no artistic director handing down a program from on high. Performers contact venues, and if a venue says yes, the show is in. That's it. That's the entire admissions process for one of the more ambitious arts festivals in the world. It sounds like chaos. It is, a little. But it's also the most honest description of how creative cities actually function, not through committees, but through people saying yes to each other.
So if you're the type who wants a plan, Fringe will accommodate you. The full program, all 31 days of it, is sitting on fringe.ee, filterable by genre, language, and how much you're willing to spend (a lot of it, gloriously, costs nothing). Circus, dance, spoken word, burlesque, stand-up in multiple languages, an open-air magic show for kids, a Kafka adaptation, something called "AUTOTUNED: The Orchestra of Cars" that I have chosen not to investigate too closely before seeing it live. There is, genuinely, something for whoever you are.
But if you're the type who'd rather just go get a drink and see what happens, Fringe will accommodate that too, arguably better. Walk around town on a Friday night, follow the noise, and odds are decent you'll end up watching something you didn't plan on watching, in a room you didn't know existed, next to people who also just followed the noise. That's the closest thing this festival has to a mission statement.
Which brings me back to Dan's question, the one I've been chewing on since he asked it. How do you Fringe?
You don't, really, not as a verb you perform. You let it happen to you. You let a whole city hand you its stage for a month and you decide, moment to moment, whether you're a performer, an audience member, or just someone who wandered in for a beer and left with a story. Most nights in Tallinn, that line is thinner than you'd think.
The Tallinn Fringe Festival runs August 18 through September 18. Find the shows that interest you the most. Let the rest find you.

Editor: Helen Wright

2026-08-24
05:43:43 UTC
14:43:43 KST

Ukraine said it was ready to coordinate with Türkiye on civilian shipping safety in the Black Sea, where repeated attacks have hit Turkish-owned and Turkish-flagged vessels.
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi offered condolences to the families of seafarers killed in recent incidents, noting that Turkish citizens were among the victims.
“We are ready for the necessary contacts and coordination with Türkiye to clarify the circumstances and help ensure the safety of civilian shipping,” Tykhyi said.
The statement did not identify who carried out the attacks or what weapons were used.
Tykhyi blamed the deterioration in Black Sea security on Russia, accusing Moscow of turning much of the sea into a conflict zone through attacks on Ukrainian ports and civilian infrastructure.
He urged shipowners, operators and crews to follow navigational warnings and avoid areas closed to maritime traffic, as well as Russian ports and territorial waters.
The statement followed the death of Turkish chief cook İlker Lazoğlu, 47, aboard the Ro-Ro vessel “Ural” near Russia’s Novorossiysk port.
Turkish media reported that Lazoğlu had been evacuated to “Ural” after an earlier attack on the cargo ship “Necibe.”
“Ural,” which rescued 18 crew members from the vessel, was later struck, killing Lazoğlu and injuring eight others.
Responsibility for either attack has not been officially established.
In another recent incident, Turkish-operated container ship “RMS Team” was hit by a drone in international waters while sailing from Gemlik to Novorossiysk.
Operator Akkon Lines said 11 crew members were rescued, while one remained missing.
The incidents followed drone attacks on the Turkish-owned civilian vessels “Yaşar” and “Nadezhda” after they departed Novorossiysk on Aug. 3. Several crew members, including Turkish citizens, were injured.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said at the time that it was seriously concerned that the war was spreading across the Black Sea and affecting civilian vessels.
It called on both Russia and Ukraine to take concrete measures to ensure navigational safety.
The attacks have also begun to disrupt Turkish commercial shipping in the region, according to industry representatives.
Salih Zeki Çakır, chairman of the Istanbul Institute for Maritime Strategies and Research and Trabzon Shipyard, told DW Türkçe that more than 700 Turkish-flagged cargo ships and smaller coastal freighters operate in the Black Sea.
“Our vessels have almost completely halted operations because the safety of crews and cargo cannot be guaranteed,” he said.
Çakır estimated that around 50 Turkish-flagged ships and coastal freighters had been damaged in attacks since the war began in February 2022.
He warned that continued disruption could affect shipments of energy products, grain, coal and steel, while the use of alternative routes would increase transport costs.
He also said damaged vessels stranded offshore posed an environmental risk because of the fuel they carried and called on Ankara to engage both Moscow and Kiev.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan earlier this month called for a mechanism allowing Russia and Ukraine to declare a moratorium on attacks against commercial shipping.
He said Ankara had relayed a Ukrainian proposal to Moscow.
Russia subsequently rejected the idea of a partial Black Sea ceasefire, while saying it had received no "formal" proposal.

130,000 or 230,000? The migration figures One Nation is trying to explain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:40:45 UTC
14:40:45 KST

in brief
- One Nation MPs presented conflicting figures regarding their proposed annual net overseas migration targets.
- Party leader Pauline Hanson clarified that the official policy remains a strict cap of 130,000.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has faced questions over his party's immigration target, claiming fellow MP David Farley misspoke when he revealed their figures were "not too different" from Labor's.
The MP for Farrer told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday that One Nation's stated figure of 130,000 net overseas migration annually into Australia did not include those who enter under a Pacific labour scheme, aged-care nurses, and other in-demand skilled workers.
He conceded that those groups would add roughly 100,000 people, bringing their total to 230,000 — 5,000 fewer than the current Labor budget projections.
Party leader Pauline Hanson intervened just hours later, writing on social media that One Nation's policy is to reduce net overseas migration (NOM) to 130,000.
Speaking to Channel Seven's Sunrise program on Monday, Joyce added that Farley simply made a mistake while explaining the numbers.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Show me a political career where people haven't made a mistake, and I'll show you a person who's not told the truth," Joyce said.
"I'm not going to throw anybody under a bus. When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that's what happens. God knows, I've done it enough."
The debate over Australia's migration figures has intensified in recent months, with a recent Redbridge/Accent Research poll, conducted for the Australian Financial Review, indicating that voters trust One Nation and its traditionally restrictive approach to handle migration better than Labor or the Liberal Party.
However, the disjointed nature of One Nation's ongoing public discourse on the topic has prompted claims that the party is "incoherent" and "not fit to govern" from federal minister Pat Conroy.
What is One Nation's immigration target?
Since its 1997 inception, cutting immigration has been seemingly a foundational pillar of One Nation policy. During her first speech to federal parliament, Hanson alleged Australia was in danger of being "swamped by Asians", that migrants never assimilated, and that multiculturalism should be abolished.
Its website currently states One Nation would "cut immigration by over 570,000 people" through "capping visas at 130,000 per year".
In a social media post on Sunday, Hanson wrote that NOM would be cut to 130,000 — a figure the party has previously clarified to SBS News. This number would be achieved by reducing international students, temporary graduate visas, and a "much more targeted" skilled migration program, Hanson said.
Those figures are different to the ones put forward by Farley, who said One Nation is focusing on "the NOM in its true form", as separate to labour programs "that drive our economy".
"The raw number is not too different [to current projections], but the reality is, where do we need them?" he asked.
"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."
Joyce further affirmed Hanson's view that One Nation's policy remained at 130,000 people annually for NOM.
SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment.
Where do Labor and the Coalition stand on immigration?
NOM hit 306,000 in the 2024-2025 period, down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000.
Labor is yet to unveil its plan to restrict migration, but has previously set an official cap of 185,000 places on the permanent migration program. Treasury figures project that NOM will fall to 225,000 by the 2027-28 financial year.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was set to detail Labor's plan to ensure that forecast was met, but pulled out of a National Press Club address at the last minute over fears about the implications cuts would have for certain sectors.
"Our policy will be released when Tony Burke is in a position to do so," Conroy told ABC Radio National on Monday. "But we've been very focused on getting the right migration mix to grow the economy as well as the broader interests of Australia."
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap NOM at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.
Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam told ABC Radio National that the Coalition is being "fairly methodical" in assessing its figures but that he would not "put a date" on when it will reveal details.
Duniam attacked One Nation for being cavalier with its migration figures, saying it had not detailed the impact such reductions would have on industries like agriculture, which relies on working holiday visa holders for seasonal labour.
"It was the same leader of One Nation who said in an interview about a week ago as well that she did not care about the impact on business any change to the migration system would have," Duniam said.
What's in a NOM?
NOM is difficult for governments to control because it is a measurement of human behaviour rather than a fixed quota.
NOM is calculated by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) based on the movement of people, subtracting overseas departures from overseas arrivals. To be included, a person must remain in the country for any 12 out of 16 months.
Citizens, permanent residents, temporary visa holders, and asylum seekers are included, as are backpackers and working holiday makers who stay for more than a year.
In 2024-2025, 568,000 people entered Australia, according to the ABS, down 14 per cent on the previous year.
Of that cohort, 88,000 were permanent visa holders, 53,000 were New Zealand citizens, and 64,000 were returning Australians. At the same time, 263,000 people left the country.
As Hanson stated, "short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration".
However, using Farley's figures, many of the 100,000 additional workers he says would be able to enter the country — such as workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme — would be included in NOM.
PALM workers can enter under a short-term placement of up to nine months or a long-term placement of one to four years.
The visa caps One Nation plans to set would place policy restrictions on NOM, but they can't control it entirely. Australians suddenly returning home en masse from abroad would, for example, elevate the figure regardless of visa caps.
Migration experts have long cautioned that linking migration to housing shortages is a flawed argument and that, in fact, migrant workers are essential to increase housing stock.
"If we don't have workers doing the jobs we need, if we don't get the right skill set into our country, then we all are worse off," Duniam said.
"One Nation has zero regard for that, as evidenced by the multiple positions they've had on migration policy all over the last few weeks."

Dog Stars and Dark Matter: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:36:53 UTC
14:36:53 KST

From the pastel portraiture of Norwegian artist Asta Nørregaard, to the post-apocalyptic action of Ridley Scott's 'The Dog Stars', here's what's on this week's cultural agenda.
As we near the end of August, a new season approaches — but don't go ordering any pumpkin spiced lattes just yet.
The remains of summer are still lingering, and bring with them more unusual exhibitions, mind-bending TV series, and blockbuster action.
From Apple TV+'s second season of the multiverse thriller Dark Matter, to the release of Interpol's hauntingly introspective new studio album, this week's releases give us something to get stuck into as the summer sun slowly begins to wane.
In case you missed it, there's also our list of the best exhibitions to see in Europe — some of which end soon, so make haste! And for the contrarian music lovers out there, our ranking of the most overrated albums is not so much a recommendation, but might inspire some re-listening.
Until next time, here are your upcoming highlights.
Exhibitions and events
Asta Nørregaard: Truth and Beauty
When: Until 18 October
Where: National Museum (Oslo, Norway)
In the late 19th century, Asta Nørregaard became one of Norway's most famous portrait artists. After studying in Germany, she went on to paint everyone from her fellow artist Edvard Much, to Norwegian monarch King Hakoon VII; each subject depicted with delicate detail and pastel-hued personality. These form the crux of The National Museum's exhibition, which also highlights Nørregaard's keen eye for fashion and lesser-appreciated religious works. For both fans and the uninitiated, it's an opportunity to experience the breadth of a previously overlooked artist's career — and reappraise its impact. Find out more here.
Jürgen Addiers: I Have No Idea What I Am Doing
When: 27 August - 20 September 2026
Where: M HKA Museum of Contemporary Art (Antwerp, Belgium)
The title of Belgian artist Jürgen Addiers' new exhibition is impossible to forget. Not only does it sit inside a sculpture of metal spheres that hang from the museum's ceiling — it's also a sentence we have all, at some point, felt.
But as Addiers also articulates, that's not such a bad thing. The unknown is a freedom of sorts; a place where experimentation is most possible and imagination can grow. Through his mixed media, absurd collages and abstract installations, a blend of humour and doubt emerge that, together, acknowledge the strange juxtapositions of existence. Find out more here.
Bonus highlight: Fans of Monet and Renoir should visit the National Gallery's 'Painting Side by Side' exhibition in London, which ends 15 September.
Movies
The Dog Stars
Where: Cinemas
When: 28 August
After a virus wipes out most of humanity, a pilot named Hig (Jacob Elordi) sets up fort in an abandoned airport hangar with his dog and weapon-wielding friend, Brangley (Josh Brolin). Amidst avoiding violent scavengers and grappling with trauma, a mysterious radio message brings hope — setting Hig on a treacherous journey into the unknown. Based on a post-apocalyptic book of the same name by Peter Heller, Ridley Scott steers this action-packed film adaptation that also stars Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce and Allison Janney.
Bonus highlight: Gregg Araki's I Want Your Sex, a bombastic ode to exploring pleasure, is released in UK and Ireland cinemas
TV series
Dark Matter (season 2)
Where: Apple TV+
When: 28 August
Based on the bestselling 2016 book by Blake Crouch, Dark Matter follows a physicist named Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton), whose entire life is suddenly upended when he's abducted into an alternate reality. A contemplation on existence, identity, and the veil between our choices and life paths, this compelling series makes the multiverse a metaphor for confronting deeper psychological fears. Season 2 sees its characters venture stray from the original source material — and cements Apple TV+ as the current kings of sci-fi TV.
Bonus highlight: The fifth and final season of teen mystery series Outer Banks is out now on Netflix.
Music
Interpol: This Mirror Weighs a Ton
When: 28 August
American post-punk band Interpol return with their eighth studio album, a follow up to 2022's 'The Other Side of Make-Believe'. Layered with intricate instrumentals, wandering harmonies and low-fi laments, it's a frequently haunting collection of tracks that feels ambient and calm — like slipping into a gentle abyss. It's also one of the band's most experimental efforts yet.
Bonus highlights: The darkwave sounds of American artists Boy Harsher return with their fourth album, ‘Get Mean’, released on 28 August. For a different, rockier vibe, Alabama Shakes' 'I Must Be Dreaming' is out the same day.

====================================================================================================

AI tokens getting cheaper but businesses paying more than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:36:43 UTC
14:36:43 KST

AI costs are rising for Australian businesses even as tokens get cheaper
In short:
Businesses are looking for ways to measure the return on the billions being spent on AI. Some say they are "years away" from judging bottom-line impacts.
In this story:
Australian businesses paying to use AI are weighing up what value they are getting from the disruptive technology.
"It's actually only really a relatively new thing that we have started to speak about," Anna Volkova, the head of people and culture at HR software company HiBob, told ABC News.
The platform has seen wins from using artificial intelligence, but it has been difficult to judge that against the mounting cost.
With AI capabilities changing so quickly, Ms Volkova said the business can "never catch up" with the need to redesign how it works to get the most out of it.
This has made it hard to work out precisely if the money is being spent effectively.
"We'll probably start to see impact to our bottom line in maybe two or three years, and I think most businesses are in that boat."
Jeremy Pell, whose firm Elastic helps companies to manage the cost of AI, agreed with that estimate.
"We're in a really interesting time at the moment," he said.
"Businesses are forced to pay this additional investment into AI, but they haven't yet reaped the 'bottom-line' benefits of the cost savings yet."
Last week, Assistant Minister for Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton described the value flowing out of Australia via AI as a "distant sucking sound".
In a speech at the ANU Crawford School of Public Policy, he said Australians were already spending $5-8 billion each year on artificial intelligence.
"With the overwhelming majority of those payments flowing offshore, in effect, we are creating a new import bill. An import bill for intelligence."
That is just the start, with the government estimating local spending on AI could "plausibly" reach $20 billion to $40 billion annually within a decade.
Tokens adding up to billions
Even a few years ago, AI was not a line item companies had in annual budgets.
Now, in the current reporting season for ASX-listed companies, you can measure it in billions.
The technology spend at Australia's biggest bank, the Commonwealth Bank, increased from $2.3 billion in the 2025 financial year to $2.4 billion in this most recent financial year. It lists savings too.
"Measured gross benefits from AI use cases, including reinvested capacity, were [around] $200 million in FY26," its results presentation noted.
"Gross benefits from AI use cases are expected to double in FY27, and to exceed investment."
On Wall Street, investors are asking whether the billions invested by US tech giants in AI will ever be justified by returns, creating concern about an AI-fuelled stock market bubble.
Stu Scotis, AI leader for consulting firm Deloitte, said the equation of how to spend an IT budget is getting tougher.
Clients are weighing up long-term information technology costs — like storage and refreshing laptops — with a new, runaway expense.
"What we used to plan for as a static activity is now somewhat variable," he said.
Mr Scotis said current conversations are around "tokens": units of data processed by AI, or essentially the amount of grunt used to compute tasks.
Complex requests use more tokens, simple ones fewer.
The cost of tokens has plummeted in recent years, with increased competition, more efficient chips and more supply.
An unprecedented amount of data centre construction has increased the computing power available in the world.
Adding in more energy-efficient microchips, increased competition and the technology improving how much it can compute per token, it is now cheaper than ever.
As the below chart from research institute Epoch shows, the cost of the most powerful models has fallen the fastest.
Epoch used the "Massive Multitask Language Understanding" benchmark to rank AI large language models.
The price for large language models GPT-4 Turbo level or better (the most powerful, shown by the blue line) fell from $US15 ($20.90) for one million tokens in November 2023, to 17.5 US cents (24.4 cents) per million in February last year.
Despite this trend, what companies are spending on AI is rising.
That is because firms are finding new tasks for AI to take on, leading to increasingly difficult computations, requiring more tokens per request.
AI not necessarily cheaper than workers
Mr Scotis put it another way: Human workers are paid in dollars, digital workers — or AI models — are paid in tokens.
"You want to get value for the digital workers and their output," he explained.
That means companies investing in AI need to examine the "value, outcome or growth" that comes from the tasks they complete, just as companies evaluate the work of human employees.
"You start to get pretty clear, measurable outcomes that mean your investment in AI dollars or AI tokens actually pay a return."
He said the human workers should not be too worried about being replaced.
"The cost of a digital worker doesn't necessarily mean it's cheaper than a human," he said.
"The complexity of the task, the length of time which a digital worker runs can, in some instances, be more expensive than a person."
Mr Scotis said firms needed to make a judgement "as to where you want to invest that type of work in your organisation, and does it make sense to do so".
It is a question being weighed in boardrooms right now.
How do companies pay for AI?
There are multiple ways that companies pay for artificial intelligence.
Some use "seats", paying per employee that accesses the technology.
This model is often used with platforms like Microsoft's Copilot, where AI abilities can be unlocked in existing programs, like writing documents in Word or juggling numbers in Excel spreadsheets.
The most common way to pay is by tokens.
The frequency with which employees are using AI models and the amount of tokens used in the queries is a new and increasing cost for businesses — which many of them will not have been paying for in even last financial year's report.
"That's the cost metric these businesses are grappling with," said Elastic's Jeremy Pell.
Different model, different prices
Another variable is that some of the cutting-edge or "frontier" AI models use more tokens.
That has led to companies using different models for different tasks, to avoid paying top dollar for tasks a more basic model can handle.
Some firms have also become more deliberate about the use of AI, sometimes capping the amount of tokens employees can use in a certain time frame.
"Businesses can no longer do AI for AI's sake,"
"It's a matter of making sure that you are driving the business forward and these initiatives are driven and tied to the business's return on investment … It's working out which bits are useful."
'Scattergun' AI approach
AI expert Jon Whittle has warned the "scattergun" approach business has taken to using AI means the cost calculations are becoming more difficult, even as the price of tokens falls.
"I don't think companies are being very strategic right now about their AI use cases," he told The Business.
"They're just trying to find any place where they can use it, and that's why they're having costs increase so much."
Professor Whittle, a former technical lead at NASA, director of CSIRO's AI capability and founder of Australia's National AI Centre, said a particular issue was that AI itself did a poor job at estimating the amount of tokens required.
Research has shown estimates can differ "by a factor of 30" running the same request on the same technology.
"I think that's the number one thing keeping [chief financial officers] up at night right now,"
"It turns out that even the AI itself is not very good at predicting the cost that a particular AI task will take."
Speed increases as AI crunches data faster
From her Sydney office, Anna Volkova says the major advantage her firm currently gets from AI is speed.
By connecting artificial intelligence to the software tools the company already uses, staff have been able to do more, at greater pace.
But the bill is mounting.
She said, eventually, the business would likely need to evaluate usage "by need", not "limiting responsible experimentation" but looking for uses that maximise what staff get out of using AI as a tool.
"I think the things that we're looking for in terms of really seeing the return for our people … is it making their work better, easier?" she asks.
"Is it helping our leaders make decisions faster?"
It turns out the questions business leaders are asking about AI are very human.

DR Congo and M23 fighters agree to roadmap for peace talks, Switzerland says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:28:14 UTC
14:28:14 KST

Both sides had previously signed an agreement in Doha last year, but fighting has continued in mineral-rich eastern DRC, a region that has endured years of conflict.
The Democratic Republic of Congo and the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group have agreed to a roadmap for peace talks, according to a joint statement published on Sunday.
"The Parties developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement and committed to flexibility and creativity within the existing structure," the statement published by Switzerland, which had hosted the negotations, said.
"They reaffirmed their commitment to pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution through the implementation of the Framework Agreement," it added.
The two sides signed a US-brokered framework agreement last year in the Qatari capital Doha, but fighting has continued since, prompting both to gather in Switzerland last week for a new round of talks.
The closed-door talks took place from 17-21 August, bringing together representatives from the United States, Qatar, Switzerland, the African Union Commission and Togo, which served as African Union mediator.
The two sides said they had "agreed on the importance of a standardised method for reporting allegations of ceasefire violations," with a first ceasefire verification mission due in Minembwa in DRC's South Kivu Provnce on Monday.
Both also agreed to create a "mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement."
Multiple armed groups have fought over territories in Eastern DRC, which are rich in minerals critical to much of the world’s technology, including the Rwandan-backed M23, which seized large swathes of the region last year.

English cricket investigates reported nightclub incident involving test bowler Brydon Carse

Videos circulating on social media on Sunday appeared to show Carse in handcuffs and being led away from a club by police officers.

New Zealand to consider banning children under 16 from social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:22:19 UTC
14:22:19 KST

New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon has said his party will introduce a bill in parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance.
The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents.
“We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Luxon said in a statement on Monday.
“Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.”
It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners – the New Zealand First party – saying it would not support it.
“We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country,” New Zealand First’s leader, Winston Peters, who is also the country’s foreign minister, said on X.
In December, Australia became the world’s first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta’s Instagram and Facebook.
That legislation had been a “colossal failure”, Peters said, adding that keeping children off social media should be the responsibility of parents.
“I won’t pretend that it will be simple or that it will be perfect,” Luxon said at an event.
“We won’t get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it’s just way too important not to at least try.“

China opens exhibition hall on language preservation, diversity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:46 CST
14:21:46 KST

CHANGSHA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays.
The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions.
More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display.
The exhibition features original sound recordings representing 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, said Chen Xuliang, deputy Party secretary of the Hunan Museum.
Visitors can listen to regional dialects, folk songs and field recordings of some endangered languages, while interactive installations allow them to explore the development and diversity of languages across China, Chen added.
The exhibition draws on materials collected through a national language preservation project launched in 2015 to document and preserve the country's diverse languages and dialects. It is the world's largest project of its kind, according to experts.
An alliance was also launched on Monday, bringing together universities and research institutions to promote the use of language technologies in areas including education, scientific research and cultural preservation. ■

Opinion: What 9.39 seconds says about human ingenuity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:18 CST
14:21:18 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- At the second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, China's Tien Kung Ultra humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds at the finish line, shattering the 9.58-second men's 100-meter world record set by Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt 17 years ago.
The comparison is irresistible, though the two feats are hardly equivalent: Bolt shows how fast the human body can run; the robot shows how far human ingenuity can go.
At the current stage of humanoid robot development, running remains a formidable challenge. The robot must generate force, absorb repeated impacts and maintain dynamic balance while coordinating multiple joints simultaneously. Speed tests every technical limit: the faster the machine moves, the less time it has to recover from a mistake.
That makes the pace of improvement remarkable. At last year's Games, Tien Kung Ultra took 21.5 seconds over the same distance. One year later, it had more than halved that time.
Progress on that scale rarely comes from a single breakthrough. Over the past year, engineers upgraded the robot's joints, refined its structure and reworked its control algorithms for high-speed running. They have also improved its navigation, allowing it to hold its course at speed without relying on track markings.
Breaking the human record, however, is never the ultimate goal of engineering. Every improvement reveals the next weakness. Even Saturday's 9.39-second run pointed to the next challenge: the robot had a slower start, although its higher top speed allowed it to pull ahead later in the race.
Competition helps accelerate that process. It provides clear targets, common benchmarks and visible results. Once one team raises the bar, everyone else has a new standard to meet -- and proof that a higher level of performance is attainable.
Ultimately, the goal of humanoid robot innovation is not simply to make robots move like humans, but to enable them to work alongside people and take on useful tasks in the real world.
A factory robot does not need to win a sprint, nor does a service robot need a medal. But every gain in speed, stability and precision on the competition floor can bring robots one step closer to becoming genuinely useful beyond it.
That is what gives 9.39 seconds significance beyond the stopwatch. The speed record captures how far the machine has come in a year; behind it are countless human decisions, experiments and refinements that made that progress possible. The next test will be how far those advances can go beyond the track. ■

Feature: Chicago concert bridges cultures through Chinese, American folk songs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:13 CST
14:21:13 KST

CHICAGO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The familiar strains of "Shenandoah" brought tears to Marci Jarog's eyes during a downtown Chicago concert on Saturday. For a song she thought she knew by heart, something was different this time.
Performed in a newly arranged symphonic choral version featuring a Chinese community chorus, the American folk classic offered Jarog a fresh perspective on a melody deeply rooted in American musical tradition.
"I thought I had heard this song a million times already, and then today I heard it differently," Jarog told Xinhua after the performance. "I think that hearing an unexpected cultural representation of 'Shenandoah' was even more moving than anything I would have expected."
More than 500 musicians, singers, dancers and community artists took part in the concert titled "Bridges We Build, Memories We Keep" at Chicago Symphony Center, drawing an audience of more than 2,000. The event was organized by the Midwest Asian Health Association.
Among the highlights were the world premieres of newly arranged symphonic choral versions of the American folk song "Shenandoah" and the Chinese folk song "Jasmine Flower."
"Music has a unique power to connect us across cultures, generations, and memories," said Elizabeth Jia, artistic director of the concert.
"I wanted those traditions to listen to one another, speak to one another, and ultimately create something that none of them could create alone," she said.
The concert brought together Western classical repertoire, Chinese art songs and instrumental works, opera, choral music and dance, taking audiences on a journey across different musical traditions.
Internationally acclaimed violinist Liu Yang performed an excerpt from the Chinese violin concerto "The Butterfly Lovers." Chinese baritone Hu Sihao, a member of the Patrick G. and Shirley W. Ryan Opera Center at Lyric Opera of Chicago and a prizewinner of China's Golden Bell Awards, also took the stage alongside soprano Boya Wei and other featured artists.
"It was fantastic. It was very well put together, and everyone was very professional," Jackie Carreras, who attended the concert at the invitation of a friend, told Xinhua after the performance.
"It's just beautiful to learn about different cultures, such as the Chinese culture, so I really enjoyed it," she said.
For Shelly Carter, the concert left her wanting to learn more. "It was like the whole world was up there, that mixed a lot of culture," she said, adding that she hoped to learn more about Chinese music and culture in the future.
As two folk traditions met in newly created symphonic arrangements and artists from different cultural backgrounds shared the same stage, the concert became more than a performance -- it served as a musical bridge connecting cultures, generations and memories. ■

====================================================================================================

Independent Ukraine at 35: State-Building Under Immense Pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:21:00 UTC
14:21:00 KST

On Aug. 24, 1991, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, a decision overwhelmingly ratified months later by more than 90% of voters across every oblast. To treat this breakthrough as a modern fluke, however, is to miss the deeper reality: independence restored political and cultural sovereignty rooted in Kyivan Rus, the Zaporozhian Sich and the Ukrainian People’s Republic of 1918.
Three and a half decades later, Ukraine’s development can be assessed not only through its crises but also through the institutional, civic, cultural and social changes that have taken place since independence. The record is uneven, but it includes important achievements: competitive politics, an active civil society, renewed cultural confidence and the consolidation of a broader national identity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine is often examined through the lens of corruption, flawed governance, and incomplete reform. Those problems remain part of the record. A balanced assessment, however, should also take account of what has been built: a resilient society, a democratic civic culture, a distinct modern identity and a state that has continued to function under severe pressure.
Laying the Foundations (1991–1996)
The foundational moment of modern independent Ukraine was the clarity of its inception. On Dec. 1, 1991, voters across the country overwhelmingly endorsed independence in a national referendum. The result gave the new state a clear democratic mandate and helped bring the Soviet Union to a peaceful end.
Russian Drone Strike on Kharkiv Train Kills 1, Injures 4
It was a difficult task for Ukraine to create a functioning state amid the economic turmoil of the post-communist transition, but the early steps toward this goal provided a rudimentary framework for its democratic development.
The Constitution, adopted in 1996, anchored the republic to democratic principles, human rights, and the separation of powers. That same year, the introduction of the hryvnia stabilized the monetary system and provided a practical symbol of statehood.
Ukraine also made a major geopolitical decision by voluntarily surrendering the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal under the Budapest Memorandum. The decision placed Ukraine within the post-Cold War security order and strengthened its claim to international legal protection.
Democratic Mobilization and the Maidan
Formal institutions provided the framework of the state, while civil society became one of its main sources of accountability. Since independence, public mobilization has repeatedly shaped the direction of Ukrainian politics.
The first major watershed came in late 2004 with the Orange Revolution. After widespread allegations of electoral fraud, large demonstrations in Kyiv’s Independence Square led to a legal rerun of the presidential election. The episode showed that public mobilization had become an important check on political power.
A decade later, in the winter of 2013–2014, the Revolution of Dignity began as a protest against the suspension of an EU Association Agreement and grew into a broader movement for accountability, rights and European integration.
The deaths of scores of protesters during the Revolution of Dignity marked a defining moment in Ukraine’s post-Soviet development. The events increased public support for democratic accountability and closer links with Europe.
European Orientation and Security Reform
Ukraine’s European orientation became more concrete after 2014. The Association Agreement and visa-free travel with the European Union tied domestic reform to a broader framework of legal, economic and administrative alignment.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion, this trajectory accelerated: Ukraine applied for EU membership in February 2022, received candidate status in June 2022, and formally opened accession negotiations in June 2024. The process remains demanding, but it has given Ukraine’s reform agenda a clearer institutional direction.
Security reform followed a similar pattern. The experience of war after 2014 pushed Ukraine to professionalize parts of its armed forces, deepen cooperation with NATO members, and adapt its command, training and logistics practices.
These changes did not resolve all weaknesses, but they meant that the resistance after February 2022 rested on years of preparation rather than improvisation alone.
This European trajectory also shaped domestic modernization, particularly in public administration, digital services and economic governance.
Digital Governance and Economic Dynamism
Beyond politics, Ukraine’s 35 years of independence have included notable modernization. Over the past decade, the country has developed a sizeable technology industry and expanded its digital public services.
- E-Governance (Diia): Ukraine became a model for digital public services. The platform reduced administrative friction by introducing legally recognized digital passports and moving business registration, tax filing and healthcare management online.
- Technology Sector: Software engineers and entrepreneurs created internationally competitive companies and a strong outsourcing base.
- Agricultural Logistics: Ukraine’s agricultural sector supplied major markets in Africa, Asia and the Middle East, cementing the country’s role in global food security.
These changes show a society and state adapting to the demands of modern administration, economic activity and public service.
Cultural Resurgence
Independence created space for a broad cultural revival, the rejection of Russification imposed by Moscow, and a reaffirmation of national identity. The Ukrainian language, literature and art, which for decades had been relegated to a secondary or regional status in imperial and Soviet narratives, gained greater public exposure.
Ukrainian writers such as Serhiy Zhadan helped Ukrainian literature gain international visibility, with Andriy Kurkov, a Ukrainian writer of Russian descent, becoming an esteemed literary ambassador. Ukraine also emerged as a major European force in music, winning the Eurovision Song Contest three times: in 2004 with Ruslana, in 2016 with Jamala, and in 2022 with the Kalush Orchestra.
Across cinema, contemporary art and fashion, Ukraine developed a modern cultural profile that combined established traditions with experimentation. The Ukrainian language also gained wider public use and became an important marker of civic identity.
Prominence in Sports
Ukraine’s sporting record has also contributed to its international profile. Oksana Baiul’s 1994 Olympic figure-skating gold was the first for independent Ukraine; Lilia Podkopayeva followed with gymnastics success in Atlanta. Andriy Shevchenko became one of Europe’s leading footballers, while Vitali and Wladimir Klitschko and, later, Oleksandr Usyk made Ukraine prominent in professional boxing. Ukrainian athletes have also achieved recognition in athletics, winter sports and other Olympic disciplines.
Resilience and Civic Unity
A central test of statehood is whether institutions and society can continue functioning under sustained external pressure. Since 2014, and especially since the full-scale invasion of 2022, Ukraine has faced that test directly.
Ukraine’s record over 35 years should therefore not be reduced to the fact that it has spent roughly a third of its independent life resisting Russian aggression. That resistance is central, but it depends on earlier developments: institution-building, civic identity, cultural revival, administrative modernization and a public commitment to sovereignty.
Civilian mobilization became a major feature of the response. Volunteer networks supported logistical and humanitarian needs, while the Armed Forces adapted rapidly and gained extensive combat experience.
The full-scale war also accelerated Ukraine’s military and technological adaptation. Facing a larger enemy and inconsistent Western aid, Ukraine increased its production of domestic drones, improved feedback between soldiers and engineers on the battlefield, and used unmanned systems at sea and in the air to compensate for Russian strengths.
These changes helped blunt Russian advances, constrain the Black Sea Fleet and enable strikes on military, logistical and energy-related targets inside Russia, extending the costs of the war beyond the front line.
In maintaining its sovereignty, Ukraine produced several broader outcomes:
- International Coalitions: Ukraine’s defense renewed international attention to the principles of self-determination and territorial integrity.
- National Cohesion: Regional differences remained, but support for the state and its symbols became more broadly shared.
- Inclusive Political Nation: Russia’s overt aggression, which began in 2014, precipitated the crystallization of an inclusive Ukrainian political nation.
Taken together, Ukraine’s 35 years of independence show a record broader than war, corruption or reform failure. It includes state-building, regular electoral competition, repeated civic mobilization, cultural consolidation and gradual modernization amid severe internal and external constraints.
Assessing the Republic’s Trajectory
Thirty-five years is a short period for a state-building project. In that time, Ukraine has given institutional form to a national idea, tested its political system through elections and public protest, and developed a society capable of defending the state when required.
This process remains incomplete. Ukraine’s future security and development will depend partly on the depth of its integration with European and Euro-Atlantic structures, as well as on continued domestic reform.
At 35 years of independence, Ukraine is neither simply a fragile post-Soviet state nor only a country defined by war. It is an independent European state with significant unresolved challenges and a substantial record of institutional, civic, cultural, and social achievement.
The author is completing a book examining Ukraine’s first 35 years of modern independent statehood, provisionally titled “Indomitable Ukraine 1991–2026: The Reemergence of a European Nation.”

US: Wildfire forces mass evacuations near Reno, Nevada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US: Wildfire forces mass evacuations near Reno, Nevada
August 24, 2026
A fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes near Reno in the US state of Nevada over the weekend.
An unknown number of homes have been destroyed and at least six people have been injured.
Officials have expanded the "GO NOW" zone to include almost 90,000 residents as conditions make the fire unpredicatable.
What do we know about the Hawk Fire in Nevada?
The fire started Saturday morning off Hawk Meadow Trail and spread rapidly through the Peavine Peak area northwest of the city, growing to between roughly 13,000 and 15,000 acres by Sunday.
About 42,000 residents were ordered to evacuate, with another 45,000 told to be ready to leave, officials said. The evacuation zone stretched to the edge of the University of Nevada in northwest Reno, a city of more than 280,000 people near the California border.
At least six people were injured — three first responders and three civilians — local authorities said. Officials said the fire was human-caused but have not released further details.
"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas," fire chief Richard Edwards told AFP.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the National Guard, deploying two helicopters and 60 troops to assist firefighting and security efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said, according to Reuters.
Human cost of the wildfire
The fire has already destroyed homes. Cari Kieffer told AP her family fled with only minutes to spare, grabbing clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes, but leaving behind birth certificates and childhood photos.
"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," she said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."
"We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."
Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from about 60,000 the day before, AP reported. Parts of US Route 395 were closed, two hospitals evacuated patients, and officials monitored whether the county jail would need to be evacuated. The Reno-Tahoe airport remained outside the evacuation zone, with flights operating normally.
The blaze adds to a wave of fire activity across the drought-stricken Western United States this year. Fifteen new fires broke out across Nevada on Saturday alone.

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv
- Published
Andy Burnham is marking his first foreign visit as prime minister with a trip to Kyiv - and will hand over blueprints so Ukraine can build its own long-range missiles.
The prime minister will chair his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.
He is also set to accept an award on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine and to take part in independence day events.
Crucially for the war effort, he will announce his government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French equivalent of the UK's Storm Shadow.
Burnham will be reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people.
Ahead of his visit on Monday, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.
"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."
He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
It comes after Moscow warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.
Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.
The long-range Scalp missile weighs 1,300kg and is 16.7ft (5.10m) in length. It is capable of hitting targets around 150 miles into Russia - not as far as Ukraine's deep strike drone capability but it is a significant step in showing the willingness of international partners to share weapons technology.
The maker describes them as designed to hit pre-planned, stationary targets. It can be used day and night in all weather, and has advanced navigation systems.
MBDA adds that it is in service with the Royal Air Force, the French Air Force, Italian Air Force and has been used in Iraq, Syria and Libya.
Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles.
On Sunday, he said they have requested 360 of the missiles, but are "working with countries on additional options".
Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.
The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".
In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."
Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".
The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.
The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.
Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.
A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.
It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.
Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.

Hong Kong urged to adopt trait-based dog tiers, DNA checks after fatal attacks
Proposal calls for risk tiers, certified handlers, muzzles or possible confiscation of highest-risk dogs as authorities review fighting-dog rules
Hong Kong should introduce a tiered risk framework and carry out DNA testing and physical assessments to identify dogs with aggressive breed traits, a veterinary surgeon and a lawmaker have said following three fatal canine attacks within a week.
The calls made on Monday come after the latest fatal mauling at a pet training centre, where a 33-year-old woman was attacked by a dog suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog and was later found dead last week.
Preliminary inspections by authorities revealed the dog shared genetic traits with the pit bull terrier, a banned fighting breed in the city. Yet, the dog’s microchip indicated it was a mongrel.
Speaking on a radio show, veterinarian Lai Cheong-sang said Hong Kong should replace the city’s breed-specific categorisation system with a trait-based, tiered system to classify dogs’ danger levels and assign corresponding control measures.
“If a dog is suspected of having the potential to cause danger after a risk assessment, it can be required to undergo mandatory training, be leashed or otherwise constrained, and receive regular assessments,” he said.
He also called for a certification system for people who keep or train high-risk breeds.
