Moscow is increasing pressure on Israel over the future of the Alexander Courtyard in Jerusalem’s Old City, as Russian Ambassador to Israel Anatoly Viktorov made an unusual visit to the disputed compound on Saturday.
Viktorov arrived with a large delegation that included nuns who had traveled from Russia, family members and several embassy employees.
The visit came days after the Russian Embassy in Israel said the process of re-registering Russian ownership rights over the Alexander Courtyard was in its “final stages” and that the issue was now “purely legal.”
Viktorov made Moscow’s position even clearer in an interview last week with RTVI. “The courtyard is ours, Russia’s courtyard. There is no need for negotiations on this. We only need to complete the legal procedures,” he said.
His remarks suggest that Moscow considers the ownership question settled and views the remaining dispute as merely a matter of completing the legal process in Israel. Israeli officials, however, stress that the matter is still under professional review and that it is too early to determine whether, or when, the process will be completed.
Officials familiar with the issue cautioned against interpreting the ambassador’s visit as evidence that a decision has already been made to transfer the compound to Russia. They said that alongside the legal and diplomatic process, Moscow is also waging a public campaign aimed at creating the impression that the outcome is already inevitable and increasing pressure on Israeli decision-makers.
One assessment is that Russia is seeking to exploit the current political window in Israel, calculating that after the election a decision could become more difficult, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu is no longer prime minister. Officials familiar with the matter therefore say Moscow has recently intensified both diplomatic and public pressure surrounding the site.
Viktorov’s arrival at the Alexander Courtyard with nuns who had traveled especially from Russia may form part of that effort. The visit gives Moscow’s claim a highly visible public dimension and conveys the message that Russia already sees the property as an asset moving toward its control.
That impression has been reinforced by Ukrainian nuns who currently operate the compound. They said Russian clergy recently asked them, “When are you leaving?” a remark they interpreted as a sign that the Russian side believes an Israeli decision may be close.
The Alexander Courtyard is a historic Russian compound in the heart of Jerusalem’s Old City, a short walk from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Covering about 1,300 square meters, it includes the Church of St. Alexander Nevsky, inaugurated in 1896, as well as buildings and archaeological sites of religious and historical significance.
The land was purchased during the Russian Empire, and the compound was established in the late 19th century by the Imperial Orthodox Palestine Society, known as the IOPS. After the Russian Revolution, a long-running dispute emerged over ownership of Russian properties acquired in the Holy Land during the czarist era.
In recent years, Moscow has demanded that Israel recognize an Ottoman-era registration in the name of the “Glorious Russian Kingdom” as granting present-day rights to the Russian Federation. The organization that established the compound disputes that claim, arguing that ownership rights belong to it and do not automatically pass to the Russian state.
In 2020, during a Netanyahu government, an order designated the Alexander Courtyard a “holy place.” At the same time, Israel moved to renew registration of the property in the name of the Russian Federation. A petition filed by the IOPS halted that process and effectively preserved the status quo.
Two years later, Russian President Vladimir Putin personally wrote to then-prime minister Naftali Bennett asking him to act to transfer the rights to Russia, underscoring the importance the Kremlin attaches to the issue.
In late 2024, Netanyahu revived the work of a ministerial team examining the dispute. The team includes Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Justice Minister Yariv Levin, while the National Security Council and Prime Minister’s Office are coordinating the process. In November 2025, a special interministerial committee held a hearing attended by the parties. Russia participated actively and has since been waiting for the official protocol and an update on the next steps.
‘Another foothold in the heart of Jerusalem’
The dispute over the Alexander Courtyard extends beyond the legal question of ownership. A study published last month by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, written by Ella Itkin and Arkady Mil-Man, warned that the activities of the Russian Orthodox Church in Israel go far beyond religion.
According to the study, the Russian Church has historically served as an instrument for advancing Moscow’s diplomatic interests, while ties among the church, the Kremlin and Russian security services have grown stronger under Putin. The researchers also pointed to ties between the IOPS and senior figures in Russia’s political and security establishment.
The organization is headed by Sergei Stepashin, a former Russian prime minister and former head of the Federal Security Service, or FSB. According to the study, Ambassador Viktorov is also affiliated with the organization.
The authors argued that, given the close cooperation between the Russian Church and Putin’s government, and because they say Israel is under no legal obligation to transfer the compound to Russia, Israel is unlikely to gain any strategic benefit from doing so. They also cited Moscow’s close relations with Iran and other actors hostile to Israel.
The researchers warned that handing over the Alexander Courtyard could give Russia another foothold in the heart of Jerusalem and that a Russian victory in the case could lead to future demands for additional properties linked to Russia’s historical presence in the Holy Land.
The Alexander Courtyard also became part of public discussion surrounding the case of Naama Issachar, an Israeli woman imprisoned in Russia and released in January 2020. During negotiations for her release, reports suggested that transferring the Alexander Courtyard to Russia was part of understandings between Netanyahu and Putin.
There is no public evidence that the property transfer was formally included in the deal, although various officials have said over the years that the matter was discussed in talks between Jerusalem and Moscow. Officials familiar with the issue say Putin sees the compound as personally and symbolically important.
For the Russian president, transferring such a prominent historic Russian property into Moscow’s hands could be presented as a significant diplomatic and symbolic achievement in Jerusalem, particularly at a time of acute confrontation between Russia and the West.
Against that backdrop, Viktorov’s unusual visit takes on added significance. Formally, the process remains unresolved, and Israel has not announced any decision to transfer the compound to the Russian Federation.
But the ambassador’s arrival with a large Russian delegation, coupled with the questions reportedly directed at the Ukrainian nuns about when they intend to leave, suggests Moscow wants to convey that, from its perspective, the battle over the Alexander Courtyard has entered its final stage.

Norway will drill in Arctic regardless of EU's position, says energy minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:13:24 UTC
14:13:24 KST

Norway will drill in Arctic regardless of EU's position, says energy minister
OSLO, Aug 24 - Norway will continue developing its oil and gas resources in the Barents Sea regardless of the European Union's support for a moratorium on Arctic hydrocarbon supplies, and no longer sees itself as Europe's "green battery", Energy Minister Terje Aasland told Reuters.
Following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Norway has become Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, meeting around 30% of gas demand of both the European Union and Britain.
Last year, the country's gas production was near record levels, while oil output reached its highest level since 2009. Official forecasts, however, show production falling sharply after 2030 unless new resources are discovered and developed.
"In today's geopolitical and security environment, and given the resource situation, I believe continued activity in the Barents Sea serves both Norwegian and European interests," Aasland said in a Reuters interview ahead of ONS, Norway's biannual energy conference, which begins in Stavanger on Monday.
The European Union currently supports a ban on new drilling in the Arctic on environmental grounds but is considering revising its policy in response to concerns about energy security.
Aasland said Norway aims to maintain petroleum production and exports at roughly current levels until at least 2035, and Barents Sea production will be key.
"If Norway is to remain a long-term supplier of oil and gas to Europe..., then the Arctic must be part of that discussion," he said.
In talks with EU officials, Norway has argued that the parts of the Barents Sea opened to petroleum activity are also ice-free like in the North Sea, and so less prone to oil spills and other environmental impacts, and are helping to sustain jobs and settlement in the country's northern regions bordering Russia.
Aasland believes Norway's arguments are being heard in Brussels, but added that it was the country's sovereign right to develop the Barents Sea resources even if the EU continued to support a moratorium.
"We would develop these areas, and then it will be up to the EU whether they should have a moratorium on buying that gas or oil," Aasland said.
Arctic oil would be sold into global markets regardless, while gas could be exported worldwide as liquefied natural gas from Equinor's Melkoeya LNG plant near Hammerfest, he added.
International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol has also urged the EU to reconsider its opposition to new Arctic oil and gas developments, arguing that future supplies will be needed to support energy security.
Critics of such a move argue that new Arctic projects would take many years to come online and would do little to address Europe's near-term energy challenges.
GREEN BATTERY "A FLAWED IDEA"
In addition to oil and gas, Norway produces a surplus of renewable energy most years from an extensive network of reservoirs and waterways feeding hydroelectrical plants, which it has exported to Europe via cross-border power cables.
Norway has previously presented itself as "the green battery" of Europe, but the minister says this idea is now outdated as Norway alone can't balance the European power market.
"It was a flawed idea," Aasland said.
The idea helped drive the construction of new power interconnectors, including links to Britain and Germany, but has drawn some opposition in Norway as European electricity prices have escalated.
Deeper integration with Europe's power system left Norway more vulnerable to continental price swings.
Aasland said Norway will not build new interconnectors but remains committed to strong power sector cooperation with Europe.
He urged countries on the continent to strengthen their stable power supply, weakened by coal and nuclear plant closures and a lack of investment in new gas-fired generation.
Doing so will lower prices and build greater reciprocity when it comes to power flows between different countries.
"The future lies in having a very strong and integrated system," Aasland said. REUTERS

Demonstrations in the capital New Delhi, triggered by the leak of the national medical entrance test, turned violent on 20 July when thousands of protesters attempted to march towards parliament.
Indian police used excessive force, including electric shock devices and pellet guns, against youth-led protests that forced the education minister to resign last month, Amnesty International said on Monday.
A report from the rights' group clashes with the police account that force was used only after protesters turned violent, and comes after India's Supreme Court set up a panel on Thursday to investigate violence by both police and demonstrators.
Demonstrations in the capital New Delhi, triggered by the leak of the national medical entrance test, turned violent on 20 July when thousands of protesters attempted to march towards parliament.
Amnesty said witness testimony and visual evidence it had verified confirmed the use of "pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas launchers, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against protesters" in Delhi and the eastern state of Bihar.
Amnesty said it had also verified two instances of a police officer "unlawfully using lethal force against a crowd" in Bihar's Siwan district. No one was killed.
"The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines," it added.
Amnesty said that there were "isolated incidents of protesters throwing stones," but that the "heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control."
Delhi Police said in a Supreme Court hearing last week they had used force only after protesters "resorted to violence."
They said anti-social elements "masquerading as aggrieved students" caused "grievous injuries" to security forces.
On Friday, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi staged a sit-in outside a Delhi police station with a 19-year-old protester who said he was injured by pellets during the July demonstration.
Gandhi demanded a police investigation into the shooting and officers later registered a case over the complaint.
Led by the online Cockroach Janta Party, the protests broadened from anger over exam irregularities into a wider movement over unemployment, opportunities for young people and what critics describe as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's increasingly authoritarian rule.
The protests proved to be the biggest challenge that Modi has faced after winning a third term in 2024.

How Jewish extremists use siege tactics, violence to push Palestinians from homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:09:34 UTC
14:09:34 KST

Mahmoud and Aida Tubasi can see their homes from the house where they now live, but they cannot return to them. “There, over there,” Mahmoud said, pointing toward two stone houses and a cluster of cypress trees on a hill at the northeastern edge of Jalud, a Palestinian village near Nablus where he has lived all his life.
Nearly a month has passed since the couple left. Their account is not of one sudden attack but of something slower and more systematic: months of threats, arson, stone-throwing, roadblocks and isolation that, they say, gradually made ordinary life impossible. By the time they finally walked away, Tubasi said, there was nothing left to sustain them. “No water, no flour, no rice,” he said. “We knew it was over, and we left.”
The Tubasis’ story is part of a broader pattern emerging across parts of the West Bank, where extremist settlers have established outposts deeper inside areas nominally under Palestinian administration. Palestinian residents and Israeli rights groups say the outposts are frequently followed by confrontations, intimidation and violence that drive residents away from farmland, isolated homes and, in some cases, entire properties.
“We are not Americans. We are ordinary Palestinians,” Tubasi said, contrasting the lack of attention his family received with the international focus on nearby Qusra, where U.S. citizen Louay Abu Rida became the center of a confrontation after settlers surrounded his home. “We have no foreign citizenship, and my wife and I don’t speak English. What happened in Qusra is nothing compared with what we went through, and almost nobody came.”
Outposts move in, violence follows
Under the Oslo framework, the Palestinian Authority exercises civil control in Area B while Israel retains overriding security responsibility. Area A is formally under Palestinian civil and security control. Yet according to mapping by Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now, 26 settler outposts have been established in Areas A and B, some bordering Area A itself. The group estimates that settlers have taken control of about 100,000 dunams, roughly 25,000 acres, in the two areas.
A report by Israeli rights group Yesh Din suggests that the geography of settler violence has shifted in tandem with the expansion. The organization said 62.6% of the settler violence incidents against Palestinians it documented in the first half of 2026 occurred in Areas A and B. In 2025, by contrast, 67.6% of documented incidents were concentrated in Area C, which is under full Israeli control, while 32.4% occurred in Areas A and B.
Yesh Din research director Yonatan Kanonich described the trend as a pressure mechanism that pushes Palestinian residents away from agricultural land and isolated homes and toward the centers of established towns and villages. “The deeper the settlement, the deeper the violence,” he said. The incidents documented by the organization include arson attacks on homes, vehicles and crops, beatings, stone-throwing, Molotov cocktails and live fire.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee recently used unusually strong language when discussing such attacks. “When you engage in activity designed to create fear in an individual, a society or a community, that is the dictionary definition of terrorism,” he said in interviews with Israeli media.
‘They threatened to burn us’
For the Tubasi family, the pressure began on April 3. Mahmoud said he had built two houses on the family’s land, one for himself and Aida and another about 25 meters away for their sons Wael and Qais and their families. Construction began in 2017, and the family moved in two years later. Tubasi said the family owns the land and obtained permission from the village council to build.
Then a new settler outpost appeared on a nearby hill. “The first night the settlers came, they poured fuel on the doors of the houses, set them on fire and ran away,” Tubasi said. “We woke up terrified and managed to put out the flames.”
Two weeks later, he said, settlers erected a makeshift structure beside the homes and remained there. Stones were thrown at the houses, loud music was played at night and the family received threats. “They told us, ‘We will burn you like the Dawabshe family,’” he said, referring to the 2015 arson attack in the nearby village of Duma that killed a Palestinian toddler and his parents.
The family sent the children and their mothers away. Later, Tubasi said, settlers broke through a wall and set fire to a storage room. Israeli troops would occasionally dismantle the settlers’ structure, he said, but the settlers returned when the soldiers left.
By late June, the family’s only road to the village had been blocked with rocks and spikes. Their water and electricity were cut. Tubasi said the family repeatedly complained to Palestinian liaison officials, the Israeli Civil Administration, the army and police, but each authority pointed to another. “They passed us around like a ball,” he said.
The pressure spreads
Similar accounts have emerged from other Palestinian communities. In Jaljulia, a village north of Ramallah deep inside Area A, residents say the establishment of an outpost about 10 months ago transformed what had previously been a quiet area.
In May, settlers claimed 120 sheep had been stolen. Residents said settlers subsequently took about 900 sheep from Palestinian pens. During confrontations that followed, soldiers opened fire and killed 16-year-old Yusuf Kaabneh, according to the account provided in the report. A month later, a mosque was set on fire and the word “revenge” was spray-painted on its wall.
Resident Yusuf Muzahim said settlers now enter village farmland with livestock, damaging crops and confronting farmers. “They come with rifles and pistols and threaten us,” he said. “We film them, and they laugh in our faces.” Residents say they provided photographs, videos and license plate numbers to Yesh Din, but the attacks have continued.
Leaving on foot
The Tubasis held out until July 22. The day before, Mahmoud said, Israeli soldiers arrested his two sons on suspicion of throwing stones at settlers. The following day, Mahmoud and Aida decided they could no longer stay.
“There was nothing left,” he said. “No water, no flour, no rice. Nothing. Just my wife and me, and we are 60 years old. We understood it was over.”
They asked for permission to bring in a vehicle to remove their belongings, but Tubasi said the request was refused. So they walked out carrying only some clothes.
Settlers entered the houses shortly afterward, Tubasi said, before soldiers removed them. Israeli troops have since maintained a presence there, while settlers remain nearby.
The IDF said the allegations were being examined and that forces were operating around Jalud and Qusra “to prevent lawbreakers and rioters from reaching the area and to preserve the fabric of life in the region.”
For Tubasi, the larger question is what happens once the soldiers, cameras and outside attention disappear. “We thought the world would stand by us,” he said. “It turns out nobody cares about us.”

Poll: 43% support Ülle Madise as next president

Unknown Publisher

Poll: 43% support Ülle Madise as next president
Forty-three percent of respondents support frontrunner Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise becoming Estonia's next president, while 36 percent do not, according to a Norstat poll commissioned by the Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut.
The results of the survey showed that 43 percent of respondents chose "yes" and "rather yes" when asked if they supported Madise's election, while 36 percent answered "no" and "rather no." Twenty-one percent of respondents did not give an answer.
Madise is most popular with Reform voters (83 percent), followed by opposition party SDE (69 percent), non-parliamentary party Parempoolsed (69 percent), and Isamaa (57 percent).
The majority of respondents from opposition party EKRE (79 percent) do not support Madise's election, and half of Center (50 percent).
In the poll, respondents were also given a list of names and asked who they would like to see as the next president.
Respondents' preferences were as follows:
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise 29 percent, EKRE's Mart Helme 12 percent, TalTech Rector Tiit Land 9 percent, diplomat Hannes Hanso 5 percent, entrepreneur Indrek Neivelt 3 percent, diplomat Jüri Luik 2 percent, Gen. (Ret).Riho Ühtegi 2 percent, diplomat Jonatan Vseviov 2 percent, Deputy Director-General of the European Commission's Directorate-General for the Internal Market and Industry Maive Rute 0.6 percent, CEO of Estonia Pianos Indrek Laul 0.3 percent, diplomat Matti Maasikas 0.2 percent.
Fifteen percent would like to see some other candidate, while 20 percent had no preference.
Citizens support direct presidential elections
Respondents were also asked whether the president should be directly elected by the people. Seventy percent of respondents said "yes" or "rather yes," 22 percent said "rather no" or "no," and eight percent said, "don't know."
Direct presidential elections are most popular among voters of EKRE (97 percent), Center (88 percent), Isamaa (74 percent) and Parempoolsed (54 percent).
It was below 50 percent for respondents who support Reform and SDE.
The survey also showed that 66 percent of those polled think the president should initiate new legislation to change the voting procedure to direct elections.
The Norstat poll was conducted online from August 19 to 20 among Estonian citizens aged 18 and older and included 1,002 respondents.
The first round of the presidential election will take place on September 2.

‘Nature makes every colour in the world’: Meet the company brewing an end to toxic chemical dyes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:02:05 UTC
14:02:05 KST

The fashion industry's toxic petrochemical dyes often end up in oceans. Could colours be 'brewed' from nature instead?
The fashion industry is among the most polluting on the planet, and dyeing fabric a big reason why. The process consumes huge volumes of water, energy and chemicals, leaving a lasting mark on the environment.
"The industry uses upward of 70 highly toxic chemicals in the dyeing process," Orr Yarkoni, CEO and co-founder of Colorifix, tells Euronews Earth.
He explains that this figure covers not just the dyes themselves but the additional chemicals needed to help colour bond to fabric. "Over 30 of them are irretrievable, meaning no matter what you do to the water after you use them, they stay in the water, so they'll end up in the ocean."
According to Yarkoni, the industry's reliance on synthetic dyes dates back to the 19th century, when manufacturers shifted away from natural alternatives.
"The industry moved to using cheap, effective chemistry that unfortunately proves to be quite toxic for life in general, including humans," he says. Moving away from these chemicals has proven slow, largely due to a lack of viable alternatives that can operate at scale.
Brewing colour like beer
Colorifix's approach borrows directly from nature's own methods of producing pigment, without extracting it from plants or animals. "We borrow the information of how the pigment or dye stuff is made in nature," Yarkoni tells Euronews Earth.
The company inserts that genetic code into bacteria, which are then grown in fermentation tanks. "Very similar to how you make beer, but instead of alcohol, we're brewing the colour," he explains.
Once harvested, the biological dye – along with the biomass used to help it bond to fabric – replaces the synthetic chemicals typically used in the dyeing process.
Yarkoni says this delivers significant environmental savings, citing figures specific to polycotton: "We're seeing upward of 77 per cent savings in water, 51 per cent savings in energy, and 31 per cent savings in emissions by doing things biologically."
He is careful to stress that natural origin does not automatically mean a product is safe. "Natural does not mean non-toxic," he says, noting that Colorifix tests every dye it produces for cytotoxicity, skin irritation and allergenicity, going beyond standard testing required for synthetic dyes.
"We don't want to repeat the mistakes of the past of pushing with something that looks good and causes serious problems down the line."
Producing dyes that meet the performance demands of the textile industry has also been a challenge. Colours must resist fading in sunlight, survive repeated washing and not rub off onto skin.
"We developed hundreds of colours," Yarkoni says, adding that Colorifix now offers a full colour range for synthetic fibres such as polyester, with a more limited but growing palette for cotton and other cellulosic fabrics.
From lab to industry
Colorifix has moved beyond research and into commercial use, with major fashion brands adopting the technology, according to Yarkoni. The company has also begun shipping its dyes as ready-to-use concentrates, rather than requiring manufacturers to install fermentation equipment on site.
"We're releasing these products now as concentrates... that means we can ship the product ready to use in the dye machine without having to do any additional processing on site," he says.
Yarkoni credits Colorifix's recognition as an Earthshot Prize finalist with raising the company's profile among manufacturers and brands. "It's helped really highlight our solution to the problem and bring more awareness to brands and manufacturers," he says. "We've had outreach from all over the world following the exposure."
Looking ahead, Yarkoni argues that petrochemicals should be reserved for uses where no natural alternative exists, rather than applied broadly across industries such as fashion: "Colour is one of the worst things to make out of petrochemicals because nature makes every colour in the world, and rivers still run clean".

New daily diabetes pill that helps with weight loss launches in UK pharmacies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:01:52 UTC
14:01:52 KST

A new daily pill that treats diabetes and helps with weight loss will be available in UK pharmacies from Monday.
Pharmacists said the move would be welcome for people who cannot use weight-loss jabs, but also issued a warning over the growing problem of fake, unlicensed or counterfeit versions of GLP-1 tablets.
Orforglipron, known as Foundayo and made by the US pharmaceutical firm Eli Lilly, was authorised by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) earlier this month. The UK is the first country in Europe to approve it, after approving another weight-loss pill in June.
“The UK is the first country in Europe where Foundayo is now available,” said Khalil Asmar, the vice-president of cardiometabolic health at Lilly Northern Europe. “We’re pleased that this means there is another oral treatment option for eligible UK patients alongside licensed injectable treatments.”
The drug will initially be available through private prescription, with Eli Lilly saying it is working with the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) on its assessment of Foundayo for a potential rollout on the health service in England.
Th drug is licensed for people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or above, or those with a BMI of between 27 and 30 and at least one weight-related condition. It can also be used to improve blood sugar levels in patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The pill is taken once a day, at any time, with no food or water restrictions.
Henry Gregg, the chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said: “This is another significant day with a second weight loss pill available from today in certain pharmacies. This is particularly significant for patients who cannot or do not want to take an injectable medicine and could make weight-loss treatment available to a wider range of patients.”
However, there are concerns about the marketing of fake, unlicensed or counterfeit drugs, which can be easier to produce in pill form than injectables. Last year, the MHRA seized £250,000-worth of unlicensed weight-loss pens and ingredients from a factory in Northampton, and Eli Lilly is suing various suppliers it accuses of participating in an illegal hidden market for its drugs.
Patients are being urged to ensure that they access weight-loss treatments only through safe and regulated pharmacies.
Gregg said: “There must now be a redoubling of efforts within government and the NHS to use pharmacies to make sure more eligible patients in clinical need can get weight loss treatments on the NHS, rather than the current postcode lottery that exists for weight management services via GPs.”
The MHRA approved the first GLP-1 pill for weight loss, a tablet form of Wegovy, in June.

LAX, JFK, DXB: Everything you need to know about airport codes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:01:24 UTC
14:01:24 KST

Miley Cyrus famously hopped off the plane at LAX with just a dream and a cardigan, but have you ever wondered what airport codes are actually used for?
While airport codes used to be something you’d only see on your boarding pass and luggage tags, nowadays, the three letters are absolutely everywhere. You can rep your home city with phone cases, décor, t-shirts… I’ve even seen airport code shoelaces.
But have you ever stopped to wonder how those three letters were chosen, or why we need them in the first place?
With airport codes hitting the headlines as Palm Beach International Airport changes to DJT following its renaming after current president Donald J. Trump, we thought it was time for a deep dive…
What is an airport code, and what is it used for?
An airport code is a unique three-letter geocode that corresponds to a single airport around the globe.
The geocodes are assigned by the International Air Transport Association (IATA), and there are around 11,300 in the IATA Airline Coding Directory. These codes aren't just assigned to airports, either – they can also be used for heliports, rail stations and bus stations.
Introduced in the 1930s, airport codes were originally just two letters but became three in the 1940s as the number of airports grew.
“These universal codes are essential to the functioning of the aviation and travel industries, ensuring that systems involved in reservations, scheduling, ticketing, cargo documentation, and other operations speak the same language,” the IATA notes on its website.
How are airport codes chosen?
Around 40 to 50 codes are newly assigned annually.
The standard procedure is to use the first three letters of the location’s name, but if that is already taken, the airport will need to choose an unassigned combination that preferably starts with the first letter of the location’s name.
For example, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol’s IATA airport code is AMS, Frankfurt International Airport’s is FRA, and Dublin Airport’s is DUB, while Dubai International Airport is DXB, because DUB was already taken.
It worked out in Dubai’s favour, though, as the airport is commonly known by its code, much like JFK in New York or LAX.
Some airport codes instead come from the airport’s name, as is the case with Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).
Exceptions to the rule
Notable exceptions to the rule include Canadian airports, where the code for most major airports starts with Y.
This is because when deciding the three-letter codes, it was decided to use the two letter code from before alongside a Y at the front if the area had a weather station.
That’s how we’ve ended up with codes like YOW for Ottawa and YVR for Vancouver.
Why do airport codes change?
While the IATA notes that airport codes “are considered permanent and are almost never changed”, over the past 12 months, some 750 changes have been made.
Some examples of airports that have changed code include Don Mueang International Airport, which was originally known as Bangkok International Airport and had the code BKK. Its code is now DMK, while Suvarnabhumi Airport, the busier airport serving the Thai capital which opened in 2006, is now BKK.
John F. Kennedy International Airport was originally known as Idlewild Airport, and had the code IDL. It adopted the code JFK when it was renamed after the late president in 1963.
You can browse all of the world’s airport codes on the IATA website.

The new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, faces a critical test this week amid anxiety in government bond markets over inflation and Donald Trump’s tax and spending plans.
As the world’s most powerful central bank prepares for its annual Jackson Hole conference, analysts said bond traders would be looking for signals from Warsh over its commitment to fighting inflation.
The Trump-appointed head of the US central bank has previously signalled reluctance to “spoon-feed” financial markets over how it plans to set interest rates to keep fast-rising prices in check.
However, anxiety over Trump’s handling of the economy and investor fears that his war with Iran is stoking inflation have rocked global financial markets amid a dramatic sell-off in US government bonds.
Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said: “Investors will be looking for a comfort blanket when Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh addresses the Jackson Hole meeting.”
James Smith, an economist at ING Bank, said: “By offering less commentary on where rates are headed … [Warsh] risks injecting yet more volatility into an already febrile bond market.”
Warsh is expected to give a highly anticipated speech on Friday at the Fed’s annual symposium in the Rocky Mountains resort of Jackson Hole, against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets.
The gathering of the world’s most powerful central bankers in the Grand Teton national park is a blue riband event in the financial calendar, as a vital platform for the Fed chair and other top officials to signal their policymaking approach.
However, Warsh has signalled reluctance to use his speech for the “more traditional setup” of dropping hints over how the US central bank may respond to inflationary pressures when its officials next meet to set interest rates in September and December. Instead, he has said his Jackson Hole speech could be “focused on bigger questions”, including concerns over productivity and demographics.
However, the meeting comes as selling pressure intensifies in the $30tn (£22tn) US government debt market despite efforts by the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, to assuage investor worries after he committed to at least double Washington’s purchases of US Treasury bonds.
With investors fretting over the inflationary impact of the Iran war and the US national debt surpassing $40tn for the first time, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on long-term US Treasury debt at first fell, before rising back towards the highest levels since 2007.
Warsh was accused by investors of sending confusing signals in his first press conference as Fed chair in July, after he expressed his commitment to curbing inflation without giving details.
The Fed held rates in July, and trading in financial markets reflects investor expectations for a hold again in September, although a rise is thought possible. Markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by the middle of next year.
Trump, who appointed Warsh, has called on the Fed to cut rates, fuelling investor concerns over interference at the central bank.
Stephen Brown, an economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said Warsh maintaining a tight-lipped approach could be risky. “He might even stick to the official subject of the symposium, ‘Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy’, in which case his speech could be something of a snoozefest.
“That said, even that approach would risk giving the impression that Warsh is not taking inflation risks seriously, so there could still be volatility in markets.”

‘An amazing relief’: implant offers hope for those with refractory angina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

“It’s an amazing relief, both physically and emotionally, to be able to live my life again normally, without feeling that I’m limited all the time in what I can do.”
Cristian Jensen is describing the difference that an implant inserted in his chest – to reduce the symptoms of his debilitating angina – has had on his life.
The 64-year-old used to have five angina attacks a week, each involving a sharp, acute pain that reminded him of the heart attack he once had. Now he has an attack every week or two.
He used to have to limit the amount of exercise he did, in case strenuous activity induced an attack. Now he’s walking further and faster and no longer worries about climbing stairs.
“It’s made a huge difference to my confidence,” the packaging designer adds. “Angina is a reminder that something isn’t right with your body. It’s like a sharp pain in the middle of your chest that stops you doing what you are doing.
“The fear that the pain of an episode of angina could be a heart attack. Suddenly not having that anxiety at the back of your mind changes your life.”
Angina, a common form of heart disease, involves pain in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arm.
Jensen had a long and troubled history of heart problems before consultant cardiologist Dr Ranil de Silva fitted him with the implant – a coronary sinus reducer (CSR) – at the Royal Brompton hospital, a renowned centre of specialist NHS heart and lung care in London, in 2021.
In 1990, he was diagnosed with angina at an unusually young age – at just 28 – after an angiogram showed he had blocked arteries.
Open heart surgery helped. “That fixed me, for a while at least,” he says. “I was angina-free for 17 years until I had a heart attack in 2007.” That led to him having the first of what became eight stents put in, to help his arteries stay open and his heart to keep pumping blood around his body.
But in 2015 he began taking drugs to lower the high level of bad cholesterol in his bloodstream – fatty deposits that narrow the arteries. He also started using another drug, a spray called gylceryl trinitrate (GTN), to banish the pain each of his angina attacks brought.
Jensen is one of an estimated 300,000 people in England with refractory angina. That is angina that remains problematic despite the patient having drugs, stents and heart bypass surgery.
When Jensen’s symptoms persisted, de Silva suggested he have the implant fitted. Despite the large number of people with the condition, only a handful have had what is still an experimental treatment.
The small, hourglass-shaped device is implanted near the heart using keyhole surgery through the patient’s neck. It works by narrowing a vein at the back of the heart. That helps to redirect the person’s blood flow to the parts of the heart muscle that are getting too little oxygen. Each device costs the NHS £11,400.
A new study – the largest of its kind worldwide to date – has found that the device brings about a significant fall in chest pain in 75% of people with refractory angina within six months of its implantation.
“In this respect it is potentially a gamechanger,” says de Silva, who co-led the study with his colleague Dr Kevin Cheng. It was based on observation of 491 people with refractory angina between 2014 and 2024, 474 of whom had the implant fitted at 19 hospitals in England and Scotland.
Most patients went home the day of the procedure or the day after and serious complications were rare, the study also found.
According to de Silva, it shows that the device can greatly reduce the debilitating symptoms of refractory angina that significantly compromise quality of life and the ability to undertake normal day to day activities, and can help people avoid being admitted to hospital and boost their mental wellbeing.
“Many patients report their lives being transformed and that it helps them to achieve the quality of life they wish for, that they were unable to enjoy prior to the reducer implant – they get their life back,” says de Silva.
Despite the apparent success of the implant, and that only “a tiny fraction” of the 300,000 people with refractory angina have had one fitted, it is too early to yet see CSR as a standard treatment for people with this very painful form of coronary artery disease, he says.
More trials are needed and the NHS needs to approve the funding needed to expand access, he adds.
Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and the British Heart Foundation’s clinical director, said: “The findings are reassuring as they show that in routine clinical practice the device is being delivered safely and is resulting in fewer symptoms for patients.”
The device “offers hope for people living with this challenging condition”, she said.

Courgette kraut and fermented pepper sauce: Šárka Otevřel Camrdová’s Czech pickle recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

Preserving the abundance of summer produce is a wonderful way to extend the season long after the gardens have faded. Opening a jar in the colder months offers more than just something good to eat; it also holds joy, patience and memories. When winter comes knocking, we are ready with something sweet, sour or salty waiting on the shelf, reminding us that summer will return and the sun will shine again.
Courgette kraut
This kraut can be used much like traditional sauerkraut, though its flavour is milder and its texture more delicate. Sauteed with onions in a little butter or lard, it makes an excellent accompaniment to roast meats and sausages; it can also be added to potato pancakes or used as a filling for savoury pies and pastries.
Prep 5 min
 Cook 40 min
 Ferment 2 weeks
 Makes 3-4 x 650ml jars 
2kg courgettes
2 tbsp (25g) granulated sugar 
  1½ tbsp (25g) salt 
65ml distilled white vinegar (8% acidity) 
1½ tsp caraway seeds, crushed 
Wash the unpeeled courgettes and pat them dry. Cut the courgettes in half lengthways, scrape out the seeds and shred or coarsely grate the flesh into a bowl.
Mix the sugar, salt and vinegar, then pour this over the courgettes. Sprinkle in the caraway seeds, mix well and set aside for 15-30 minutes. Adjust the seasoning to taste, adding sugar or vinegar as required.
Transfer the courgettes to sterilised jars, leaving a space of about 2cm between the veg and the rim of the jar, and making sure everything is completely covered in the liquid. Cover the jars tightly, place them on a rack or folded tea towel in a large pot, add warm water until it comes about three-quarters of the way up the sides of the jars, and keep at a steady at 85-90C (185-195F) for 15 minutes. Carefully lift out the jars, leave to cool completely, then store in a cool, dark place for about two weeks before use.
Fermented bell pepper sauce
You can modify this recipe to suit your taste, by using different types of bell peppers, for example, or replacing some of the peppers with tomatoes, or adding other herbs and spices. You can also use this recipe to make your own hot sauce – just replace the bell peppers with chilli peppers. Fermented bell pepper sauce has a flavour that is reminiscent of the Balkan red pepper condiment ajvar, which means you can use it in a similar way: as a sauce for grilled meat and kebabs, burgers or sandwiches; as a dip for different vegetable side dishes; as an accompaniment for bulgur and couscous; or spread it on toast.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 30 min
 Ferment 5 days+
 Makes 3 x 750ml bottles 
1l water
  1 tbsp (20g) salt
  6 red or orange bell peppers, halved lengthways, stalks, pith and seeds removed and discarded, flesh washed and cut into chunks
3 sprigs flat-leaf parsley, or lovage
  1 onion, peeled and cut into wedges
  3-5 garlic cloves, peeled and halved
  3-6 bay leaves (optional)
To make the brine, put the water in a saucepan, bring to a boil, then leave to cool completely. Add the salt and stir until it’s all dissolved.
Divide the pepper pieces between three sterilised jars, then add a parsley sprig, a few pieces of onion and garlic, and a bay leaf or two, if using, to each one. Leave at least a 3cm gap between the contents of the jar and the rim. Pour the brine over the vegetables – the pepper pieces should be completely covered to prevent contact with the air, so, if need be, use a sterilised fermentation weight to keep them in place. Leave some space between the salt solution and the rim of the jar to allow room for the formation of foam on the surface of the liquid.
Close the jars with their lids, but do not tighten them. Put the jars on a tray or baking sheet and leave in a dark place at room temperature (preferably at 18-21C/65-70F) to ferment for five to seven days: the exact time will depend on the temperature of the room (a warmer temperature speeds up the fermentation process). Check and taste the contents of the jars regularly (always use an impeccably clean fork) – the peppers are ready when no more bubbles form or the foam dissipates, and they should now have a pleasantly sour and mildly spicy taste.
Fine-strain the contents of the jars and collect the liquid. Discard the bay leaves. Puree the vegetables and herbs until thick and creamy, diluting the sauce, if need be, with some of the reserved liquid. Fill sterilised bottles with the sweet pepper sauce and use immediately or store in the fridge.
- 
  These recipes are edited extracts from God is a Pickle: Recipes and Stories for Preserving the Seasons – A Culinary Journey Through the Czech Republic, by Šárka Otevřel Camrdová, published by Gestalten at £35. To order a copy for £312.50, go to guardianbookshop.com

Half of Taiwan households have 2 or fewer people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Households with two or fewer members accounted for 51.6% of all households in Taiwan in 2025, marking the first time the figure has surpassed half, according to the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
One-person households accounted for 17.33% of all households. Two-person households made up 34.27%, with both reaching record highs, per UDN.
The figures reflect changing attitudes toward marriage and childbearing, along with Taiwan's persistently low birth rate, contributing to a major transformation in the country's family structure. In July, birth rates dropped for the 31st consecutive month, falling by more than 10,000 in the first seven months when compared to the same period last year
The annual household survey examines the size and composition of households, as well as housing conditions and facilities. The data is used by government agencies as a reference for developing policies related to families, housing, and social welfare.
Three-person households were 23.21%. One-person households surpassed four-person households, which represented 16.63% for the first time.
In the 1980s, four-person households were the most common type, accounting for between 25% and 27% of households. Five-person households also accounted for about 20% of households in the early 1980s before beginning a steady decline, per UDN.
By the late 1990s, the proportion of four-person households had begun to decline and eventually fell below 20% in 2020. The latest figures highlight the continuing shift away from larger traditional family households toward smaller households, driven by demographic and social changes.
DGBAS data also showed that Taiwan's homeownership rate declined for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, falling to 83.95%. Due to previous adjustments to the statistical definition of homeownership, the 2025 figure was the lowest recorded since 2010.

Ukrainian ambassador: If Russia says it wants to kill you, you best believe it

Thirty-five years ago, Ukraine chose freedom, but for twelve of those years, Ukrainians have been forced to shed their blood to fight against Russian aggression and its imperial vision of the world, says Ukrainian Ambassador Olha Nikitchenko in an interview with LRT.lt. Ukrainians never sought to become heroes, she argues, they simply had no other choice: “If we stop fighting, then we stop existing.”
Ukraine is bringing war closer to Russia, Russian people with long-range strikes into its territory. Even Vladimir Putin acknowledged that there is some damage, but still it looks like he has a firm hold on power in Russia. Do you think these attacks are actually changing his calculations with, for example, negotiations?
Definitely, because these attacks and these long strikes, we call them the long-range sanctions, they are definitely making all of the difference. We are bringing the war actually into Russia. It's not even closer Russia, but into Russia. <…>
And it makes all the difference because Putin can acknowledge this or he may not, but it doesn't change the truth that economically Russia is very much into decline right now. Sanctions are working, long-range strikes are working. So whatever he or his allies are telling themselves, this is definitely working. <…>.
But as they say, winter is coming, and there are very serious warnings about another very difficult winter for Ukraine, particularly as Russia is still targeting energy infrastructure, which is not repaired. What worries you the most about this upcoming winter in Ukraine?
What we've seen last winter was the most hard and terrible winter for Ukraine, and I hope it stays this way. I do hope we will have it easier. But if you look at what is happening, it certainly does not seem so because we are in for a very hard period.
<…> Basically, I would say that the two things that worry us the most. The first is the air defense, because Russia targets energy infrastructure, and energy sector in terms of generators, transformers, energy capacity. So these two priorities are interlinked. So we do very much need more stronger air defenses, anti-ballistic missiles for the Patriot systems, the IRIS-Ts, the NASAMS, and everything along these lines. So it still remains very much essential.
There is also the new “Freya” initiative, the anti-ballistic initiative launched by Ukraine, and it is ongoing now, but it still requires time to create that. Ukrainian Energy Support Fund has mobilized more than two billion euros so far, but we are still short 500 million euros to live through the winter.
I would actually say that the challenge is broader than the energy, because Ukraine has still to keep schools and hospitals running. It has to finance its defense, maintain macroeconomic stability. That gives us a little more of a broader perspective on how we should go through winter, because as of now 68% of the Ukrainian budget goes into the defense priorities, and it is extremely important for us to continue having the international budgetary support to keep the state actually running and to keep our people living.
You have to spend a lot of time explaining Ukraine’s situation and what support it needs. What is the most frustrating or difficult thing that you still need to explain to people about the support that Ukraine needs?
Here? Nothing. (smiles)
When I was just posted in Lithuania, I was preparing for all my meetings, for the first meeting with the president, the prime minister, I was making notes, and I had a very big list of the arguments of why they should be helping Ukraine and why it is important.
But I found myself that in every meeting when I just started saying all this everybody would just stop me and say, “Ambassador, yeah, we know that. Like, tell us what you need.”
We do share a very special bond, and it's not just because I'm the ambassador here, but because of our common history, common values. Because Lithuania understands very much what the Russians are and what “Russkiy Mir” brings to people.
So I'm not explaining here why it is needed, I'm just saying what we need. And Lithuanians never hesitate and say, “Oh, well, that might be too difficult” and “That is impossible.” They just say, “Let us see what we can do”. And we are extremely grateful for that.
All of my meetings, all of my speeches here start with a thank you: “Ačiū labai”.
Because even in Ukraine, if you would stop a random person on the on the street, and if you would ask to tell what countries are most helping Ukraine, I am sure that you would get Lithuania in the top three.
There have been recently warnings, particularly for Baltic states and Poland, that Russia might start false-flag operation, perhaps even with Ukrainian drones. What do you think Lithuania is doing right while preparing for this scenario?
I can say that you are doing a great job actually. I also would like to say that we're already helping you with sharing experience that we had learned very painful way. And while we share it, we certainly hope you would never have to use it. <…>
You have a great concept of total defense, which includes the civil defense, defence of energy objects, military defense. We're sharing with you processes of how to keep the state functioning during wartime. All of our institutions are in deep connection about the sharing of knowledge and experience at any point should, I wouldn't say the big word invasion but should any of these circumstances occur here.
And what do you think Lithuania could do better?
It's not what you could do better, but it is kind of also learning on our case and on our mistakes, is that if Russia tells you that it wants to kill you, believe it. So that just maybe be more vigilant.
I'm not saying that they will come here tomorrow, but being more aware of that this is an actual threat. This is not something potential. This is not something that might happen. Before the 2022 and before 2014 nobody believed that there could be such an offensive in Europe, that Russia would actually do it because it doesn't make sense: it's very costly, it’s not beneficial. There were a lot of things that showed that it should not happen, and yet it did.
So for this, for Lithuania and for other NATO countries, I would just say that just be aware that nothing is impossible with Russia. <…>
How do you think Putin sees world order in the future?
Well, Putin sees himself as the collector of the Russian lands, and in his perception Russian lands is a very broad thing. So this is of course Ukraine, Baltic states, but it goes more and more and more. We can think that he opens his map and thinks that the world is his.
He would want to win the war to have Ukraine because he would be happy to have Soviet Union restored. That is actually what he said in Munich and again, everybody ignored this. All of his speech was dedicated to how a huge of a mistake was the collapse of the Soviet Union. And everybody was just, “Well, ha ha” ...
But again, you should listen to what they are saying because usually they mean it.
I would think that that is his dream, to be a collector the Russian lands, to restore Soviet Union, to get some more countries along the way into that.
But come on, Ukraine is not going to let it happen. (smiles)
I want to ask about the negotiations. With President Donald Trump's attention currently focused on Iran, the negotiations between Ukraine and Russia have basically stalled. Do you see any signs that they might move forward?
We are certainly not the ones who are stalling them. We are ready to continue this process on different levels. The president is ready to meet Putin in some neutral place and to conduct negotiations.
But Russia is the one who doesn't want peace negotiations nor the ceasefire. Our position is that we are ready for the unconditional immediate ceasefire, because the goal of this is not just the ceasefire for a couple of years so they can regroup but long lasting, just of course and comprehensive peace.
But if you look at what is happening in Russia right now, it certainly does not look like a country that is preparing for any kind of peace or any kind of negotiations, diplomatic solution.
Because we all know that and our president was saying, that they're getting ready for a large wave of mobilization, up to 500,000 people, after September Duma elections, if I can call tem way. They are increasing their missile production, and they are also conducting a very large military campaign within kids and youth as well.
None of their actions show us that Russia is somewhere even barely thinking about any peace activities or negotiations.
That is why diplomacy should be combined with pressure, with strength. So that at some point they have to understand that actually leading the war is going lead to breaking up of Russia. It's not cost effective, it has already ruined their economy, they are internationally isolated. There's nothing good for them coming out of this war.
Ukraine is marking 35 years of independence, but for more than 12 of those years Ukrainians have been fighting Russian aggression. After eight years of war in the Donbas, Russia launched its full-scale invasion four and a half years ago. How do you and Ukrainians keep finding strength to fight for your freedom?
We don't have a choice. We didn’t find it anywhere, it is just within us. We don't have a choice. If we stop fighting, then we stop existing, so that basically doesn't give us any room for flexibility in this matter.
But I really don't like how everybody says, “Oh my God, you are such heroes. You are so strong”.
We didn't choose that. We don't want be heroes. We want live a normal life. We don't want to fight. We don't want our people to die. We don't want question ourselves, are we going to wake up tomorrow. We just want to live, develop and build a democratic European state where our children can live, where our children can study, where we can build something because Ukrainians as a nation are mostly about building. We love building, we love creating.
We are not into fighting, but of course, when somebody comes into our land, we all get up and we fight. <…>

Kazakhstan’s new ruling party projected to win elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:59:58 UTC
13:59:58 KST

Kazakhstan's new ruling Adilet Party has taken a decisive lead in early exit polls, with more than 70% of the vote, in the country's early elections for its unicameral parliament, which could give it roughly 105 of the 145 seats in the new legislative chamber.
Five parties are projected to enter Kazakhstan’s new 145-member Kurultai, according to early exit polls. Parties needed at least 5% of the vote to win seats in the new legislature.
The election was Kazakhstan’s first parliamentary vote under the new Constitution, which replaced the bicameral Parliament with a single-chamber Kurultai.
The three exit polls put Adilet’s support between 70.7% and 72.3%, positioning the party for a commanding majority in the new 145-member unicameral Parliament, the Kurultai.
In other words, the poll projects around 109 seats for Adilet in Kurultai, giving the party a dominant majority.
The newly established Adilet Party, formed in April, absorbed Amanat, the country’s largest political party, ahead of the election.
Amanat has been the ruling party in Kazakhstan for almost 30 years. Formerly named Nur Otan, the party was created in 1999 from the electoral campaign headquarters, which supported ex-president Nursultan Nazarbayev in presidential elections of 1999.
The Adilet Party is now the country's most influential political force. It supports the new Constitution and nominated the largest number of candidates - 186.
The chair of the leading Adilet Party, Aibek Dadеbay, thanked voters after the first exit poll results were released.
"During the election campaign, we visited all regions and met with thousands of people across the country. At every meeting, we heard directly about the issues that matter to people, as well as their views and suggestions. Every opinion matters to us. All the proposals we received will be taken into account in our future work," he said.
Under the new electoral system, voters chose from seven political parties contesting the election. Unlike under the previous system, independent candidates could not run, with all Kurultai seats contested through party lists.
Who were the other parties competing in Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai election?
A total of seven political parties took part in the election, putting forward 545 candidates.
The first exit poll, conducted by the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development, put Auyl at 6.2%, Respublica at 5.2%, Ak Zhol at 5.1% and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party at 5%. The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 2.8%, while Baitaq got 0.9%.
The poll projects 12 seats for for Auyl, 9 for Respublica, 8 for the Nationwide Social Democratic Party and 7 for Ak Zhol. The People’s Party of Kazakhstan and Baitaq are not projected to win seats in the new Kurultai, exit polls show.
The Aq Zhol Democratic Party fielded 63 candidates. Founded in 2002, it advocates political and economic reforms, supports entrepreneurship and private business, and calls for strengthening the role of Parliament.
The Respublica Party, established in January 2023, nominated 75 candidates. The party focuses primarily on entrepreneurship, business and economic development.
The People’s Party of Kazakhstan fielded 72 candidates. Its platform centres on social policy, protection of workers and support for vulnerable groups.
The Auyl Party nominated 69 candidates. Founded in 2000, it has a clear political niche in the agricultural sector.
The Baitaq Green Party fielded 47 candidates. Founded in September 2022, it focuses on environmental protection and green development.
The Nationwide Social Democratic Party nominated 33 candidates. Founded in 2006, it entered Parliament for the first time in 2023.
Assessing the preliminary results, Indira Aubakirova, Head of the Institute of Legislation and Legal Information, said Adilet had used all available platforms effectively, making its lead over the other parties very expected.
"The People’s Party of Kazakhstan, to my surprise, received around 3%. There could be several factors behind this. Firstly, the new generation is entering political life, and it no longer shares these views. At the same time, the natural decline of the older population is also having an impact, meaning that there are fewer," she said.
Among the main contenders were Aq Zhol and Respublica, two parties that have traditionally focused on the interests of entrepreneurs and the business community.
"It would seem that Aq Zhol has such a rich background. It has been on the political scene since 2002. But Respublica is a much younger party, launched in 2023, and it positioned itself very correctly and built its election campaign in a very competent way."
A new vice president
On election day, President Tokayev also made several important statements about the country’s political future, including the appointment of Kazakhstan’s first vice president.
The position of vice president, like the new Kurultai, was introduced under the new Constitution.
Asked by journalists at a polling station when the country would learn the name of the new vice president, Tokayev said he would officially announce the appointment within seven to ten days.
Tokayev also said he plans to launch the Qazaqstan Khalyq Kenesi Secretariat or Kazakhstan People’s Council. The new body is intended to strengthen and develop work previously carried out by the Assembly of the People of Kazakhstan.
"I am confident that the work of the Kazakhstan People’s Council will be productive. The country should turn into a major construction site. Large construction projects will be implemented in every regional centre, district and city. Polyclinics, children’s rehabilitation centres and other social facilities will be built," said Tokayev.
"In Astana will appear such important facilities as a new bridge, the Dombra Palace and the Water Resources Research Centre. All cities need to be improved," he added.
The president’s comments came as Kazakhstan has already been accelerating construction and infrastructure projects across the country.
For example, just days before the election, several strategically important infrastructure projects were opened.
In Arkalyk, an airport has reopened after more than 30 years, restoring air links to the city after decades without regular flights. The airport in Pavlodar was also renovated.
In Kostanay, authorities carried out the technical launch of what is described as the country’s largest indoor water park. The facility includes seven swimming pools and can accommodate up to 500 people.
In Almaty Region, a new multimodal logistics centre was opened. The project attracted 28.1 billion tenge in investment and covers more than 26.5 hectares. It has the capacity to handle up to 100,000 containers a year.
The centre also includes railway infrastructure, a container terminal, warehouses and road logistics facilities.
The Parliamentary elections come as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its role in Central Asia. For Kazakhstan, this is closely linked to its ambitions to expand trade, attract investment and develop transport routes between Asia and Europe, including the Middle Corridor and oil export routes.
Will Tokayev seek another presidential term?
One of the most closely watched questions on election day concerned Tokayev’s own political future.
Asked whether he would continue his presidential term and seek another election, Tokayev said he could give a more specific answer at a later stage.
"The Constitutional Court made such a decision. It is lawful, of course, and I have the legal right to be re-elected in accordance with the law," Tokayev said.
"But as for the upcoming election, whether I will run or not, and in which year, it is premature to speculate on that at this point."
The question is significant because the new Constitution changed the rules governing the presidency.
Tokayev’s current term remains the focus of political attention, while the constitutional changes have opened a new debate about the country’s political future.
International observers
A total of 777 international observers followed the voting process. Among them was Caraman Angelica, Chairperson of the Central Election Commission of Moldova, who highlighted the digitalisation of the electoral process and measures introduced to make voting more accessible.
"Polling stations also follow modern standards of digitalisation. Each invitation has a QR code. It provides access to more detailed information on the Central Election Commission’s website," noted Caraman Angelica.
"We also noticed some positive practices. Every polling station has a special booth for people with disabilities. Voters can use special tools to cast their ballots independently and keep their vote secret. These include a voting template and audio instructions. This helps make the voting process more accessible and easier to understand," she added.
The comments come as Kazakhstan presents the election as the first major vote under its new constitutional framework and a key step in the transition to the new single-chamber system.
The first Kurultai will now become the country’s central legislative body, with 145 deputies serving five-year terms.
The final election results must be announced no later than seven days after voting (by August 30, 2026, according to the law).
Kazakhstan’s new political system will work in practice and whether Tokayev’s reforms will translate into tangible changes in government and people’s everyday lives.

TN CM Vijay announces 3 free LPG cylinders, expands free bus travel for women
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday announced a set of welfare measures in the state Assembly, including three free cooking gas cylinders a year for eligible beneficiaries and an expansion of the fare-free bus travel scheme for women.Under the cooking gas scheme, the amount for the three cylinders will be credited directly to the bank accounts of eligible beneficiaries.Vijay announced the launch of the Vetri Payanam scheme, expanding the existing fare-free bus travel programme for women across the state.Under the scheme, women will be allowed to travel free of charge on Express, LSS and Deluxe government buses operating in metropolitan and urban areas. Vijay had earlier outlined several welfare measures in his election manifesto, including six free LPG cylinders a year for every family, up to 200 units of free electricity, a monthly assistance of Rs 2,500 for women below the age of 60, and family health coverage of up to Rs 25 lakh.

Ukraine’s Solar Return: Astrologer predicts a year of transformative decisions and possible negotiations for the country

Ukraine’s Solar Return: Astrologer predicts a year of transformative decisions and possible negotiations for the country
Kyiv • UNN
Kseniia Bazylenko predicts transformation, political decisions and possible negotiations for Ukraine. She also expects economic and social challenges.
Over the next year, Ukraine will face a period of profound transformation, important political decisions and possible negotiations, while the country will remain at the center of international attention. Professional astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko told UNN about this, analyzing Ukraine's solar return chart.
Details
According to her, the solar return chart is complex, but does not indicate a dead end. On the contrary, it points to the need to review previous decisions, restructure state processes and move to a new stage.
I do not see it at all as a chart of a dead end. On the contrary, this is a solar return chart of profound transformation. A year in which many things will have to be changed, reviewed and restructured
The astrologer drew attention to the fact that the solar return is forming near a period of eclipses. In the astrological tradition, such periods are considered a time of accelerating processes and intensifying accumulated contradictions. According to her, this does not mean inevitable catastrophes, but it may force the country to address issues that have long been postponed.
Ukraine will remain at the center of global attention
Bazylenko believes that Ukraine is unlikely to move away from the forefront of international events. According to her, this is indicated by the strong emphasis on the first house of the solar return chart, where the Sun, Mercury and Ketu are located.
At the same time, the astrologer interprets Ketu next to the Sun as a symbol of accumulated results from the past. Therefore, in her opinion, the coming year may become a period of summing up the previous stage and taking responsibility for decisions that have already been made.
The country's leadership will play a special role. In the astrological tradition, the Sun is associated with power, while the presence of Mercury, according to Bazylenko, enhances the importance of negotiations, diplomacy, legislation, documents and information.
She also links these trends to the economy, emphasizing the importance of the quality of state governance, transparency of decisions and the fight against corruption.
Regarding the war, the astrologer sees no grounds to say that military tensions will disappear completely during the year. At the same time, she believes that the possibility of negotiations will remain.
The war may continue, but the window for negotiations remains open
According to her, much will depend on the political will of Ukraine's leadership, the position of its partners, the parties' readiness to reach agreements and Kyiv's ability to defend its own interests.
Alliances and changes in government
The astrologer separately drew attention to the position of Rahu, which in her interpretation symbolizes the direction of development. It is located in the partnership sector, so Bazylenko identifies the creation of new alliances, the strengthening of coalitions and the deepening of relations with international partners as among Ukraine's main tasks.
At the same time, she emphasizes that strengthening international ties should not mean losing one's own identity.
To preserve ourselves — and learn to become stronger together with others
Changes may also affect the system of government. According to Bazylenko, there are two possible scenarios: the current leadership may become an agent of reforms and restructuring of the system, or, if the system is unable to change from within, the transformations may affect the model of governance itself.
At the same time, she noted that this does not necessarily mean a change of specific politicians, but rather a test of the state system's ability to respond to new conditions.
Society will face emotional exhaustion
According to Bazylenko, one of the most tense indicators is the position of the Moon, which in mundane astrology symbolizes the people. In her view, this may indicate a high level of emotional fatigue in Ukrainian society.
People may react especially sharply to decisions that they perceive as unfair or detached from real life.
The state is first and foremost its people
She also describes the economic indicators as tense. This concerns household incomes, the cost of living, trade, logistics, agriculture and the state's ability to provide for basic needs. At the same time, Bazylenko does not consider the chart to be an indicator of an economic catastrophe.
In her assessment, international agreements and partner support could become important stabilizing factors. She describes the economic formula for the year as a combination of limited domestic capabilities, competent governance, assistance from partners, and economic restructuring.
Among other areas, the astrologer highlights the labor market and medicine. She predicts pressure on traditional forms of employment, but at the same time believes that new ways of working may develop. In medicine, she says, Ukraine’s accumulated experience in treating injuries, rehabilitation, and prosthetics could serve as the foundation for new technologies and methods.
Bazylenko also named children’s safety as one of the year’s priorities. She emphasized the importance not only of physical safety, but also of psychological well-being, education, and opportunities for recovery.
Children must not become those who pay the highest price for adults’ decisions
Ecology and its importance
The astrologer identifies water resources, critical infrastructure, and environmental issues as a separate area of focus. She stressed that she does not interpret these indicators as a forecast of a specific catastrophe, but merely as an area that deserves greater attention throughout the year.
According to her forecast, migration processes will also remain an important part of the country’s life. Some Ukrainians may continue to live, study, and work abroad, while the return of people and the arrival of those wishing to contribute to Ukraine’s reconstruction may intensify.
Summing up the forecast, Bazylenko called the coming year not a quiet one, but a turning-point period in which Ukraine may move from the consequences of the previous stage toward the formation of a new model of the state.
I see both serious risks and very strong potential for transformation here. This year may become not simply a continuation of the previous period, but a boundary between two stages in the country’s history
She added that the main question of Ukraine’s solar return chart is not what exactly will happen to the state, but whether the country will be able to use the consequences of the past to build a new stage of its development.

World’s oldest person celebrates 117th birthday with family and friends in Britain
