World’s oldest person celebrates 117th birthday with family and friends in Britain
- Ethel Caterham, the world’s oldest person and first British to reach 117, celebrated her birthday with family and friends in Surrey.
- She lived through major historical events, survived Covid-19 at age 110, and credits her longevity to avoiding arguments.
- Caterham became the oldest living person in April 2025 and received a birthday card from King Charles on her 116th birthday.
AI generated
The world’s oldest person, Englishwoman Ethel Caterham, celebrated her 117th birthday on Aug 21 with her family and friends.
Caterham, who lives in a care home in Surrey, about 40km away from the British capital London, also chalked up another milestone – she is the first British person to reach that age.
“I’ve had a lovely day celebrating with my family and friends, and I look forward to seeing what next year brings,” she told British national news agency PA Media.
The world’s oldest man, 113-year-old Joao Marinho Neto, was among the well-wishers. He held up a celebratory photo of Caterham from his home in Brazil, reported Guinness World Records.
Born on Aug 21, 1909, Caterham is the last living subject of King Edward VII and has lived through two world wars, the sinking of the Titanic and the Russian Revolution.
She also survived the Covid-19 pandemic, when she became the oldest person to contract the virus at the age of 110 in 2020.
The second youngest of eight children, Caterham moved to India at the age of 18 to work as a nanny for a British family.
She met British Army Major Norman Caterham at a dinner party in 1931, and they married two years later.
The couple spent some time in Hong Kong before settling down in Surrey, England, with their two daughters.
Caterham’s husband died in 1976, and she also outlived her daughters.
She currently has three granddaughters and five great-grandchildren.
Caterham became the world’s oldest living person in April 2025 following the death of the Brazilian nun, Sister Inah Canabarro Lucas, at the age of 116.
At that time, she revealed her secret to living a long life.
“Never arguing with anyone, I listen, and I do what I like,” she told the Associated Press in May 2025.
On her 116th birthday in 2025, Caterham received a special visit from Britain’s King Charles, who gave her a birthday card.
During the visit, Caterham recalled when Queen Elizabeth invested him as the Prince of Wales in 1969, when he was 21.
“All the girls were in love with you and wanted to marry you,” she told him, prompting a laugh from the British monarch.
Despite her latest milestone, Caterham is still not the oldest person ever.
That honour belongs to French woman Jeanne Calment, who was 122 years and 164 days old when she died in 1997, according to Guinness.

Germany's Wadephul to urge Rubio to take more active role on Ukraine
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul plans to speak to his US counterpart, Marco Rubio, by phone to urge him to become more personally involved in diplomatic efforts related to the war in Ukraine, he told radio broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.
Wadephul, who was recently in Ukraine, told the broadcaster that US diplomacy had so far been handled largely by presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
"I may be able to encourage him (Rubio) myself to do more there," the German minister said, adding that Berlin was pursuing other channels to help restart negotiations.
Ukraine hit Russian fighter aircraft, two vessels in Black Sea
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian MIG-29 fighter aircraft and two Russian vessels in Black Sea overnight, Ukraine's drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said.
Brovdi said on the Telegram app that one of the vessels attacked was a tanker, and the other was a bulk carrier.
EU approves further €6.1 billion for Ukraine's defence
The European Commission approved a further €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in financial aid for Ukraine to procure new defence systems, such as air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.
The EU said this latest aid package came on top of €16 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion had already been disbursed.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a statement.
EU's Costa, UK's Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day
European Council President Antonio Costa and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv to mark the country's independence day, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
The visiting dignitaries also included Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldova's President Maia Sandu and Estonia's President Alar Karis, Sybiha said on X, posting photos of the officials arriving at the Kyiv station.

South Korean president’s approval rating hits record low as decline extends to 6th week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:43:35 UTC
13:43:35 KST

Faisal Mahmud
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s approval rating fell to its lowest level since he took office, extending its decline for a sixth consecutive week, according to a Realmeter poll released Monday.
The survey, conducted from Aug. 18-21 among 2,026 adults, showed Lee’s approval rating falling 2.8 percentage points from the previous week to 40.2%.
His disapproval rating rose by the same margin to 56.9%, the Korea Herald reported.
Realmeter attributed the decline to growing public distrust over the government’s housing policies, political clashes involving judicial and constitutional issues, and security concerns following the scaling back of South Korea-US joint military exercises.
The pollster also noted weakening support for Lee among conservative voters and people aged 70 and above.
A separate Realmeter survey of 1,009 adults conducted Aug. 20-21 showed support for the ruling Democratic Party of Korea falling 6 percentage points to 41.9%.
Support for the opposition People Power Party, meanwhile, climbed 4.5 points to 37.6%, narrowing the gap between the two parties.
Both surveys were conducted using wireless automated response systems. The presidential approval poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Leg-length gap forces para table tennis champion to halve training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:43:25 UTC
13:43:25 KST

The Moradabad athlete has won 27 national and 10 international medals and recently clinched gold at the 1st UTT Para National Ranking Table Tennis Championship 2026-27 in Indore.
NEW DELHI: A three-inch difference in his leg lengths, persistent back pain and other physical problems have forced 29-year-old Kunal Arora to cut his table tennis training by more than half. Yet, the thalassemia major patient and international para table tennis player is set to leave for Finland on August 26 with the Indian team, even as doctors have advised him to get a prosthetic extension to improve his alignment and mobility.The Moradabad athlete has won 27 national and 10 international medals and recently clinched gold at the 1st UTT Para National Ranking Table Tennis Championship 2026-27 in Indore.Arora will also be felicitated on Sunday by the Thalassemia Patients Advocacy Group (TPAG), in collaboration with Thalassemics India, at an event in New Delhi honouring thalassemia patients for their achievements and resilience.Diagnosed with thalassemia major at birth, Arora said severe iron overload led to two major leg surgeries in 2010. The difference developed gradually as he grew after the surgeries, leaving his left leg around three to four inches shorter than the right.A July 22 prescription records a three-inch left-side limb-length discrepancy and recommends an extension prosthesis with an Axion carbon-fibre foot and laminated socket.
Arora said the imbalance has caused spinal curvature, persistent back pain and mobility problems, with doctors recommending the device to improve alignment and daily mobility. He said it would also help during training, though it is unclear if he can wear it in competitions. The prosthesis is estimated to cost Rs 2,66,910 including GST, which his family cannot afford.“My father is a small businessman and my mother is a homemaker. I completed my graduation from Delhi University in 2021 and I am continuing with table tennis. I also help my father with his business whenever he needs me,” Kunal told TOI.The physical problems have cut his training from 7-8 hours in two sessions to about 2.5-3.5 hours in one session. “The difference in my leg length causes pain and affects my daily activities as well as my training. I am now hoping for support to get the prosthetic extension, which costs around Rs 2.7 lakh.
I want to continue playing for India and need this support to manage my mobility and training,” he said.Arora has represented India internationally since 2014 and is seeking sponsorship for international tournaments, which he says would help him compete more frequently and work towards the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games and Paralympic Games. For now, he is managing without the prosthesis and plans to give his measurements in the first or second week of September. The device is expected to take about a month to prepare.“Life gave me thalassemia major, but also a choice: to be defined by my diagnosis or my determination. I chose the paddle,” Arora said.

Weidel also reaffirmed the AfD's opposition to a planned combustion-engine ban and rejected measures targeting human-caused climate change.

UN expert urges peacekeepers in Palestinian territories as settler attacks surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:39:45 UTC
13:39:45 KST

UN expert urges peacekeepers in Palestinian territories as settler attacks surge
UN special rapporteur for Palestine Francesca Albanese has called for the deployment of an international protection force in the Palestinian territories in response to a rise in attacks by Israeli settlers.
“An International Protection Presence in West Bank/east Jerusalem and Gaza is absolutely URGENT,” Albanese wrote in a post on X on Monday.
“Third states have an obligation, per the ICJ, to act to end Israel’s unlawful occupation,” she said, using the acronym for the Hague-based International Court of Justice. She called on the offices of the UN secretary-general and the General Assembly to help bypass the “paralysis” of the organization’s Security Council, where the US has vetoed a number of resolutions critical of Israel.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are considered illegal under international law by the UN and most of the international community. Israel disputes this. The settlements are also widely viewed as an obstacle to establishing a viable Palestinian state. In 2024, the ICJ issued an advisory opinion saying Israel should end its occupation of Palestinian territory “as rapidly as possible.”
On Sunday, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, condemned Israel’s plan to build more than 1,200 housing units under the E1 settlement project, saying it would “divide the West Bank in two, isolating East Jerusalem, and further eroding the viability of a two-state solution.”
Israel has taken an increasingly hawkish stance since the war in Gaza began with a Hamas attack in October 2023, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying last year that “there will be no Palestinian state to the west of the Jordan River.”
More Israeli outposts have since been approved in the West Bank, which far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich hailed as “a revolution” in settlement expansion.
Settler violence has also surged. There were around 190 attacks against Palestinians per month in the first months of 2026, according to UN data cited by The Guardian. A 17-year-old Palestinian was killed and another wounded by gunfire on Friday during an altercation with settlers.

Over 20 Marvel stars back campaign to free senior terrorist Marwan Barghouti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:38:24 UTC
13:38:24 KST

More than 20 actors who have appeared in Marvel Studios films and television series have joined an international campaign calling on Israel to release senior terrorist Marwan Barghouti, one of the most prominent Palestinian prisoners held in Israel.
Among the best-known names backing the “Freedom for Marwan” campaign are Benedict Cumberbatch, who plays Doctor Strange in the Marvel Cinematic Universe; Mark Ruffalo, who portrays the Hulk; and Don Cheadle, who plays War Machine.
They have been joined by Cate Blanchett, Tilda Swinton, Tatiana Maslany, Daniel Brühl, Ian McKellen, Hugo Weaving and Kingsley Ben-Adir.
The campaign was launched late last year by Barghouti’s family with the support of civil society organizations in Britain. The Marvel actors join more than 200 cultural figures from around the world, including actors, musicians, writers and directors, who have signed a letter supporting the campaign.
Barghouti, a senior Fatah figure and former secretary-general of the movement in the West Bank, has been imprisoned in Israel for more than two decades. Israeli forces arrested him in Ramallah in April 2002 during the Second Intifada, when he was a leader of Tanzim, Fatah’s armed faction.
In 2004, an Israeli court convicted Barghouti of five counts of murder for his role in four terrorist attacks that killed four Israelis and a Greek monk. He was also convicted of attempted murder and membership in a terrorist organization and sentenced to five consecutive life terms plus an additional 40 years.
Despite his imprisonment, Barghouti remains one of the most recognizable figures in Palestinian politics and has repeatedly been cited as a possible successor to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas.
His name has also surfaced repeatedly in negotiations over prisoner exchanges. Hamas has sought his release in past negotiations, while Israel has refused to free him.

During his visit to Kyiv, Burnham will provide Ukraine with the technology to produce SCALP missiles.
Kyiv • UNN
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will announce in Kyiv the disclosure of SCALP technologies to create assembly lines in Ukraine. London will also continue its military support.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is arriving in Kyiv on August 24 for his first foreign visit in office and will announce permission to disclose classified information about British components of SCALP missiles to create assembly lines in Ukraine. The British government reported this, UNN writes.
Details
Burnham's visit is taking place on Ukraine's Independence Day. In Kyiv, he is expected to meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing for the first time, together with other world leaders.
The main defense decision during the visit will be the British government's authorization for defense company MBDA to disclose classified information about components of the SCALP long-range missile. This is intended to allow Ukraine and France to establish local assembly lines for such missiles on Ukrainian territory.
Britain is opening access to SCALP technology
SCALP is the French version of the British Storm Shadow missile. Both systems use shared French and British technologies.
The British government said the decision continues its support for Ukraine after the United Kingdom became the first country to provide Kyiv with long-range weapons in 2023 for defense against Russian aggression. The disclosure of technical information is expected to allow missile assembly in Ukraine to continue.
On the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence, the Ukrainian people should have no doubt: the United Kingdom supports you today and for as long as necessary
Burnham separately said that the United Kingdom would continue to support Ukraine in developing long-range strike weapons as part of the Breakstop project. According to him, London would also continue working with international partners on Ukraine's long-term security.
During his stay in Kyiv, the British prime minister will also take part in events marking Independence Day and co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing. The United Kingdom says it has allocated a total of £25 billion in funding to support Ukraine, including £16 billion in military aid.

UN rapporteur calls for international protection force in Gaza, West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:36:49 UTC
13:36:49 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese called Sunday for an “international protection presence” in the occupied West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, saying such a deployment was “absolutely urgent.”
“Third states have an obligation, per the ICJ, to act to end Israel’s unlawful occupation,” Albanese wrote on the US social media platform X, referring to a July 2024 advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice that deemed Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory unlawful and said states must not assist in maintaining it.
Albanese also questioned whether UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ diplomatic efforts and the General Assembly’s “Uniting for Peace” mechanism could overcome the Security Council’s deadlock on the conflict.
The mechanism allows the General Assembly to consider international peace and security issues when the Security Council cannot act because of a lack of unanimity among its permanent members. The council has repeatedly been unable to take action on Gaza and the West Bank amid vetoes by the US.

MPs from the Eesti 200, Isamaa, Reform and the Social Democratic Party (SDE) factions will submit 74 signatures in support of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise on Monday at 11 a.m.
Among members of the parties supporting Madise, SDE's Züleyxa Izmailova and Isamaa's Priit Sibul, Andres Metsoja and Helir-Valdor Seeder did not sign the nomination.

Netherlands unveils underground stabilization facility project to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:32:00 UTC
13:32:00 KST

Netherlands unveils underground stabilization facility project to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day
According to a Ukrinform correspondent in The Hague, Dutch and Norwegian volunteers are working to implement this project in Ukraine.
“This is a single facility that will serve as a stabilization center for the wounded while also housing several operating rooms. Emergency surgeries will be able to be performed there. The main goal is to increase the chances of survival for Ukraine’s defenders,” said Jaap Scholten, a Dutch volunteer and co-founder of the Protect Ukraine Foundation, in an exclusive comment to Ukrinform.
He also noted that the total cost of the project is 2.5 million euros, and 750,000 euros have already been raised.
“We can’t say exactly where it will be located, but yes, the site where it will be built has already been determined. However, we don’t want to help the Russians, so we’re not naming it. And it’s important to note that this isn’t a hospital where patients will stay for a long time. They’ll only be there for a certain period, after which they’ll be transported to a military or other specialized hospital. Usually, they try to stabilize the wounded already in the ambulance and then at a stabilization point. But this facility will allow us to take it one step further. For example, it will be possible to perform certain surgeries, which will significantly increase a soldier’s chances of survival, rather than having to wait another three, four, or five hours until they are transported to a military hospital. That is the idea,” he said.
According to Zita Yankovich, a member of the Protect Ukraine Foundation’s board responsible for medical issues, drones have radically changed the conditions for evacuating the wounded. Even evacuation vehicles can become targets, which is why transporting the wounded to hospitals takes significantly longer.
“We used to talk about the ‘golden hour,’ when a wounded person had to be rescued within the first hour. But now that’s often impossible, because it’s simply not possible to quickly remove a person from the battlefield. So this project involves building a medical complex about 6–8 meters underground. For security reasons, its exact location and technical details are not being disclosed. The plan is to equip the facility with six operating rooms where surgical procedures can be performed, as well as to provide blood transfusions, anesthesia, and other emergency care. Most importantly, doctors will be able to work there safely,” she emphasized.
According to her, Russia’s war in Ukraine—particularly the widespread use of drones—has led to a change in the nature of injuries. Medical personnel are increasingly dealing with severe trauma, amputations, and internal bleeding caused by shrapnel. At the same time, stabilization points near the front lines are often set up under extremely challenging conditions—in makeshift underground facilities where medical personnel work with minimal resources and constant risk.
“About 2 million euros are needed to build the medical complex itself; the remaining funds will go toward medical equipment, supplies, and transportation, including armored vehicles for the safe evacuation of the wounded. The project aims not only to strengthen Ukraine’s medical capabilities on the front lines but also to protect doctors and medical personnel working in close proximity to combat operations. “We want to save as many lives as possible among Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom—and for our freedom as well,” she emphasized.
Also during the event, Khrystyna N. (call sign “Ice Queen”)—a Dutch-Bulgarian senior combat medic who has been working on the front lines for four years— and Nataliia Tsyplytska—a former Ukrainian combat medic and executive director of the organization “Vdachni”—shared their personal experiences working in the combat zone and evacuating the wounded. They also showed the audience photos and videos depicting the real-life conditions under which medics work and the process of evacuating the wounded.
As reported by Ukrinform, a Dutch volunteer received the Order of Merit, Third Class, for his support of Ukraine.
Photo: Iryna Drabok

UK’s Burnham to visit Kyiv on 1st foreign trip as prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:31:50 UTC
13:31:50 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Kyiv on Monday in his first foreign trip since taking office, reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine as it marks the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union, according to several British media reports.
The BBC reported that Burnham will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and chair his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing" established by France and the UK under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer. He is also expected to accept an award on behalf of the British people recognizing Britain's support for Ukraine.
"On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes," Burnham said ahead of the visit. "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
The government is also expected to announce that defense company MBDA can declassify information on British components used in the long-range Storm Shadow missile, allowing Ukraine to pursue domestic production of its French equivalent, Scalp-EG.
The weapons, with a range of around 150 miles (241 kilometers), have been used against heavily fortified targets in occupied Ukrainian territory and Russia.
Burnham’s visit comes amid intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine and growing tensions between Moscow and London. Russia recently warned of "consequences" over British-made drones used in Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory.
Moscow also confirmed that its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post after seven years. Russia's Foreign Ministry accused Britain of pursuing a "path of confrontation," while a NATO official told The Telegraph that Russia has intensified destabilization campaigns against allies through cyberattacks, assassination attempts and sabotage.
"NATO continues to boost its resilience and is applying and enhancing the tools at our disposal to counter hybrid actions," the official said. "At every stage, we will ensure that the Alliance is prepared to deter and defend against any threat and to keep our one billion citizens safe."

SAO PAULO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Jose Manuel Lopez scored twice as Palmeiras extended its lead at the top of Brazil's Serie A on Sunday with a 4-1 home win over Vasco da Gama.
Lopez opened the scoring in the 47th minute before Vitor Roque converted a penalty and Mauricio added a third goal just inside the hour.
Argentina international striker Lopez struck again a minute from time ahead of Facundo Colidio's stoppage-time consolation goal for the visitors.
The result leaves Palmeiras with 51 points, six clear of second-placed Flamengo, which has a game in hand. Vasco is 19th in the 20-team standings with 22 points.
Elsewhere in Brazil's Serie A on Sunday, Coritiba won 2-1 at home to Corinthians, Mirassol drew 1-1 at Santos, Chapecoense won 1-0 at home to Sao Paulo, Bragantino secured a 1-0 home win over Gremio, and Bahia prevailed 2-0 at Vitoria. ■

Scorching heat expected in much of Japan: weather agency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:31:15 CST
13:31:15 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Scorching heat is expected to grip much of western and eastern Japan on Monday, the weather agency said, urging people to take extra caution against heatstroke.
Due to a high-pressure system, sweltering weather is expected in much of the country, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), with a heatstroke alert in place for 31 prefectures, from Tokyo and Chiba in the Kanto region through Okinawa in southwestern Japan.
The JMA forecast daytime highs of 39 degrees Celsius in Hita City, Oita Prefecture, and 38 degrees Celsius in cities including Saga, Yamaguchi and Nara.
The mercury is also forecast to jump in areas of Kumamoto Prefecture that were hit hard by a massive earthquake in late July, with daytime highs to reach 38 degrees Celsius in Kumamoto City, 37 degrees Celsius in Amakusa City and 36 degrees Celsius in Hitoyoshi City. ■

China renews alerts for rainstorms, typhoon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:31:04 CST
13:31:04 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) on Monday renewed a yellow alert for rainstorms and a blue alert for the 19th typhoon of this year, with heavy rainfall and strong winds forecast to affect multiple regions of the country.
From 8 a.m. Monday to 8 a.m. Tuesday, torrential rain is expected to lash parts of Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Taiwan, Hainan, Jiangxi, Hunan, Hubei, Yunnan, Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, according to the NMC.
Intense downpours will hit southeastern Zhejiang, the eastern coastal areas of Fujian, northern Guangdong, most parts of Taiwan Island, and eastern Liaoning, with some areas in Taiwan likely to see exceptionally heavy rain of 250 to 300 millimeters.
The affected areas will experience short-term heavy rainfall, with hourly precipitation reaching 20 to 50 millimeters, accompanied by thunderstorms and gales, the NMC said.
Meanwhile, the 19th typhoon of this year was located at 5 a.m. Monday in the Beibu Gulf, about 185 kilometers southwest of Beihai City in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with maximum winds of 23 meters per second near its center.
It is expected to track eastward from Monday night and then travel northward at a speed of 5 to 10 kilometers per hour, gradually approaching the coastal areas from Guangxi to the western Leizhou Peninsula in Guangdong Province.
The NMC has advised local governments to take precautionary measures.
China has a four-tier color-coded weather warning system, with red representing the most severe, followed by orange, yellow and blue. ■

====================================================================================================

KPMG Australia to cut hundreds of jobs amid audit leaks scandal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:31:02 CST
13:31:02 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Australian branch of international accounting and consultancy firm KPMG on Monday said it will cut hundreds of jobs after revenue fell as a result of an audit leaks scandal.
KPMG Australia reported total revenue of 2.26 billion Australian dollars (1.6 billion U.S. dollars) in its full-year results for the 2025-26 financial year, down 0.9 percent year-on-year.
It said that revenue grew in four of its five divisions, but that consulting revenue fell by 16.9 percent after the firm was barred from new government contracts over the misuse of confidential client information.
As a result, KPMG Australia said it plans to reduce its workforce by approximately 5 percent, affecting 360 employees and 27 partners.
"We need to be clear about the outlook. We expect difficult market conditions to continue in FY27 and beyond," Chief Executive Officer John Sams said in a statement.
"Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes," he added.
Senator Deborah O'Neill in March shared allegations in parliament from a whistleblower that KPMG partners had repeatedly used clients' confidential information to win lucrative audit contracts.
The firm in May said it had been aware of the allegations since 2024 and that its internal investigation was not rigorous enough.
O'Neill told a parliamentary inquiry into the allegations earlier in August that many more whistleblowers had come forward to raise concerns about misconduct at KPMG. ■

Iceland to vote on resuming EU accession talks amid fears over Trump
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:30:27 EEST
13:30:27 KST

Iceland to vote on resuming EU accession talks amid fears over Trump
Kyiv • UNN
On August 29, Icelanders will vote on resuming EU accession talks amid concerns over Trump's policy toward Greenland. The key disputes concern sovereignty and control over fisheries.
Icelandic voters will decide on August 29 whether to resume negotiations on the country's accession to the European Union amid rising geopolitical tensions and concerns over U.S. President Donald Trump's policy toward Greenland. Associated Press reports, UNN writes.
Details
The referendum will be the first direct vote by Icelanders on resuming negotiations on EU membership. Iceland, with a population of about 400,000, is a NATO member, participates in the EU single market through the European Economic Area, and is part of the Schengen Area.
Iceland's Foreign Ministry is "optimistic" about joining the EU in 202818.03.26, 23:03 • 5547 views
One of the factors that accelerated the referendum was Trump's statements about Greenland. The American president has repeatedly spoken about the need for the United States to control the Danish autonomous territory, and in one speech he called Greenland Iceland several times.
We can no longer truly trust the United States. Trump was not joking about Greenland. There was a lot of fear in Iceland because if he takes Greenland by force, we will probably be next
Sovereignty and fishing remain the main issues
Supporters of EU membership believe that closer ties with Europe could strengthen Iceland's security and protect it from geopolitical instability. Among the possible economic benefits, they cite a more stable currency, lower interest rates, and inflation.
Opponents of accession emphasize the preservation of sovereignty. Iceland gained independence from Denmark in 1944, and control over its own laws and natural resources remains an important part of national policy.
Iceland's independence is the most valuable resource we have. The ability to create our own laws and decide how to do everything is extremely important
Fishing is a separate issue. Iceland has extensive fish resources in the North Atlantic, and concerns about losing control over them have remained one of the main arguments against joining the EU for many years. Icelandic opponents of membership fear that European trawlers will gain access to its waters under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Defense Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir said that Iceland would not agree to a deal that did not guarantee the country's full control over its own fisheries.
Iceland has already attempted to join the EU. Negotiations began after the country submitted its application in 2009 amid the global financial crisis, but they were suspended in 2013 and formally ended in 2015.
If Icelanders support resuming negotiations in the referendum, a years-long process with the European Commission will begin. It will assess the country's compliance with 35 groups of criteria, including in the areas of finance, fisheries, transport, agriculture, and rights and freedoms. The final agreement must be approved by all EU member states, after which the decision on accession will again be put to a vote in Iceland.

Another case of acute liver damage in counterfeit peptide user
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:25:20 UTC
13:25:20 KST

Doctors fear possible contaminated counterfeit peptide batch after seventh case of acute liver damage
In short:
There are fears a "contaminated batch" of counterfeit peptides is causing hospitalisations for acute liver toxicity.
The latest patient became seriously unwell after taking unapproved peptide labelled as retatrutide.
What's next?
Doctors are testing the counterfeit peptides linked to the liver failure cases, amid warnings that unapproved products can cause serious harm.
Another black market peptide user has suffered a severe liver injury, with doctors concerned a possible "contaminated batch" might be to blame.
The latest case means seven Victorian patients have now been hospitalised for acute liver toxicity, after using a counterfeit of the weight loss peptide retatrutide.
Liver transplant specialist Marie Sinclair, who has treated liver failure patients in Victoria, said another patient had recently become seriously unwell after taking an unapproved peptide labelled as retatrutide.
"We have seen a recent case again, fairly similar to previous cases, where after a second dose of unregulated retatrutide there was severe liver injury," Dr Sinclair said.
"It's uncertain as to why this has happened, but one possibility is that there could be a contaminated batch of [counterfeit] retatrutide that is in Victoria.
"It's one possible explanation … we don't have any testing results to support that, it's purely a hypothesis at this stage."
Dr Sinclair said she had commissioned testing of counterfeit peptides used by liver failure patients.
"This is something I think we are going to continue to see with peptides if the unregulated market continues," she said.
Dr Sinclair said the affected patients sustained liver injuries "within a few weeks" of taking the black market retatrutide.
"They may become yellow or jaundiced, which is very frightening for patients, and they can become very unwell," she said.
The Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) chief medical advisor Robyn Langham told the ABC "the localised nature" of the liver issues in Victoria suggested "a batch problem".
"We are seeing reports of acute liver failure which might be related to some batch issues certainly from Victoria," Professor Langham said.
She said the cluster of liver harm cases did not appear to be happening elsewhere in Australia.
Professor Langham warned consumers black market retatrutide was a "counterfeit product" and taking it was a risk.
"The retatrutide that's being sold is not the retatrutide that's currently in clinical trials," she said.
Professor Langham said her comments were not the result of an investigation.
Peptides are small chains of amino acids which act as signalling agents in the body, telling it to carry out certain processes such as hormone release or tissue repair.
There are regulated peptide medications including insulin and GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic.
This year there has been a boom in social media promotion of counterfeit, unapproved peptides, which are not safe for human use.
Victoria's health department has been contacted for comment.
It previously warned products labelled "retatrutide" may contain contaminants that could have "toxic effects".
The ABC contacted all other state and territory health departments to ask if there had been any cases of liver toxicity associated with unapproved peptide use.
Canberra Health Services confirmed it had detected liver damage from products sold as retatrutide, but would not say how many "due to the low numbers involved".
US-based pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly is the sole owner of the patent for retatrutide and is currently running clinical trials.
"Lilly continues to warn the public about the potential dangers of fake medicines," Manny Simons, general manager of Lilly Australia, said.
"Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."
Adolescents 'injecting' counterfeit peptides
Professor Langham said it was important to note there were no good batches or safe unapproved peptides — the risk of serious harm applied to all the products.
"There are hospital admissions happening across the country because of the use of unapproved peptides," she said.
"The risks are real, they are not theoretical."
Professor Langham said the TGA was particularly worried about young people using unapproved peptides being promoted on social media.
"What concerns us most is that adolescents, young children are buying these and injecting them into themselves, so goodness knows what is happening," she said.
"[The counterfeit products] have not been tested in clinical trials, they have not been tested in terms of their manufacturing, and they've not been tested for their safety and people are injecting these into their body."
The TGA said more than 94,500 unapproved peptide products had been destroyed this year, in collaboration with Australian Border Force.
Last week, the TGA and New South Wales Police seized more than $120,000 of "illicit peptide and anabolic steroid products" from premises allegedly linked to a social media influencers.
In April, authorities seized $2 million worth of steroids and peptides.

Ebola responders were chased with machetes, while the outbreak in Congo has already spread across an area larger than France
Kyiv • UNN
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ebola has infected more than 5,500 people and claimed 2,642 lives. Attacks, strikes, and refusal to isolate are complicating the response.
Rescuers who tried to bury an Ebola victim in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo were chased with machetes, while the outbreak had already spread across an area larger than France. Bloomberg reports this, citing data from the authorities of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the UN and humanitarian organizations, UNN writes.
Details
Just over 100 days after the outbreak was declared, more than 5,500 people have been infected and 2,642 have died. Julien Harneis, the UN’s senior Ebola coordinator, said the scale of the epidemic is growing faster than the response capacity.
The outbreak is spreading faster and more widely than the response to Ebola
According to him, the epidemic already covers an area larger than France.
Attacks complicate the fight against the epidemic
The violence has already forced some rescuers to leave the affected areas. Last week, the Uganda Red Cross Society evacuated staff from the Congo after an attack on an Ebola response team near the epicenter in Ituri province. One worker was seriously injured, one response vehicle was destroyed, and two others were damaged.
A burial team was also attacked in North Kivu, leaving several people injured and one person dead. In other areas, families obstructed the examination of bodies, took the deceased away from treatment centers and blocked the work of burial teams.
There are also problems with isolating infected people. Fourteen patients left treatment centers in Ituri, while the authorities separately recorded 14 cases of refusal to isolate in various health zones.
Workers are on strike
At the same time, some medical workers are on strike because of unpaid salaries. Five screening points were not operating in Haut-Uele, while workers from public organizations in North Kivu and Tshopo have not received payments for months.
Médecins Sans Frontières is calling for intensified case detection and infection control directly within communities. According to the organization, more than 60% of deaths since the beginning of the current outbreak have occurred outside healthcare facilities.
The authorities in Congo are also preparing to expand the use of the Ervebo vaccine. The first 16,520 doses arrived in Kinshasa as part of a shipment of more than 50,000 doses. At the same time, the vaccine is not approved against the Bundibugyo strain, which caused the current outbreak, so its potential effectiveness is still being assessed.

Gauff beats Pegula for 2nd Cincinnati Open title; France’s Fils beats American Tiafoe in men’s final
MASON, Ohio (AP) — Coco Gauff defeated fellow American Jessica Pegula, 6-2, 6-4, to capture her second women’s Cincinnati Open title on Sunday, and Arthur Fils of France defeated American Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0, in the men’s final for his first Masters 1000 title.
In Saturday’s semifinals, Pegula beat defending champion Iga Swiatek and Gauff defeated Sara Bejlek to set up the first all-American women’s final at the Cincinnati Open in 56 years.
The last time two American women played in the Cincinnati final was in 1970, when Rosie Casals beat Nancy Richey.
Pegula’s best finish in Cincinnati came in 2024, when she lost to Aryna Sabalenka in the final.
Gauff, who won the 2023 title beating Karolina Muchova, stormed out to a 5-0 lead in the first set on Sunday before winning 6-2. Pegula battled back to within 5-4 in the second before Gauff closed out the win. Gauff won five of six break points.
“I think it was a long journey, but I’m happy,” Gauff said. “I think it’s night and day, the player I was last year to now. I don’t think that this is an indicator that I’m going to do well in New York. Just knowing the quality ones that I had this week, hopefully I can use that experience.”
Gauff had five wins in straight sets in Cincinnati.
“I thought she just played at a really high level and didn’t really have many dips,” Pegula said. “I didn’t really think I played bad. The more you construct the point (against her), the worse it is because she almost likes to run. It was tough today. A dangerous, confident Coco is going to New York.”
The head-to-head series between Gauff and Pegula is now tied at five apiece. Sunday was their second meeting in a final, with Gauff winning at Wuhan last year.
The Fils-Tiafoe match was the first time two Black players have met in an ATP Masters 1000 final.
Fils is the third Black man to win a Masters 1000 title, joining Ben Shelton, who won twice in Canada, and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga, who won in Paris in 2008 and Canada in 2014.
At 22 years old, Fils is the youngest French champion in Masters 1000 history. He became the second French player to win a Cincinnati final, joining Guy Forget in 1991.
“Very happy with that,” Fils said. “It’s been a tough last year. I didn’t play the French Open (due to a hip injury). I lost early in Washington. People think that I’m done. But here we are. I got the title.”
It was the second time Tiafoe has appeared in the Cincinnati Open final, losing to Jannik Sinner in 2024. He was looking to become the first American male to win in Cincinnati since Andy Roddick in 2006.
“I’m going to have two Cincinnati finals trophies at the crib,” Tiafoe said. “I wish they were both champion ones. Losing on Sunday sucks. I’ve had a tough summer. I was able to play five great matches and beat quality players.”
Fils overpowered Tiafoe early in the first set on Sunday, winning 12 of 13 points to take a 3-0 lead. Tiafoe was dominant in the second, rolling to a 3-0 lead.
Tiafoe used the time break before the third set to stretch and receive massage treatment on his upper left leg and lower back.
“My hip bothered me a little bit, but that’s neither here nor there,” Tiafoe said. “It’s not about how I feel. I’ll be alright in a week (for the US Open).”
Tiafoe saved three championship points in the final game before Fils closed out the victory.
The Frenchman had 11 aces and won 71% of his points on first serve. He improved to 10-0 in deciding sets this year and 8-0 against American opponents.
Fils also won his only previous meeting with Tiafoe in Miami last year, also in three sets.
“It feels very good to have a trophy next to me, especially Masters 1000,” Fils said. “Never won one before. You just have to stay positive and find a way to make it work. Being positive is going to help me in the next weeks in the US Open.”

3-year college degrees grow more popular in the US, saving time and cash. But critics aren’t sold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:01 UTC
13:23:01 KST

3-year college degrees grow more popular in the US, saving time and cash. But critics aren’t sold
Giles Sims, 34, was sick of getting passed over for jobs because he didn’t have a college degree.
But with a wife and a widowed mother to help support, he needed a quick solution. So the laid-off web developer turned to one of a growing number of three-year degree programs.
“I can’t afford to be out of the workforce for four years. That just seems like forever, and the three-year made it seem less daunting,” said Sims, a student at Ensign College, a private Salt Lake City school that recently changed all its bachelor’s degrees to require fewer classes than a traditional four-year degree.
The condensed programs have exploded in popularity. As of this spring, 26 U.S. states have a college that offers at least one reduced-credit, three-year bachelor’s, according to the nonprofit research group RAND.
Advocates say these programs are a solution to the college affordability crisis and a godsend for non-traditional students like Sims.
Critics, however, worry that they’ll narrow too much what students learn, confuse employers, limit graduate school options and create headaches in fields that require state licenses.
The American Association of University Professors, for one, says the programs devalue the meaning of a college credential.
“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” said Todd Wolfson, AAUP’s president.
A new option to graduate more quickly, but with reduced credit
For decades, colleges have offered accelerated programs that let students finish faster, often by forgoing long summer breaks, maximizing transfer credits and condensing semester-long courses into shorter, five- to 10-week terms.
But those programs maintained the same course load, measured as credits. The new programs let students finish faster by completing as few as 90 credit hours. That shaves a year off the typical 120-hour bachelor’s degree.
Three-year bachelor’s degrees are common in other countries including the United Kingdom, India, France and Italy. But they can create complications for graduates seeking admission to U.S. graduate schools, which sometimes require extra coursework.
Some of the earliest colleges in colonial America, modeled after English institutions like Oxford and Cambridge, initially had three-year degrees, said John Thelin, the author of “A History of American Higher Education.” By the 19th century, the four-year format had taken hold, partly because there wasn’t an established system of public high schools to prepare students, Thelin said.
“The colleges would have to kind of start from scratch,” he said.
A change in accreditation opened the door to shorter degrees
The idea of bringing three-year degrees to the U.S. got attention in 2009 when Robert Zemsky, the founding director of the Institute for Research on Higher Education at the University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education, argued in a Newsweek cover story that three-year degrees could shake up a broken system.
But there was a roadblock, he recalled recently. “Accreditors said, ‘College is 120 credits, not 90 credits,’” he said.
Years passed. And in 2022, amid mounting concerns about college affordability, Zemsky helped revive the idea. The College-in-3 Exchange was born, and dozens of higher education institutions joined the network to look for ways to help students get degrees faster.
The Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities was the first accreditor to say yes in 2023, when it approved reduced-credit programs at Ensign and Brigham Young University-Idaho. Other accreditors quickly followed.
As of May, 119 reduced-credit programs had been publicly announced, according to the RAND analysis, which was conducted to help education officials in Ohio as they weigh the feasibility of reduced-credit degrees.
It comes at a time when tuition and fees averaged $11,950 for in-state students at public schools and $45,000 at private nonprofits last school year, although many students get discounts that reduce the price, according to a report from the College Board, the nonprofit that oversees the SAT.
Some degrees are easier to compress
Private nonprofit schools offer three-quarters of the reduced-credit programs, frequently online. Typically, they compress the majors by reducing electives. Business degrees in fields such as marketing and management are the most common, followed by computer and information sciences.
Other majors, such as engineering, with its extensive math requirements, have been harder to shrink. And RAND found just six reduced-credit degrees in teacher education, which involves real-world experience requirements and state licensure.
Jill Cohen, 42, lives on a ranch in rural Yoder, Colorado, and is completing her teaching degree through one such program at Indiana Wesleyan.
She quit her old job selling life insurance and turned to teaching after a farming accident nearly claimed her life. Already, she is in the classroom, teaching middle school English, as she works on the degree through a special “Grow Your Own” program designed to address staff shortages.
Because her home is busy — she has twin 12-year-olds, along with a menagerie that includes horses, goats and chickens — she appreciates the streamlined degree.
“Why do I need to take, you know, underwater basket weaving when I could just take the evolutionary structure of the English language — what I’m going to be teaching,” she said.
However, programs with state licensing requirements are one of the biggest worries for Jenna Kramer, a policy researcher at RAND.
Indiana Wesleyan, which has a growing slate of reduced-credit offerings, said its education programs are specifically designed to meet Indiana licensing requirements. Students from elsewhere will need to check if the programs meet their state requirements, said Pam Downing, the school’s director of communications, in an email.
The RAND report also found the programs are so new that there are no standard practices for admitting three-year degree recipients into graduate school.
Students acknowledge it’s a gamble
Gabriella Staten, a 20-year-old student in the reduced-credit digital marketing program at Mount Mary University, a Catholic women’s institution in Milwaukee, estimates it will save her at least $20,000. While she sometimes wonders whether employers will take her degree as seriously as a four-year degree, she decided she could prove herself.
“Even if they were to look a little bit down on the three-year pathway, I can show them otherwise with the work,” she said.
Wesley Hardy, who is three semesters into a bachelor of applied science in accounting at Ensign, also sees the pros and cons. He likes that the three-year format will get him into the workforce faster.
But he noted that the requirements to become a certified public accountant — something he has considered — vary by state. Many require 120 semester hours to sit for the exam and 150 to become licensed. Graduate school often is needed.
Bruce Kusch, president of Ensign, said he has talked to multiple college presidents and doesn’t anticipate that graduate school will be a problem. But Hardy, 22, has questions about how it would work.
“Would I have to take extra classes?” he asked. “It’s definitely something I’ve thought of.”

What to know about Iceland’s vote on whether to restart talks to join the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:01 UTC
13:23:01 KST

What to know about Iceland’s vote on whether to restart talks to join the EU
REYKJAVIK, Iceland (AP) — When U.S. President Donald Trump said he wanted a “piece of ice, cold and poorly located,” the people of Iceland had every reason to worry even if he was referring to Greenland.
Their concern was not only that the object of Trump’s desire was their nearest big neighbor, but that he repeatedly called it Iceland — four times.
That gaffe, as Trump continued to press for control of Greenland earlier this year, could help push the fiercely independent Iceland and its 400,000 people closer to Europe as voters decide Saturday whether to restart talks to join the European Union.
“We can’t really trust the U.S. anymore,” said Hildur Knútsdóttir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership. “Trump was not joking about Greenland. There was a lot of fear here in Iceland because if he takes Greenland with force, we’re probably going to be next.”
Iceland’s decision is whether to continue going it alone successfully and maintain control of precious natural resources like its lucrative and well-managed fisheries, or to strengthen ties with Europe to better insulate the country from geopolitical instability and gain economic benefits such as the more stable euro currency and lower interest rates and inflation.
Iceland, which is a member of NATO, already participates in the EU’s single market through the European Economic Area and is part of the Schengen free-travel zone.
Sovereignty is at the heart of the divide
For both sides of the debate, it’s really a matter of sovereignty, said Hulda Thorisdottir, a political science professor at the University of Iceland.
Opponents argue that the nation that won its independence from Denmark in 1944 enjoys all the benefits of European integration with no drawbacks. Why surrender that when they’re doing so well? she said.
“The independence of Iceland is the most precious resource that we have,” said Haraldur Olafsson, a physics professor who is chairman of Heimssýn, a Euroskeptic group that opposes EU membership. “The possibility of making your own law and deciding how things are done is essential.”
EU proponents, however, see it through the lens of a rapidly changing world in which shifting alliances pose a security risk. Being outside the EU makes Iceland vulnerable and that threatens its sovereignty, Thorisdottir said.
Foreign and Defense Minister Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, who supports joining the EU, said when she asks people from smaller countries such as Ireland, Finland or Luxembourg, whether they feel they’ve lost their sovereignty, “they look at me like I’m a crazy woman” and say membership has made them stronger.
This is not the first time Iceland has considered joining the EU
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir’s center-left coalition government was elected in 2024 on a platform that called for a vote on EU membership.
Icelanders did not vote on the decision to apply for EU membership in 2009, after the country’s debt-burdened banking sector collapsed during the 2008 global financial crisis. Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a center-right government came to power, and they formally ended in 2015.
The referendum is a first step to potentially joining the 27-nation bloc. Voters will answer a simple yes-or-no question: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?
If voters reject the proposal, the issue would be put to rest. A yes vote would lead to a yearslong negotiating process with the European Commission assessing 35 sets of criteria from financial systems to fisheries, transport networks, agricultural regulations, and freedoms such as speech and religion.
Any agreement would need to be approved by all current EU member nations and then voters in Iceland would have the final say on whether to join.
The fish factor could be a deal breaker
The descendants of Vikings who settled Iceland have been living off the sea for centuries, and fishing remains part of the country’s cultural identity. They fought the so-called Cod Wars with Britain to win control of their fishing grounds in the 1970s.
Their rich North Atlantic fishing grounds have always been a key sticking point to joining the EU over concerns they would have to join the Common Fisheries Policy that would allow Spanish, Dutch and other trawlers into their waters.
Any deal with the EU that doesn’t protect Iceland’s fishing rights is seen as dead in the water, but Gunnarsdóttir and other officials are confident any deal will offer an exemption for Iceland’s fisheries.
“We are a superpower when it comes to fisheries,” she said. “We will not sign any agreement which will not underline our sovereignty and full control of our fisheries.”
Heiðrun Lind Marteinsdóttir, the CEO of Fisheries Iceland, said the seafood trade organization doesn’t oppose joining the EU if there is a permanent opt-out from the fisheries policy, but she said that would be unprecedented.
“I think we need to be very realistic on the negotiation process and what we can get out of the negotiations,” she said. “To be honest, I think, we’re aiming high.”
Others in the industry are more skeptical that any protection of Icelandic fisheries would be lasting — especially for open water species like herring, capelin and mackerel that migrate between different fishing zones.
“We are going to see European fishing vessels here in Iceland,” Einar Sigurdsson, chairman of Isfelag fishing company, predicted.
Trump’s Greenland obsession sped up election timetable
The government had planned to hold the vote by next year but moved it up after Trump’s repeated overtures about taking over Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark, a longtime U.S. ally.
The U.S. State Department reassured Iceland officials that Trump meant Greenland during his repeated slip of the tongue at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Gunnarsdóttir, the foreign minister, said.
It didn’t help that William Long, the newly arrived U.S. ambassador in Reykjavik, once joked that Iceland would become the 52nd U.S. state and he’d be its governor. He apologized, but the remark prompted thousands of Icelanders to sign a petition urging the prime minister to reject his appointment.
Gunnarsdóttir said Trump’s saber-rattling emphasized the importance of the EU’s collection of small and large nations standing as one with Greenland and Denmark.
“That is so important for us to see a group of like-minded nations stand together on principles and values,” she said. “That is also what I’m looking at when I see the European Union in this volatile world.”

Uganda and Burundi military officials visit Israel to discuss Gaza troop deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:01 UTC

Uganda and Burundi military officials visit Israel to discuss Gaza troop deployment
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Military officials from Uganda and Burundi visited Israel last week to discuss deploying troops to Gaza as part of an international security force envisioned by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace for the fragile ceasefire, according to officials.
A Board of Peace official told The Associated Press that Ugandan officials joined a Burundian military delegation, and that Uganda is finalizing details of its participation after its parliament approved the troop contribution this month.
Nothing has been finalized with Burundi, but the official said they look forward to starting the process.
“We shared significant knowledge with one another, and the Burundi representatives expressed interest in our mission,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to discuss talks with potential troop-contributing countries ahead of any agreement.
A Burundian military official told the AP that three other senior military officers led the delegation to Israel and that Burundi appeared intent on joining. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
It was not clear what Uganda or Burundi might be offering or what they might receive in return. Spokespersons for their militaries did not respond to requests for comment.
Progress on the international force has been slow
If Burundi moves ahead, the African nations would be the latest to join the international force for Gaza after Morocco, Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania made commitments. Uganda has committed around 1,200 personnel, and Morocco has committed up to 500. Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania in total have committed around 80.
Indonesia earlier said it was preparing to send 8,000 troops — by far the largest commitment — but put that on hold after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
The 20,000-strong force would be led by U.S. Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers. Troops committed remain far short of that goal.
Last month, Trump announced a deal for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza. According to the deal, the International Stabilization Force would be deployed to areas of the Palestinian territory administered by an incoming technocratic committee, and Israeli forces would withdraw.
The force would help monitor the ceasefire, train Palestinian police and secure the delivery of aid, among other tasks.
The ceasefire that took effect in Gaza last October has stalled due to disagreements regarding Israel’s withdrawal from the strip and Hamas’ disarmament. A U.S. delegation met for hours earlier this month with the Hamas leader and then with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to press them forward. Hamas has agreed to the new U.S. deal.
Netanyahu has rejected it, saying Israel will not withdraw from any of the roughly 60% of the territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. Even after Netanyahu’s meeting with the U.S. team, which included negotiator Jared Kushner, officials offered no concrete commitment by Israel.
Uganda and Burundi have peacekeeping experience from Somalia
Paul D. Williams, director of the security policy studies program at The George Washington University, said Uganda and Burundi have gained considerable peacekeeping experience through long-term deployments in Somalia as part of an African Union force resisting the al-Qaida-linked al-Shabab extremist group.
Their countries’ leaderships have “shown they are willing to tolerate high numbers of casualties without withdrawing,” he said.
Williams added that, with the mission in Somalia winding down, both countries will be searching for ways to accrue financial and material support for their militaries: “Deploying to Gaza with U.S. support is one way to do that.”
A Ugandan military officer with knowledge of the upcoming deployment said troops were being selected to go to Gaza. The officer spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the press.

Falzetta reported from Nairobi, Kenya.

Iraq proposes joint security council between Iran, Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Laith Al-jnaidi and Tarek Chouiref
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Iraq has proposed creating a joint security council between Iran and Saudi Arabia, a senior Iraqi official said Sunday, citing a “crisis of trust” between the two regional powers.
Qasim al-Araji, national security adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, said Baghdad had presented the proposal to both Tehran and Riyadh.
“The problem between the two countries is a crisis of trust,” al-Araji told state broadcaster Iraqiya TV.
He gave no further details on the proposed mechanism, while neither Iran nor Saudi Arabia immediately commented.
Al-Araji also said that bringing all weapons under state control was a “purely Iraqi strategic decision,” stressing that decisions of war and peace rest exclusively with the Iraqi state.
The Iraqi army announced on June 3 the formation of a committee tasked with bringing weapons under state control, a longstanding security and political challenge amid the presence of armed factions operating both within and outside the Popular Mobilization Forces.
The proposal comes amid heightened regional tensions and days after Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan discussed developments in the region, stressing the need to contain escalation and resolve disputes peacefully.
On July 27, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed several drones launched from Iraqi territory that attempted to target oil facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh.
Riyadh blamed “Iran-affiliated militias” for the attacks and said it reserved the right to respond.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered security agencies the same day to investigate information provided by Saudi Arabia about the launch of the drones from Iraqi territory.

Torrential rain  triggered by Typhoon Narra caused widespread flooding across southwestern Guangxi region over the weekend, forcing tens of thousands of people to relocate as forecasters warned of more downpours in the days ahead.
Some 54,000 people have been relocated because of the flooding, including 8,087 moved to emergency shelters, state broadcaster CCTV said.

Heavy rain is expected to persist across parts of southern China through Wednesday, with areas of Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan and Fujian forecast to receive torrential rain, CCTV said.
China postponed the launch of its uncrewed Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which had been expected as early as Monday from Hainan's Wenchang Space Launch Site.

NEW DELHI: Former Union minister P Chidambaram on Monday said the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls could leave 10% of India’s eligible population — or nearly 10 crore people — without the right to vote, after a former diplomat detailed difficulties he faced establishing his citizenship during the exercise in Punjab.Navdeep Suri, who served as India’s Ambassador to Egypt and the UAE and High Commissioner to Australia, questioned what the experience of a common citizen might be if he himself faced difficulties despite having represented the country in three nations.“Based on the outcomes so far, at the end of the S.I.R. process, 10% of India’s adult population will be ‘citizens’ but without the right to vote, thanks to the ECI. That is nearly 10 crore people. The ECI has created a new category of ‘non-voting citizens’,” the senior Congress leader wrote, referring to Suri’s post.
Earlier, Suri said his details did not match the 2003 electoral rolls used for verification because he was posted in London at the time and had not participated in that revision.“Sharing my experience with #SIR in Punjab. Went to BLO, submitted Voter ID and Aadhaar card, was assured that everything is in order.
Got a message today from a volunteer saying some details don't match with SIR in 2003!!” Suri posted on X.According to the former diplomat, officials later asked him to produce his passport as proof of citizenship.“Spoke with BLO, was told that I should come and collect the notice. And then come again with unspecified documents that show I am an Indian citizen... I happen to have documents other than voter ID and Aadhaar card.
But can’t help asking: If I have trouble establishing my citizenship after representing India in three countries, what’s the fate of the common citizen? Ease of Living, I presume!” he added.Meanwhile, the Punjab Chief Electoral Officer assured citizens that receiving a notice was not a cause for concern.“As part of the ongoing SIR process, notices are being delivered to voters where required. Received a notice? Don't worry! Simply check the details, submit the required documents, and complete the process,” the Punjab CEO stated on X earlier.The draft electoral roll for Punjab was published on August 13. The state is currently undergoing the second phase of the SIR, which involves reviewing the draft electoral rolls and filing claims and objections.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will co-chair the meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv on Monday, along with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Ukraine on Monday on his first international visit since taking office last month.
The Labour Party leader's visit comes as he announced that the United Kingdom will help support Kyiv with its domestic production of long-range missiles.
The UK has "agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on Brtish-made components for the long-range missile, SCALP, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine," a statement said.
The decision to release the classified information on the missile, which uses both British and French technology, would allow France and Ukraine to move forward with the Ukrainian assembly of the missile.
"It also complements the major UK effort to rapidly develop low-cost advanced long-range strike weapons for Ukraine through Project Brakestop," the statement added.
Along with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Burnham will co-chair the meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, which brings together countries supporting Kyiv.
The meeting will be held in a hybrid format, with some participants attending in person and others via video conference.
The office of Irish prime minister Micheal Martin indicated that he would participate remotely.
On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Nordic and Baltic leaders and held bilateral talks focused on joint defence cooperation.
Zelenskyy also welcomed US Senators Richard Blumenthal and James Lankford to Kyiv. The president said he briefed the pair on the continuing ballistic missile threat from Russia and the need for improved air defences.
European Council President António Costa is also expected to be heading to Ukraine along with other international guests including Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden.
The meeting comes ahead of Ukraine's Independence Day celebrations on Monday.
"On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes," Burnham said in a statement.
The UK has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, pledging around £25 billion (€29.2 billion) in support to date, including £16 billion (€18.7) in military aid.

Taiwan machine tool orders see improvement

2026-08-24
04:03:23 UTC
13:03:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s machine tool industry is seeing a recovery in orders as market conditions improve, with several manufacturers expecting stronger operations in the third quarter, CTEE reported Sunday.
Machine tools are used to shape metal and other materials into precision parts for a wide range of products. They play a key role in manufacturing, as many industrial machines and products rely on components made using these tools, according to Gugu Fund.
Order visibility at many companies has extended to at least two to three months, while some manufacturers have bookings stretching into 2027. Component-related manufacturers, including Hiwin Technologies Corp., Chieftek Precision Co., and Tbi Motion Technology Co., have reported better order visibility and stronger revenue growth than other companies in the sector.
All three companies are benefiting from continued orders from the semiconductor and automation industries and are targeting double-digit revenue growth this year. Their backlogs extend into at least the fourth quarter.
Tongtai Machine & Tool Co. has benefited from strong orders for printed circuit board drilling machines. PCBs are the boards on which electronic components are mounted and interconnected, while drilling creates the holes needed to connect different circuit layers and install components, according to Stockfeel and Business Weekly.
The company has also made progress in semiconductor applications, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging. This has increased its total order backlog from NT$2.8 billion (US$88 million) at the start of the year to NT$3.2 billion.
Meanwhile, manufacturers of large-scale equipment are also seeing longer order visibility. Honor Seiki Co. and Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co. have delivery schedules of at least six months, with some orders extending beyond a year.
Honor Seiki said its order backlog stands at about NT$1.7 billion to NT$1.8 billion, with new bookings mainly coming from the aerospace and basic processing industries in China and India. The company expects operations to improve in the third quarter and for the full year.
Shieh Yih reported a loss in its core business in the second quarter, partly because some customers postponed shipments until the third quarter due to higher freight costs. It expects its core operations to return to profitability in the third quarter.
Taiwan Takisawa Technology Co. said its bookings extend through the end of the year. Its orders mainly come from manufacturers of AI server cooling plates and liquid-cooling systems, as well as Chinese producers of robot reducers and components for robotic hands.
Looking ahead, global supply chain shifts and emerging markets are reshaping Taiwan’s machine tool industry. Growth is expected to come from new markets and higher-value applications, according to the Industrial Economics & Knowledge Center.
Semiconductor equipment, aerospace, AI servers, drones, and humanoid robot components are emerging as potential growth areas. Manufacturers are also shifting toward integrated solutions that combine automation, AI, digital monitoring, and multiple machining processes.
Taiwanese machine tool makers including Anderson Industrial Corp., Awea Mechantronic Co., Goodway Machine Corp., Kao Fong Machinery Co., Tongtai, and Shieh Yih are diversifying their businesses to capture new growth opportunities.

Report urges Taiwan to lean more on city diplomacy to deepen Europe ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:03:17 UTC
13:03:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should pursue more ‘paradiplomacy’ to deepen its ties with Europe, according to a Central European Institute of Asian Studies (CEIAS) report.
The Slovakia-based think tank defines paradiplomacy as “the international activities of sub-state actors that may operate alongside, complement, or at times even diverge from central government foreign policy.”
Taiwan currently has 33 partnerships in Europe, including in Poland, Germany, France, Latvia, Czech Republic, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belgium, Denmark, Hungary, and Italy, CEIAS said. These local-level ties give Taiwan another way to connect internationally, especially since its formal diplomatic options are limited, it said.
Sister-city ties, in particular, allow Taiwan to collaborate with European cities on areas like innovation, green development, urban planning, and public health, CEIAS said. Regular exchanges and projects can also promote Taiwan as a more widely accepted, reliable partner, it added.
CEIAS said that for European partners, working with Taiwanese cities offers access to advanced industrial systems, opportunities to share knowledge, and avenues to attract investment. “These partnerships are, therefore, less about symbolic recognition than about practical cooperation in areas where Taiwanese expertise overlaps with local European policy and economic priorities,” the think tank said.
Additionally, as Europe works to reduce dependence on China and diversify its supply chains, local-level ties with Taiwan offer a flexible and inexpensive way to expand cooperation, CEIAS said.
The think tank said that Taiwan has not yet used paradiplomacy to its fullest potential in Europe due to practical constraints and political factors. Taiwanese cities have at least 34 partnerships in Japan, while in the US, there are more than 100, it said.
The Taiwanese diaspora in Europe “is smaller, more fragmented, and generally less connected to local political institutions,” the think tank said.
While Taiwan’s representative offices do help with outreach, efforts by overseas Taiwanese communities to influence local or regional governments are still limited, CEIAS said. However, Taiwanese businesses, industries, and research links are increasingly helping drive city-to-city and regional cooperation, making up for the limited influence of overseas diaspora lobbying, it said.
The think tank said that the Smart City Summit & Expo in Taipei and Kaohsiung is an effective tool to facilitate global cooperation. “The expo attracts the attention of municipal leaders beyond the formal partners of Taiwanese cities, often serving as the first point of exposure for foreign municipal leaders to Taiwan,” it said, adding that their participation often results in city-level projects or agreements.
CEAIS also suggested more Taiwanese cities join the Pact of Free Cities, which was established in 2019 to share best practices in city planning and local government management. So far, only Taipei and Taoyuan are members.
Overall, the think tank recommended that Taiwan strengthen existing partnerships and expand outreach in areas where national-level diplomacy is limited.
