Shein will debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September, the fast-fashion retailer said on Monday, in a long-awaited listing that would value the group at close to $27bn.
Founded in China and now headquartered in Singapore, the online retailer secured Beijing’s approval last month to make its initial public offering in Hong Kong.
Its valuation has dropped by about 70% from a near $100bn private market peak four years ago, as it aims to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) in its Hong Kong IPO launched on Monday.
Shein is selling 280m shares between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 per share, the filings showed, valuing it at close to $27bn at the top of that range. The company will announce the final price on 31 August and start trading on 1 September. With the funds raised from the market, Shein said it aims to finance its technological capabilities as well as boost its international presence.
Known for selling $5 dresses and $10 jeans to shoppers in about 160 countries, the marked decline in valuation comes after Shein faced questions over slowing growth, rising costs and changing market conditions.
Plans to list in New York and London had been held back in recent years by regulatory hurdles, according to media reports.
The firm moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.
But it still benefits from China’s unique combination of a huge, low-cost textile manufacturing sector and a highly sophisticated e-commerce logistics network.
By the end of last year, its European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users, making Shein one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside China’s AliExpress (193 million users) and Amazon (about 180 million users).
In November, the group made waves with its first-ever physical outlet, a dedicated space in the storied BHV department store in Paris.
Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence to keep the tense situation from getting out of hand.
Demonstrators slammed what they alleged were inhumane working conditions at Shein’s suppliers, the environmental costs of selling clothes not made to last, and unfair competition against brick-and-mortar retailers struggling to stay open.
The company says it holds its suppliers to strict compliance standards and does not tolerate forced labour.
Shein also drew criticism last year in France over the discovery of childlike sex dolls on its platform. The company pledged to cooperate with French authorities and announced it was banning all sex dolls on its platform.
In June, French authorities imposed two fines on Shein totalling more than 22m euros ($25.1m), citing problems with product traceability, environmental labelling and delivery times. At the time Shein said it would contest the “disproportionate” penalties, arguing that no consumer harm had been established.
Overall, Shein has paid over 210m euros in various French fines over the years, and Italy has also imposed fines alleging misleading environmental claims.

Photo of Disraeli among missing parliamentary works of art, FoI request finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:01:50 UTC
13:01:50 KST

A photograph of Benjamin Disraeli, an engraved portrait of William Wilberforce and a cartoon of Barbara Castle have all been misplaced by the UK parliamentary authorities, a freedom of information (FoI) request has revealed.
The Press Association has been given a list of more than 65 works of art that have been missing since 2024. They also include a photograph of Margaret Beckett, the UK’s first female foreign secretary and the first woman to lead Labour, and a satirical cartoon by Martin Rowson from the Conservative leadership battle of 1995.
A parliamentary spokesperson said it was a working collection, which meant that objects moved around frequently. None of the works had been permanently written off, they said.
The photograph of Disraeli, Queen Victoria’s favourite prime minister, was taken by John Jabez Edwin Mayall. Mayall was a prolific Victorian portrait photographer who captured the images of many of the era’s best known figures.
Art UK, which catalogues Britain’s publicly owned art, lists 212 Mayall works in UK collections including portraits of Charles Dickens, Karl Marx, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the soprano Anna Bishop, the scientist Michael Faraday and the explorer David Livingstone.
Mayall also made a fortune photographing Victoria and the wider royal family with his carte de visite portraits feeding the 19th-century “cartomania” collecting craze.
The misplaced Disraeli photograph is likely to be the same as one in other collections, including the Royal Collection, showing a tired, heavy-lidded Disraeli in his 60s.
The missing print of Wilberforce, the most celebrated campaigner against the slave trade, was made by the printmaker William Holl and his brother Francis.
The Rowson cartoon is from the 1995 Tory leadership campaign when John Major resigned as party leader, telling opponents to “put up or shut up”. It shows Major seeking to lance the literal “boil” of the contest, as his deputy Michael Heseltine and challenger-apparent Michael Portillo look on.
Rowson said the issue of cartoons going missing was not uncommon. He said a cartoon of the Foreign Office Christmas party in 2004, sent to the then junior minister Denis MacShane at his department, “never got beyond reception”.
Rowson said: “It’s a shame but it’s hardly the crown jewels – and the point about cartoon originals is that they’ve been published already: the artefact is probably the impression in the newspaper, as that’s its ticket to posterity.
“The original is the modern equivalent to one of Hogarth or Gillray’s copper plates used to create the – reproduced – satirical print. That’s why we belong more properly to journalism than art.”
He said the misplaced work was “small beer compared to one of my cartoons which was part of a touring exhibition of work by members of the British Cartoonists’ Association, all of which were destroyed by a Nato airstrike in the Serbian public library it had reached on its British Council sponsored tour in 1998.”
The missing satirical cartoon of Barbara Castle depicts her as Florence Nightingale.
The number of works involved is much fewer than the 224 reported missing after a similar FoI request in 2018. At the time it included portraits of William Pitt the Younger, and a wartime oil painting by William John MacLeod of the scene after parliament was bombed.
A parliamentary spokesperson said: “There is little evidence of works of art going permanently missing from the Parliamentary Art Collection. As a working collection, artworks are frequently moved between their recorded locations and are often subsequently found, meaning none of the items currently recorded as missing have been written off or are considered a financial loss.
“Parliament continues to reduce the number of artworks recorded as missing through ongoing audits.”
They said five of the “missing” works had been found this year. The art collection is one of four parliamentary heritage collections, which contain 26,000 objects including furniture and decorative arts.

‘I’ll probably feel emotional’: Kindertransport centenarian prepares to revisit site of family separation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:00:52 UTC
13:00:52 KST

Gabriele Keenaghan still remembers the day in April 1939 when she said goodbye to her grandmother at a Vienna railway station for a Kindertransport to Britain – tears were strictly forbidden.
“I was apprehensive and I was worried because Nazis in black uniforms were on the platform,” she said. “I was only 12 years old so I think they were frightening … terrifying.
“People had been told that there were to be no emotional scenes, they didn’t want any emotion shown by anyone. I tried not to cry. It was very difficult. My grandmother … she smiled.”
This week Keenaghan will mark her 100th year by returning to Vienna’s Westbahnhof, a place which changed, if not saved, her life, and there might be tears.
“I haven’t thought about how I’ll feel – I probably will feel emotional.”
Keenaghan, a retired head teacher, is speaking at her home in North Shields before what will be an epic trip to Vienna with several generations of her family.
The plan, hatched for her centenary, was nearly scuppered because Lufthansa cancelled routes from Newcastle. Fortunately, a good samaritan came to the rescue offering the use of a private jet, and the family admit they have been bowled over by the generosity.
Keenaghan is 99 but you would never guess.
She was awarded the British Empire medal for her services to Holocaust education, recounting what is a remarkable life story in the hope it might bring “kindness, tolerance and acceptance of diversity” in others.
Keenaghan, an only child, said she did not even know she was Jewish until after the Nazis invaded Austria.
Her mother, Hildegard, was a Catholic who died suddenly in 1935. Her father, Josef, was Jewish and manufactured heating stoves.
The young Gabriele was a boarder at a Catholic convent school run by nuns when the Nazis came and told pupils they would all be moving.
“The authorities came into the convent to tell us which schools we had to go to. We were all standing in the hall and names were called for this school, that school. At the end, I was the only one left standing. And I thought: ‘What’s happening to me?’”
She was told she would have to go to a Jewish school and a yellow star of David was sewn on to her coat. “I hadn’t realised that my father was a Jew. I didn’t know. I don’t think I even knew what being a Jew meant.”
It was bewildering and people treated her horribly, she said. “They called me a ‘dirty little Jew’ and I was a sensitive girl. It was upsetting.”
Keenaghan never saw her father again. He was deported to Łódź in Poland and was almost certainly murdered in an extermination camp.
Her grandmother, also called Gabriele, made arrangements for her granddaughter to be taken out of Austria on a Kindertransport, the scheme which brought about 10,000 Jewish children to Britain as refugees.
Alone and scared but also probably excited, she remembers, she left with 150 other children, taking the train to the Netherlands and then a boat to Harwich.
Keenaghan was a good student and quickly picked up the language. One of her first jobs was as a nanny to an affluent family in Woldingham, Surrey.
She has vivid memories of VE Day as all the village’s nannies – there were many – were given the day off and went to London to be part of the celebrations.
“It was really euphoric,” she said. “I’ve never experienced such excitement and joy. People were dancing in the street. They were climbing trees.
“We were in front of Buckingham Palace and out came the king and queen and the two princesses, Elizabeth and Margaret. Princess Elizabeth was the same age as me … she would also be 100 this year had she lived.”
Keenaghan went on to train as a teacher in the north-east and met her husband, Ken, and raised a family in Wallsend. She became a middle-school head teacher and clearly has fond memories of her career and the children and teachers who were part of it.
She has returned to Austria annually to see relatives, especially her grandmother, who died in 1974.
The one place she and her family have not been to is the station.
Keenaghan’s actual official birthday is in November, when Vienna would be far too cold. “I’m going to be like Queen Elizabeth. I’m going to have two birthdays,” she said.
There will be family members on the plane, including Keenaghan’s two daughters, Pat and Christine. Others will travel separately.
Both daughters have vague memories of their great-grandmother, although they were very young.
“The story goes that I used to call her Noddy Grandmother because I didn’t realise she couldn’t speak English,” said Christine. “I would speak to her all of the time and she nodded a lot.”
Keenaghan has spoken many times to children about her experiences. “I hope they have learned something from it,” she said. “But do we ever learn? Look at the world, look at the state it is in now.”

====================================================================================================

Scrapping of Berlin swimming day for Black children becomes latest in long list of race-linked pool rows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:00:52 UTC
13:00:52 KST

It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre.
But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats.
Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some.
“Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”.
It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions.
Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check.
The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children.
Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said.
Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party.
In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.”
In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds.
The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children.
The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all.
In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities.
“People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.”
The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair.
Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.”
As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues.
“It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.”

Marine Le Pen's career has been resurrected – and she is a bigger threat than ever | Mujtaba Rahman
Unknown

04:00:52 UTC
13:00:52 KST

France loves a battle-scarred survivor. Charles de Gaulle, François Mitterrand and Jacques Chirac clawed their way back from political failure to become presidents of the republic. There is a significant chance that Marine Le Pen will be next.
Now that the Paris appeal court has unshackled her from an electoral ban for fraud, the far-right veteran has double appeal in the race for the French presidency next year. She will run, as always, as an outsider and a scourge of the political elites – despite continuously holding electoral office since 1998. She can also now pose as a “miraculous survivor”, a “mother courage” and “a battling granny”, as senior French political figures, including former ministers, described her to me during recent conversations in Paris.
Le Pen will be a much more formidable candidate than her young understudy Jordan Bardella might have been. The other candidates were wary of Bardella, but they did not fear him. They do fear a resurrected Le Pen.
Her party, the National Rally (RN), has a new campaign slogan: “Renaissance”. The rebirth of Le Pen’s political career, the party says, foretells the rebirth of France.
One might almost think Le Pen had been acquitted of fraud on 7 July. She was not. The judges essentially ruled that voters, not the courts, should decide who is president. They reduced Le Pen’s five-year ban from electoral politics, imposed by the Paris criminal court last year, to time already served.
She is now a twice-convicted embezzler of more than €4m in EU funds. If her final appeal to France’s highest court is heard rapidly and rejected, she might have to campaign next spring wearing an electronic tag on her ankle.
And yet. Two opinion polls since her reprieve suggest that she could defeat all imaginable opponents in the two-candidate second round next year.
Previous polls were almost as good for Bardella, but there were reasons to believe that he would not stay the course. The two-week-long second-round campaign traditionally stress-tests the capacity of the candidates not just to govern France but to represent it. Voters will wonder: do they have a stature présidentielle? Bardella will be 31 in September. He has been an RN party apparatchik since he dropped out of college at the age of 19. Would voters have been able to imagine this talented but glib young man toe-to-toe with a Vladimir Putin or a Donald Trump?
That question – presidential weight – is especially important for older voters. Of the 50 million registered French voters, 28% are over 65. Unlike younger people, they turn out in huge numbers.
A recent Ifop poll showed Le Pen beating the former prime minister Édouard Philippe, the strongest of the many candidates looking to carry Emmanuel Macron’s centrist torch, by 54% to 46% in the second round. She had almost exactly the same lead among the over-65s. It is the first time any poll in any national election put the RN ahead with the “grey vote”.
Bardella was also popular with older voters but his appeal to young and old was starting to fade. He comes from a working-class, Italian migrant family but had begun to show a Nicolas Sarkozy-like attraction to the high life, including, reportedly, a romance with an heiress from Italy’s remnant nobility.
Le Pen was born into a wealthy family and political business but cultivates an image as a gruff-voiced people’s champion, a single grandmother living with her best friend, a breeder of cats and, above all, a survivor.
There is, however, another issue that is crucial for older voters: economic stability. Le Pen’s feeble TV debate performances on the economy in 2017 and 2022 helped Macron to defeat her.
The RN’s economic policies remain an incoherent jumble of high social spending and low taxes, free markets and state interference. Bardella tried to shift the party towards a more traditional rightwing, low-tax policy and a more reformist approach to the EU, taking inspiration from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni.
But Le Pen’s return means a return to “Marinomics” and a policy of wrecking the EU from the inside. With France €3.5tn in debt and permanently teetering on the brink of fiscal crisis, the prospect of a far-right government may disturb older and better-off voters.
Le Pen will have an obvious riposte. Macron bamboozled you twice all with his clever people’s talk, she will say. Look where that got you: another €1tn in debt. Time to give a down-to-earth woman a chance. I could hardly do worse.
But she could. Much, much worse.
A President Le Pen or a President Bardella would take France and the EU into dangerous new territory. Bardella, at least, appeared aware of the difficulty of being so outlandishly anti-EU, and of trying to govern with slogans. Le Pen does not.
A Le Pen presidency from next May is not a certainty. But it is, for the first time in seven decades of the family’s involvement in politics, a strong possibility. The comfort blanket for mainstream parties of right, left and centre – the implausibility of a 31-year-old slightly more pragmatic President Bardella – has been snatched away.

  Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

Three-quarters of secondary schools in England are breaking the rules on food offered to pupils by serving chips, burgers and hash browns too often – and sweets and crisps at breakfast time, according to a report.
“Shocking” breaches of school food standards have been exposed on Monday, in a new analysis of the food provided at almost 400 state secondaries undertaken by Bite Back, a food charity set up by the chef Jamie Oliver.
D’Arcy Williams, Bite Back’s chief executive, said the picture of schools’ widespread noncompliance with the government-set standards that emerged from its analysis was alarming.
Three out of four menus it analysed at 391 state secondary schools in England contained at least one breach of the standards. Most involved schools offering unhealthy foods more often than is allowed.
At 206 schools (53%), products high in fat, sugar or salt that are meant to be banned altogether – such as crisps, Oreos, Mini Cheddars, chocolate bars and pastries – were being offered to pupils to buy as snacks, including at breakfast time and at lunchtime. Schools are allowed to sell only nuts, seeds, plain vegetables and plain fruit as snacks.
The research also found that:
There were 224 schools (57%) providing meat products such as burgers, nuggets, sausages and goujons more often than the twice a week permitted by the standards.
Hash browns, which as a fried starchy food should be a menu option only twice a week, were being offered more often than that at 144 schools (37%).
There were 123 schools (31%) using chocolate in solid form, such as chocolate chips or chocolate coating, as an ingredient in dessert or bakes, despite it being banned.
“These findings are very alarming and expose a system that is fundamentally failing our children,” said Williams.
“It is shocking to find crisps and chocolate being pushed at breakfast time or processed meats like sausage rolls and bacon baps being served far more frequently than the rules allow.
“Young people have been telling us for years that their school food is ‘beige, bland and boring’ and now we have more evidence that they are being surrounded by unhealthy food throughout the school day.
“Schools should be a sanctuary for health and learning, yet the current postcode lottery of food quality is undermining that mission.”
But in other findings that parents may find reassuring, only eight schools (2%) were flouting the ban on selling confectionery such as KitKats, Haribo sweets and Maltesers as standalone items. And even fewer – just three schools (1%) – were selling banned sugary drinks such as Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Fanta and Sprite.
Campaigners for healthier food voiced concern at the findings. Katharine Jenner, the executive director of the Obesity Health Alliance, said: “Schools should be one of the places where we can be confident children are being given nutritious food. Yet this research suggests too many are still being routinely exposed to processed meat, fried foods, pastries and confectionery beyond what the standards allow.
“Children are already growing up surrounded by unhealthy food across the wider food system, from what is marketed to them to what is promoted in shops. If we can’t even get the food environment right in schools, where children spend such a large part of their lives, then we have a serious problem.”
Ministers are preparing to unveil an overhaul of the school food standards, which child health and anti-obesity organisations have been seeking for years.
At the start of the new academic year in England next month, there will be a major expansion of access to free school meals instigated by the Labour government. From now on, all pupils from a household where someone is receiving universal credit will qualify in England.
The Department for Education acknowledged that schools did flout the standards. A spokesperson said: “We want every child to be healthy, happy and ready to learn, and nutritious food plays a vital role in helping them achieve that.
“That’s why we are delivering the most ambitious overhaul of school food in a generation, making sure children have access to healthy, balanced meals, get more of their five a day and are protected from the harms of eating too much ultra-processed food.
“We know not every school is following these standards, which is exactly why we will introduce a strengthened enforcement regime, alongside requiring every school to publish their food policy and menus online to improve transparency for parents.”

Chinese scientists have developed a new tabletop X-ray ghost imaging method that allows them to capture real-time “see-through” video of fast-moving objects.
The team’s system could be used to capture dynamic objects such as rotating aircraft engines or biological movements like a beating heart.
Importantly, this could all be accomplished with a lower radiation dose and simpler set-up than traditional X-ray methods.
“In contrast to other available X-ray imaging techniques for moving objects, our method can be implemented with a conventional tabletop X-ray source,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Communications Physics on August 15.
“The set-up is simple, relatively inexpensive and easy to operate.”
The researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shanghai Jiao Tong University said their method had “great potential” for medical imaging as well as non-destructive imaging of moving mechanical components.

The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
At the peak of the Hormuz crisis, Kapa Research asked 300+ shipping leaders about the future. They see influence shifting East, turmoil as beneficial and an AI race ahead.
This past May and June, while the Strait of Hormuz crisis was at its peak and a fifth of the world’s traded oil was looking for a way around the blockage, researchers from Kapa Research were interviewing the businesses that move the cargo. We spoke with 314 shipowners and C-suite executives from the world’s leading shipping groups and asked them how they see the years ahead.  The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94 percent express optimism about their company’s prospects, and 70 percent believe global shipping is in better shape today than it was five years ago.
The Global Shipping Outlook 2026 is Kapa Research’s quantitative study of the industry’s leadership, with respondents across every major shipping region, from Europe’s main maritime centers to the United States and Asia. Because fieldwork ran at the height of the crisis, the survey is a rare real-time record of how shipping leaders think under pressure.
Geopolitical crises in Ukraine, the Red Sea and the Middle East are named the most serious problems for shipping today by 76 percent of respondents, the top concern in every region we surveyed. Yet when we asked what the Hormuz crisis means for their own company, 40 percent said it creates new opportunities and only 23 percent see significant obstacles.  Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business. The logic is pragmatic. Conflict pushes ships onto longer routes, longer routes absorb vessel supply and freight rates rise while demand for goods persists. Shipping moves against the cycle. When instability rises, so do revenues.
The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94 percent express optimism about their company’s prospects.
The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76 percent expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, which covers the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and Covid-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: “Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.”
We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54 percent to 46 percent. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such candor is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it.
Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76 percent of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17 percent choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69 percent, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62 percent and a near-universal 96 percent call its role important for strengthening global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17 percent rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers.
The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping, the president of China, stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of +44, ahead of Narendra Modi, the prime minister of India, at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the center of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment.
Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business.
The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimization are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and Internet of Things sensors, is scaling, and a third, artificial intelligence (AI) analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70 percent still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). AI is the divide to watch: 65 percent of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7 percent use it extensively and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight tonnes, 79 percent work with AI, against 50 percent in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.”
No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37 percent, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change: 72 percent of companies intend to employ more women at sea and 74 percent now call ESG (environment, social, governance) performance important to their overall business strategy.
Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.
One response from the interviews
Shipping carries about four-fifths of world trade, so the way its leaders think matters far beyond the industry. What they told us at the peak of a crisis is that volatility is now structural, that the center of maritime gravity is shifting East, and that they plan to keep moving through whatever comes. Governments, corporations and international organizations facing the same instability have lessons to draw from their resilience.

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
Syria’s foreign minister meets with an Israeli delegation led by the chief of the Mossad to de-escalate tensions after an Israeli strike near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has met with Israeli intelligence officials in Jordan, according to Syrian state media, as the two sides work to de-escalate tensions following an Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border.
Syria’s Sana news agency, citing a diplomatic source, said the talks were mediated by the United States and involved a “high-level Israeli delegation”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

The AFP news agency reported that al-Shaibani met the head of Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman.
According to Sana, the discussions “focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations” as well as “reviving negotiations for a lasting security agreement between the two sides”.
They also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Turkiye and to prevent their rivalry from spilling onto Syrian territory, Sana reported.
The US has sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa for more than a year. Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and sent troops into a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
It also bombed the Abu Duhur airbase in northwestern Idlib on Thursday, claiming the attack was to prevent Turkish troops from deploying at the base, a claim Syria and Turkiye have denied.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also traded barbs since the incident, with tensions high between the two leaders.
According to Sana, the Syrian side stressed during Sunday’s talks “that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests”. The Syrian side rejected “any arrangements or mechanisms that would restrict these sovereign rights,” it said.
Syria’s immediate priorities in the talks remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before al-Assad’s overthrow and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement, Sana reported.
The Syrian officials also reaffirmed Damascus’s sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, it added.
Israel’s ‘red lines’
Israeli media reported that the talks were “positive” and said Israeli officials had adopted a number of red lines going into talks.
These include preventing Turkish military activity in Syria, keeping the Syrian side of the Golan Heights demilitarised, “ensuring the security” of Syria’s Druze community and preventing the Syrian army from acquiring certain strategic weapons systems.
They also conditioned any withdrawal from Syrian territories occupied by Israel on “diplomatic achievements”.
During previous rounds of US-mediated talks, Syria and Israel had agreed on a joint mechanism to share intelligence and defuse tensions. But the negotiations froze at the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, without a date set for resumption.
In an interview published ahead of the meeting, al-Shaibani told Reuters news agency that Damascus did not trust Israel, but that the door remained open for diplomacy. He said Syria had cut off contact entirely after the Israeli attack on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Al-Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only UN forces would be present.
Hassan Mneimneh, a political analyst and researcher at the Middle East Institute, told Al Jazeera that the current round of talks was unlikely to de-escalate tensions given Israel’s track record.
“It’s quite the opposite, meaning now that Syria has indicated its desire to have the situation de-escalate, Israel is likely to bring in more demands and have the Americans basically negotiate these new demands with Syria, against any kind of expansion of Turkish presence in the north and beyond the north,” he said.
Mneimneh added that Syria was “afraid that the country will become a battlefield” between Israel and Turkiye and was concerned about Israel’s territorial grab in the country, stretching “all the way to Hermon, to Jabal al-Sheikh in its totality almost, and all the way to three southern provinces”.
So, from the Syrian perspective, Mneimneh added, the talks with Israel seem to be aimed at avoiding “the disintegration of Syrian authority” as well as ensuring any conflict between Israel and Turkiye does not prevent Syria from “forming, establishing, consolidating polity after the fall of” al-Assad.

Fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz at the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as Iranian and US blockades restrict traffic through the chokepoint for energy shipments.

That compared with Friday's figure of 16 transits, with two empty very large crude carriers (VLCCs) entering the Gulf with the tracking devices switched off, one heading to Iraq and the other to Bahrain, the data showed.
A VLCC carrying 2 million barrels of Emirati crude exited the strait on Thursday.
Eight very large gas carriers transited the strait over the past three days, the data showed, six of them entering empty while the others carried liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) loaded from Iran and exited the Gulf.
Traffic 'well below normal levels'
Overall traffic volumes remained suppressed in the week to August 21, as vessels aborted transit plans or switched routes through the strait's north after attacks, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said in a report.
A total of 89 vessels exited the strait while 103 entered over the seven-day period, the report, based on Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, showed.
"Traffic remains well below normal levels, with AIS-detected transits approximately 90% below pre-conflict baselines and declining since the June 24 to June 26 peak," it added.
Tanker traffic, at 45% of the total, continued to dominate movement through the strait, the agency said. Of these, 56% were tankers that carry crude oil, oil products or chemicals while LPG carriers accounted for a further 24%.
Since July 6, the UKMTO has reported 23 incidents of projectile strikes, leading to bridge, engine-room, and structural damage across vessels in the strait and its vicinity.
A total of 24 commodity vessels sailed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Sunday, down from Saturday's figure of 32, which was an increase from 22 on Friday, Kpler data showed.
Two VLCCs entered the Red Sea on Saturday with one carrying Iraqi Basrah crude and the other empty, it showed.

Syria to dismantle Assad regime's chemical weapons legacy 13 years after deadly attack - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:55:53 UTC
12:55:53 KST

Thirteen years after the chemical weapons gas attack on Ghouta, Syria's government says it is entering a new phase in dismantling the bitter legacy of the Assad regime’s chemical weapons program.
Statements issued over the past week by Syrian officials, together with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), reflect a shift toward cooperation with international investigators and renewed efforts to hold those responsible accountable. The international community supports Syria in this endeavor.
The developments come as Syria continues its broader effort to rebuild relations with Western countries following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They also represent one of the clearest examples of the new authorities in Damascus seeking to distinguish themselves from the previous government that ruled Syria for more than five decades.
According to SANA, Syria’s state media, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani announced that Syria is beginning "a new phase" in dealing with the country's chemical weapons legacy.
"Tomorrow, the Syrian Arab Republic begins a new phase in addressing the burden of these weapons, as we have initiated the necessary technical and operational measures to eliminate them in cooperation with international partners," Shaibani wrote.
Ghouta attack symbolic of the Syrian Civil War
He added that the work would proceed along with efforts to identify those responsible for the attacks. This will mean efforts to prosecute the perpetrators, and hold them accountable. Why does this matter? The announcement coincided with the anniversary of one of the worst, most horrid, days of the Syrian civil war.
On August 21, 2013, rockets carrying a chemical sarin nerve agent struck areas of Eastern and Western Ghouta outside Damascus. This was an area held by the Syrian rebels. More than 1,400 civilians were killed, according to reports. Thousands more suffered poisoning and other affects.
The Ghouta attack became a key moment in the Syrian conflict. Images of families dying in their homes, children gasping for air, and overwhelmed hospitals circulated around the world. The attack showed the regime would use chemical weapons. It also gave the world a chance to stop the regime. However, the US, UK, and others held back from airstrikes. Hundreds of thousands more people would be killed in the war.
The Assad regime denied responsibility, feeding conspiracy theories.
The Assad family's rule, at the time, stretched back more than half a century. Hafez al-Assad seized power in 1970 and built an authoritarian state dominated by the Baath Party and the security services. After his death in 2000, his son Bashar inherited the presidency, promising reform but instead preserving much of the existing political system.
When peaceful protests erupted in 2011 as part of the Arab Spring, the regime responded by attacking the civilians. It received support from Iran, Hezbollah and Russia.
As the conflict intensified, allegations of chemical weapons use became increasingly frequent.
According to a statement published by SANA, more than 200 chemical weapons attacks occurred between late 2012 and the fall of the Assad regime, resulting in the deaths of more than 1,500 people.
International investigations by the OPCW and the United Nations attributed attacks to the Assad government, including the sarin attack on Khan Shaykhun in 2017 and chlorine attacks in other parts of Syria. The United States and Britain eventually responded with missile strikes targeting facilities linked to Syria's chemical weapons program.
OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior said this week that recent discoveries of previously undeclared chemical munitions demonstrate both the scale of the remaining work and the importance of continued cooperation. According to SANA, Dallafior said discussions with Syria's ambassador to the OPCW had focused on the next steps, adding that recent progress showed "what can be achieved through serious cooperation."
She also emphasized that the OPCW remains committed to ensuring that chemical weapons never again inflict such suffering. The new Syrian government appears eager to demonstrate that cooperation.
Accountability in chemical attacks could change region's outlook
SANA reported that Syria has restored full cooperation with the OPCW following the fall of the Assad government and is now pursuing technical measures to eliminate the remaining elements of the former chemical weapons program.
Damascus says accountability will remain a central priority. Interior Minister Anas Khattab stated that authorities have already arrested several individuals connected to the chemical attacks while continuing efforts to locate additional suspects. "No criminal will escape punishment, regardless of how much time passes," Khattab said, according to SANA.
The emphasis on accountability extends beyond Syria. Syria is a symbol of how a country can do the right thing. France has become one of Damascus's principal partners in documenting crimes committed during the civil war. The joint Syrian-French statement commemorating the Ghouta anniversary reaffirmed both countries' commitment to combatting chemical weapons' use, the reports said.
The statement also described French President Emmanuel Macron's July 2026 visit to Syria as opening "a new phase" in bilateral relations after years of relations being broken due to the Assad regime.
For Syria's new leadership, confronting the chemical weapons legacy serves several purposes. It helps rebuild international credibility, for one.
Justice matters because chemical weapons are not simply another type of weapon. Since World War I, the international community has regarded them as uniquely bad because they deliberately inflict indiscriminate suffering on civilians. acceptable under any circumstances.
Holding those responsible accountable is therefore about more than Syria's past. It reinforces an international norm that has existed for decades. For Syria, accountability offers victims and survivors the possibility of justice after years of impunity.
For the region it is a test of whether one of the world's norms, the prohibition on chemical weapons, can ultimately be enforced. In a changing world order, this matters.

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:53:01 UTC
12:53:01 KST

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs
HONG KONG (AP) — Computer programmer Fei Zhaojun’s boss asked him if artificial intelligence could soon replace humans in coding jobs. Two weeks later, he was laid off from his job in Beijing, together with about 160 of his colleagues.
It’s an increasingly common scenario as artificial intelligence, supported by government policies, reshapes China’s massive job market. Some economists believe that might eventually undermine the overall strength of the world’s second largest economy.
Rapid adoption of AI in many fields, from computer programmers to script writing and physical tasks, is pushing people out of their jobs or leaving them afraid that it might. China is at the vanguard of AI adoption as government policies encourage people and businesses to use AI applications and robotics in all aspects of life, so people like Fei are figuring out how to adapt.
“There appears to be far less anti-AI sentiment in China (than elsewhere). Most people seem either positive, neutral, or mildly interested in AI,” said Shujing He, a Beijing-based senior analyst at advisory and research firm Plenum.
“Individuals who worry about being replaced, as well as those who have already left traditional workplaces, are often eager to experiment with AI-enabled businesses and independent ventures,” she said. “The level of interest is striking.”
Until recently, Fei had doubted AI could do programming work perfectly, even though his bosses thought it was close enough.
“Mid-level coders’ job are essentially replaceable in most of the cases,” said Fei, 40. “Even if it is a disaster that leads to replacing all humans, at this stage, you just have to use it as everyone else is using it.”
Now he’s making vlog-style short videos during a career break while figuring out what he wants to do next. He’s not making a living off of his videos, which are about ordinary people’s lives, but hopes that they might help others.
If you can’t beat them, join them
Du Qinchun, a part-time translator, has been helping to train an AI model to do translations. That’s brought him more work, at least temporarily.
“But it’s true that the pay in the industry has been cut by more than half compared to what it was years ago,” said Du, who is based in southwestern China’s Chengdu city.
The trend is so evident that popular college programs in foreign languages have increasingly fallen out of favor as AI-powered translation tools have become more widespread.
The share of Chinese industrial enterprises saying they use AI models and “agents” jumped to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024, according to the market intelligence firm IDC.
“China’s vibrant open-source model ecosystem fosters greater AI application innovation in industrial settings, gradually closing the gap between foundational model capabilities and real-world enterprise value creation,” said Yanze Du, an IDC senior research manager in Beijing.
Humanoid robots can now, for example, sort parcels in postal centers, although still on a small-scale basis, and are pushing the boundaries in performing more human tasks such as directing traffic and making coffee. Food delivery robots are also gaining ground across the country, potentially threatening the livelihoods of millions of Chinese food delivery workers.
Generative AI increasingly is used for creation, production and distribution in China’s short drama industry. The number of live-action short and vertical video series designed for mobile phones fell about 75% in the first quarter of this year from a year earlier, according to Chinese media reports.
“Tasks that once required specialized training can now be performed by almost anyone with access to AI tools. This is particularly evident in software development and multimedia creation,” said Plenum’s He. “As a result, workers whose roles are narrowly concentrated in these areas may face greater displacement risk.”
A report from International Labor Organization, meanwhile, found that women face higher risks of losing employment due to use of AI than men, as they tend to work in areas more suitable for automation, such as assembling electronics, and remain underrepresented in science and technology.
AI has mixed effects on the slowing economy
Under China’s “AI Plus” initiative and its five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing to infuse AI across many industries, aiming to gain an edge in China’s technology rivalry with the U.S.
“What is specific to China is that the government is really into diffusing AI across the economy, so AI may get into different domains more quickly comparing to other countries,” said Zilan Qian, a research associate at Oxford China Policy Lab.
China’s economic growth has already been slowing. Consumer spending has lagged partly due to people becoming reluctant to spend because they’re worried about losing their jobs. It’s added to problems stemming from a prolonged downturn in the housing market that has undermined household wealth.
China’s tech industries may be innovative with high productivity, but they may not generate many new jobs, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.
“AI is likely to lift productivity across the board but could have a severe disruptive effect on employment, worsening the employment growth problem and resulting in a detrimental effect on social stability,” he said.
Similar to their U.S. rivals, Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. The outlook for the broader jobs market remains uncertain: China’s overall urban unemployment rate hovers around 5%, but unemployment for people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, is roughly triple that.
That said, in the longer run, some experts say unemployment rates could fall, since China’s population of 1.4 billion is rapidly aging and shrinking.
By 2050, China is projected to have fewer than two working-age adults to support each retiree, compared with more than 2.5 in the U.S., said Xuenan Cao, a professor at San Francisco Bay University whose focus includes technology and society.
“Automation could partially offset a shrinking workforce rather than being purely a threat to it,” Cao said.
Some embrace AI to find new ways to make a living
Wang Zhicheng, 32, often used AI for brainstorming and fact-checking in his previous job as a scriptwriter for a company that produces 3D animated educational videos and interactive exercises for children.
After its parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, he chose to resign and work independently, making illustrated children’s books.
While AI sometimes saved time the scripts it generated, they often felt strange, Wang said. Episodes tended to be repetitive and formulaic and the level of detail devoted to knowledge varied widely.
“You can treat AI as a tool just like (Microsoft) Word,” said Wang, who has started his own studio making picture books and other creative works. “Humans are still the decision makers on which one to pick or pursue among all that AI generates.”
High school chemistry teacher Yang Zheng said he doesn’t consider AI as a threat to his job even though students use AI for help with their homework.
“Teachers cannot be there all the time,” he said. “It is a good thing for students as it generates in real-time so that students can ask follow-up questions,” said Yang, 29. “It often gets things wrong, but it improves over time.”
____
Fu Ting reported from Washington. AP video producer Wu Jia in Beijing contributed to this story.

New coalition of states could form around Trans-Arctic Corridor — expert

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. A new coalition of states could form around the development of the Trans-Arctic transport corridor, which is already turning into not only an economic but also a geopolitical project, Irina Strelnikova, director of the Center for Interdisciplinary Arctic Studies at the Higher School of Economics, told TASS.
"The scenario is entirely realistic. There are certain caveats to consider, but I would say that it is already taking shape as a geopolitical project, and the economic component, indeed, is gaining momentum alongside the geopolitical one," she said when asked about the potential formation of a new coalition of states centered on the Trans-Arctic transport corridor.
China, India, and the United Arab Emirates could become potential participants in this alliance, Strelnikova said, adding that Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan are also showing interest in expanding transport chains and accessing new markets.
Forming a stable coalition requires an alignment of the states’ economic interests, the expert noted. The project must offer tangible benefits to participants, including access to resources, new markets, and the development of logistics capabilities.
Strelnikova cited political will and the readiness of states to reach agreements on contentious issues as another condition. In particular, she believes potential coalition members need to set aside their differences regarding the legal status of the Northern Sea Route.
The expert also mentioned geopolitical competition, US sanctions pressure, and the risk of fragmented cooperation, whereby instead of a unified coalition, separate partnerships between Russia and China, India, and the UAE would develop, as potential obstacles.

CANBERRA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- South Australian authorities on Monday reported a second suspected case of H5N1 bird flu in a seal, one day after the state reported Australia's first case in a mammal.
South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said on Monday that the long-nosed fur seal was found at the Pages Conservation Park, a protected area consisting of the North Page and South Page islands located about 18 km off the state's south coast.
The department said that samples have been sent to the Australian Center for Disease Preparedness for confirmatory testing.
It comes after the federal government on Sunday announced that Australia's first confirmed case of the highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza strain in a mammal had been confirmed in a long-nosed fur seal found dead in mainland South Australia on Wednesday.
South Australian Minister for Climate, Environment and Water Emily Bourke said that the two cases were incredibly concerning. The state government on Thursday said that over 1,000 birds had been found dead in suspected H5N1 mass mortality events on three islands, including North Page and South Page.
"We've seen devastation in seals around the world when it comes to bird flu," Bourke told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) radio on Monday.
According to the National Parks and Wildlife Service, the Page islands are home to one of three large colonies of endangered Australian sea lions in South Australia. The Invasive Species Council has warned that the H5N1 outbreak could be an extinction-level event for the species.
Bourke said that the strain circulating in South Australia potentially arrived in the state from Heard Island, a remote sub-Antarctic Australian territory.
The Australian Antarctic Program said in June that around 13,000 of the estimated 17,000 elephant seal pups on Heard Island had died from H5N1 avian influenza.
Federal Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt told ABC television on Monday that the cases in seals were not unexpected and authorities expect to see more mass mortality events. ■

Feature: On the Gobi, western China's oil city Karamay serves up tennis dreams
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:36 CST
12:43:36 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Karamay's name, derived from the Uygur language, means "black oil," reflecting the resource that shaped the city's development.
Rising from a remote stretch of the vast Gobi Desert, the city grew around its oil fields and developed into a modern industrial hub.
Beneath the vast skies of this once-isolated city, another passion has taken root. Over the decades, tennis has grown from a pastime for a small circle of enthusiasts into an established part of local sporting culture, turning Karamay into an unlikely center for the sport in inland China.
SEED TAKES ROOT
Karamay, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is one of modern China's most important energy bases. With a population of fewer than 500,000, the city is home to Xinjiang Oilfield, which has maintained annual crude oil production of more than 10 million tonnes for 24 consecutive years.
Like many of his peers, Alipjan Awut grew up in a family connected to the oil industry.
Inspired by the teamwork and determination of the oil workers around him, he found joy in pursuing a common goal on the football pitch. As a midfielder, he led attacks and captained his primary school team.
"Football is a team sport. It tests cooperation and brings different people together," said the 36-year-old. "But nothing can surpass tennis in my heart."
As oil workers from across China settled in the Gobi city, they brought with them their lifestyles and hobbies. Since the 1980s, tennis has gradually taken root in Karamay, growing from a pastime among a small group of enthusiasts into a sport embraced by the wider community.
At 12, Alipjan got his first taste of tennis when a PE teacher spotted his athletic ability and invited him to pick up a racket for Karamay's first citywide school tennis competition.
"At that time, we didn't even have our own rackets. The school provided them. I just thought it was fun," Alipjan recalled.
After just over a month of training, he finished fifth in the city competition, turning his initial curiosity into a lifelong passion.
With few professional coaches available, Alipjan found his own ways to improve. Whenever a tennis tournament was broadcast on television, he would sit in front of the screen, studying every detail of the players' movements, footwork and technique.
The sport also took him beyond his hometown. During school holidays, coaches brought young players from Karamay to eastern Chinese cities with stronger tennis programs, where the team often drew curious looks.
"They were often surprised to see players from Xinjiang on the tennis court," Alipjan said. "We knew there was a gap, but we wanted to change that perception."
GROWING UNDER SUN
After graduating from university, Alipjan returned to his hometown and became a tennis coach at an amateur sports school.
As part of efforts to make tennis more accessible, Karamay expanded its facilities. A sport once constrained by a lack of courts now has nearly 40 venues across parks, communities and schools, some capable of hosting national competitions.
Alipjan has become busier than ever. More than 100 young players now train at his school, many of whom discovered tennis through short tennis programs offered at local schools.
"Those with potential will be selected into our elite training group, and they do not need to pay any fees," he said.
Among the young players he coaches, one stands out: Alfudin Hasimjan, his younger cousin. Before turning seven, Alfudin had never seriously played any sport, but he quickly fell in love with tennis.
"I don't know why, but I feel like I have some talent for tennis," the youngster said with a smile.
At 14, Alfudin is already over 1.8 meters tall and has won titles in his age group in Xinjiang. He spends almost every summer day on the court, where the intense Gobi sun has left him deeply tanned, but his passion remains undiminished.
"It is a sport under the sun," Alipjan said. "Whether they play for fun or dream of going further, we hope children can stay active. That is what we want to achieve."
As more young players picked up rackets, tennis became increasingly embedded in Karamay's sporting identity. The city has since been recognized by Chinese tennis media as one of the places with the greatest potential for the sport's growth.
BEYOND THE GOBI
At the ongoing 15th Xinjiang Games, nine regions sent under-18 players across two age groups, marking a record turnout. Karamay remains a strong force, but its dominance is facing growing challenges.
Once numbering fewer than 50 players, Xinjiang's youth tennis community has now grown to about 500, with specialized clubs emerging to provide greater support for the next generation.
"Urumqi, the regional capital, is developing quickly, with more courts, coaches and families embracing tennis," Alipjan said. "I'm not worried. The more people play, the stronger Xinjiang tennis will become."
Still, Alipjan knows Karamay has a long way to go to reach the level of the world's leading tennis regions. For him, that gap has always been motivation to improve.
In 2024, Alipjan became a senior coach certified by the Chinese Tennis Association. For him, building a tennis ecosystem in Karamay remains a long-term endeavor.
"Honestly, it is a long process," he said. "But one day, I hope players from my team can also step out of Xinjiang and represent this region on a bigger stage." ■

Pro-Palestinian protesters sentenced over blocking Golden Gate Bridge traffic in 2024

Pro-Palestinian protesters sentenced over blocking Golden Gate Bridge traffic in 2024
WASHINGTON – Seven protesters who blocked traffic on the Golden Gate Bridge in a 2024 pro-Palestinian protest against Israel’s assault on Gaza have been sentenced to 30 days, with credit for time already served.
They were convicted in July of misdemeanour charges by a San Francisco jury that remained deadlocked on the more serious charge of felony conspiracy.
Defence attorneys said demonstrators acted out of a moral responsibility to oppose the devastation from Israeli strikes on Gaza and Washington’s support for its ally.
San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said the protest caused a safety risk for those stuck in traffic, and there should be consequences when laws are broken.
“Throughout history, civil disobedience has mostly involved accepting legal consequences,” Superior Court Judge Teresa Caffese was quoted as saying by KQED.
“In that spirit, those who blocked the bridge and disrupted the lives of hundreds of commuters should be treated respectfully, but should also be prepared to accept the consequences of their actions.”
The sentences included half the time in county jail, while the remaining days can be served at a work release programme operated by the San Francisco Sheriff’s Office. There will be four days’ credit for previous time already served. The sentencing also included six months of probation, and fines and restitution of more than US$1,000 (S$1,270).
The defendants will remain free while the case is appealed, SFGate reported.
Defence attorneys argued that protesters resorted to blocking the bridge after writing letters and appealing to congressional representatives produced no result.
The jury convicted the seven protesters on misdemeanour counts, including false imprisonment, obstruction of thoroughfare, unlawful assembly and, in one defendant’s case, refusal to disperse.
The jury did not reach a verdict on the most serious charge of felony conspiracy, an agreement between two or more people to commit a crime coupled with an overt act, which could have carried a sentence of up to 15 years. Prosecutors said they will not retry the charges. REUTERS

KUWAIT CITY, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 150 people gathered Sunday evening at the China Cultural Center in Kuwait for the Chinese & Kuwaiti Tea Art and Treats Tasting event, where they savored teas and sweets and learned about tea-making traditions in both countries.
Jointly organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait and Kuwait's National Council for Culture, Arts and Letters (NCCAL), the event was part of Kuwait's 18th Summer Cultural Festival. It aimed to introduce Chinese and Kuwaiti tea traditions and promote cultural and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
Attendees sampled Chinese green, black, white and oolong teas, accompanied by Chinese sweets. A separate tasting area featured Kuwaiti and Arab beverages, including karak tea, loomi tea and Moroccan mint tea, along with local and Arab sweets.
In his speech, Chinese Ambassador to Kuwait Yang Xin noted that this year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and cultural exchanges constitute "a bridge connecting the hearts of the two peoples."
Speaking to Xinhua at the end of the event, Yang said the occasion represented "a window into China's time-honored culture and a means of promoting cultural exchanges and friendship between China, Kuwait and the Arab world."
NCCAL Secretary-General Mohammad Al-Jassar noted that presenting Kuwaiti and Arab tea traditions alongside Chinese tea reflects the links between cultures and shared daily customs.
The Chinese tea ceremony opens a window into an authentic aspect of Chinese culture and showcases rituals and values passed down through generations, Al-Jassar said.
Liu Jinhong, director of the China Cultural Center in Kuwait, said the center was pleased to see "tea as a bridge to introduce the rich tea cultures of China and Kuwait," noting that the tradition of welcoming guests by serving tea represents a shared value between the two cultures.
Kuwaiti tea cultural expert Sarah Maher AlMajed, a certified tea sommelier and tea master, gave a presentation on Arab tea culture, beginning with an overview of the trade and cultural routes through which tea spread from China to the Arab world.
Nasser Alsaqer, a Kuwaiti enthusiast of Chinese tea culture, shared his experience of studying tea-making in China. He explained the process of Chinese tea production, from picking fresh leaves through processing and manufacturing.
The event also featured a tourism booth showcasing routes and resources related to tea culture in China. It was part of the Tea for Harmony program organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait throughout 2026. ■

Murder-suicide suspected as woman, 66, found dead after husband jumped from building

His wife, who worked as a cleaner, was later found collapsed in the living room of their flat in the same block. She had sustained serious injuries to her head and body.
Wan Chun-hong, acting assistant district commander of Kwai Tsing district, said the couple were pronounced dead at the scene.
“According to a preliminary forensic examination, the force believes the man died after falling from a height, while the woman died after being struck on the head with hard objects. She is believed to have died between 7pm and 11pm that night,” Wan said.

====================================================================================================

Shin Bet must protect Eisenkot before political violence brings Israel another tragedy - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:20:51 UTC
12:20:51 KST

Israel knows the devastating effects that incitement and political violence can wreak on the fabric of a taut society. It can tear it in two.
One only has to look back to November 4, 1995, when prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, the target of vicious incitement campaigns over his support of the Oslo Accords, was gunned down by far-right ultranationalist Yigal Amir. Israel has not been the same ever since.
Although the country has not experienced another political assassination, the specter remains always just under the surface. Security for elected officials was heightened, and warnings from Israel’s security services about the threat of political violence have accompanied every election campaign since that dark day in November 1995.
That’s why the decision, as reported by N12 on Saturday night, by Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief David Zini not to provide Yashar Party head Gadi Eisenkot with a security detail is so perplexing and worrisome.
Eisenkot has emerged as Benjamin Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the October 27 poll. The decision was reportedly made despite regular threats directed at Eisenkot on social media and warnings from the defense sector that Iran and other hostile actors may attempt to target current and former senior officials.
Eisenkot’s campaign field director wrote to Zini and other security officials in June saying the Yashar leader had been forced to hire a private security firm because he was not receiving state protection.
According to the N12 report, Zini’s representatives told Eisenkot’s staff that while the Shin Bet would not provide him with a security detail, the agency would assign a liaison and gather intelligence if concerns emerged about an exceptionally serious incident. However, the request for permanent protection was denied.
Netanyahu, Lapid, leading candidates in 2022 election, both received full security detail
In the last election campaign in 2022, both leading candidates, Yair Lapid and Netanyahu, were provided with full security details - Lapid as sitting prime minister and Netanyahu as a former leader as part of the lifelong package for past heads of government.
Following Zini’s decision, Eisenkot’s campaign submitted its objections in writing to the Shin Bet, Israel Police, and the attorney-general, warning that physical threats against the former IDF chief of staff were escalating, and he called for the decision to be reversed.
“The atmosphere on the Israeli street, as well as on social media, is becoming increasingly heated, and threats are emerging and multiplying,” the letter said.
Just last week, N12 reported that Zini was considering providing Eisenkot with an armed detail amid indications that Iran was increasing efforts to harm Israeli leaders as elections drew close.
The decision not to grant Eisenkot state protection during the campaign is playing with fire. One only has to scroll on social media or watch one of the TV news talk shows to see that the level of vitriol on all sides of the political fence is reaching alarming proportions.
Zini's decision politically motivated?
The suggestion has been raised by the Eisenkot team that Zini’s decision was politically motivated. The letter sent by his team in protest alleged that the government, the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs, and the committee’s chairman “are failing to fulfill their personal responsibility for political and ulterior motives and are avoiding carrying out their duties.”
Eisenkot’s campaign further alleged that a consideration in denying the security detail was a desire to avoid images of Eisenkot looking “prime ministerial” by appearing in public surrounded by security personnel – images which could boost his stature in the public eye.
Although that sounds somewhat conspiratorial, it’s worth noting that the chairman of the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs is Netanyahu, and its members consist of Defense Minister Israel Katz, Justice Minister Yair Levin, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Education Minister Yoav Kisch.
Zini has already faced claims that he’s a Netanyahu appointee who has pledged allegiance to the prime minister. Now is the time to smother those charges and demonstrate that the decisions of the Shin Bet are being made with solely professional considerations in mind, and not according to political alliances.
Granting Gadi Eisenkot a state security detail leading up to the October 27 election is the surest way to clear the air. And more importantly, doing so will help ensure that another devastating national tragedy has less of a chance of taking place.

Australia see spike in near-misses amid air traffic controller shortage

2026-08-24
03:20:03 UTC

Australia see spike in near-misses amid air traffic controller shortage
Staffing gaps are fuelling safety concerns as Sydney Airport records four aircraft close calls in the past month
Since late July, incidents at Sydney Airport included a passenger jet aborting its take-off because there was a plane in its path. In a separate close call, an aircraft that was taxiing had to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding with another jet.
Short-staffed control towers have long been a problem globally, but nowhere is the urgency of the matter more on display recently than in Australia. The growing number of incidents is pressing the need for authorities worldwide to crank up hiring and adopt new tools like artificial intelligence.
“Air traffic control staffing levels are not at the level required,” said Andrew Marshall, president of the Australian and International Pilots Association, which represents the flight crew at the nation’s flag carrier, Qantas Airways. “Whilst pilots are the last line of defence in aviation safety, it isn’t an appropriate long-term solution.”
The problem is there is no quick way to fill the shortfall of air traffic controllers in Australia, largely because it takes years for a new recruit to be fully trained. Meanwhile, flight demand continues to grow.
That is becoming the case worldwide as the lack of controllers has turned into one of the aviation industry’s biggest frustrations. More than 70,000 new controllers will be needed globally by 2034, according to forecasts by aviation training provider CAE.
