Taiwan labor insurance rate to rise to 13% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:13:12 UTC
12:13:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The labor insurance contribution rate will rise by 0.5 percentage point to 13% in 2027, reaching the statutory ceiling under the Labor Insurance Act.
The increase will raise insurance costs for employers and workers nationwide, with nearly 626,000 businesses expected to incur an additional NT$13.147 billion (US$413 million) in costs next year, while more than 10.51 million workers will see higher rates, per UDN.
Under the current system, the 13% rate includes a 1% employment insurance component, meaning the ordinary labor insurance rate itself will rise to 12% next year. Labor insurance premiums are shared among employers (70%), workers (20%), and the government (10%).
Premiums are calculated according to an insured salary scale rather than directly on an employee's actual salary. The maximum monthly insured salary for labor and employment insurance is NT$45,800.
With the average insured salary of NT$36,511, the 0.5% increase will raise an employer's monthly contribution by an estimated NT$127.79 per worker. Workers will pay an additional NT$36.51 per month, or about NT$438.14 annually.
The increase is expected to generate approximately NT$23.021 billion in additional labor insurance revenue annually.
Employers are also preparing for a possible minimum wage increase next year. Businesses have argued that mandatory labor-related contributions already represent a significant financial burden.
Labor insurance provides social security coverage for insured workers, including eligible foreign and migrant workers. Benefits include payments for ordinary injury or sickness, disability, old age, and death, per a Bureau of Labor Insurance press release.
For ordinary injury or sickness, eligible workers can receive benefits equal to 50% of their average monthly insured salary for up to six months, with an additional six months available under certain conditions.
Occupational injury and disease benefits are now administered separately under the Labor Occupational Accident Insurance and Protection Act. Eligible workers can receive compensation equal to 70% of their average monthly insured salary, subject to statutory limits and conditions.
Labor insurance also provides old-age benefits, including monthly pension payments or lump-sum benefits for eligible workers. Disability and survivor benefits are available to qualifying insured workers and their families.

Advertisement
Investment market volatility is ‘here to stay’ unless global recession strikes: analyst
Rich investors put on notice as AI advancement and geopolitical risks continue to change market structure, causing instability, says Nomura
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Wealthy investors should be ready for higher volatility “for years” as uncertainties around artificial intelligence (AI) development and geopolitical risks are set to persist, according to a major private bank.
In the past few years, asset prices underwent several roller coaster rides, from US Liberation Day last year to the sell-off of semiconductor shares and US Treasury in recent months.
But volatility came after changes to the market’s structure “over the decades” and was expected to be “here to stay”, said Julia Wang, North Asia chief investment officer of Nomura International Wealth Management, in an interview with the South China Morning Post.
“(Periodic high volatility) is already a result of structure changes to the market, so it’s unlikely to change, unless we have a global recession,” said Wang, who joined the international wealth management arm of Japan’s largest investment banking and brokerage firm in November last year, to advise the offshore investments of clients with at least US$20 million of potential investable surplus.
While Wang reaffirmed Nomura’s positive outlook on AI and the global economy, AI was one of the key pushes behind the ups and downs.
She explained that expectations for outperforming gains from the future productivity driver resulted in crowded trading and leverage, which usually would be followed by market sell-offs.
Semiconductor shares could be a good example. After hitting a record high in late June, the memory chip-heavy Korea Composite Stock Price Index plunged 22 per cent last month, sending a Hong Kong-listed SK Hynix-leveraged exchange-traded fund to dive 71 per cent over the month.

New York Times highlights problems with three key factors of global food system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:56:55 UTC
11:56:55 KST

NEW YORK, August 24. /TASS/. The global food system relies heavily on three key factors, with challenges being observed regarding each of them, The New York Times (NYT) wrote.
"The system we currently have in place depends on three things: seamless trade, cheap energy, stable climate," Evan Fraser, a professor at the University of Guelph, in Ontario, told the publication. "Today, it seems none of these assumptions are met," he noted.
Uninterrupted trade in agricultural products is complicated by the fact that the Black and Red Seas, through which commodities, including wheat, are transported, are currently zones of active combat, the newspaper said. Moreover, Europe, a major agricultural producer, is experiencing extreme heat, which is reducing crop yields. In turn, Australia, a key wheat producer, is facing a fertilizer shortage due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, American farmers are contending with drought, which is also affecting crop yields.
In May of this year, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization warned of the threat of a serious global food crisis due to problems stemming from the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.

CHICAGO (AP) — Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”
The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction.
Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.
“There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss.
Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.
“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”
Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.
He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
“I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, “so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.”
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.
Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.
Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.
Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.
“If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said, “and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too.”

BERLIN, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Substitute Marin Ljubicic scored twice as Union Berlin came from behind to beat second-tier Eintracht Braunschweig 4-2 in the first round of the German Cup and give new coach Mauro Lustrinelli a winning competitive debut on Sunday.
Braunschweig twice took the lead through Max Marie, but the Bundesliga visitor responded on both occasions before Ljubicic turned the tie around late in the second half.
The host went ahead in the 11th minute when Marie reacted quickly to Martin Entrup's touch and finished low past goalkeeper Matheo Raab.
Union leveled in the 31st minute, with summer signing Zeno Van Den Bosch rising to head home Josip Juranovic's corner.
The second-tier side regained the lead nine minutes into the second half when Entrup again supplied Marie, who calmly completed his brace.
Union responded through another set piece in the 63rd minute. Ljubicic flicked on Juranovic's corner and Tom Rothe converted from close range.
The substitute then put Union ahead nine minutes later, reacting quickest after goalkeeper Ron-Thorben Hoffmann had initially denied Ilyas Ansah.
Braunschweig pushed for an equalizer in the closing stages, but Ljubicic struck again in stoppage time to secure the win.
Union begins its Bundesliga campaign at home to Eintracht Frankfurt next Saturday.
Elsewhere in the first round, fourth-tier SSV Jeddeloh II produced the day's biggest upset by stunning second-tier Heidenheim 5-2, while Rot-Weiss Essen knocked out St. Pauli 2-0. Bundesliga sides Borussia Monchengladbach, Mainz and Freiburg advanced comfortably. ■

YAOUNDE, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Seven people were killed and 10 others injured Sunday when an intercity bus collided head-on with a truck in Cameroon, officials said.
The crash occurred in Sikoum in the Sanaga-Maritime division of the Littoral region, where the commercial capital Douala is located. The bus was carrying residents from the same neighborhood in Douala who were returning from a funeral, said Esther Ngo Yemba, Sanaga-Maritime divisional delegate for transport.
State media Cameroon Tribune reported that the bus driver fell asleep at the wheel, causing the vehicle to veer into the opposite lane and crash into the oncoming truck.
The crash comes just days after 16 people were killed and 40 others injured in a separate accident on the Yaounde-Bafoussam highway.
Deadly road accidents are frequent in Cameroon, often linked to poor road conditions and reckless driving. Ministry of Transport data shows that around 1,500 people die in road accidents in the country each year. ■

S. Korean banks' net income falls in H1 amid lower non-interest income
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:45:51 CST
11:45:51 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' combined net income fell in the first half as securities-related losses offset record-high interest income, financial watchdog data showed Monday.
The net income of local banks stood at 13.8 trillion won (10.0 billion U.S. dollars) in the January-June period, down 6.4 percent compared to the same period of last year, according to the Financial Supervisory Service.
Their interest income grew 8.3 percent to hit the first-half high of 32.2 trillion won on the back of higher net interest margins (NIM) and larger interest-bearing assets.
The NIM gained 0.04 percentage points to 1.56 percent in the first half on a yearly basis, while the interest-bearing assets swelled 6.4 percent to 3,628.1 trillion won.
Non-interest income dipped 43.4 percent to 2.9 trillion won as securities-related earnings swung into a deficit amid rising interest rates.
Amid lingering inflationary pressure, the Bank of Korea lifted its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent in July, marking the first monetary tightening in about three and a half years, since January 2023.
Loan-loss expenses rose 8.6 percent to 3.5 trillion won in the cited period.
Return on assets for domestic banks, a key gauge of profitability, retreated 0.10 percentage points to 0.65 percent, and the return on equity declined 1.15 percentage points to 8.89 percent. (1,000 won equals 0.72 U.S. dollars) ■

After Wildberries, Ukraine launches drone campaign on Russia’s Ozon
MOSCOW - Ukraine has struck warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon on consecutive days, with the firm reporting another logistics site set aflame on Aug 24.
Ukraine has for weeks mounted a campaign targeting Russia’s Wildberries – the country’s top online retailer – alleging it supplied components to the military.
Ozon is Russia’s second-largest online marketplace, with its pick-up points and delivery boxes ubiquitous across the country.
Both companies have been dubbed “Russia’s Amazon”, due to their control over a huge swath of the fast-growing e-commerce sector.
Ozon said on Aug 24 that a “major fire” was burning at one of its logistics centres in the southern Krasnodar region after a drone attack.
“All systems operated as designed, and we promptly evacuated staff. Preliminarily, there are no casualties,” the company said in a Telegram message.
On Aug 23, Ozon reported that a fire had broken out at its logistics hub in the central Orenburg region after a drone attack.
“Operations at the warehouse are currently suspended,” the company added.
The strike came a day after an Ozon centre in the neighbouring Samara region was hit.
The company said an unspecified number of its workers were wounded in that attack.
Ukraine’s military on Aug 22 said it was launching a new campaign targeting the company.
“After Ukrainian units hit the 15 largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it is now Ozon’s turn,” the defence ministry said in a statement.
A logistics centre next to an Ozon facility on the outskirts of Saint Petersburg was also hit.
The attacks on the warehouses – typically easier to reach than heavily defended military installations – have already delivered economic losses worth billions of dollars.
Several facilities were packed with flammable products and were destroyed by the attacks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Aug 19 pledged support for Wildberries amid the strikes, saying the government would help rebuild logistics hubs hit by Ukrainian attacks.
Russia has railed at the attacks on its “civilian infrastructure” more than four years into its full-scale offensive on Ukraine that has killed thousands of civilians and flattened cities across the country’s east and south. AFP

‘Hang in there’: Chinese boys offer US$1.5 to struggling store owner, sparking wave of support
To express his gratitude, Chen treats the three ‘angel investors’ to a meal, a fishing trip, offering each a red envelope
Three boys from southeastern China offered 10.5 yuan (US$1.5) to a convenience store owner on the brink of closing, igniting a wave of public support.
Five years after borrowing money to establish his convenience store in Guangzhou, Chen decided to shut down the shop as business continued to decline.
On August 12, three primary school boys visited the store, as they often did, to buy drinks. During a casual conversation, they learned that Chen was preparing to close the establishment.
One boy suggested that Chen take his business online, while another proposed they combine their pocket money to support him.
The trio then counted their savings and placed 10.5 yuan on Chen’s counter, despite his persistent refusals, before running off with a message of encouragement: “Hang in there!”
The sight of the crumpled banknotes brought Chen to tears.

Taiwan Navy to hold large-scale exercise next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:24:27 UTC
11:24:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Navy will conduct a large-scale exercise from Sept. 9 to 24 in waters off southeastern Taiwan.
According to a Fisheries Agency notice, the Navy will carry out live-fire drills against sea and air targets. They are scheduled for Sept. 9–10, 16–18, and 21–24.
No specific weapons were listed, but the notice said fighter jets, helicopters, and reconnaissance drones will be deployed.
The Navy has designated three warning zones. Zone 1 is located in waters east of Taimali in Taitung to Eluanbi in Pingtung. Zone 2 extends from the Taitung–Pingtung border eastward to waters off Green Island and Orchid Island. Zone 3 is situated in waters east of Chenggong and Taimali in Taitung.
In the past three years, the military has deployed a range of weapons during precision munitions live-fire drills, including Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles and Patriot and Sky Bow air defense missiles, per Liberty Times. Last year, the Kuai Chi attack unmanned surface vessel and Chien Hsiang-series attack drone were unveiled during drills.
The exercise announcement comes two weeks after China held navigation exercises, including communications and at-sea replenishment, with an Indonesian Navy frigate in waters east of the country. Taiwan's foreign ministry condemned the move, saying that China disregarded “international norms and responsibilities” and escalated regional tensions.
There has been an increase in Chinese gray zone and military activities near Taiwan’s eastern waters this year. In late July, Chinese coast guard vessels, the Xiushan and Chongming, were found 280 kilometers and 80 km east of Lanyu, respectively. The Chinese coast guard claimed they were conducting a routine law enforcement mission.
National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said in July that China has deployed a record of more than 110 military and coast guard ships along the First Island Chain.

Taiwan plans to continue free counseling program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:24:23 UTC
11:24:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to continue its mental health support initiative in 2027, with NT$429 million (US$13.5 million) proposed for the effort, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Sunday.
Launched in August 2024, the scheme provides people aged 15 to 45 with three free counseling sessions. The allocation is expected to benefit about 100,000 people next year, according to UDN Money and the Ministry of Health and Welfare.
The service was introduced as suicide rates among young and middle-aged people have risen in recent years. Health ministry figures point to growing psychological strain linked to the demands of fast-paced modern life, according to Health News.
The 15-to-45 age group encompasses several major life transitions, from education and entering the workforce to relationships and starting a family. Clinical psychologist Hsu Chun-wei (許峻維) said common concerns discussed in counseling include daily stress, interpersonal and romantic conflicts, academic and workplace demands, and difficulties related to career changes. Symptoms of depression and anxiety are also frequently reported.
Hsu said psychologists and psychiatrists are among the professionals involved in the initiative. The three free sessions are designed to allow participants to discuss their difficulties and, when necessary, connect them with appropriate social resources.
The service is available to Taiwanese citizens aged 15 to 45 as well as foreigners eligible for Taiwan's National Health Insurance. Eligible individuals can make appointments by phone or inquire about the service directly at participating medical institutions, Hsu said.
More than 80,000 people had used the service by the end of October 2025, receiving more than 200,000 counseling sessions. The number of participating institutions had also increased from 523 when the scheme launched to 616.
Funding for the initiative is included in the Cabinet's recently proposed NT$3.9 trillion central government budget for 2027. The package includes more than NT$1 trillion each for national defense, social welfare, and local governments, along with additional allocations for 10 major areas, including cash payouts, population policies, and public infrastructure, according to Capital Futures.

During the talks, Damascus stressed that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild its national army and determine partnerships without restrictive mechanisms.
Syria reiterated that the occupied Golan is Syrian territory, stating that the immediate priority remains the withdrawal of Israeli forces to lines held before December 8, 2024 and the full reactivation of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.

Homes crack as London heatwaves trigger record subsidence claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:12:05 KST

Homes crack as London heatwaves trigger record subsidence claims
Five successive heatwaves have led to a surge in structural damage claims in the UK capital this summer
Londoners are facing historic levels of subsidence risk after five successive heatwaves dried out the clay soil on which much of the British capital is built.
Insurance claims tied to subsidence – a phenomenon associated with bouts of hot, dry weather that shrink the soil and destabilise the foundations on which buildings stand – hit a record last quarter, according to data provided by the Association of British Insurers (ABI). On average, households claimed £20,000 (US$27,200) for the risk, more than in any previous quarter and a 15 per cent jump from the same period in 2025, the ABI said.
Laura Hughes, head of general insurance at the ABI, said the upwards trend is likely to continue. “We expect to see more subsidence cases because of the hot weather,” she said in an interview.
Londoners have taken to social media to express their dismay. On Reddit, people offered personal accounts telling of “horrendous cracking” in their homes, and “doors sticking” due to subsidence. One said it was “genuinely scary” to discover that their kitchen had moved as the foundations of the home shifted.
Another Reddit user described the response of a structural engineer they contacted for help. “Before I could finish explaining he laughed and said, ‘You and 20,000 other people in southeast London’,” the person wrote.
“It’s crazy, what’s happening now,” said Otso Lahtinen, chief executive of Geobear, an engineering firm that is regularly called in to repair damage caused by subsidence. “It’s the new norm, and it seems it will happen more often in the next 20 to 30 years.”

Police examining how long the suspect deceived women online

Police suspect that, as part of those relationships, the suspect caused some of the women to perform sexual acts on themselves.

According to police, the person behind the profile and male identity throughout the period was the same young woman.
Investigators believe the suspicions do not center on a single incident or a short period of time. Police are examining the possibility that the alleged pattern continued for years and are working to determine whether additional women had relationships with someone who presented himself as “Orel Hazan” and were harmed in a similar manner.

Her attorney, Erez Bar Zvi, said after the hearing: “I am glad that with the agreement of the police, my client was released under conditions. We are confident that once the facts become clear, the case will be closed with nothing.”

Can Kenya’s AI ambitions coexist with Naivasha’s water needs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:09:40 UTC
11:09:40 KST

Can Kenya’s AI ambitions coexist with Naivasha’s water needs?
As Kenya courts data-centre investment, communities fear growing pressure on an already stressed water system.
Naivasha, Kenya – For communities living around Naivasha, water is not an abstract resource. It sustains families, livestock, farms and schools.
That reality has taken on new significance after plans for a major Microsoft-G42 data centre in Olkaria, near Lake Naivasha, stalled in May 2026 over concerns about available power capacity.
Microsoft and United Arab Emirates-based artificial intelligence company G42 announced the project in 2024 as part of a $1bn digital investment package for Kenya. The proposed facility was to run on geothermal energy and eventually scale to as much as 1 gigawatt of capacity.
The uncertainty has also prompted questions about what another major industrial user could mean for water in a region where residents already report shortages.
Microsoft and G42 said the proposed data centre campus would run entirely on renewable geothermal energy and incorporate water conservation technology. The companies did not disclose a project-specific water consumption figure in their 2024 announcement.
Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen) communications director Frank David Ochieng told Al Jazeera that the data centre remains at the design stage and that he could not comment further until the project is ready to proceed.
For residents like Musa Olorkedienye, who spoke to Al Jazeera, water scarcity is already a daily concern. He says communities around Olkaria have seen changes in access to water, including the loss of reliable piped supplies that residents previously received from KenGen.
“Currently, we are relying on water vendors to get water, our animals are walking for kilometres, and we fear things could get worse as demand for water rises,” Olorkedienye says.
Pastoralist Isaac Leshishi, who also spoke to Al Jazeera, says increasingly harsh weather is adding to the pressure.
Why Olkaria?
The choice of Olkaria was closely tied to energy. The area is home to Kenya’s major geothermal operations, making it an attractive location for a power-intensive facility.
KenGen operates the Olkaria geothermal complex, while Microsoft and G42 planned to power the proposed data centre entirely with geothermal energy.
A lake under pressure
Naivasha is a freshwater lake in Kenya’s Rift Valley whose catchment supports agriculture, tourism, livestock and domestic water use. Its basin also hosts geothermal development and other economic activity.
Grace Kimani, a patrol leader with Lake Naivasha and Oloiden, told Al Jazeera that the reservoir is under growing pressure from population growth, agriculture, water abstraction, climate variability, pollution and ecosystem degradation.
“The planned Microsoft-G42 data centre in Olkaria could bring jobs and investment, but its water demand raises concerns about adding pressure to already competing needs, particularly during dry periods,” she said.
Kimani said there is limited public information about the project’s expected water demand, source and cooling technology. She said transparency and an assessment of its cumulative impact on water resources would be important.
She also called for water-efficient or water-free cooling, water recycling and the use of treated wastewater, as well as sustainable abstraction limits and community involvement in monitoring.
Silas Wanjala of the Lake Naivasha Riparian Association, who spoke to Al Jazeera, said the region is heavily dependent on groundwater and that declining water flows are adding to the pressure.
“These industries, especially EcoCloud, which deal with data, will consume a lot of water at a time when rivers are drying, and demand for water is on the rise,” Wanjala said.
Olkaria EcoCloud Data Centre is a local partner in the G42-led development. In 2024, the Kenya News Agency reported that G42, Microsoft and EcoCloud signed a letter of intent for the wider data-centre initiative, with EcoCloud described as a local partner that had previously signed a memorandum of understanding with G42.
Wanjala points to past fluctuations in Lake Naivasha as a warning.
“This lake in 2010 nearly dried up due to over-abstraction, and this could be repeated due to high demand for water by these investors in Olkaria,” he says.
His concern comes against a wider backdrop of water scarcity in Kenya. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations says Kenya has about 527 cubic metres (527,000 litres) of freshwater available per person, below the 1,000-cubic-metre threshold for water scarcity, and estimates availability could fall to about 475 cubic metres per person by 2030.
The figures do not show what effect the proposed data centre would have on Lake Naivasha. They provide context, however, for why the prospect of another major water user is drawing scrutiny in a region where demand is already high.
How much water would it use?
The amount of water the proposed Microsoft-G42 facility itself would require remains unclear.
The project announcement provides no projected consumption figure.
Existing industrial use offers some context.
A KenGen environmental and social impact assessment records that 195,165 cubic metres of water were abstracted from Lake Naivasha in July 2023 for domestic and commercial uses at Olkaria and for operations and domestic use at Eburru.
Of that total, 153,918 cubic metres were used for commercial operations at Olkaria. The assessment records the abstraction as within Water Resources Authority (WRA) permitted levels.
Those figures relate to existing KenGen operations, not the proposed data centre.
For farmer Eskimos Kobia, who spoke to Al Jazeera, the potential competition extends beyond households and livestock. He says farmers, pastoralists, schools and investors will all face greater pressure as demand increases.
Kimani said climate variability has also led to fluctuations in lake levels, with periods of flooding followed by prolonged dry conditions.
“Water quality is affected by agricultural run-off, untreated wastewater in some areas and invasive species,” she says.
Investment versus local concerns
Not everyone in Naivasha opposes the investment.
Absolom Mukhuusi of the Naivasha Professional Association, who spoke to Al Jazeera, says the technology sector could bring jobs, infrastructure and new businesses to the area. But he says economic benefits should not come at the expense of local communities.
“Even as we welcome the investors, our biggest fear is what happens to our water bodies and communities as water is diverted to Olkaria for the heavy users,” he says.
Could technology help?
Geologist Kenyatta Otieno, who spoke to Al Jazeera, sees another potential benefit.
He recalls the pressure large flower farms once placed on the lake’s ecosystem, saying many have since left or scaled back their operations.
Otieno says the proposed centre would have included a resource centre to monitor lake levels and weather patterns. Such monitoring, he says, could help identify the highest water level over time and guide riparian land zoning.
“The centre being built with water conservation in mind would be futuristic as Naivasha is generally a water-scarce area. It would be a model for future development,” Otieno said.
Kenya already has regulators responsible for managing competing demands. The WRA regulates water abstraction and issues water-use permits, while the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) oversees environmental impact assessments under the country’s environmental regulatory framework.
Attempts by Al Jazeera to obtain comments from WRA and NEMA officials were unsuccessful. Efforts to reach Microsoft-G42 officials and Kenyan government officials for comment on the project’s status and water requirements were also unsuccessful.
For now, the project’s eventual scale, design and water requirements remain unclear, according to KenGen.
“We are now competing with the multibillion [-dollar] companies for water, and we fear that we shall be the losers in the long run,” Leshishi said.

Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:02:28 UTC

Ebola cases in DRC hit 5,515 as Pope Leo urges global action to save lives
Case fatality rate climbs to nearly 48 percent in the DRC, meaning almost one in two people infected with Ebola are dying.
DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 5,515 confirmed cases of infection and killed 2,642 people, with 51 new cases detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, according to the latest government figures.
The update on Sunday came as Pope Leo called for international action to help contain the epidemic, which is now the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC’s history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How the deadliest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak can be stopped
- list 2 of 3DR Congo miners risk Ebola to make a living
- list 3 of 3Ebola continues to spread in the DRC as 16,000 vaccine doses arrive
Declared in mid-May, it is the DRC’s 17th Ebola epidemic and was designated a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization (WHO), its highest alert level, also covering neighbouring Uganda.
The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, which was the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.
According to government figures, the case fatality rate in the DRC has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to nearly 48 percent now, meaning almost one in two people infected are dying.
Contact tracing, however, has improved sharply, from 30 percent in June to more than 85 percent.
The disease has also proved deadly for those fighting it. About 160 health workers have been infected, and about 45 have died, according to the WHO.
Efforts to contain the outbreak, however, have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population and a lack of critical infrastructure.
Vaccines arrive in DRC
There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo, which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks.
The WHO has pledged 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed for Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. According to the global body, early data from animal trials suggest it may offer some protection against Bundibugyo.
Some 16,250 doses of the vaccine arrived in the DRC on Friday.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and other officials said the response in the DRC needs to be scaled up two to threefold to contain the outbreak and reach every affected area.
They also called for more support and protection for front-line health workers, including protective equipment, timely payment, and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill.
Abdulsalami Nasidi, a public health consultant who helped establish the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Al Jazeera that the outbreak was “getting out of hand”.
He blamed weak infection control measures and a lack of trust between authorities and affected communities for the continued transmission.
“This is no longer just a national or regional issue; it is a global issue. If it spreads to neighbouring places with lower immunity, it will be a disaster,” Nasidi added.
The WHO currently rates the risk to the global public as low, but warns that the danger inside the DRC remains very high.
Despite the surging cases, Uganda and several health zones in DRC’s Ituri and South Kivu have interrupted transmission, which the WHO said is evidence that rapid detection, decisive leadership, and community cooperation can break the chain of transmission.
At the Vatican on Sunday, Pope Leo offered prayers for the DRC, “in light of the spread of the Ebola epidemic, which is sadly claiming many lives”.
The pontiff also called for global action to help save lives.
“I urge the international community to respond in a way that also involves local communities in prevention efforts to save as many lives as possible,” he said.

Britain told EU citizens to trust its settled status system. Then it mixed up identical twins.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

LONDON — The U.K.’s Brexit settlement scheme left a woman stranded at a foreign airport — after confusing her for her identical twin sister and stopping her from boarding her flight home.
The error is the latest in a string of problems caused by the system’s design affecting tens of thousands of EU citizens living in Britain.
When Brexit hit, EU nationals already resident in the U.K. at the time were given “settled status” granting them the right to stay once free movement ended.
Advertisement
But instead of getting a physical document to prove their status, the Home Office decided they would only be given a digital “eVisa” stored on a Home Office computer.
Just one problem: the information in the eVisa computer isn’t always correct. The Home Office system sometimes gets confused, including, POLITICO has learned, between identical twins.
Known issue
The system’s problem with identical twins is a “known issue,” the Home Office told Nidia Webb over the phone as she tried to work out why she had been stranded in a foreign country.
When Webb, who has lived in the U.K. for eight years, tried to fly home from a holiday in Spain earlier this month, she was denied boarding at the gate.
The problem? Her settled status wasn’t showing up in the system. The flight departed without her.
After spending hours on the phone with a Home Office helpline, the problem became clear.
Advertisement
“My digital settled status had become linked to my identical twin sister’s details rather than my own, meaning my status could not be properly matched to my identity,” she told POLITICO.
“I was informed that this is a known technical issue affecting some twins within the Home Office system.” The Home Office did not dispute her account and said it would be contacting her to ensure the issue was resolved.
Webb was assured over the phone that she would get an update when the issue with her eVisa account had been fixed. But in a result which failed to inspire confidence, the Home Office sent the confirmation email to her twin sister.
The Home Office system sometimes gets confused, including between identical twins. | Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images
“I had no idea the issue had been corrected until I was allowed to board my flight home,” Webb said — a fact which compounded an already stressful situation.
“Had I not spent hours on the phone trying to resolve the matter, I have no idea how long I could have remained stranded abroad,” she added.
Webb was forced to pay for a new flight home out of her own pocket — money her travel insurer said she should try to recover from the Home Office.
Advertisement
The eVisa database keeps a record of a person’s full name, date of birth, nationality, and a facial photograph. But these traits are by definition often a very close match for identical twins, including Webb, whose name is similar to that of her sister.
Many such cases
Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, which campaigns for the rights of EU citizens living in the U.K., said problems with the eVisa system sometimes left people unable to prove their identity when they needed it most.
“We have seen many cases where someone else’s immigration status is entangled with another person’s eVisa account. We had hoped, after repeatedly raising this issue, that the Home Office had taken more steps to prevent it happening. It just shows how, despite claims that the eVisa system is highly resilient, it can fail people at the critical moments they need it to work,” she said.
Hawkins said it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status” and described the digital-only system as “rushed,” adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.”
While a Home Office spokesperson did not dispute Webb’s account, they defended the eVisa system, arguing it had worked for many people.
“Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status,” the spokesperson said. “As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.”
Advertisement
More than 76,000 people have their names, immigration status, or photographs mixed up in the U.K.’s immigration database, the Guardian reported in 2024. This number includes other nationalities subject to eVisa and not just EU citizens.
As identity and border systems are increasingly digitalized, twins are facing more problems across the board, say campaigners. “Too often twins are considered as one as opposed to as individuals and we urge those making these technological decisions to consider twins’ individuality,” Rafi Cooper, head of communications at Twins Trust, said.

Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

A helicopter prepares to drop water on a fire at Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries' complex near Podolsk, outside Moscow, on Aug. 16, 2026. | Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP via Getty Images
For most of Russia’s years-long war against Ukraine, Russian civilians have been relatively insulated from Kyiv’s attacks. That is changing.
Since July, Kyiv has broadened its long-range drone campaign beyond conventional military targets, intensifying strikes on Russia’s oil and gas industry and hitting the vast warehouses of Wildberries, Russia’s answer to Amazon.
While these are primarily intended to cause economic damage, in the words of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, “to bring the war back home – to Russia,” they also mark another important shift. Ukrainian authorities are increasingly seeing Russian civilian casualties as a price they are prepared to pay for taking the war deeper into enemy territory.
Advertisement
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.
Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.
Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.
Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images
There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.
“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”
Advertisement
“But we know that Russia has been systematically targeting Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure and civilian districts with the deliberate intent to cause civilian casualties,” she added. “That’s an important underlying distinction to draw.”
On Friday, a Russian drone attack on a busy shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, left 16 people dead and more than a 130 wounded, including children. The strike was a double-tap — that’s when second attack on a target is conducted around half-an-hour later and is designed to catch first responders, a tactic used frequently in northern Syria.
The damage done to a shopping mall following a Russian strike in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine is pictured on Aug. 22, 2026. | Yan Dobronosov/AFP via Getty Images
Since the war began, Russian officials have consistently denied their forces intentionally target civilians and Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has instead accused Ukraine of deploying troops and heavy weapons close to civilian infrastructure.
Russia has “a clear pattern” of targeting Kyiv and other urban centers with large civilian populations, Rosemary DiCarlo, the U.N. under-secretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the U.N. Security Council in July.
The U.N. has verified that at least 16,874 Ukrainian civilians, including 820 children, have been killed since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale assault on the country in 2022. Ukrainians believe the toll is likely higher, arguing there are many unrecorded deaths near the front lines and on territory occupied by Russian forces.
Advertisement
DiCarlo also expressed concerns about Ukraine’s drone attacks. “Any attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a clear violation of international humanitarian law,” she said.
It is an argument that infuriates Ukrainian officials, who bristle when asked about the risks to Russian civilians with the tactical switch. Even asking the question triggers accusations of echoing Moscow propagandists. “You are helping Russia by pushing this civilian stuff,” a presidential aide said. He declined to answer when asked whether Ukrainian commanders adhere to any pre-strike procedures to assess risks to civilians.
The change in tactics has alarmed some European officials, according to Adrian Karatnycky, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and author of Battleground Ukraine, who regularly meets with senior European officials and diplomats. “They have always been low-risk and fearful of Russian escalation,” he said.
The shift, he added, has been enabled by Ukraine’s growing ability to manufacture its own long-range drones and by cuts in U.S. assistance that have reduced Washington’s leverage over Kyiv. “There will be noncombatant casualties, but in an existential war you can’t fight with a hand tied behind your back,” Karatnycky said. “Ukraine’s ability to counterpunch is a relatively new phenomenon.”
How will the Ukrainian attacks play out in Russia — will they weaken Putin politically? Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former U.K. diplomat now at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, said Kyiv must try to minimize civilian casualties with the long-range drone campaign.
“There are some risks,” he said. “As we know from the history of warfare, the bombing of civilians tends to actually harden people’s resistance rather than weaken it. Just think of the London Blitz, but also Ukraine now. And second, there is a danger of losing what still is a remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine.”
“But you cannot wage war without casualties,” he added.

Half of Hong Kong’s public bodies omit emissions data, green group finds
The Green Earth’s study of 82 public entities finds that while 41 publish emissions data, about eight use outdated emission factor
Half of Hong Kong’s government departments and public bodies have not disclosed their greenhouse gas emissions data and some calculations have been based on outdated information, a green group has found.
The findings from The Green Earth have prompted calls for stronger carbon reporting and the setting of reduction targets across the public sector to align with the city’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality before 2050.
The non-profit group’s study of 82 public entities found that while 41 published emissions data, about eight entities relied on an outdated emission factor.
An emission factor is a standard multiplier used to calculate the amount of greenhouse gas generated from an activity.
The city’s two utility providers, CLP Power and HK Electric, each publish their own emission factors, which are adjusted with changes in the energy mix.
Using outdated factors could lead to overestimated emission reductions, said Steven Chan Wing-kit, the green group’s assistant environmental affairs manager.

====================================================================================================

Germany’s establishment has a plan to contain the far right. Sort of.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ulrich Siegmund walks past election campaign placards at the Alternative for Germany campaign launch for state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, on June 4, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — It’s not the kind of photo op German Chancellor Friedrich Merz would likely want to frame for his office wall: him standing next to Ulrich Siegmund, the far-right politician a national magazine recently labeled the country’s “most dangerous man.”
And yet, such a picture might soon be hard for Merz to avoid. On Sept. 6, Siegmund is set for a sweeping victory in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. If his far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secures an outright majority in the state parliament, Siegmund will likely become premier, and his party will have broken through the political “firewall” that has kept it out of all federal and state governments since its founding in 2013.
It would be a historic triumph for the AfD and a shock to Germany’s political system.
Advertisement
As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press.
Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said.
The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support.
So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD?
POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name.
The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it. State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record.
Advertisement
The conversations for this article were dominated by a single concern: domestic security, especially the protection of intelligence information, given the AfD’s advocacy for closer ties with President Vladimir Putin’s Russia.
According to Social Democrat Georg Maier, who serves as the state of Thuringia’s interior minister, Siegmund’s party has “good channels” to Moscow. “If the AfD provides the minister-president in Saxony-Anhalt, the champagne corks will be popping in the Kremlin,” he told POLITICO.
AfD supporters listen to Siegmund during a campaign event in Dessau-Roßlau, Germany, on Aug. 19, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Although there is no playbook yet for containing an AfD government, the thinking in Berlin and several state capitals has already moved well beyond the abstract.
Option 1: Hold extra informal meetings
One way to limit the AfD’s access to sensitive discussions could be to simply have more discussions. In addition to the gathering of state premiers that Siegmund would be expected to chair for a year, Germany’s states regularly coordinate through a network of ministerial “conferences.” Among the most important is the conference of interior ministers, where some of the country’s most pressing security and intelligence matters are discussed.
One possibility being considered is to keep holding the regular meetings of the interior ministers but also organize separate gatherings for particularly sensitive issues. Only Germany’s 15 other interior ministers would attend these meetings, without the representative from Saxony-Anhalt. Several ministers confirmed this hypothetical scenario to POLITICO.
The idea builds on a long-established practice in German politics. State governments are informally grouped into so-called “A” and “B” states, depending on which political camp holds the governing majority: Social Democratic-led governments on one side, conservative governments on the other. Before major conferences, both camps coordinate internally.
Advertisement
Applied to the AfD, this model would put the ostracized government on one side and everyone else on the other.
Christoph Degenhart, a professor emeritus of constitutional law and former judge at Saxony’s Constitutional Court, said the idea is definitely conceivable. “How long that would work and whether the courts would tolerate it is, of course, another question.”
Option 2: Erect a wall
One of the biggest worries regarding the AfD is its closeness to Moscow, according to Maier.
Specifically, the minister’s biggest concern is an AfD-led interior ministry. Whoever runs such a department, he said, gains access to highly classified information. And yet, excluding the entire state from Germany’s domestic intelligence network would not be possible; public safety, including protection against terrorist attacks, would rule that out.
“But we can build Chinese walls into our joint information systems, barriers that block certain information,” said the minister. He laughed briefly. “‘Chinese walls’ fits perfectly here. The AfD doesn’t just have a soft spot for Moscow,” he added.
What information would Maier wall off? “We would have to keep all intelligence relating to right-wing extremism and the entire area of espionage away from the AfD,” he said. Such a “preventive segmentation” would be legally possible, he added, citing legal advice he has obtained. It could also be implemented relatively quickly. “Government formation is not going to happen overnight,” he said.
Advertisement
Patrick Harr, a spokesperson for the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, rejected all accusations of closeness to Russia. “That’s complete nonsense,” he said. “We don’t have a red telephone to Moscow.”
“We talk to everyone, whether West or East,” he added. “That doesn’t mean we’re going to hand over files. Anyone who claims otherwise is talking nonsense. If and when we get access to such information, we understand our responsibility as a party of government.”
But Konstantin von Notz, a Green member of the Bundestag and deputy chair of its intelligence oversight panel, pointed to Austria’s far-right Freedom Party’s (FPÖ) time in government as a cautionary example. After entering government in 2017, the FPÖ took control of the interior ministry. The following year, police raided Austria’s domestic intelligence service and seized sensitive data, including information from allied agencies.
Thorsten Frei, right, Friedrich Merz, center, and Markus Söder, left, speak to media in Berlin on July 29, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Germany could face something similar under an AfD government, said von Notz, if for example the country’s allies suspected Russia would be able to access the database used by Germany’s domestic intelligence services to exchange information on extremists, spies and other security threats.
“The British, the Americans, the Poles, the Ukrainians — nobody would share information with us anymore for fear that everything would be passed on to Moscow,” warned the Green politician.
Advertisement
Option 3: Cut off their funds
Another instrument mentioned both by AfD figures and the party’s opponents is Germany’s fiscal equalization system, which helps poorer states with money from wealthier ones and additional federal funds.
Saxony-Anhalt has depended on this system for decades. In 2025, it received around €2.8 billion according to preliminary figures — nearly one-fifth of its state budget.
Reducing or even halting such payments would be one way to make life harder for an AfD government, or to coerce the party to behave in ways the political establishment finds acceptable. Within the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch, this scenario is seen as a real risk.
The legal hurdles, however, would be high. Danyal Bayaz, the Green finance minister of Baden-Württemberg, one of Germany’s wealthier contributor states, chose his words carefully. “The fiscal equalization system is anchored in the constitution and is not an instrument that can simply be changed according to the political weather,” he said.
He then added a caveat: A federal state based on solidarity, said Bayaz, depends on shared commitments to the rule of law. If a state government were to call those principles into question, or pursue legally dubious special paths, that would affect trust and cooperation with the federal government and other states, “including in financial matters.”
Bayaz’s spokesperson stressesdthat this was the minister’s personal assessment, not an agreed position of the state government — a coalition led by the Greens, with the CDU as its junior partner.
Advertisement
Option 4: Deploy the nuclear option
The most powerful constitutional instrument would be Bundeszwang, or federal coercion. Under Article 37 of Germany’s Basic Law, the federal government, with the consent of the Bundesrat — the chamber representing the states — may take “necessary measures” to compel a state to fulfill its legal obligations. In plain English: Berlin could force a state government to obey federal law.
The provision has never been used. In the reporting for this story, no one interviewed brought it up on their own — perhaps out of conviction, perhaps out of fear that merely mentioning it would play into the AfD’s hands before the elections.
Within AfD’s right-wing intellectual circles, federal coercion has long been treated as a realistic scenario. In 2025, publisher Götz Kubitschek, whose estate lies in Saxony-Anhalt and who the New York Times once labeled “the prophet of Germany’s new right,” told POLITICO this is what he would expect to see happen.
The entrance to the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Cologne, Germany is pictured on Sept. 22, 2025. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images
A potential trigger can only be guessed at. If, for example, an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt failed to provide for even the most basic needs of asylum seekers, the federal government could intervene with binding orders to restore those services, eventually through a federal commissioner with the authority to issue instructions to the state and all its authorities.
Would all this work?
Whatever Germany’s political establishment does to contain the country’s first AfD government, this fall or later, the risks are obvious. Measures meant to defend liberal democracy could also feed the AfD’s central grievance and that of many of its voters: that the establishment refuses to accept the party even when it wins.
Public opinion on this is more divided than it once was. A representative poll from July found that only 42 percent of Germans still considered it right for the Social Democrats and the CDU to refuse cooperation with the AfD; another survey showed that support for the exclusion strategy had fallen to 46 percent, down from 54 percent in early 2025.
Advertisement
Doing nothing out of the ordinary may well be the safest option for established parties. The AfD has spent years thriving in opposition, turning its rivals’ mistakes and broken promises into political fuel. But it has never governed. Once in office, it could become mired in incompetence and internal infighting, sparing its opponents the need for special defensive maneuvers.
Key figures in the AfD’s own orbit are aware of this danger. “They have to prepare like the biggest overachievers,” Kubitschek told POLITICO in 2025 regarding Siegmund’s state party. Benedikt Kaiser, another influential far-right intellectual and aide to an AfD member of the Bundestag, also advised caution if the party wins an outright majority: “In the first 90 days of government, the AfD has to pursue a politics that does not create fear,” he said, mentioning “family benefits, free school meals, things like that” as examples.
Even as Germany’s political establishment considers ways to contain an AfD state government, the party’s intellectual leaders are fretting over a more immediate concern: Simply governing could prove a more effective constraint on the party than any measure the country’s political mainstream can devise.

Sean Grayson, former Illinois deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:53:01 UTC
10:53:01 KST

Sean Grayson, former Illinois deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
CHICAGO (AP) — Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff’s deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence.
Grayson’s attorney, Daniel Fultz, confirmed that his client died earlier Sunday but declined to provide any further details.
Grayson, 32, was convicted of second-degree murder in October in the fatal shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman who had reported a possible prowler outside her Springfield-area home. Body camera video of the July 2024 encounter showed Massey crouching in her kitchen and apologizing moments before Grayson shot her in the face.
He was sentenced in January to the maximum 20 years in prison.
Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer before Massey’s killing, and his attorneys said at his sentencing that the disease had spread to his liver and lungs. In May, only months into his sentence, he sought medical release under an Illinois law for prisoners with terminal illnesses or serious medical conditions. The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request last month.
Massey called 911 early on July 6, 2024, to report someone prowling outside her home. Grayson and another Sangamon County sheriff’s deputy responded.
Video showed Grayson directing Massey to remove a pot of hot water from the stove. As she held the pot, Massey told the deputies, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.”
Grayson threatened to shoot her, drew his handgun and ordered her to drop the pot. Massey apologized and ducked behind a kitchen counter before Grayson fired three times.
The other deputy, Dawson Farley, later testified that he did not consider Massey a threat and drew his own weapon only after Grayson did.
Grayson was fired after the shooting and charged with first-degree murder. Jurors convicted him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder after Grayson argued that he feared Massey would throw the hot water at him.
Massey’s killing drew national attention and protests and raised questions about how Grayson had moved through several law enforcement agencies before being hired by the Sangamon County Sheriff’s Office.
Illinois lawmakers later passed the Sonya Massey Act, requiring law enforcement agencies to more closely review an applicant’s previous employment records before hiring an officer.
The Justice Department also opened a civil rights investigation after Massey’s death and later reached an agreement with Sangamon County, its sheriff’s office and other agencies requiring changes to policing and emergency response. Those changes included additional training for interactions with people with behavioral health disabilities and development of a mobile crisis response program.

TRIPOLI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Libya's Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed al-Menfi has referred United Nations reports on oil smuggling and illegal exports to the country's Prosecutor General Al-Siddiq Al-Sour for investigation, according to an official statement released Sunday.
The reports, issued by the UN Security Council's Panel of Experts, allege illegal exports of crude oil and petroleum products, fuel smuggling and the diversion of fuel from designated channels. They also contain information on entities and networks allegedly benefiting from proceeds generated by such activities.
Al-Menfi called for a comprehensive and independent judicial investigation, particularly into Arkenu Chemicals Company and related entities and individuals for possible criminal offenses.
The referral also demands probes into the contracts and arrangements cited in the reports, including the quantities of oil involved, revenues generated and beneficiaries, and whether such revenues entered the state's official financial channels.
The Presidential Council further requested tracing related funds and assets inside and outside Libya and activating international judicial cooperation mechanisms.
It also stressed the need to safeguard evidence and protect witnesses, experts and whistleblowers involved in the investigations. ■

The ‘GO NOW’ evacuation zone has expanded to the edge of the University of Nevada, Reno, and another 45,000 people in an adjacent ‘GET SET’ zone have been urged to leave and prepare to stay away for several days.

How has AI and tech changed your life? Australians share their stories — as it happened
Technology is creeping into every facet of our lives. Whether it is for better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder, but it is certainly here to stay.
Australians are grappling with the prospect of AI replacing jobs, breaching privacy, and creating misinformation and digital exclusion, while also developing technology designed to make everyday tasks easier.
We heard your stories and experiences in our live blog below, plus put your questions to Curtin University cybersecurity expert Mihai Lazarescu and the ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson.

What do you see as the biggest threat to you or your family?

Are there environmental guardrails in place for data centres?
My main concern with AI at the moment is the environmental impact of data centres that AI use. The ongoing resource demand of data centres for electricity and water risk accelerating the effects of climate change. Is there anyway we can ensure that we contribute relatively less or not at all to this environmental degradation? And what planning guardrails are in place in Australia to prevent this?
- Edward
Thanks for the question Edward. Here is what AI reporter Cam Wilson has to say:
You're not the only one worried about this! Power is probably the thorniest issue facing policy makers right now. Water, too, is a concern although I would say not to quite the same scale.
It boils down (no pun intended) to the fact that AI needs an enormous amount of power to be trained and to run. It's a huge, unanswered question about whether we can source enough power to feed all the data centres that companies are proposing, let alone sourcing that new capacity with renewables.
The Albanese government first said its proposed AI rules would require large data centres to bring enough new grid capacity to make up for their demand. Recently, it's been saying that this new capacity needs to be renewables. It's facing a fight with the states, and potentially the data centre sector too, so it's far from guaranteed.

Many of you have been sharing your concerns about AI, from its impact on critical thinking to how much you tell us it's being used in universities.

Naomi
As a teacher, I am concerned about the impact that AI will have on society's critical thinking skills. Social media has already impacted our attention spans, and now AI is able to complete high cognitive tasks at the click of a button. How can we as a society protect our minds, and foster a culture of learning and cognitive resilience?
AJ
As a Masters student at university, it is really concerning how professors are encouraging us to use AI for everything, including assessments, and telling us that we are falling behind if we don't use AI. A lot of my classmates are entirely reliant on AI to complete all their work and will likely graduate with a degree and high marks without putting in effort.

Quite a few of you have brought up Google's AI-generated search results. It's certainly one of the ways AI is appearing in our day-to-day lives, even when we don't seek it out.

AI may be tightening jobs market, but some roles could see stronger demand
While AI is fast becoming ubiquitous in everyday life, there's still limited evidence it has caused widespread job losses.
That's according to a recent Deloitte report, which dubbed 2026 "the year of AI" and offered hope to some occupations it predicts will see a stronger demand when combined with AI.
Those jobs, which are listed below, includes roles like CEOs, teachers and nurses where "AI can boost productivity, but the human element is still critical," Deloitte Access Economics partner David Rumbens said.
However, the list of jobs most exposed to AI has also grown.
What was once concentrated in clerical and administrative roles now extends into professional and managerial occupations, many requiring higher levels of education and expertise.
You can read more of this story by the ABC's national work reporter Bronwyn Herbert.
Key Event
Can workplaces use AI to record us?
My manager has advised that our calls will soon be recorded for preparing training data. I'm concerned about giving my voice, my words, to my workplace and AI vendors to have ownership over. Can workplaces own our words, and can this part of our identity just be harvested and given away?
- Sam
As workplaces integrate AI into everyday technology, people are weighing up the benefits versus concerns. ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson has answered this question from Sam.
That's an interesting (and a little unsettling) one! The short answer is there might not be a lot you can do.
The longer answer is there's a bit of law that can impact recording for AI training. Some Australian states have laws against one person in a conversation recording the other without permission. There's Australia's privacy law, which essentially rules that, most of the time, data can only be used for the purpose that it is collected for. But if your boss has told you about it and made it clear it's for training AI models, neither of those protections would apply.
My suggestion would be to ask for as much information as possible about what they're collecting and for what purpose. Then you can go see your union or community legal centre for some advice. Also, please send me an email because I am very interested in this, too!
Regional and remote communities still dealing with mobile black spots
We've been talking a lot about how new technology has been impacting Australians.
But what about when they lose access to old technology?

Good question, Ian! Associate Professor Lazarescu has an answer below.
There is no way to avoid bias in the results, and yes, money will be a big factor.
It is, in my opinion, a critical issue with all the models that are being trained in the sense that one can manipulate the training to get a specific outcome.
To make matters worse, the vetting of the training data is non-existent. The models just read in what they are "fed" and no-one has the means or time to check if the data is correct or valid.
My advice is to take everything that the AI generates with a mountain of salt.

US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:34:41 UTC
10:34:41 KST

A US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as the Trump administration remains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.
On Tuesday, the Marine Mineral Administration (MMA), an agency under the US department of the interior, released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28m hectares (69m acres) of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.
The leases would allow companies to explore the seabed and potentially extract deposits of critical minerals – known as polymetallic nodules – that could be used in batteries, electronics and defence technologies. Many environmental groups have opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.
The Northern Mariana Islands is a self-governing commonwealth of the United States, while Guam is an unincorporated territory of the US.
The governor of the Northern Marianas, David Apatang, has said his government would approach the Trump administration’s proposal “with extreme caution”.
Apatang, while acknowledging the strategic importance of critical minerals, said it was necessary that “no activity, survey or otherwise, takes place without rigorous scientific baseline studies, complete transparency, and explicit protections for our marine resources”.
He said his administration would “thoroughly examine the proposed terms over the next 60 days to ensure that the ecological integrity of our waters and the long-term wellbeing of the [Northern Marianas] are fully safeguarded”.
The Guardian approached the Marine Mineral Administration for comment.
In an earlier statement, the MMA said it had completed an environmental review of proposed commercial leases for critical minerals in the Marianas area. The MMA said it would consider comments from the governor.
A statement from the office of the governor of Guam acknowledged the Trump administration’s focus on national security and strategic needs, but added: “National security cannot mean asking the people of the Pacific to accept environmental risks before those risks are fully understood.
“We’re unequivocally opposed to the deep sea mining efforts in this region,” said Guam’s lieutenant governor, Joshua Tenorio.
He told the Guardian: “The department of interior is giving assurances that mining activity is not going to commence with the awarding of these licences, [but] I think that this is a matter where we can’t really trust that because this has been rapidly evolving.”
The proposed lease notice for deep sea exploration in the Marianas region came just weeks after the initiation of a leasing process for 12.4m hectares (31m acres) of American Samoa’s seafloor, with plans to award contracts in November.
The governor of American Samoa, Nikolau Pula, said his government remained opposed to deep sea mining, noting that untested extraction processes could harm the territory’s tuna industry, which fuels its economy.
On 19 August, environmental groups in American Samoa and Hawaii launched legal proceedings against the US government to halt the proposed auction of seafloor permits around the islands, alleging that federal agencies failed to evaluate the destructive impact mineral extractions could have on marine ecosystems.
In a Hawaii court, Fa’asao Ameika Samoa and the Conservation Council for Hawaii warned that the extraction machinery “can destroy nearly all life in its path” and “stirs up sediments that can introduce toxic substances into the food web and smother seafloor ecosystems”.
“Even just exploring for seabed minerals introduces extremely loud noise into the marine environment that can harm marine mammals and other wildlife,” the complaint reads.
The Marine Mineral Administration was approached about the concerns over the American Samoa leasing process.

Shares of Alibaba fell eight percent to HK$113.00 soon after the stock market opened on Monday morning, and hours after the company announced the launch of an HK$80-billion, or US$10.2 billion, share placement to fund artificial intelligence-related development.
The shares closed at HK$123.00 on Friday.
The share placement by the Chinese e-commerce and cloud computing giant would mark the largest-ever primary follow-on offering by a Hong Kong-listed company.
It would rank as the world's third-largest primary follow-on share sale this year after offerings from Alphabet and Intel.
The company said it intends to use 100 percent of the net proceeds from the placement to invest in its "full stack" AI capabilities, a category that includes chips, infrastructure and the development and deployment of AI models.
A term sheet reviewed by Reuters showed Alibaba planned to sell 710 million ordinary shares at HK$112.70 a share. 
That represented a 3.6 percent discount to its Friday's closing price.
In its announcement, Alibaba did not reveal additional details on its investment plans by category of its planned AI-related investment.
It did not comment beyond its regulatory disclosure.
Last week, Alibaba reported its results for the April-to-June quarter, saying it had already spent nearly half of its three-year capex investment plan. 
It said its expected payback on AI-related investments was on track to fall to 2.5 years from three years, driven by surging demand.
Alibaba's net profit for the quarter fell 75 percent from a year earlier as it ramped up its AI-related capital expenditures.
"In order to be able to capture that future growth, we first need to make these capex investments to build out the necessary compute capacity," CEO Eddie Wu said on an earnings call.
The company's share offering has been met with strong demand from investors, including sovereign wealth funds, two people familiar with the deal told Reuters. 
The share placement was not registered under US securities laws as an offshore transaction, meaning American investors were not eligible to participate, Alibaba said. (Reuters)
