Remembering Zhu Rongji and understanding his legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:30:06 UTC
10:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Publisher's Pen
Remembering Zhu Rongji and understanding his legacy
The late Chinese premier showed genuine love and support for Hong Kong and kept ‘one country, two systems’ dear to his heart
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Tammy Tam is the Publisher of the South China Morning Post, overseeing both editorial and business strategy and operations to drive the publication’s development and commercial growth. 
“History doesn’t repeat itself but it often rhymes.” This famous quote, widely attributed to Mark Twain, keeps playing in my mind as China mourns the death of former premier Zhu Rongji and reflects on his legacy.
It was early afternoon on August 12 when I received a message from a friend on the mainland that made my heart sink: “Our much-respected Premier Zhu left us this morning!”
As we anxiously waited for the official confirmation that would launch us into a frantically busy news day, my mind went back to those years when I, as a journalist, had multiple opportunities to encounter Zhu up close. I was as impressed by his statesmanship, wisdom and wit on the international stage as I was touched by the genuine love he showed Hong Kong.
Zhu became the fifth premier of China in March 1998 as the country was undergoing a tremendous transformation from decades of a planned economy to a “market economy with Chinese characteristics” under then-president Jiang Zemin. It was only about nine months after Hong Kong’s return to Chinese sovereignty following more than a century of British colonial rule.
It was an uncertain but exciting time, when the “one country, two systems” governing principle for Hong Kong was being rolled out. The implementation of the special formula designed by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and officially recognised in China’s constitution – which empowered the establishment of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and the legislation of the Basic Law – was well received but still a work in progress.
Back then there were plenty of concerns, doubts and political narratives about it being “over” for Hong Kong, and some of that remains to this day, although the facts speak louder about the progress the city has made and its transformation for the better after its return to the motherland. Zhu and Jiang kept one country, two systems dear to their hearts, and China’s current leadership has neither changed that approach nor intends to.

Rush to vaccinate little penguins against H5N1 as another seal is diagnosed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:22:08 UTC
10:22:08 KST

In brief
- Five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on Monday, including a long-nosed fur seal.
- 5,000 little penguins in Victoria are receiving a vaccine to protect them against the deadly virus.
Bird flu has likely spread to a second seal, one day after the first mammal in Australia was confirmed to have contracted the virus.
Five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on Monday, including a long-nosed fur seal at The Pages Conservation Park, the state's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said in a statement on Monday morning.
The Pages — which covers two small islands between Kangaroo Island and the mainland — is a haven for the endangered Australian sea lion.
The fur seal has been tested for bird flu, with results expected in the coming days.
The first positive case of the virus in a mammal was confirmed on Sunday in a long-nosed fur seal at Beachport, 300km south of Adelaide, which authorities believed was contracted from wild birds.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Before the new case was announced, Environment Minister Murray Watt said the spread from birds to mammals was inevitable and the government was examining whether further vaccination programs were needed.
"We are likely to see mass mortalities of birds and mammals, and I know that is a very distressing thing for Australians to hear. But we also need to be realistic," he told ABC TV on Monday.
"This is what we've seen happen overseas. Australia is very fortunate that we've been the last continent on Earth to have this strain of bird flu happen. But we are likely to see those kind of events as we have overseas."
Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the federal government was investigating whether bird flu vaccines were available for use in mammals.
"There are trials underway in North America, in California and Hawaii, and this is using a vaccine that's been developed for cattle," she told ABC radio.
"There certainly is nothing commercially available, but we do continue to look at that research."
Bird flu vaccinations have been rolled out to at-risk species, including the little penguins on Victoria's Phillip Island.
Many were corralled into pens to receive the first of two vaccinations on Sunday night.
With case numbers on the rise, authorities have stepped in to do what they can to defend the 5,000-strong colony.
The penguins' nightly ritual of returning to the same burrow, along the same path, made them ideal candidates for vaccination, Phillip Island Nature Parks reserve manager Ben Thomas said.
As a world-first in scale, the process has taken some experimentation and fine-tuning.
"We've had our teams out late into the night for a week now and learning a lot along the process," Thomas said.
"We started on some of the quieter penguin pathways to fine-tune the whole process and get it working as quickly as we can, so we can process as many penguins as we can each night.
"We've now moved to the western end of the penguin parade, where the larger numbers are, and it's working really well."
A further 600 penguins were vaccinated over the weekend, taking the total number that have received a first dose at Phillip Island and St Kilda to about 1,000.

"The British announcement is a small step in a much larger and longer-term project that could lead to Ukraine making its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile in several years' time. But the move is likely to trigger further criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high," the Guardian noted.
Burnham will also announce that the UK will help France establish long-range missile assembly lines in Ukraine, a move French President Emmanuel Macron promised last month.
The UK announcement is a small step within a much larger, long-term project that could eventually enable Ukraine to produce its own long-range versions of the Storm Shadow cruise missile.
The Guardian suggested that the move is likely to trigger another wave of criticism from Moscow at a time when tensions between the UK and Russia are already high.
Background:
- Last week, Russia accused the UK of deliberately escalating the conflict by allowing Ukraine to carry out attacks using British-made drones, warning that the deeper UK's involvement becomes, "the higher the price it will pay".
- Over the weekend, it emerged that Russia had recalled its ambassador to London without appointing a replacement, prompting speculation that Moscow was reducing its diplomatic presence in the UK.
- Burnham stressed that Russian threats would not weaken UK's support for Ukraine, saying last week: "We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need, and that won't change."
- On 24 August, Burnham will use a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, comprising 34 countries that have pledged to help ensure Ukraine's security in the event of a peace deal with Russia, to underline this commitment.
- The meeting will be chaired by Burnham and Macron, who will join by video link. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will also take part in the online conference, during which leaders will discuss ways to help Ukraine withstand the recent wave of long-range attacks.
- During his stay in Kyiv, Burnham will attend events marking Ukraine's Independence Day, details of which are being kept secret amid fears of a major Russian attack. The UK PM is also expected to receive an award in recognition of his country's support for Ukraine.

National rental prices rise to half average Australian income
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:13:04 UTC
10:13:04 KST

Rents increase to more than half median take-home pay across capitals
In short:
Housing advocacy group Everybody's Home has found renting a unit now costs more than half the median take-home pay of a single worker in every Australian capital city.
For someone earning $70,000, median Sydney rent would take 69 per cent of their weekly pay, while even Adelaide — the cheapest capital — would cost more than half their pay.
What's next?
The advocacy group is calling for more social housing and limits on rental increases.
The average apartment now costs half of the average Australian income to rent, with prices exceeding the 30 per cent housing stress mark even for six-figure earners, according to a new report.
Housing advocacy group Everybody's Home has found renting a unit now costs more than half the median take-home pay of a single worker in every Australian capital city.
The 2026 Priced Out report found apartments on average nationally cost $614 per week, making up 56 per cent of the take-home income of someone earning $70,000 — close to Australia's median income of $74,100.
Everybody’s Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said this was a "crisis that continues to get worse for the country's renters".
"We now see people earning really high incomes are still spending more than a third of their income on rent. If you are earning $130,000 a year, you are still spending more than a third on rent," she said.
"If you are earning an average income between $70,000 and $80,000 and living in a capital city, you are spending two-thirds of your income to afford the average rent.
"We are seeing across the board renters can't avoid rental stress anywhere in the country, which is dire."
The report found northern WA, the Gold Coast and Sydney were the three most expensive places to rent, followed by the Sunshine Coast and Perth.
"For a long time Sydney was ground zero for the crisis and it is still really bad news, shocking if you are a renter in Sydney," Ms Azize said.
"This year one of the most expensive... capital cities in the country is Perth and WA across the board has some really dire results.
"The Gold Coast has been surging every year that we have done this report and it is getting expensive to rent on the Gold Coast, even if you are earning $130,000 a year, you can't afford to rent on the Gold Coast. You would need to be in a couple or a multi-income family to make that work."
The report found, for someone earning $70,000, median Sydney rent would take 69 per cent of their weekly pay, while even Adelaide — the cheapest capital — would cost more than half.
Since the March 2025 Priced Out report, rents on average have increased by $48 a week — almost $2,500 a year.
This year's report found for an employee on $40,000, that increase would be the equivalent of 4.4 weeks of work per year; an employee on $70,000, 3.1 weeks and for someone earning $130,000 1.6 weeks.
Changes and recommendations
Changes to housing policy in this year's budget were predicted by the government to result in a median rental increase of $2 a week.
However, Ms Azize said rents had been surging by about 10 per cent every single year.
"I think it's a bit of an insult to people's intelligence when the industry comes out and says that any rent increases from here are going to be down to these changes," she said.
"Any renter in Australia knows that they get whacked with a huge rent increase every single year."
However, she said changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were positive overall.
"They're changes that we've been pushing for a really long time," she said.
"They're really good news for anyone who wants to make the housing system fairer, especially those renters who are trying to save to buy.
"But what these results show us is that the federal government and state and territory governments especially now really need to turn their attention to renters and taking some steps to limit rent increases because there's really only so much that people can afford to pay."
The report recommends several recommendations, including the Australian government committing to build 940,000 public and community homes over the next 15 years; introducing limits on the number and amount of rent increases during a tenancy and ending no-grounds evictions.
"For the past four decades we've seen the federal government especially really step back from funding housing, from playing a role, and they're leaving it entirely to the private sector," Ms Azize said.
"We can see that over that same period renting has become incredibly expensive.
"So we need to see the government step back in.
"When you look around the world at the countries that are actually doing a good job of turning around their housing crisis or better yet avoiding it altogether, they're the countries where the government is playing a really big role in providing housing. They're not just leaving it to the private sector."

KPMG to cut almost 400 jobs after audit leaks scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:06:37 UTC
10:06:37 KST

KPMG to cut almost 400 jobs from Australian arm as it loses contracts after audit leaks scandal
In short:
Accounting firm KPMG is cutting hundreds of jobs after revenue fell as a result of a recent audit inquiry.
One number to know:
Accounting firm KPMG says it will cut 27 partners and about 360 staff from its local arm, and revamp its structure as it grapples with lower revenue from lost contracts following the audit leaks scandal.
The firm's revenue fell from $2.28 billion the previous year, to $2.26 billion in the 2026 financial year, and KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams expected more revenue falls.
KPMG has been unable to retain most of its ongoing government contracts after allegations KPMG audit partners misused client data and then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it.
In March, Labor senator Deborah O'Neill shared with parliament a whistleblower's allegations that confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus.
And earlier this month, the firm's current and former partners were hauled before a federal inquiry probing why the firm allegedly shared client information and ignored the whistleblower's allegations when they first surfaced.
The job cuts at KPMG's Australian arm were widely expected as the firm reportedly sought financial support from KPMG International to remain solvent.
KPMG is one of the "big four" accounting firms, which have taken a hit to their bottom line from getting fewer ongoing government consulting contracts, following the earlier tax leaks controversy at PricewaterhouseCoopers.
Mr Sams said in a statement the firm was cutting 5 per cent of its workforce, primarily in its consulting arm, "in response to continued economic weakness, difficult market conditions and the impact of the firm's conduct and whistleblower matters".
This includes 27 partners and about 360 employees.
"This is not a decision that has been taken lightly, and we know it will have a very real impact on people,"
With demand for consulting remaining weaker, "most of the roles affected will be in our consulting business".
"Changes to our business and the professional services landscape have also reduced the need for some roles in business services," he said.
"Our immediate focus is on treating everyone impacted with care, dignity and respect. We are providing practical support and making wellbeing support central to the process."
More job cuts could follow
The firm will also restructure so that its mid-market and private deals team joins deal advisory and infrastructure, while its advisory team joins consulting.
These changes would align KPMG Australia more closely with its global advisory services.
The firm will also begin consultation on "a small number of award-based roles".
Mr Sams said more cuts could follow.
"The changes announced today are an important step in the longer work of renewing and rebuilding our firm,"
The firm was undertaking "internal and external reviews" in the wake of the whistleblower's allegations, which he said "will be completed in the coming months".
"Their findings will inform the next phase of our action plan and help ensure we take all necessary action," he said.
Mr Sams thanked the firm's staff after a "very challenging year".
"They [KPMG employees] continued to deliver outstanding work for more than 13,000 clients, while supporting one another through a difficult period for the firm," he said.
"Our total revenue was slightly lower than last year, and below our expectations."
Consulting takes a hit, audit and tax divisions grow
While consulting took a hit, revenue grew in four out of five divisions, led by audit and assurance, up 11 per cent, and tax and legal, up 10.9 per cent.
"We also continued to invest significantly in technology and build our AI capability, helping our people work more effectively and deliver better outcomes for clients."
But the firm needed to "be clear about the outlook".
"We expect difficult market conditions to continue in FY27 and beyond,"
"Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes," he said.
"The professional services sector is also changing rapidly as client expectations evolve, AI reshapes the way services are delivered, and government spending on consultants remains lower.
"We also recognise the challenges created by our own failings, and the work we must continue to do to rebuild trust.
"While these conditions are likely to persist, we remain focused on what we can control. We will continue to monitor performance closely, act when needed and consider carefully how the firm needs to be set up for the future."

SYDNEY, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A man has been arrested after police seized explosives, a firearm and ammunition from a home in the eastern Australian state of New South Wales (NSW).
The NSW Police Force said in a statement on Monday that a search warrant was executed at a home in the city of Wagga Wagga, 380 km southwest of Sydney, on Thursday after officers located small quantities of cocaine and MDMA during a search of a 30-year-old man.
During the search of the home, police allegedly located two improvised explosive devices.
The bomb disposal unit was deployed and the location was subsequently declared safe. The search resumed and officers allegedly found a privately made firearm, ammunition, cannabis seeds and testosterone.
The 30-year-old man was charged with 16 offenses, including two counts of manufacturing military-style weapons without a permit, which carry a maximum penalty of 20 years' imprisonment.
Police said he was refused bail during an initial court appearance on Friday and will return to court in October. ■

Ukraine: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv in show of support on Ukraine's Independence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
01:04:00 UTC
10:04:00 KST

Ukraine news: UK PM Burnham arrives in Kyiv to show support
Published August 24, 2026last updated August 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Andy Burnham visits Kyiv on his first overseas trip since becoming the UK's prime minister
- Burnham is set to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing and meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
- Ukraine has been calling for its allies to supply more air defenses and apply more pressure on Russia, which has escalated its attacks on civilians in recent weeks
- The meeting coincides with the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence from the Soviet Union
- Ukraine hits facilities belonging to Russia's second-biggest e-commerce website Ozon
- The United Nations Security Council is scheduled to hold a special session on Ukraine later on Monday
Here is a roundup of the main developments related to Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, August 24, 2026:
Burnham arrive in Ukraine for independence day
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa have arrived in Kyiv.
Burnham is on his first international visit since becoming prime minister.
He was welcomed by Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, at the train station.
Burnham and Costa will meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later and attend Ukraine's Independence Day celebrations.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldova's President Maia Sandu and Estonia's President Alar Karis, along with Sybiha, were also in the Kyiv to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence.
Russia says it hit fuel tanker near Odesa
Russia's Defence Ministry has said its forces struck a tanker carrying fuel and lubricants for Ukrainian troops at the port of Pivdennyi near the southern city of Odesa.
The ministry said the attack also hit port infrastructure used to unload and store military cargo.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the Russian claims.
Ukraine stepping up attacks on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon
Ukraine has struck warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon on three consecutive days, with the company reporting another logistics center on fire.
The attacks mark an expansion of Kyiv's campaign against Russian logistics infrastructure after weeks of strikes on Wildberries, the country's largest online retailer.
Kyiv has accused Wildberries of supplying components to the Russian military.
Ozon said a "major fire" broke out at one of its logistics centers in the southern Krasnodar region following a drone attack.
"All systems operated as designed, and we promptly evacuated staff. Preliminarily, there are no casualties," the company said on Telegram.
On Sunday, Ozon said a drone attack caused a fire at its logistics hub in the central Orenburg region, forcing the warehouse to suspend operations.
That came a day after another Ozon center was hit in neighboring Samara, where the company said an unspecified number of employees were wounded.
WATCH — Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia?
Russia has a growing manpower problem in its war against Ukraine. Rumors are spreading, and recent border queues near Georgia are drawing comparisons to the chaos of 2022.
Is Russia quietly preparing another draft? DW's Shannon Redstall explains.
Why is Ukraine struggling to defend itself against Russian air attacks?
In recent weeks and months, Russia has intensified its airstrikes on Ukraine, regularly firing dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, often at civilian targets.
To defend itself, Ukraine relies on advanced, foreign-made weapons systems — most importantly, US Patriot missiles.
The US war with Iran has depleted its own stockpiles, and Washington has resisted providing Kyiv with large numbers of missiles, leaving Ukraine more exposed to Russian bombs.
Even before the war with Iran, US support for Ukraine had wavered after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Trump, who had an angry public spat with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House, has sought to mend ties with Russia's Vladimir Putin, and ordered a pause of US military aid to Kyiv.
Over the weekend, Zelenskyy revealed that deliveries of Patriot interceptors had dropped by 50% since 2023.
"Over the entire year of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 — 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," he said. "For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264."
Debris from Ukrainian drone kills two children in southern Russia: governor
Falling debris from a Ukrainian drone attack landed on a childcare facility in Krasnodar, southern Russia, killing two children, the regional governor said early on Monday.
Seven other children and two adults were wounded in the attack, Veniamin Kondratyev said on Telegram. He added that a fire started at a warehouse after a drone fell on it.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, said there was a "major fire" at one of its logistics centers in Krasnodar as a result of a drone attack.
Another Ozon logistics complex in Dagestan was also hit, sparking a massive fire, Ukrainian monitor Exilenova+ reported. If confirmed, it would be the third Ozon facility to be struck on Monday.
Ukraine has also hit warehouses belonging to Russia's other major e-commerce website, Wildberries, in recent weeks.
While Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure, it has also struck commercial hubs and warehouses, which are easier targets and less heavily defended than military or energy sites. The attacks have inflicted losses worth billions of dollars.
Russian strike on Kharkiv kills 3
At least three people were killed after a Russian attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv, the local governor said on Telegram.
Oleh Syniehuhov said eight people were rescued by the emergency services, which were still working to identify other potential casualties.
Kharkiv is Ukraine's second-largest city, and lies around 30 kilometers (about 18 miles) from the border with Russia.
IN DEPTH: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?
Empty pumps, long waits: Attacks on oil refineries have left Russia increasingly short of fuel. Dissident Russian economists say growing anger about shortages among ordinary Russians could help end the war in Ukraine.
Learn more about how Ukraine's drone strikes inside Russia are triggering a fuel crisis that could bring about the end of the war in this report.
Ex-Ukrainian minister didn't call for elections until dismissed from government, lawmaker tells DW
Dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for elections earlier this week, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy comes under unprecedented pressure domestically.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion began more than four years ago. Zelenskyy has resisted holding elections while the country remains at war with Russia.
Ukrainian Member of Parliament Yevheniia Kravchuk spoke to DW from Kyiv about the prospect of Ukraine holding elections while still fighting the Russian invasion.
Here's what Kravchuk had to say about Fedorov's appeal for elections:
"You know, Mykhailo wasn't speaking about elections when he was in the government for seven years, almost seven years. So, the first time he started to speak about it was when he basically lost his position in the government during the reshuffle."
On the prospect of a wartime poll, she said:
"War is not a normal situation for people, for elections — it's not normal to live. But we have to; it's been almost five years.
Martial law does put restrictions, and these restrictions are there for a reason. And it is because Russians are throwing missiles at supermarkets."
Watch this video for more of Yevheniia Kravchuk's interview with DW News, as well as insight from Harry Nedelcu, a geopolitics expert at Rasmussen Global consultancy in Brussels:
EU pledges 'as much support as necessary'
The European Union has pledged its continued backing for Ukraine as the country celebrates its 35th Independence Day on Monday.
"We will continue to provide as much support as necessary, for as long as necessary — during the war, in peace negotiations and in reconstruction," EU Council President Antonio Costa said, according to an EU statement.
Costa added that EU sanctions on Russia were impacting its war coffers, and pledged to "intensify the pressure" until Moscow ends its war of aggression.
He also reiterated the bloc's position that Ukraine will one day become an EU member.
"Ukraine’s future in the European Union is the best guarantee of security and long-term democratic stability — for Ukraine and for Europe as a whole."
Costa will personally attend the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv on Monday.
UK PM Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv in first trip abroad
The United Kingdom's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is visiting Ukraine on Monday, on his first international trip since taking office.
Burnham, who will co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine's foreign backers, is also set to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Several other world leaders, including co-chairs German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, as well as European Council President Antonio Costa and leaders from the Nordic and Baltic countries, will take part in the meeting, some of them in person and others remotely via video conference.
The meeting comes as Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union (USSR).
During his visit, Burnham will confirm that the UK has agreed to allow European weapons manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on British parts of the SCALP long-range missile to set up assembly lines in Ukraine, Downing Street said in a statement.
"On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes," Burnham said in a statement.
"Our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security," the British leader added.
The UK has been one of Ukraine's strongest international backers since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Britain has pledged more than 25 billion pounds ($34 billion, €29 billion) in military and civilian support so far and was the first nation to provide long-range strike weapons to Ukraine for defensive purposes in 2023, Downing Street said.
Burnham's trip to Kyiv comes after Zelenskyy traveled to the UK last month as the new prime minister's first foreign guest.
Welcome to our coverage
Thank you for joining us as we bring you updates from the war in Ukraine, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv on Monday.
The meeting comes as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who is under mounting political pressure at home, has been urging his country's Western allies to increase their air defense supplies amid intensifying Russian airstrikes.
Burnham, who welcomed Zelenskyy to the UK as his first international guest last month, is expected to reassert the UK's support for Ukraine's defense against Russia's invasion.
Burnham's trip, his first outside of the UK since taking office in July, coincides with Ukraine's 35th independence day.

The United Kingdom's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is visiting Ukraine on Monday, on his first international trip since taking office.
Burnham, who will co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine's foreign backers, is also set to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Several other world leaders, including co-chairs German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, as well as European Council President Antonio Costa and leaders from the Nordic and Baltic countries, will take part in the meeting, some of them in person and others remotely via video conference.

The UK has been one of Ukraine's strongest international backers since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Britain has pledged more than 25 billion pounds ($34 billion, €29 billion) in military and civilian support so far and was the first nation to provide long-range strike weapons to Ukraine for defensive purposes in 2023, Downing Street said.

A party led by allies of Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev won a landslide in parliamentary elections on Sunday, hours after he hinted that he may stay in power beyond his current term.
The Adilet party won 71.8 per cent of votes in the election to a new single-chamber parliament, according to an exit poll released on state television. The Auyl party representing agrarian interests was second with 6.4 per cent.
“I have the right to be re‑elected in accordance with the law,” Tokayev told reporters earlier, after casting his vote, in response to a question on whether he would seek another term. “Perhaps next year I’ll be able to give you a more specific answer.”
Adilet, which means Justice, is led by one of Tokayev’s former top aides with backing from business leaders who have gained influence during his presidency. It was founded only in May, and the former ruling Amanat party, which won the 2023 parliamentary elections, announced in June that it was merging with Adilet.
Seven parties contested 145 seats allocated by party list for a five-year term in the new parliament. Five had cleared the 5 per cent threshold, according to the exit poll conducted by the Institute of Eurasian Integration, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 1 percentage point. Voter turnout was 74.19 per cent, according to the country’s central election commission.
The new chamber is the latest element of a constitutional overhaul initiated by Tokayev following deadly 2022 riots that he called an attempted coup in the giant former Soviet republic of about 20 million people. It replaces the previous bicameral parliament, following a referendum in March that also established the post of vice-president, who would succeed the head of state in the event of an early departure from office.

Why Moderna’s and Merck’s cancer vaccine is a breakthrough for mRNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:50:00 UTC
09:50:00 KST

Why Moderna’s and Merck’s cancer vaccine is a breakthrough for mRNA
- Moderna and Merck's mRNA-based cancer vaccine showed success in a large trial, lowering melanoma recurrence and boosting hope for mRNA cancer treatments.
- The vaccine is personalised, using tumour mutations to train the immune system to target specific cancer cells and prevent recurrence after surgery.
- mRNA vaccines differ from other treatments by preparing the immune system to recognise unique tumours; research continues for other cancers and rare diseases.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The announcement by Moderna and Merck & Co that a messenger RNA-based cancer vaccine had lowered the recurrence rate for melanoma in a final-stage trial is a watershed moment for cancer vaccine research.
It is the first time that an mRNA-based cancer vaccine has succeeded in a large-scale study.
While the companies did not disclose details about the results, the success has bolstered hopes that mRNA-based shots could some day play a broad role in fighting one of the world’s leading causes of death.
The results also signal a second act for a technology that encountered widespread scepticism during the Covid-19 pandemic among those angered by vaccine mandates or uneasy about the shot’s rapid development.
The technology continues to get pushback today, including from influential figures like US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
But investors and many in the scientific community were cheered by the new findings. Moderna shares rose 177 per cent the day the news was announced.
The results could boost enthusiasm for cancer vaccine research in general.
Such vaccines have been pursued for decades by scientists, but they have frequently had lacklustre results in all-important human trials.
How do mRNA vaccines work?
Traditionally, vaccines have worked by exposing the immune system to a weakened or inactivated form of a disease-causing organism, or to a harmless piece of one, so that the body learns to recognise and fight it.
Vaccines using mRNA take a different approach.
They temporarily turn some of the body’s cells into tiny vaccine-making factories.
The shots contain laboratory-made mRNA, which carries instructions telling those cells to make a particular protein associated with the disease.
The immune system recognises that protein and produces antibodies to attack it.
In the case of Covid-19 vaccines, the mRNA instructs cells to make the spike protein found on the surface of SARS-CoV-2.
That trains the immune system to recognise the spike and respond quickly if it later encounters the virus.
How can an mRNA vaccine treat cancer?
It turns out that essentially the same mRNA technology used for Covid-19 and the flu – which is also being studied for other infectious diseases – can be employed to train the immune system to attack cancer.
This type of vaccine is not used to prevent cancer, but would instead be deployed to treat cancer already present, often to prevent a recurrence in patients who have had surgery.
Such vaccines contain mRNA with instructions for making fragments of mutated proteins produced by cancer cells.
Once inside the body, the mRNA instructs cells to produce the mutated protein fragments, so-called neoantigens.
The goal is to prompt the immune system to recognise the mutated proteins, triggering an immune response against the cancer.
Why are mRNA vaccines personalised?
Cancer cells typically contain mutated proteins that, in theory, can be recognised by the immune system.
But no two tumours are exactly the same, and mutations can vary widely among patients with the same type of cancer.
Over the years, it has proven difficult to come up with a one-size-fits-all vaccine that consistently generates a strong immune system response against tumours, although researchers are still working on it.
Among other problems, tumours might be able to evade an immune response targeted against a single distinguishing feature.
To create personalised vaccines, scientists take samples from an individual patient’s tumours and put it through an algorithm to determine which mutations are most likely to result in an immune response.
For the Merck and Moderna shot, the companies can put up to 34 mutations into a personalised shot, which is sent back to the patient’s doctor to administer to the patient.
“Thirty-four is quite a lot of chances, of shots on goal,” said Jane Healy, head of oncology early development at Merck, which has been working with Moderna on the cancer vaccine approach for more than a decade. That ensures the vaccine is “covering a sufficient amount of the spectrum of a patient’s cancer”.
How are mRNA cancer vaccines different from other cancer treatments?
Cancer vaccines work in a very different way from other cancer treatments such as chemotherapy, targeted pills and immunotherapy.
Chemotherapy poisons fast-dividing cells, while newer targeted medicines block particular growth-promoting proteins on cancer cells.
Bestselling immunity-boosting drugs already on the market, including Merck’s Keytruda and Opdivo from Bristol Myers Squibb, are antibodies that disable a key method that cancer cells use to evade an immune response against them.
But off-the-shelf immunotherapy drugs do not prepare the immune system to recognise and target an individual’s specific tumour.
This is what personalised cancer vaccines aim to do, which technically are treatments, not preventative shots.
Because it is thought this approach will work well against small volumes of cancer cells, many vaccines, such as the Merck-Moderna trial in melanoma, aim to prevent recurrences in patients who are at high risk of the cancer coming back after surgery.
Much is still unknown about the melanoma results, including the magnitude of the benefit.
Findings from the vaccine trial will be reported at an upcoming scientific meeting. In particular, scientists do not yet know whether people who got the vaccine will live longer, and the trial is continuing in order to gather long-term results.
What other diseases are mRNA treatments being tested against?
In addition to melanoma, Merck and Moderna are testing their personalised cancer approach for lung cancer, bladder tumours and kidney cancer.
Meanwhile, Germany’s BioNTech and Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche Holding are testing their own mRNA-based personalised cancer vaccine to treat both pancreatic cancer and colon cancer.
BioNTech is working on a different mRNA technology that uses a standardised shot to treat patients with advanced lung cancer and head and neck cancer.
Rare diseases are another potential use for mRNA technology.
Moderna is testing its mRNA technology to treat metabolic diseases including propionic acidemia and methylmalonic acidemia. BLOOMBERG

The Israeli army has used as much ammunition in less than three years of war as it did over the previous three decades, the Israeli newspaper Maariv reported, pointing to mounting strain on its personnel, equipment, and finances.
Israeli Air Force activity during the period was also equivalent to roughly nine years of operations under normal conditions, whilst tanks and armoured personnel carriers have gone through thousands of engines, the newspaper said.
Maariv said military hardware could be replaced or repaired but warned that the toll on personnel was far harder to reverse.
The army alone, excluding other Israeli security agencies, has lost 1,138 personnel, whilst 11,730 others have been recognised as suffering physical or psychological injuries, according to the report, with thousands more suffering psychological trauma likely to be added.
Personnel fatigue
Signs of strain are also emerging among career soldiers, with a significant number offered command positions opting instead for less demanding rear roles or leaving military service altogether.
Meanwhile, the Israeli army is keeping an average of 53,000 reservists on active duty each day.
Maariv said a single month of reserve service last year cost around 2.1 billion shekels ($703 million), equivalent to the price of seven F-35 fighter jets or 70 Merkava tanks.
Israeli forces are currently deployed across what the newspaper described as three "security belts" in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, in addition to the occupied West Bank, which consumes the largest share of military manpower.
Five Israeli battalions are deployed along the so-called yellow line in Gaza, covering roughly 60 percent of the enclave, alongside two reinforced battalions on the border.

Stranded French tourist dies in Death Valley during 47 deg C heat
Alexandra E. Petri

- The tourist, Pierre Michel Formosa, collapsed after walking about 2km; his companion reached help and alerted authorities who found Formosa deceased.
- Death Valley is known for deadly extreme heat; similar heat-related deaths have occurred recently at Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona.
AI generated
DEATH VALLEY, California – A French tourist visiting Death Valley National Park in California died after he and a companion were stranded on a remote road as temperatures reached 47 deg C, the National Park Service said on Aug 21.
The tourist, Pierre Michel Formosa, 68, and his travel companion, who was also from France, were headed on West Side Road on Aug 17 when the car got stuck in mud near Queen of Sheba Mine Road, the National Park Service said in a news release.
The two men walked across the salt flats towards Badwater Road to find help. Temperatures reached 46.7 deg C, with little chance of finding shade.
After about 2km, Formosa was unable to continue walking, the park service said. His friend, whom the authorities did not identify, continued towards Badwater Road, where he was helped by a passing driver.
Formosa’s companion reported what happened just after 2pm local time, and park service rangers and an Inyo County deputy began a search. A California Highway Patrol helicopter joined the search and found Formosa about 2.4km from Badwater Road.
Formosa was pronounced dead at the scene, the park service said.
The park service did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Aug 23. The Inyo County coroner, whom the National Park Service said would determine the cause and manner of death, did not respond to requests for comment.
The park is known for its extreme heat. The park’s website notes that summertime temperatures in Death Valley can reach as high as 54 deg C, with nighttime temperatures of up to 32 deg C.
The deaths of at least four hikers were reported in June at Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona from what appeared to be heat-related illnesses as temperatures peaked, officials said.
On June 16, the authorities found a 67-year-old man and a 68-year-old woman dead on the North Kaibab Trail.
On June 12, a 72-year-old man died on the South Kaibab Trail, officials said.

Independence Day of Ukraine – 35 Years of Freedom: How the State Was Born and What Defined Its Journey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:40:47 EEST
09:40:47 KST

Independence Day of Ukraine – 35 Years of Freedom: How the State Was Born and What Defined Its Journey
Kyiv • UNN
On August 24, 2026, Ukraine will celebrate the 35th anniversary of its independence. The country has journeyed from a post-Soviet state to a symbol of the struggle for freedom.
On August 24, 2026, Ukraine will mark the 35th anniversary of its independence. During this time, the country has journeyed from a young post-Soviet state to a country that has become one of the key symbols of the struggle for freedom in the world. Despite wars, economic crises, revolutions, and Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has not only preserved its independence but also formed its own political nation. UNN recalls how Ukrainian independence was born and which major achievements have become symbols of the past 35 years.
How Ukraine Became Independent
At the end of the 1980s, the Soviet Union was rapidly losing control over the union republics. The movement for sovereignty was growing increasingly stronger in Ukraine, and on July 16, 1990, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Ukraine.
The decisive moment came in August 1991. Following the failure of the attempted coup in Moscow, the Ukrainian parliament adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine on August 24. It was supported by 346 members of parliament.
From a Young State to a Country Fighting for Freedom
Over 35 years, Ukraine has endured difficult trials. The state developed its own economy, established the Armed Forces, adopted a Constitution, built democratic institutions, and gradually integrated into Europe.
At the same time, the country experienced two revolutions—the Orange Revolution in 2004 and the Revolution of Dignity in 2013–2014—which shaped its European development path.
After the occupation of Crimea and the outbreak of the war in Donbas in 2014, Ukraine launched large-scale military reform, and since February 24, 2022, has been defending its independence in a full-scale war against Russia.
35 Years of Independence: Key Moments in Ukraine’s History
Among the most important:
– the proclamation of Ukraine’s independence in 1991;
– the adoption of the Constitution of Ukraine in 1996;
– the renunciation of the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal;
– the Orange Revolution of 2004;
– the Revolution of Dignity of 2013–2014;
– the signing of the Association Agreement with the European Union;
– obtaining visa-free travel with the EU in 2017;
– the establishment of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine and the receipt of the Tomos;
– Ukraine obtaining EU candidate status in 2022;
– the beginning of negotiations on accession to the European Union;
– full-scale resistance to Russian aggression, which has become a symbol of the struggle for freedom for the entire world.
What Defined the 34th Year of Independence
Ukraine spent its last year of independence amid a full-scale war, yet continued to strengthen its international standing and develop its own defense capabilities. The state retained the support of key allies, expanded cooperation with the United States and European countries, and continued its path toward full membership in the European Union.
One of the main events was the opening of negotiations on Ukraine’s accession to the EU. At the same time, international partners continued to allocate multibillion-dollar assistance for defense, the country’s reconstruction, and the development of Ukraine’s defense-industrial complex.
At the same time, Ukraine substantially increased the production of its own long-range weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles. Ukrainian Defense Forces regularly struck military facilities, airfields, logistics centers, and enterprises of Russia’s military-industrial complex, demonstrating the ability to hit targets far beyond the front line.
Despite daily Russian attacks, Ukraine preserved the resilience of its state institutions, economy, and society. The 34th year of independence once again proved that the struggle for freedom remains for Ukrainians not only a historical choice but also a daily reality.
A Symbol of Resilience
Today, Independence Day carries a much deeper meaning for Ukrainians than it did in 1991.
If independence was then a political decision, it is now being fought for every day on the battlefield, on the diplomatic front, in the economy, through the volunteer movement, and through the work of millions of citizens.
Over 35 years, Ukraine has journeyed from a newly established state to a country that has become one of the main symbols of the struggle for freedom and the right to determine its own future.

The warring nations have not conducted military strikes against each other for weeks, but they also have not engaged in meaningful talks to end the six-month-old conflict.

“If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei wrote in a social media post. “Iran will regard any country’s participation in or support for America’s economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war.”
Bessent previously urged China to cooperate with the US, noting that China receives half of its oil imports from the Gulf region. A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington responded with a statement that “sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem”, while calling for diplomacy.
Iran’s economy was already under pressure from international sanctions before the US and Israeli attacks destroyed parts of its infrastructure.
Though Tehran remains outwardly defiant, Iranian officials have warned that further economic punishment could increase hardships, reignite unrest and further erode the Islamic republic’s legitimacy.

What is celebrated on August 24 in Ukraine and around the world

What is celebrated on August 24 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On August 24, Ukraine celebrates Independence Day, while around the world it is Alopecia Awareness Day. Saints are also honored, and unofficial holidays are observed.
On August 24, Ukraine celebrates its main national holiday — Independence Day. Around the world, this day is observed as International Alopecia Areata Day, reports UNN.
Independence Day of Ukraine
The country's main national holiday, established to commemorate the adoption by the Verkhovna Rada of the Ukrainian SSR of the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine in 1991. Ceremonial events, tributes to the memory of freedom fighters, and patriotic activities take place in all cities.
International Alopecia Areata Day
A campaign to raise public awareness of the autoimmune disease that causes hair loss and to support people affected by it.
Day of Engineering and Technical Professionals
In a number of countries and companies, the contribution of engineers, architects, and designers to infrastructure development is celebrated today.
World Strange Musical Instrument Day
An unofficial holiday for enthusiasts of experimental and avant-garde music, dedicated to rare, exotic, or handmade instruments that produce unusual sounds.
National Peach Pie Day
A popular culinary holiday, especially widespread in the United States, dedicated to baking sweet summer pies with fresh peaches.
International Rose Day / Bath Celebration
An unofficial day of relaxation dedicated to self-care and aromatherapy.
Day of Hieromartyr Euplus
According to the new calendar, on August 24 Orthodox believers commemorate Hieromartyr Euplus, who suffered for the Christian faith during the reigns of Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, as well as Venerable Martyr Zinaida. Venerable Theodosius of the Caves is also commemorated. In the folk calendar, this day was often called "Euplus Day" or the day for gathering early apples and preparing cellars for the cold weather.
According to the old calendar: on August 24, people commemorate Saint Martyr Archdeacon Lawrence (Lawrence Day). People believed that calm and quiet water on Lawrence foretold a warm autumn, while heavy rains indicated a harsh and rainy winter; traditionally, girls also collected morning dew on this day for beauty and health.

China postponed the planned launch of the "Chang’e-7" lunar mission, which was intended to study the Moon’s south pole, in particular to search for water ice in permanently shadowed craters. The China Manned Space Agency reported this on Sunday, UNN writes.
Details
The spacecraft was initially scheduled to launch in the coming days from the Wenchang Spacecraft Launch Site on Hainan Island. However, the space agency said that the mission did not meet the launch conditions and could not take place during this year’s planned launch window.

As part of the mission, scientists planned to study permanently shadowed areas of the Moon and conduct environmental and resource research on its south pole. According to China’s Xinhua news agency, one of the key objectives of "Chang’e-7" was to achieve technological breakthroughs.

The program’s previous mission — "Chang’e-6" — delivered rock and soil samples from the far side of the Moon to Earth in 2024. This was the first instance in history of samples being returned from this part of Earth’s satellite.

Why social media giants are on trial in the US for hooking kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:25:00 UTC
09:25:00 KST

Why social media giants are on trial in the US for hooking kids
- Lawsuits accuse social media giants like Meta and Google of designing addictive platforms that harm young users' mental health, leading to significant legal penalties and demands for operational changes.
- Trials reveal internal company documents showing awareness of addiction risks and manipulation tactics, while companies deny allegations and emphasise safety measures and user responsibility.
- Legal actions seek billions in damages, regulatory changes, and platform adjustments to protect children, with comparisons drawn to Big Tobacco's historic addiction lawsuits and potential huge financial consequences.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A flood of lawsuits against social media giants claims that by engineering their platforms to be hard to resist, the companies are causing serious harm to young users.
In the first personal injury case to go to trial, a Los Angeles jury in March found Meta Platforms and Google negligent in the design and operation of their platforms – awarding US$6 million (S$7.6 million) to a 20-year-old woman in a landmark verdict.
Many US states have also taken legal action against social media companies on behalf of the public.
At a trial that began on Aug 18 in federal court in Oakland, California, 29 states suing Meta are seeking penalties of as much as US$1.4 trillion as well as court orders to force the company to change how its Facebook and Instagram apps operate.
The trials, along with more to come in 2027, are drawing comparisons to Big Tobacco’s historic reckoning with consumer addiction three decades ago that resulted in tighter regulation of the cigarette industry.
What are the cases?
The Los Angeles trial centred on a woman who said her non-stop use of sites, including Instagram and Google’s YouTube, for more than a decade caused her to suffer anxiety, depression and body dysmorphia.
Snap and TikTok were not involved in the trial because they reached confidential settlements, but the four companies face more than 3,000 other cases brought by children, adolescents and young adults – sometimes via their parents, siblings or other family members – based on claims of psychological distress, physical impairment and death.
New Mexico’s Attorney-General also won judgments against Meta totalling US$942 million in 2026, after a jury found that the company misled young people about safety on its platforms.
The coalition of state attorneys-general lined up against Meta in Oakland alleges the company knowingly designed features that encouraged compulsive and prolonged use of its platforms by young people, while simultaneously misleading consumers about safety features on its platforms.
Another 14 states are separately pursuing claims against the company, including an ongoing trial in a case brought by Tennessee’s Attorney-General in Nashville state court. TikTok, Snap and Google have also been sued by attorneys-general over similar allegations.
Public school districts have brought more than 1,300 complaints on behalf of students.
Meta, TikTok, Snap and Google agreed in May to pay a combined US$27 million to settle a suit brought by a rural district in Kentucky that was scheduled to go to trial in June.
The next school district trial is set for February 2027.
What’s the legal foundation?
The claims filed by individual users focus on product liability, similar to those that drove decades of litigation over cigarettes, asbestos, faulty medical devices and harmful prescription drugs, with mixed success.
Rather than targeting the content that social media users see, the suits attack the platforms’ design and functionality, alleging that they are engineered to keep users constantly engaged.
The cases filed by the school districts claim that the companies have created a “public nuisance” by distracting children and undermining their education and have caused a youth mental health crisis.
How does the alleged addiction happen?
Many of the lawsuits allege that the social media giants, borrowing behavioural techniques from the gambling and cigarette industries, design endless, algorithm-generated feeds to induce young users into a so-called flow state.
In that state, users react to incessant notifications that manipulate dopamine levels, encourage repetitive account checking and reward round-the-clock use.
Addictive use of social media results in an array of psychological disorders and, in extreme cases, self-harm and suicide, according to the lawsuits.
Such addictive use delivers the most valuable prize: troves of data about young users’ preferences, habits and behaviours that are used to target them with advertisements.
How are internal records at the companies being used against them?
In 2021, Frances Haugen, a former product manager-turned-whistle-blower at Facebook, revealed internal documents showing that Meta had long known that its platforms had ill effects on young people, especially girls struggling with their body image.
Lawyers at the Los Angeles trial showed internal chats and e-mails from employees discussing the alleged addictive qualities of Meta’s products. Much of the same evidence is being used at other trials.
Records disclosed by TikTok’s parent company ByteDance, in response to lawsuits, suggest that the company knew young people were more susceptible to being lured into trying dangerous and even deadly stunts they view on TikTok because their ability to judge risk is not fully formed.
Product research at ByteDance concluded that the top reason identified by teens for participating in the challenges is “getting views/likes/comments”, followed by “impressing others online”.
What do the companies say?
They maintain that their products were not built to hook children and that they have settings and safeguards in place to protect young users.
In the Oakland case, Meta has denied the states’ allegations.
Paul Schmidt, an attorney for Meta, told jurors that the company is committed to protecting young users and has adopted new safety tools.
He also argued that while Meta “takes seriously” that children under 13 should not be on social media, the mobile app stores where users subscribe to platforms also have a gatekeeping responsibility.
Meta argued during the Los Angeles trial that social media actually helps young people connect with friends and family.
Meta and Google are appealing the Los Angeles verdict, and Meta is appealing the New Mexico verdict.
In the past, the first line of defence for social media companies has been Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, the 1996 federal statute that shields companies from liability over comments, ads, pictures and videos on their platforms.
But judges overseeing the current wave of lawsuits ruled that Section 230 does not protect the companies from negligence claims.
What consequences are the companies facing?
In the Los Angeles trial, jurors said Meta must pay US$4.2 million and that Google owes US$1.8 million.
Half of each company’s payment is compensation for the plaintiff’s losses, including the cost of therapy, and the other half is punitive damages, meant to punish wrongdoing and discourage similar conduct in the future.
That was the first of a handful of test cases selected to proceed to trial to help assess the strength of the legal arguments behind the thousands of other suits.
In the Oakland trial, the stakes for Meta are high.
The trial is focused on alleged violations of a federal privacy law and state consumer protection statutes that carry fines of as much as US$20,000 per violation – which can add up quickly when multiplied by millions of young Instagram and Facebook users.
If the company loses, it may face financial penalties ranging from US$193 billion to US$1.4 trillion.
Even the lower amount would be among the largest ever litigation payouts, comparable to the US$206 billion settlement that state attorneys-general struck with tobacco companies over cigarette addiction in 1998.
The suits filed by the school districts seek to recover past and future costs tied to the alleged harms of social media, including funding to hire additional mental health counsellors and security guards and additional training for teachers to help them identify and respond to students suffering distress.
Bloomberg Intelligence has estimated the companies’ collective exposure is almost US$400 billion.
The school districts are also demanding that the companies make adjustments to the platforms, including installing parental controls and tweaking algorithms that are designed to maximise user engagement.
Similarly, the state attorneys-general suing the companies are requesting court orders directing the platforms to dismantle what they describe as “addictive” design features that exploit children’s brain development for profit.
If the companies continue to lose trials, pressure could mount for them to pursue settlements reaching into billions of dollars per company, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. BLOOMBERG

Trump demands changes to the design of the US Navy’s most advanced aircraft carriers despite the risk of billions in costs
Kyiv • UNN
Trump is demanding that the superstructure of the Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carriers be relocated, which could lead to billions in costs and program delays. It is currently unknown which ship will be modified.
The U.S. Navy is considering changing the design of future Gerald R. Ford-class nuclear-powered aircraft carriers after President Donald Trump demanded that the island superstructure be moved closer to the center of the ship to make it resemble aircraft carriers from the World War II era. Defense Express reports this, citing The War Zone, writes UNN.
Details
The reason for Trump's demand was his dissatisfaction with the appearance of the superstructure. At the same time, its current location has not only an aesthetic but also a functional rationale.
The U.S. Navy spent four years—from 1996 to 2000—working on 75 design options for the future Gerald R. Ford-class carriers before choosing the current configuration. The superstructure was placed approximately 40 meters farther aft than on Nimitz-class ships, and its dimensions were reduced. This made it possible to increase the flight deck area by more than 11%.
This arrangement also improves the conduct of cyclic flight operations and reduces turbulence in the aft section of the ship, making aircraft landings safer.
Because the superstructure is deeply integrated into the carrier's design, moving it would require the reconstruction of systems, communications, and other elements. This could lead to additional costs of billions of dollars and further delays. A single Gerald R. Ford already costs the United States more than $13 billion.
US Navy plans to acquire 15 Trump-class battleships by 205512.05.26, 01:29 • 3971 view
The program is already behind schedule. The second ship in the series—USS John F. Kennedy—is planned to enter service by the end of 2026, although this was initially supposed to happen back in 2022.
This is not Trump's first demand to change the design of aircraft carriers. Earlier, he advocated replacing modern electromagnetic catapults with steam-powered ones. The additional costs and delays could jeopardize U.S. plans to build ten Gerald R. Ford-class ships.
It is currently unknown which aircraft carrier will receive the modified superstructure. Defense Express suggests that it could be the fourth ship in the series—USS Doris Miller.

Inside Turkey’s military machine: Tanks, drones and regional power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:20:08 UTC
09:20:08 KST

The growing tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have taken on added significance in recent days amid military activity in Syria, have raised anew a question that has become increasingly relevant for Israel's defense establishment in recent years: How powerful is the Turkish military? The answer begins with striking numbers, but certainly does not end there.
Turkey is not merely a major NATO member. It is a regional military power whose influence stretches from the Black and Aegean seas through Syria and Iraq to the Caucasus and North Africa. NATO itself described Turkey ahead of the alliance's summit in Ankara in July as the country with the "alliance's second-largest army," after the United States. Its location between Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as its control of the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits, gives that power even greater strategic significance.
According to Global Firepower data for 2026, which is based in part on estimates, Turkey has about 481,000 active-duty military personnel, 380,000 reservists and another 150,000 members of paramilitary forces. Combined, the three categories account for more than 1 million people. By the number of active-duty personnel, Turkey ranks 10th worldwide according to the index.
More than 2,280 tanks and nearly 100,000 vehicles
The ground force is the backbone of the Turkish military. According to Global Firepower, its arsenal includes about 2,284 tanks and roughly 98,000 vehicles of various types. Alongside them, Turkey maintains a large artillery force: more than 1,000 self-propelled artillery systems, 635 towed guns and 237 multiple rocket launchers. The figures represent estimated inventories and not necessarily the number of systems available for operational use at any given time.
Turkey's equipment is a mix of older Western systems and newer generations of domestically produced platforms. For decades, Ankara relied heavily on American and European weapons, but in recent years it has invested enormous sums in an effort to reduce that dependence, from tanks and armored vehicles to missiles, air defense systems, military electronics and unmanned systems.
The result is a military that seeks not only to be large but also to be capable of maintaining and upgrading a growing share of its systems on its own.
More than 1,100 aircraft and the F-35 dream
According to Global Firepower estimates, the Turkish military has about 1,101 aircraft. The figure includes 201 fighter aircraft, 84 transport planes, 301 training aircraft and 509 helicopters, including 111 attack helicopters. Here, too, the figure represents the total inventory and not necessarily actual operational readiness. The site estimates, for example, that about 141 of the 201 fighter aircraft would be available under its assumed readiness scenario.
The backbone of Turkey's fighter fleet remains its F-16s, but Ankara is pursuing two tracks simultaneously: an effort to rejoin the American F-35 fighter jet program, from which it was removed following its purchase of the Russian S-400 system, and the development of its own indigenous fighter jet, the KAAN. The KAAN made its first flight in 2024 and is one of the Turkish defense industry's flagship projects. Ankara sees it as a key component of its plan to reduce dependence on foreign fighter aircraft, although the domestic project still relies on American components, most notably General Electric engines.
At the same time, Turkey continues to press Washington to return to the F-35 program. U.S. President Donald Trump expressed openness at the NATO summit in Ankara to allowing the sale of the aircraft to Turkey, but the path remains fraught with legal and political obstacles, including over the S-400 issue. Israel strongly opposes the move out of concern that it could undermine its qualitative military edge in the region, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly voiced his opposition.
The force that changed the battlefield: Drones
If there is one field in which Turkey has quickly become a global name, it is unmanned aerial vehicles. Turkish company Baykar, the manufacturer of the Bayraktar family, turned the TB2 into one of the world's best-known drones following its use in a series of conflicts and later developed more advanced systems, including the TB3.
Turkish drones have become not only an operational tool but also an export engine and a diplomatic asset. Turkey markets its systems to dozens of countries and has emerged in this field as a significant competitor to Israeli defense industries in the global market. According to Reuters, Turkish defense industry exports reached about $10 billion in 2025, triple the 2021 figure, and Ankara is now seeking further expansion in European and global markets.
17 frigates, 14 submarines and a ship turned drone carrier
The sea is also a central component of Turkey's power projection strategy. According to Global Firepower, the navy has 192 vessels, including 17 frigates, nine corvettes and 14 submarines. Turkey operates its naval forces across three main theaters — the Black Sea, Aegean Sea and Mediterranean — and its location allows it to control the only maritime passage between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
One of the navy's most prominent platforms is the TCG Anadolu, a multipurpose amphibious assault ship and the largest vessel in the Turkish fleet. After Turkey was removed from the F-35 program, it developed, among other things, a concept under which the ship could serve as a naval base for operating unmanned aircraft.
During the EFES-2026 exercise held in May, a Bayraktar TB3 was operated from the ship as part of a combat scenario. Earlier, during a NATO exercise in the Baltic Sea, a TB3 took off autonomously from Anadolu's short deck and struck maritime targets. Through this, Turkey is seeking to develop a relatively new model of naval power: a large ship that extends its operational reach through an array of armed drones.
4,500 companies and more than 1,400 projects
One of the deepest changes in Turkey's balance of power is not in the number of soldiers or tanks but in the factories behind them. For years, Turkey was a major customer for foreign weapons systems. Today, it is seeking to become a manufacturer and exporter in its own right.
According to data published this month by Anadolu Agency, more than 4,500 companies now operate in Turkey's defense industry, compared with just 56 in 2002, while the number of defense projects has surpassed 1,400. According to the same data, the share of locally produced components and systems has risen from about 20% two decades ago to more than 85% today.
The strategic significance is substantial: Turkey is able to produce at home an increasing share of the drones, missiles, armored vehicles, warships and electronic systems it uses while also generating revenue and political influence through their export.
And how much does it spend on defense?
Turkish defense spending has been rising sharply, although the scale varies considerably depending on the definition and source. In a NATO report on 2025 defense spending, Turkey's expenditure was estimated at about $32.6 billion at that year's prices and exchange rates, up from about $28.3 billion in 2024. NATO estimated that spending amounted to about 2.33% of GDP. The figures for 2024 and 2025 were identified in the report as estimates.
Other estimates put Turkey's defense budget higher. Global Firepower, for example, estimates 2026 spending at about $51.4 billion. The discrepancy is due in part to differences in definitions, budget years and calculation methods, meaning comparisons between sources should be made cautiously.
Mass, geography, experience and industry
So what makes the Turkish military particularly powerful? First and foremost, mass. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers, hundreds of thousands of reservists, thousands of armored vehicles and the ability to mobilize manpower on a scale that few countries in the region can approach. The second advantage is geography: Turkey sits at the intersection of Europe, Asia and the Middle East and controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. It borders, among others, Syria, Iraq, Iran, Georgia and Bulgaria and lies within close reach of the Caucasus, Balkans and eastern Mediterranean.
The third advantage is operational experience. The Turkish military has spent years fighting the Kurdistan Workers' Party, carried out a series of operations beyond the country's borders, maintains forces and conducts operations in northern Syria and Iraq and has been involved, directly or indirectly, in additional theaters. The fourth is the defense industry. Unlike a large military that is entirely dependent on external supplies, Turkey is now able to produce an increasing share of its own weapons systems. That does not eliminate its dependence on foreign technology in certain areas, but it gives Ankara significantly greater freedom of action than it had in the past.
The fifth advantage is NATO. Turkey has been a member of the alliance since 1952, hosts NATO Allied Land Command in Izmir and is a key component of the alliance's southern flank. Membership provides it with joint training, common military standards, intelligence sharing and cooperation with some of the world's most advanced militaries.
Still, numbers alone can be misleading. The Turkish military has equipment from different generations, some of it old, and not every tank, aircraft or vessel listed in its inventory is fully operational. In modern warfare, the question is not simply how many platforms exist, but how many are available, how well protected they are, what intelligence is available to them and how effectively they can operate together on a single network with the air force, navy, drones, artillery and air defense systems.
But even with that caveat, the picture is clear: Turkey in 2026 is much more than a "large military." It is a regional military power with enormous manpower, thousands of combat platforms, significant air and naval forces, global leadership in drones and a rapidly growing defense industry. As relations with Israel grow more strained and Turkish influence in Syria expands, that power is becoming for Jerusalem less of a theoretical statistic and more of a strategic consideration that is increasingly difficult to ignore.

Twenty-five Ukrainian companies to be presented at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland

2026-08-24
03:19:07 EEST

Twenty-five Ukrainian companies to be presented at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland
Kyiv • UNN
At least 25 companies will represent Ukraine at the MSPO 2026 exhibition in Kielce. They will showcase drones, electronic warfare systems, communications equipment, and cyber technologies.
At the MSPO 2026 international defense industry exhibition in Kielce, Poland, Ukraine will be represented by at least 25 companies. The event will take place on September 8–11 and will be the largest in the exhibition’s history, with the number of exhibitors approaching 1,000. Defense Express reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Ukrainian manufacturers will showcase strike and reconnaissance drones, electronic warfare equipment, communications and cybersecurity systems, as well as other defense developments. Among the participants is Fire Point, which will present the long-range FP-1 unmanned aerial vehicles and the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile.
For the first time this year, Canada will be the MSPO lead nation. It will present 82 companies operating in the fields of defense electronics, aerospace, cybersecurity, and radar systems.
According to Defense Express, Ukraine’s participation in the exhibition is particularly significant amid the development of cooperation with the European defense industry. In particular, Ukraine’s defense industry is also interested in the opportunities offered by the SAFE program, to which Canada became the first non-European participating country.

Israeli drone strike kills 2 Palestinians in displacement tent in central Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:15:31 UTC
09:15:31 KST

Tarek Chouiref
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Two Palestinians were killed and several others injured early Monday in an Israeli drone strike targeting a displacement tent in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, in the latest violation of the Oct. 10, 2025 ceasefire, medical sources said.
Sources at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital told Anadolu that the tent, located near the hospital, was sheltering displaced Palestinians when it was hit.
The victims were identified as Mohammed Nasser Abu Assad and Ibrahim Nasser Abu Assad.
Israeli warplanes also carried out two strikes near the hospital, while artillery shelling targeted an area south of the Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza.
Hours earlier on Sunday, Israeli attacks across central and southern Gaza killed two Palestinians, including a child, and injured 14 others.
A medical source at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital told Anadolu that the two fatalities and seven of the injuries resulted from an Israeli strike on the town of Az-Zawayda in central Gaza shortly after the army issued an evacuation warning.
Israeli forces have carried out daily violations of the ceasefire in place since Oct. 10 which have killed 1,286 people and wounded 4,257, according to Palestine Health Ministry data.
Israel launched a war on Gaza in October 2023, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians, wounding over 174,000 and devastating about 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure.
