US envoy Barrack reverses Golan comments, reaffirms Trump's recognition of Israeli sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:53:12 UTC
07:53:12 KST

The US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack appeared to reverse his previous comments on the status of the Golan Heights in recent days, backing the US recognition of the area as Israeli territory in a statement to the Associated Press on Sunday.
“United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged,” he said, contradicting his claim in an interview with Mario Nawfal on Friday where he stated that Israel occupies the Golan Heights.
“They still occupy the Golan against the UN resolutions, against all of the international order, which has said the Golan is Syria’s,” Barrack said then, despite the US having recognized the area as Israeli for almost a decade.
The interview took place against the backdrop of Israel's strike on the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in Idlib last week. Israel claimed that Turkish troops were ready to deploy at the base, a claim that Turkey denied.
Syrian negotiations primarily on Israeli withdrawal from areas besides Golan
Israel conquered the Golan Heights in the Six-Day War, annexing the area by law in 1981. UN Security Council resolution 497, passed only days later, rejected the annexation as "null and void."
In 2019, Trump recognized the Golan Heights as Israeli, as a part of pro-Israel moves including the recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital and moving the US embassy there.
Syria never rescinded its claim to the Golan Heights, and after Ahmed al-Sharaa took power in December of 2024, the question the area's status entered the spotlight once again.
During negotiations between Israel and Syrian officials in Jordan on Sunday, the Syrian delegation asked to separate negotiations over the Golan Heights, appearing to prioritize the matter of Israel's withdrawal from areas captured after December 2024.
Barrack said strike on Syria may have been political
Barrack condemned Israel's strikes on the Idlib airbase, calling them "serious and worrisome."
In Friday's interview, Barrack suggested that Israel may have intended to provoke a faceoff with Turkey through its strike. Barrack also said the strike could have had political motives, with Israeli elections scheduled for October.
Following the attack, Barrack said the US would work to establish a deconfliction mechanism between Israel, Turkey, and Syria, insisting that increased communication would be necessary to prevent violence.
“Syria has demonstrated itself to be a responsible and stable sovereign neighbor, and a carefully structured de-escalation arrangement would contribute significantly to greater calm and predictability across the region,” Barrack told The Jerusalem Post.
Amichai Stein and Reuters contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

Yashar surges ahead of Likud as Eisenkot party outlines plans for potential government - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:53:05 UTC
07:53:05 KST

The number 26 came up before policy did. A Channel 13 poll had put Yashar on 26 seats, ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud at 23, placing a party founded in 2025 in contention to become the largest faction in the Israeli parliament. Orit Farkash-Hacohen did not describe the result as a shock.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
“I see it as a very natural process,” the Israeli parliamentarian and Yashar candidate told The Media Line.
“It’s not as if we are being overwhelmed by that. On the contrary.”
Other recent polls have differed on the size of the advantage, but most of the six surveys reviewed for this article placed Yashar ahead of Likud. The party ranged from 22 to 26 seats, while Likud ranged from 21 to 23.
Polling has elevated Yashar’s standing in the political landscape. The party is now being asked not simply why voters are turning to the former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff, but what an Eisenkot government would actually do on the economy, military service, public spending, and the recovery of regions still dealing with the effects of the years since October 7.
Eisenkot's personal appeal is not a new phenomenon in Israeli politics
Israeli parliamentarian Farkash-Hacohen, who served as tourism and strategic affairs minister and later as technology and innovation minister, said Yashar has already begun preparing for a possible move into office. The party is working on plans for its first months in government, she said, drawing on former ministers and senior public officials as well as younger members of the team.
“We are focused on preparing the plans for the first 100 days of, hopefully, a new government,” Farkash-Hacohen said, describing a cabinet whose ministers would be expected to work for the public rather than concentrate on “their own political survival.”
That governing pitch is closely tied to Eisenkot’s personal appeal. Farkash-Hacohen said she sees voters looking for an alternative not only to Prime Minister Netanyahu’s policies but also to his political style. Playing on the Hebrew meaning of the party’s name, she said Israelis “want something yashar” meaning leadership associated with integrity and public service.
Speaking with The Media Line, political scientist and educator Jack Drassinower, who specializes in Israeli politics, said the emphasis on Eisenkot himself is hardly unusual in Israel. He argued that Israeli elections have increasingly centered on party leaders rather than fine ideological distinctions, and that Eisenkot’s military background gives him an advantage at a time when security remains central to voters.
“If you ask the voter what the important issues are when going to vote, the military element is still the most important,” Drassinower said. He believes security has become an even greater priority since October 7.
Farkash-Hacohen said the first domestic task of an Eisenkot government would be to reduce the divisions that deepened in Israeli society before and after the October 7 attacks.
She accused the current government of using polarization as a political instrument and said Yashar would seek to govern beyond the constituencies that brought it to power.
“The biggest challenge for us as a leadership is to bring back the unity of Israeli society,” she said. “The people of Israel are very united, and we’re a very resilient and special kind of people. We hold each other, especially in times of challenge.”
The next issue she raised was service. Yashar wants to broaden military or national service among populations that have historically had exemptions, particularly ultra-Orthodox and Arab Israelis. Farkash-Hacohen said national service in hospitals, schools, and other institutions could be part of the model for those who do not serve in the military.
“Our mission is to bring about a strategic change in which both these populations will also contribute and take part in the very big burden that now rests on the shoulders of not all of Israeli society,” she said. “It will be a very challenging and ambitious task that we are committed to pushing forward.”
Drassinower identified conscription as one of the areas where Eisenkot has found room to distinguish himself from the current coalition without closing every door for future political negotiations.
He noted that Eisenkot has supported a much broader obligation to serve while also acknowledging that full ultra-Orthodox enlistment cannot happen immediately and that some limited exemptions could remain.
The economic platform has received less public attention, something Drassinower considers a weakness in the party’s definition so far. “If you ask me what Eisenkot’s economic position is, I couldn’t tell you,” he said, adding that the lack of emphasis may also allow Yashar to attract voters who disagree with one another on economic and religion-and-state questions.
Farkash-Hacohen, whose own background includes senior economic and regulatory positions, gave a detailed account of where she wants the party to go. The starting point, she said, is the cost of a larger long-term defense burden.
“The next decade will be very challenging economically,” she said. Israel, in her view, will have to spend more on security than it did before October 7, leaving less room for a government to avoid decisions about which programs deserve public money. “It requires us as a government, first of all, to be very clear on our priorities and how we manage the Israeli taxpayers’ money.”
Yashar would close ministries it regards as unnecessary and reduce government spending tied to coalition politics, she said. Farkash-Hacohen argued that state resources should increasingly favor Israelis who work and serve, and said the party would review subsidies that it believes discourage participation in the workforce.
The cost of living would require a different set of measures. Farkash-Hacohen singled out groceries and cosmetics as markets where concentrated corporate power and exclusive import agreements limit competition.
She said a Yashar government would seek to remove barriers to competitors, challenge exclusive import arrangements and, where necessary, force dominant groups to give up some of their market power.
Housing would be harder. “I don’t think that we will have magic solutions,” she said. Instead, she tied housing to transportation, infrastructure and the ability of people to live farther from the country’s most expensive population centers without losing access to jobs.
Better transportation, she argued, could expand the realistic housing market rather than treating the shortage as a problem that can be solved solely by construction policy.”
A future government led by Yashar would have it work cut out, expert says
Farkash-Hacohen is also working on infrastructure planning tied to energy security, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology.
A separate initiative is aimed at Israelis who have left the country in recent years, particularly physicians, engineers, researchers, and high-tech workers. She described the proposal as an “in-location” program, a play on relocation, and said she studied comparable efforts abroad to bring highly skilled citizens back.
“We have prepared a very specific program,” she said. But incentives alone, she added, may not determine whether people return. “From what we see, many of these people will be back once the leadership and the government will be changed.”
Winning enough seats to implement any of those programs would be only the first political obstacle. Israel’s parliamentary system requires a majority of 61 lawmakers to sustain a government, and Drassinower said Eisenkot’s position among voters is stronger at the moment than his authority over the parties he may eventually need as partners.
His problem, Drassinower said, “is not the larger number of votes” but reaching 61. Potential partners include leaders with their own ambitions and parties with significant ideological differences. Drassinower said that remains a vulnerability for an opposition camp whose members can agree on replacing the current government without necessarily agreeing on what comes afterward.
Farkash-Hacohen said Yashar believes a future coalition can operate around several common principles: Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, respect for the Declaration of Independence, and broader sharing of national responsibilities.
She listed education, the cost of living, military service, democratic institutions, and the rule of law as issues that would give a new government more than enough work without allowing every ideological disagreement to dominate its agenda.
Drassinower was more cautious. The experience of the previous change of government, he said, showed the danger of leaving disputes unresolved simply because partners agree that a different prime minister should be in office. “The points of disagreement were not touched,” he said of that coalition. “They were simply put under the rug.”
He sees another distinction between polling well and exercising power. “The problem, as we know, is not only to form a government, but to govern,” he said.
Yashar says northern Israel would be an early priority for the party. It released a reconstruction plan last week for communities that endured prolonged evacuation and economic disruption after October 7. Farkash-Hacohen said improved shelter would come first, followed by incentives designed not merely to bring residents back but to persuade young families to build their futures there.
“The first and foremost priority would be to perform and execute very expedited sheltering,” she said, arguing that residents need a higher standard of personal security before long-term development promises can mean much.
Yashar also proposes additional education and tax incentives, investment in tourism, agriculture, and energy projects, and special treatment for Kiryat Shmona, including added tax benefits and development initiatives.
Farkash-Hacohen said the northern plan would also depend on restoring residents’ confidence in the government’s ability to deliver on its commitments. That is a standard Yashar would have to meet if the poll numbers eventually translate into seats and those seats form a government.
The aim, she said, is “to rebuild the trust of the people of the north with their government.”

Wyndham Clark holds off McIlroy and Cantlay to capture BMW Championship for 3rd win this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:53:02 UTC
07:53:02 KST

Wyndham Clark holds off McIlroy and Cantlay to capture BMW Championship for 3rd win this year
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Wyndham Clark had Scottie Scheffler with him in the final group at the U.S. Open and Rory McIlroy at his side at the BMW Championship. Both times he started with big leads and watched them vanish. And both times, there was no mistaking who the gallery wanted to win.
Only when it was over Sunday at Bellerive, silver trophies of the BMW Championship and the Western Golf Association at his side, did Clark repeat what one of his friends told him.
“Darth Vader had more fun,” Clark said with a big smile.
Clark embraced the pressure of a tense back nine at Bellerive and accepted what his place in the game — “I’ve kind of been the underdog in all of my wins,” he said — by delivering a 5-iron that set up the go-ahead birdie and two more birdies that salvaged an even-par 70 and a three-shot victory, his third of the year.
“I know everyone maybe gives me a hard time and roots for other people,” he said. “But I feel like I’ve kind of come into my own. Three wins in one season is my best year yet —coming off my worst year ever. I’m just really pleased where I’m at right now.”
This puts him squarely in the conversation for PGA Tour player of the year considering one was a major and the other was a FedEx Cup playoff event.
But just like at Shinnecock Hills, it wasn’t easy.
He lost his five-shot lead to McIlroy in 11 holes and it was tense the last hour until Clark — without a birdie all day — followed McIlroy’s great tee shot on the par-3 16th with a 5-iron just as good. Clark made his from just outside 15 feet. McIlroy’s putt from 15 feet to stay tied missed.
“I always felt like I needed to just get my nose ahead to really try to put the pressure on Wyndham, and I couldn’t,” McIlroy said after a 69 to finish third.
Patrick Cantlay comes through to advance
Clark wasn’t the only one with cause to celebrate.
Patrick Cantlay, who came in at No. 43 in the FedEx Cup, showed plenty of moxie. Four times he bounced back from a bogey with a birdie, closing with three birdies in a row for a 68 to finish runner-up and be among the top 30 in the FedEx Cup who advance to the Tour Championship.
The winner next week at East Lake captures the FedEx Cup.
“I’m coming to a golf course that I played really well at next week,” said Cantlay, who won at East Lake in 2021 to claim the FedEx Cup. “So I’m really pleased with where my game is at and I think I’m trending in the right direction.”
Woodland’s big year to continue
Also moving into the top 30 was Gary Woodland, who pulled within one shot of the lead until topping his tee shot into a creek on the ninth hole on his way to a double bogey. He closed with nine straight pars and fought back tears as he returns to the Tour Championship for the first time since 2019 while recovering from brain surgery three years ago.
He said Saturday, when he was in the final group, took a lot out of him with the noise, the energy and the drones that triggered the kind of brain activity he tries to calm. On Sunday, he tried to embrace it and pulled through with a 69 to tie for fourth.
“I tried to enjoy it,” he said. “Outside of topping a ball — I haven’t done that for a long time — I’m just really proud.”
Robert MacIntyre closed with a 65 and tied for seventh, enough to move him into the top 30 for a return to East Lake. Those falling out of the top 30 were Rickie Fowler, Bud Cauley and Kurt Kitayama. British Open champion Ryan Fox nailed down the final spot.
Clark’s big finish at Bellerive
Clark didn’t face near the vitriol he did at Shinnecock Hills, when the New York crowd went from pulling for Scottie Scheffler in his bid for the career Grand Slam to openly rooting against Clark. There was one voice that shouted, “Get in the bunker!” when Clark hit to the par-3 13th. Otherwise, it was a clear pro-McIlroy crowd.
That was OK with Clark. He overcame three bogeys and a state of mind where he felt like he couldn’t hit the right shot or make any putt. And then he delivered his best swing — and best putt — on a 232-yard par 3 that yielded only five birdies all day.
“I wasn’t really nervous. I was kind of like ... out of it,” Clark said. “I was making dumb bogeys. I didn’t make anything on the greens. When I made the putt on the par 3, it got me back. As much as I would have loved to run away with it, it was fun to get the juices going.
“I’m really proud of myself that I didn’t let it get away.”
Clark also moved into the top six automatic spots who qualified for the Presidents Cup, joining Scheffler, Cameron Young, Russell Henley, Sam Burns and Collin Morikawa. U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker will have six picks after the Tour Championship. Cantlay surely got his attention.

A Kan 11 poll published Sunday evening found that the merger of Hadash-Ta'al and Balad into the Joint List would boost the Arab parties by one seat.
Hadash, Ta'al and Balad announced Wednesday that they had reached an agreement to run on a joint slate in the upcoming Knesset election, following lengthy negotiations marked by disagreements over the distribution of seats among the three parties.
According to the poll, the Joint List would win seven Knesset seats, while the United Arab List would win five. The current coalition would fall by one seat to 51, while the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot would remain unchanged at 57 seats.
Eisenkot's Yashar party would remain the largest party with 24 seats, up one from the previous poll, while Likud would fall by one to 23.
Naftali Bennett's Together would win 14 seats and the Democrats 10, both unchanged from the previous poll. Otzma Yehudit and Yisrael Beiteinu would each lose one seat, leaving both with nine. United Torah Judaism would win eight seats, Shas seven and Religious Zionism five, with the latter gaining one seat.
Several parties would fail to cross the electoral threshold, including Yoaz Hendel and Chili Tropper's Zionist Home, with 2.8 percent of the vote; Benny Gantz's Blue and White, with 1.8 percent; and Gilad Erdan's Unity, with 1.6 percent. All three also failed to cross the threshold in recent polls.
The poll was conducted by the Kantar Institute among 552 respondents and has a margin of error of 4.2 percent.

Change in revenue record doesn't create, end property title: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:50:49 UTC
07:50:49 KST

SC clarifies property mutation only serves revenue purposes, cannot by itself establish or extinguish ownership rights
NEW DELHI: Observing that mutation of a property in revenue records does not create or extinguish ownership, Supreme Court has said that title of property cannot be decided on the sole basis of revenue record and it must be weighed along with other evidence.A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih quashed the order of Madhya Pradesh HC which decided a title dispute on the basis of the revenue record. It said a right in immovable property cannot be treated as having been voluntarily abandoned because of a revenue entry in favour of another person. It must be independently established by the party relying on it.The bench said,“It is settled law that an entry in the revenue record neither creates nor extinguishes title and exists essentially for fiscal purposes. The order of the naib tehsildar may regulate the revenue record, but it cannot, merely by recording one person’s name in place of another, operate as a conveyance or a relinquishment of proprietary rights, and the civil court remains fully competent to determine the underlying title, which the revenue entry follows .
“The statutory presumption of correctness attaching to a revenue entry under Section 117 of the MP Land Revenue Code, 1959, is a rebuttable evidentiary presumption and not a presumption of title, and it must be weighed along with the rest of the evidence.”
It said mutation of a property in revenue record does not create or extinguish title nor has it any presumptive value and it only enables the person in whose favour mutation is ordered to pay the land revenue in question. SC said the starting point of the limitation can’t be fixed merely by identifying the date on which the revenue entry was made.

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks to ease tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:48:19 UTC
07:48:19 KST

Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks to ease tensions
AMMAN, Jordan – Syria and Israel held high-level, US-mediated talks in Jordan on Aug 23 aimed at easing tensions following recent Israeli strikes on Syrian territory, Syria’s state news agency SANA reported, citing a diplomatic source at the foreign ministry.
The talks focused on practical mechanisms to halt Israeli strikes, arrests and targeted operations, and on reviving negotiations towards a security agreement that could lay the groundwork for a broader future accord, SANA said.
The two sides also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Turkey and to prevent their rivalry from spilling onto Syrian territory.
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani told Reuters on Aug 22 that Damascus expected security negotiations with Israel to resume soon, although he added that there was a lack of trust between them.
Talks had been suspended since the start of the Iran war, while Syria cut off contact entirely after Israeli strikes on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase on Aug 18, according to Shaibani.
Washington has for more than a year sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only United Nations forces would be present, but Damascus doubted Israel’s willingness to implement the agreement.
The Israeli prime minister’s office did not reply to a request for comment on Shaibani’s remarks.
At the meeting on Aug 23, SANA said, Syria indicated that its immediate priorities remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before Bashar al-Assad’s overthrow on Dec 8, 2024, and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement.
Damascus also told the Israeli delegation it would not accept arrangements restricting its right to rebuild and develop its armed forces or determine its alliances and partnerships, SANA said.
Syria reiterated that the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights were Syrian territory but said discussions over the region’s final status were premature, according to the SANA report.
Israel has carried out repeated strikes on Syrian military sites since Assad’s fall, saying its actions were necessary to protect its security. Syria has denied posing a threat to Israel and has demanded an end to Israeli strikes and incursions.
Syria and Israel have technically been at war since 1948. Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War and later annexed it, a move recognised by the United States but not by most of the international community. REUTERS

Diego Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball sells for $3.35M at auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:44:06 UTC
07:44:06 KST

The ball used for Argentine footballer Diego Maradona's famous "Hand of God" goal and celebrated solo effort against England at the 1986 FIFA World Cup sold for $3.35 million at auction, according to Heritage Auctions.
The Adidas Azteca was used during Argentina's 2-1 quarterfinal victory over England, in which Maradona scored two of the most memorable goals in World Cup history.
The Dallas-based auction house sold the ball, which experts matched to photographs taken during the match, for $3.35 million Saturday.
The final price was well below the pre-auction estimate of at least $10 million.
Before the auction, Heritage described it as arguably the most famous ball in any sport and said it could become the most valuable soccer item ever sold.
Maradona's first goal against England became known as the "Hand of God" after he used his left hand to send the ball past goalkeeper Peter Shilton, with officials allowing the goal to stand.
Four minutes later, the Argentina captain collected the ball in his own half and dribbled past five England players before scoring a goal later voted as the FIFA World Cup "Goal of the Century."
The ball was kept for 36 years by Tunisian referee Ali Bin Nasser, who officiated the match. It was previously sold for £2 million ($2.37 million) at an auction in London in 2022.
The shirt Maradona wore in the same match sold for nearly $9.3 million at Sotheby's later that year.
The latest sale also fell short of the auction record for a ball from any sport. Shohei Ohtani’s 50th home run ball from his historic 2024 Major League Baseball season sold for $4.392 million, including the buyer’s premium.
The overall sports memorabilia auction record is held by the New York Yankees jersey that Babe Ruth wore during Game 3 of the 1932 World Series, which Heritage sold for $24.12 million, including the buyer’s premium, in 2024.

The Teasury Secretary told CNBC on Thursday that the U.S. will "collapse" the Islamic Republic with the "toughest sanctions in history."
The Trump administration demands that U.S. allies and the rest of the world stop doing business with Iran, Bessent said. The U.S. will use its "full might" against anyone who does not comply, he told CNBC.

Trump also threatened severe financial penalties against any nation that helps Iran evade sanctions, adding in a post on Truth Social that "this will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has dismissed the Trump administration's threats, according to its state media. An IRGC spokesperson said Sunday that Iran has ways "to counter the adverse effects of the enemy's war" and that it can "easily establish economic relations with countries."
"The U.S. president says that he ordered an economic war and launched the most severe economic campaign against Iran. This amounts to an implicit admission of the enemy's humiliating defeat in the military arena," the IRGC spokesperson said, according to state media.
Iran is one of the most sanctioned countries in the world, said Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets. It is unclear whether more economic pressure will change Tehran's behavior, Croft told CNBC in an interview Friday.
Iran seems to believe that it can outlast a Trump administration that wants the war to end quickly, she said. Tehran still has the ability to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz and infrastructure in the Middle East, the analyst said.
"Iran still has significant disruptive capabilities," Croft said. "The question is how is this going to change with additional economic sanctions."

Eight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:17:53 UTC
07:17:53 KST

An eight-year-old Louisiana girl has died after contracting a rare, typically fatal brain-eating amoeba after a swim in Lake Claiborne.
Lillian Smart, of Ruston, died on Saturday, one day after celebrating her birthday, her family announced in a public Facebook post on the “Love for Lillian” page.
“Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus,” her family said in the post. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from. Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”
The Louisiana department of health confirmed on 19 August that a state resident had been infected with Naegleria fowleri and said the exposure most likely occurred while the person was swimming in Lake Claiborne in Claiborne parish. Family friends later identified Lillian as the infected resident, according to reports from several local media outlets.
Naegleria fowleri infections are almost always fatal.
Lillian had been hospitalized since 15 August, KNOE reported. As her family faced the crisis, more than two dozen businesses in Ruston showed support and donated a portion of sales to the Smart family, according to the Facebook page.
Naegleria fowleri infections are extremely rare, with only a handful occurring in Louisiana since 2011.
The amoeba flourishes in warm water and is most commonly found in southern states during the summer. Only about 180 cases have been identified in the US since 1937, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In 2023, an Arkansas child died after contracting Naegleria fowleri from a country club splash pad in the state capital of Little Rock.
Naegleria fowleri can be found in warm freshwater across the country, including lakes, rivers and ponds. It is not found in salt water or in swimming pools that are properly maintained and chlorinated.
Experts say the climate crisis is causing the amoeba to pop up in parts of the US where it isn’t typical, such as the north and west. It is likely to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain.
People cannot become infected just by swallowing water containing Naegleria fowleri, and the infection does not spread from one person to another.

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.
The landslide took place at about 2am (3am UK time) in the Gbessia commune of Conakry, according to a government statement.
The death toll was 30, with six people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.
Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.
One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.
Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a World Bank report published in April.
On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara, announced that the government was closing the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to be relocated outside Conakry.
The prime minister, Amadou Oury Bah, visited the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

A CCTV video showed Nijjar’s grey pickup truck and a white sedan driving parallel in the parking lot of the gurdwara, seconds before the shooting started.Nijjar, the head of Khalistan Tiger Force (KTF), was replaced by his confidant Arshdeep Singh alias Arsh Dala. Interestingly, in the latest audio, Brar is also heard claiming the killing of Dala’s close associate, Sukhdool Singh alias Sukha Duneke, who was murdered in Winnipeg area in Sept 2023.
Raj Shekhar Jha is a journalist for the Times of India with over a decade of experience in reporting on national security, terrorism, crime and prisons.

Aussie athletes continue top form with trio of medals at Diamond League
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:04:31 UTC
07:04:31 KST

Jess Hull, Rose Davies and Eleanor Patterson all medal at Diamond League in Poland
In short:
Jess Hull, Rose Davies and Eleanor Patterson continued their Commonwealth Games form with medals at the Diamond League in Poland.
Australian sprinter Lachlan Kennedy was disappointed after failing to make the 100m final.
What's next?
Athletics eyes will now turn to the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest on September 11.
Commonwealth Games champions Eleanor Patterson and Rose Davies have kicked on from their Glasgow triumphs, along with double silver medallist Jessica Hull, as Australia's athletes have continued to shine on the Diamond League circuit in Poland.
All three made the podium at the Diamond League Silesia meet in Chorzów overnight, with high jump champion Patterson soaring to third place, Glasgow 5,000/10,000 metre double winner Davies grabbing bronze in the 5,000m and Hull running her fastest race of the year to finish 1,500m runner-up.
But there was disappointment for Glasgow sprint hero Lachlan Kennedy, who after his Australian-record run for silver at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, failed to make the 100m final in Chorzów.
Pride of place went to Olympic silver medallist Hull, who tried out new tactics, sitting back in the field in the Silesian Stadium and kicking for home at the top of the straight, only to be reeled in by Ethiopia's Tsige Duguma. She needed a 2026 world-leading time of three minutes and 55.06 seconds to pip Hull's 3:55.20.
"I got caught in the last few metres but it was a big step forwards in confidence today," said Hull, who is eyeing the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest next month.
"That's the fastest I've run all year and we have some good races to come over the next few weeks."
Davies earned her second career Diamond League podium as she pursued Italian favourite Nadia Battocletti, fresh from her own 5,000/10,000 double at the European Championships.
Davies eventually finished third in 14:55.39, pipped by Ethiopia's Freweyni Hailu and Battocletti, who won in 14:54.09.
"Every race is a step forward and to come top three at a Diamond League shows I'm in good form," Davies said.
"I really look up to Battocletti, she's a great athlete and I would love to be like her."
Patterson again defeated teammate, world champion Nicola Olyslagers, just as she had done in Glasgow when they took gold and silver.
It was a strong effort considering Patterson was battling illness, but she had to settle for third behind Ukrainian rivals, Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh and Iryna Gerashchenko.
Kennedy took his first strides back on the international circuit after his historic 9.85sec silver medal-winning run in Glasgow, but his 10.08sec run in the heats in Chorzów was not enough to earn him a place in the final, which was later won by Jamaica's world champion, Oblique Seville, in a searing 9.83sec.
"I didn't come out as well as I would've liked but I'm just trying to shake the rust off a bit. I'll get back into some training and better form — I'm happy," Kennedy said.
Triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall cleared 5.90m but it only earned him fifth place while his mate Armand Duplantis earned yet another effortless triumph with a 6.20m winner.
Queensland's two-time Diamond League champion Matthew Denny finished eighth in the discus (66.38m), as Lithuania's world record holder Mykolas Alekna won with a competition record 72.58m.
The international highlight was world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden handing Olympic champion Julien Alfred her first loss of the season to win the women's 100m, 10.78sec to 10.83.

Zelenskyy Turns To Coalition Of The Willing In Push To Bolster Ukraine's Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
22:00:18 UTC
07:00:18 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's push to bolster international support and receive additional air defenses continues on August 24 as the so-called Coalition of the Willing meets to discuss ways to pressure Russia to halt its invasion months ahead of another likely brutal winter.
The summit -- with some leaders attending in person in Kyiv and others joining by video conference -- will be held on the day Ukraine is celebrating the 35th anniversary of its independence from the Soviet Union, and comes a day after a grouping of Baltic and Nordic nations gathered in the Ukrainian capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
The Coalition of the Willing, led by London and Paris, is an informal grouping of some 34 countries supporting Ukraine. No US representative was identified as a participant in the upcoming meeting.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's office said the new UK leader will arrive in Kyiv on August 24, his first international visit since taking office a month ago, "to reiterate the UK’s unwavering commitment to Ukraine."
The statement said Britain had "agreed that defense firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine."
Ahead of the event, Zelenskyy stressed the urgency of securing European funding for Ukraine's defense -- especially against Russia's deadly ballistic missiles -- calling on the European Parliament to approve the legislation needed to unlock the money.
"We are supposed to receive 30 billion euros in European funding.... It is tied to the adoption of the relevant legislation," he said. "It is very important here that parliament works -- the entire parliament, including the opposition. Because [this money is] needed for the defense of the entire country."
French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will co-chair the meeting, which will focus on continued military support for Ukraine, air defense, and longer-term security arrangements.
Both Macron and NATO Deputy Secretary-General Radmila Sekerinska will join the summit remotely via video link.
Baltic-Nordic Support
Leaders from Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Norway convened in the Ukrainian capital on August 23. Other senior representatives from partner countries were also in attendance.
The prime minister of Norway, one of the wealthier nations of the group, pledged major assistance for Ukraine next year following a large allotment from his government in 2026.
"Norway's support to Ukraine next year will be at the level of this year: $9 billion, a record high," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store told reporters in Kyiv. The majority of it will go to Ukraine's military, the Norwegian government said.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, who co-chaired the summit with Zelenskyy, said Ukraine needs continued military support.
"Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself and resist Russian aggression. First and foremost, this means more air defense, more ammunition, and greater investment in Ukraine’s defense industry. At the same time, we must increase pressure on Russia, strengthen sanctions, and close the loopholes Russia uses to evade them,” Michal said.
Russia's full-scale invasion of February 2022 has caused major destruction to the Ukrainian economy, blasting large portions of cities -- both large and small -- while it has killed thousands of civilians and forced millions of others to flee their homes.
Without providing details, Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military has a $27 billion deficit and urged the European Union to speedily deliver the promised 90 billion euro ($105 billion) loan to cover the 2026 gap.
Europe and the US have received tens of billions of dollars in economic and military aid since Russia's invasion, but supporters worry about possible assistance fatigue by Western partners.
Seeking US Aid
With further assistance from the White House uncertain, Zelenskyy held talks with US Senators Richard Blumenthal (Democrat) and James Lankford (Republican) in Kyiv during a National Prayer Breakfast on August 23.
Zelenskyy thanked Washington for its “unwavering bipartisan and bicameral support” and said efforts were continuing in both chambers of Congress to increase pressure on Russia, including through the Lindsey Graham sanctions bill targeting Russia and Iran.
As Russia continued its missile and drone attacks across Ukraine, Zelenskyy said he briefed the senators on "Russia's ongoing terror with ballistic missiles," stressing the importance of giving Kyiv the capabilities to counter the attacks.
He said implementing a decision to grant licenses from the US for the production of Patriot systems "could significantly help."
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces on August 23 launched a massive barrage of 127 strike drones across the country overnight.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia is seeking to sharply expand its ballistic-missile production.
"I believe that Russia may have up to 1,300 ballistic missiles a year. Now they have 600-630.... They can have about 100 ballistic missiles per month. But now they don't have that yet," he said.
The figures have not been independently verified.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is working to weaken Russia's military industry, including through strikes on military targets and other measures aimed at reducing ballistic-missile production.
Early on August 24, Russian e-commerce retailer said its logistics hub in Krasnodar had been hit by Ukrainian drones and set ablaze. The company said there were no casualties.
On August 22, Kyiv's forces hit an Ozon warehouse in Samara, expanding its attacks on the sector after weeks of strikes on facilities belonging to Russian online giant Wildberries.

Shelley Fabares, ‘Johnny Angel’ singer and actor in ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ dies at 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:53:01 UTC
06:53:01 KST

Shelley Fabares, ‘Johnny Angel’ singer and actor in ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ dies at 82
Shelley Fabares, an actor who was a fixture on television for decades from her days as a young teenager on “The Donna Reed Show,” through “One Day at a Time” and “Coach,” has died. She was 82.
She died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said in a statement to The Associated Press. No cause was given.
“To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort,” her family wrote. “She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for.”
Fabares was born in Santa Monica, California, in 1944, and started acting as a young child. Her first television credit came at age 10 when she appeared on “The Loretta Young Show.” Many movies and television shows followed: She acted with Paul Newman, Frank Sinatra and Eva Marie Saint in a Producers Showcase production of “Our Town”; was in the Rosalind Russell movie “The Girl Rush” and the Rock Hudson drama “Never Say Goodbye.” Other early credits include “Annette,” “Captain Midnight” and the “Black Leather Jackets” episode of “The Twilight Zone.”
Her biggest break came when she was cast as Mary Stone on “The Donna Reed Show,” where she was a regular from 1958 through 1963. During that time she also got a recording contract and had two Top 40 hits including “Johnny Angel.” In the early 1960s, she also co-starred in three movies with Elvis Presley: “Girl Happy,” “Spinout” and “Clambake.”
“I think the years on ‘The Donna Reed Show,’ the years from 14 to 19, were so incredibly important,” Fabares told the Los Angeles Times in 1993. “Donna Reed was simply an extraordinary woman, a woman of great strength, kindness, integrity and compassion. I am not trying to make her sound like a saint, but she had the most profound influence on me. I carry her with me today.”
In the late 1970s, Fabares made an impression as Francine Webster on the CBS sitcom “One Day at a Time.” She also played James Caan’s wife in “Brian’s Song.” One of her biggest roles came when she was cast as Christine Armstrong in “Coach,” although the show took a minute to find its audience.
“I did always feel from the very beginning if they could find the right spot for us, this was a show that would last,” she said in the 1993 Los Angeles Times interview.
Fabares married twice, first to producer Lou Adler in 1964. She had been married to “M-A-S-H” actor Mike Farrell since 1984. She was also a devoted advocate for Alzheimer’s awareness, which affected her mother.
In early 1999, a visit to the emergency room for an esophageal bleed revealed that she had progressive liver failure. After spending 22 months on a waiting list, she had liver transplant surgery in October 2000.
In an interview with Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles three years after the transplant, she said she’d been “changed by the experience” and was eternally grateful to Farrell who was with her “every step of the way.”
Her family, in their statement, said “we will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives.”

Syria tells Israel it won't limit military buildup in security deal talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:52:13 UTC
06:52:13 KST

Syria told Israel that it would not accept restrictions on its right to develop its military capabilities or form alliances with other countries as part of a future security arrangement, Syria's state-run SANA news agency reported Sunday night, citing a diplomatic source.
According to the source, talks between the two countries focused on developing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli strikes in Syria and reviving negotiations toward a security agreement that could eventually serve as the basis for a broader accord.
SANA reported that Damascus stressed that it would reject any mechanisms limiting Syrian sovereignty. Its immediate priority, according to the report, is the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines held before December 8, 2024, and the full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement. The diplomatic source said any future security arrangement must also respect Syria's territorial integrity.
The report came after Mossad Chief Roman Gofman met with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Sunday in an effort to defuse tensions between the two countries following Israel's strike on Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase last week.
Reuters reported last week that Gofman and al-Shaibani had also spoken by phone several days before the strike and discussed Turkey's military presence in Syria. Axios first reported Sunday's meeting, citing two sources familiar with the matter.
In an interview with Reuters on Saturday, al-Shaibani said negotiations over a security agreement with Israel had been frozen since the start of the Iran war and that contact between the two countries was cut following the airbase strike. He nevertheless said he expected negotiations to resume soon and hoped an agreement would ultimately lead to Israel's withdrawal from Syrian territory.
Al-Shaibani said the United States was continuously pressing Israel to return to negotiations and urged Israel to seize what he called a "historic opportunity" while the door to diplomacy remains open. He said Damascus' priority is to halt Israeli attacks and that confidence-building measures are needed.
"We believe there should be contact, especially with a party that constantly threatens the security of Syria. But if this contact doesn't bring results, then we don't need it," al-Shaibani said. "We do not trust Israel currently."
Asked about the prospects for an agreement, al-Shaibani said it was "very hard to bet on Israel," but that Syria had "very great hope" of establishing stable relations with its neighbors. "Syria is extending its hand for understandings, for peace, for diplomacy" and regional stability, he said.
Israel said following the strike that Damascus was preparing to allow Turkish forces to deploy at the airbase. Syria and Turkey denied the claim, and al-Shaibani said Israel struck the base even after Syria conveyed that it would not be used as a Turkish base.
Al-Shaibani said Syria receives training and military assistance from Turkey, as well as support from Jordan, Saudi Arabia and other countries. He said Damascus was grateful for Turkey's help in rebuilding the Syrian military and "will not give up that support."
Washington has sought for more than a year to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The talks have yet to produce an agreement amid Israeli strikes on Syrian government assets and the deployment of Israeli troops inside Syrian territory, which Israel says are necessary for its security.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office did not respond to al-Shaibani's remarks.

PM 'signed people's body parts' that he would not change GST deal — as it happened
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says no changes will be made to GST distribution after a Productivity Commission report raised concerns it unfairly benefits WA.

PM says it's time for Liberal party to 'front up' to alleged Brethren connections
Albanese is talking about the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren.
The Church was in the headlines during the 2025 federal election after a number of members were accused of harassing candidates and volunteers at polling booths.
The Church has denied those allegations as well as claims published in the Nine Newspapers last week which accused members of coordinating far-right influencers to harass candidates.
The PM references a run-in he had with a far-right influencer on the first day of his campaign last year, as well as confrontation in a hotel lobby.
"In my hotel, there were people confronted, including my press secretary.., by people from the far right, the links with neo-Nazis, and the links with people being paid to disrupt an election campaign," he says.
"[They did it] not to engage in policy debate, but to undermine our democracy."
Albanese says the Liberal party must explain how and why those people were connected to their campaign.
Farley comments show Labor has immigration numbers 'about right'
We're back on immigration after the PM was asked about One Nation MP David Farley's comments yesterday about immigration, and how it aligns with Labor's policy.
Albanese says the government is working toward the 225,000 NOM figure previously forecast by Treasury.
"What David Farley said on Sunday is that he believed the numbers Labor came up with are about right," he says.

A no doubt relieved WA premier Roger Cook has been standing behind the PM during the press conference and steps up to the mic.

Key Event
Albanese says no change to WA GST distribution
Albanese is answering questions about the amount of money WA gets as part of the GST distribution.
The deal struck by then-treasurer Scott Morrison ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula, which is meant to give more money per person to states with the highest need and lowest financial means.
Earlier this month, the Productivity Commission published its interim report into the deal, calling it a "costly mistake" and recommending the government scrap it.
A number of premiers, including NSW's Chris Minns, are unhappy with the arrangement.
So - is the PM considering changing the way the pie is sliced?
"There will be no change to WA's GST arrangements while I'm prime minister," Albanese says.
"I think that WA deserves that, because WA contributes to the national economy and helps to drive that economy."

"This has been through all of our processes, many meetings and many hours... this is a once in many generations investment."
Joyce says One Nation 'sticking' to 130k immigration number
Barnaby Joyce is back, this time on News24 (previously Sky), still holding the proverbial mop to clean up what David Farley said about immigration yesterday.
He says people should "ignore" the number of people coming in to the country on the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme, because they generally stay for under 12 months, which means they are not counted in the NOM.
"They come, and they go," he says.
"We've reviewed the numbers, we've got far too many, 130,000 Net Overseas Migration is our number and we're sticking to it."
He's pressed on how a significant reduction in migrant workers might mean for productivity, but deflects to talk about energy prices.
"Go back to coal-fire power, increase productivity as a nation, stop small businesses going out of business," he says.
Data centre renewable push 'not that different' from Qld smelter deal
Industry Minister Tim Ayres is in Perth today to announce a $120 million investment for a manufacturing pilot designed to speed up build times for apartments.
While we're on the topic of development, Ayres is asked about resistance from some states and territories to sign up to minimum standards for data centres which would require developers to power the sites with renewable energy.
"I want to be respectful of the National Cabinet process, which is meeting in a couple of days' time," Ayres says.
"But we have set out our objective here to legislate AI, data centre standards for Australia, and that means not having a race to the bottom on electricity and water."
Ayres says the deal would be "not all that different" from the one struck by Queensland premier David Crisafulli to secure the future of the Boyne aluminium smelter.
Queensland is one of the jurisdictions holding out on the data centre standards.
"They're not that different really, large scale industrial electricity users and data centres," he says.
"It is now thanks to the deal with the Crisafulli government going to be powered by wind and solar."
Taylor answers question about Exclusive Brethren
Last week, a parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election heard from a director of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren.
The Church has denied allegations it secretly paid people to disrupt Labor's re-election campaign last year in a coordinated effort involving far-right influencers.
Overwhelmingly, members of the church appeared to support the Liberals during the campaign, although at the time both the church and the party denied any official affiliation.
Taylor says he's seen the reporting but doesn't answer a question about his level of concern over the allegations.
Instead, he talks about volunteers from the Rapid Relief Team, run by the church, who are helping with the Pollie Pedal, a bike ride event which raises money for charity.
Taylor is taking part in the ride.
"We're being supported by the rapid relief team and they are an extraordinary group of people," he says.
"That is an extraordinary organisation, and I am sure there are many Labor members who have been supported by that organisation because of the great work that they do."
Energy for data centres should be up to the people who build it
Taylor says the states and territories should get to decide what energy sources power data centres built in their jurisdictions, not the federal government.
On Wednesday, Albanese is expected to push minimum standards through National Cabinet which would require data centres to provide their own renewable energy sources.
Queensland and the NT are resisting, in part because they don't agree that renewable power should be the only option.
"The problem with Chris Bowen and this Prime Minister is that they always have their favourites," he says.
"We are absolutely neutral to the fuel source... we need to make sure that we have the energy to support Australian households, Australian industry, and any new data centres.
"But we won't be picking the fuel source, that should be done by people who are actually paying for it and building it."
Taylor says Labor, One Nation 'all over the shop' on immigration
Opposition leader Angus Taylor is shining bright in orange high vis today, holding a press conference at a gas-fired generator in Swanbank, Queensland.
He claims the opposition has "laid out" how it will bring the "numbers down and standards up" on immigration, despite the fact we're yet to see their policy position on the subject and apparently won't see it before the year is out.
Taylor is relying on an earlier announcement from the Coalition that immigration would be tied to housing supply.
"We'll cap migration based on housing supply, we'll put Australian values at the centre of our immigration policy," he says.
"Our opponents are all over the shop on this."
Could AI be an election sleeper issue?
At the last federal election, Tim Wilson won back the seat of Goldstein by 175 votes. The LNP held Longman by 269 votes, and in Bradfield, 26 votes determined who went to Canberra.
Tiny margins.
We've all heard about the risk of deepfakes, misinformation campaigns and foreign interference meddling in elections and compromising democracy.
But what if the more seismic change at the next election isn't just the usual flood of misleading material on social media?
Patricia Karvelas digs in to how AI and chatbots might be the next frontier to sway voters.

The government expects to settle new rules for how data centres use energy in Australia at Wednesday's national cabinet meeting, despite Queensland confirming it will remain opposed to the plan.

The Coalition's immigration policy
There are more questions than answers on immigration this week.
Liberal senator Jonno Duniam, who is leading the internal process for the Coalition's immigration policy, does not have an answer for when the public will get to see it.
"I'm not going to put a date on it," he says.
"We are in 2026, and the world in 2028, which is the first opportunity the Coalition will have at the election to form government if we win, so we need to make sure we are as relevant to that point in time as possible."
Don't expect the policy this year, he says, but maybe a "short time after that".
Conroy defends lobbying relationships
We're back talking about lobbyists at Parliament House.
Conroy insists the government has strict codes of conduct that guide its interactions with the lobbying industry, including the defence industry (his portfolio).
He says it would be unfair to exclude former defence ministers and Australian Defence Force officers who still want to contribute to policy debate.
"They obviously want to keep making a contribution to public policy, and that is their right," he says.
"I don't think people should be excluded from working in the Australian defence industry automatically, just because they happened to be a defence minister."
When will we see the government's immigration numbers?
Labor frontbencher Pat Conroy says the federal government is working to find the "right" answer for its migration policy rather than a fast answer.
Treasury has forecast a NOM of 225,000 in the financial year after this one, but Conroy won't say if that is in line with the government's own targets.
Last month Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke hastily withdrew from a planned speech at the National Press Club in which he was expected to unveil an immigration policy that included moving the families of skilled migrants into offshore processing.
We still don't have a new date for the speech, nor do we have an immigration policy, and Conroy says we won't be getting either until Burke is ready.
"I understand some in the community wanted answers to this yesterday, but it's a complex area, and it's important we get the answer right, rather than get the fast answer," he says.
"That's why Minister Burke is working through this in a serious, considered way, consulting with all his colleagues in the relevant areas."
Government to bail out SunRice
One Nation MP David Farley covered a lot of ground in his Insiders interview on Sunday, including an interaction he had with the PM after raising the issue of a struggling SunRice manufacturing plant in his electorate of Farrer.
And apparently the PM was very wiling to help.
This morning, Murray Watt confirms a bail out is being discussed for the factory, which is part of the supply chain for rice cakes.
"I can confirm that we have advised SunRice that we are prepared to co-invest with them in new investment in a rice processing plant," he says.
"SunRice has indicated that investment as well as their own would protect their jobs as well as potentially creating more."
The cost to taxpayers isn't clear yet, but we know the company has requested $15 million from the government, which it would then match.
The government says it's waiting on a formal written proposal from SunRice.
Watt defends lobbyist access
Watt is defending the government's rules around lobbyist access to parliament after a Four Corners investigation revealed dozens of former defence officials have jumped into lucrative lobbying roles or the defence sector.
Critics say there's a "revolving door" where former officials can use their connections to potentially influence the awarding of multi-million-dollar contracts.
It's prompted calls for tighter regulations and greater transparency.
But Watt says there are already strict lobbyist rules in place.
"[They] regulate, for example, the activities of former politicians, former staffers, [and] periods of time that they can't lobby and use information that they have been privy to," he says.
"And of course, any lobbyist needs to be on the lobbyist register, so there is a high degree of disclosure and transparency."
Expect more mass bird flu mortalities
Environment Minister Murray Watt is speaking with ABC News Breakfast about the first Australian detection of bird flu in a mammal.
Watt says the weekend discovery of the disease in a long-nose fur seal in South Australia is a "very serious development" but "not unexpected".
"We are likely to see more mass mortalities, which is obviously a terrible thing for all Australians who love our nature," he says.
"But we have been preparing this for some time … to make sure our populations are resilient, and we will continue to do everything we can."

Hongkong Post should focus on public service, not profit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Hongkong Post should focus on public service, not profit
The traditional self-funding operating model is no longer viable in an increasingly competitive e-commerce market
The crisis facing the city’s postal service has been a long time coming – snail mail has been slowing for postal services worldwide for decades, forcing changes to ensure survival.
That has included axing jobs and rethinking the purpose they serve in the 21st century. One of the most drastic moves came from Denmark where PostNord ended its letter delivery service at the end of 2025 to focus entirely on parcel delivery. The country is one of the world’s most digitalised nations, with 95 per cent of Danes fully integrated into its digital platforms. Ending its 400-year letter service was the correct move.
Obviously, that’s not the case with Hong Kong. We are nowhere near Denmark in terms of development and adoption of digital platforms. But if the government’s ambitious digitalisation plans bear fruit, Hongkong Post’s existential crisis will only deepen.
The government is pushing for more residents to use the iAM Smart one-stop digital services platform to access government services and others. Increasingly, there will be fewer letters to deliver. By the end of 2025, iAM Smart had already accumulated over 4 million users. Hongkong Post must brace itself to adapt to this irreversible trend, unless it wants the government’s digitalisation push to fail.

Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate as fire threatens US state of Nevada

Unknown Publisher

Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate as fire threatens US state of Nevada
NEW YORK - Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated this weekend from the area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave on Aug 23 as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state’s third-most-populous city.
About 42,000 residents have been displaced or are in active evacuations with an additional 45,000 in “be prepared to evacuate” status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late Aug 23 morning.
Local TV footage showed flames approaching roads. In eyewitness video verified by Reuters, smoke from the hills billowed over nearby residential neighbourhoods.
Fire-tracking websites showed evacuation zones extending from the Sierra Nevada hills to the University of Nevada in north-west Reno.
The fire has burned 5,261ha so far, officials said at a press conference on Aug 23. The fire was human-caused and remains under investigation, they said.
Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, said Shane Akerson, a commander leading fire and rescue operations.
Officials first received reports of a fire off Hawk Meadow Trail at about 11.15am PDT on Aug 22 (2.15am on Aug 23, Singapore time), said Richard Edwards, chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. Firefighters on Aug 22 worked amid “extreme red flag conditions,” he said.
Red flag conditions are a combination of warm temperatures, very low humidity and strong winds that raise the risk of wildfires.
“We expect those same strong conditions to come back this afternoon,” Edwards said on Aug 23.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency late on Aug 22 in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe.
“This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials,” Lombardo said in a statement.
Lombardo authorized the deployment of two National Guard helicopters to help fight fires and 60 National Guard personnel to support operations with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office, officials said.
The Reno-Tahoe International Airport remained outside the evacuation area, and commercial flights were operating normally on Aug 23. REUTERS

Meta and other social networks come under fire over accusations of harming children
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
00:29:00 EEST
06:29:00 KST

Meta and other social networks come under fire over accusations of harming children
Kyiv • UNN
29 U.S. states accuse social networks of harming children and demand up to $1.4 trillion. The companies deny wrongdoing.
U.S. states and thousands of young users are suing Meta, Google, TikTok and Snap, accusing the social media companies of creating platforms that foster addiction and harm children and teenagers. In the case against Meta, being heard in federal court in Oakland, 29 states are seeking penalties that could potentially reach $1.4 trillion, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The lawsuits allege that the companies deliberately created features that encourage young users to spend extended periods of time on the platforms compulsively. These include endless feeds, algorithmic recommendations and notifications that prompt users to constantly return to social media.
In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google negligent in the design and operation of their platforms and awarded a 20-year-old plaintiff $6 million. Overall, the companies face more than 3,000 similar lawsuits from children, teenagers and young people who report psychological and physical problems, and in some cases—deaths.
Companies deny the allegations
The plaintiffs cite the companies' internal documents. In particular, materials made public in 2021 by former Facebook employee Frances Haugen indicated that Meta knew about the negative impact of its platforms on young people. Documents from ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, also stated that teenagers, due to their underdeveloped ability to assess risks, are more likely to repeat dangerous stunts seen online.
Meta, Google, TikTok and Snap reject the allegations. The companies say they did not create their products to attract children, are implementing safety tools and are working to protect young users. Meta also argues that social media helps children stay connected with friends and family.
Separately, more than 1,300 U.S. school districts have filed lawsuits. They are seeking compensation for expenses related to problems that, in their view, are caused by social media, including additional psychologists, security and teacher training. In May, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Google agreed to pay $27 million to settle one such lawsuit.

Wife of Palestinian terrorist convicted in Israeli minister’s assassination gives birth to twins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:28:03 UTC
06:28:03 KST

Sanabel al-Ra’i, the wife of Palestinian prisoner Basel al-Asmar, who is serving a lengthy prison sentence for his role in the assassination of former tourism minister Rehavam Ze’evi, gave birth to twins Saturday in Qalqilya in the West Bank.
According to the family, al-Ra’i became pregnant through fertility treatment using sperm from her imprisoned husband that had been smuggled out of prison and frozen. Family members said the process took more than two years and involved several attempts at fertilization before the latest attempt succeeded, resulting in a twin pregnancy.
Palestinian photographer Mohammed Nazzal documented the birth. He said al-Ra’i, a former nurse, experienced a mixture of joy over the birth of her children and pain because their father remains in prison and could not be at her side.
After giving birth, al-Ra’i said she felt strong and had succeeded in “defeating the prison,” according to Nazzal.
A relationship that began through prison visits
Al-Ra’i’s relationship with al-Asmar began when she visited her brother, Shaher al-Ra’i, who had been imprisoned by Israel several times.
Her brother was placed in administrative detention — a measure Israel uses to hold suspects without filing criminal charges, generally on the basis of classified security evidence — in June 2015. His detention order was extended several times before he was released in 2017. He was arrested again this year and released in June.
During her prison visits, al-Ra’i met al-Asmar. The couple married in 2022 while he was still incarcerated. The marriage was conducted by proxy, with al-Asmar’s brother signing the marriage documents on his behalf.
Four years later, the couple’s twins have been born while al-Asmar remains behind bars.
Al-Asmar was arrested in 2002 and is serving a life sentence plus an additional 20 years for his involvement in the assassination of Ze’evi, a right-wing Israeli politician who was tourism minister at the time of his death.
Ze’evi was shot and killed at Jerusalem’s Hyatt Hotel on Oct. 17, 2001.
According to details released in al-Asmar’s case, he served as a secondary gunman in the assassination squad. His role was to provide security for the killing and shoot Ze’evi’s bodyguards if they attempted to intervene.
Ze’evi was killed by members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, or PFLP, a Palestinian terrorist organization. The group said the assassination was retaliation for Israel’s killing of its leader, Abu Ali Mustafa, in an Israeli missile strike in the West Bank city of Ramallah earlier that year.
Sperm reportedly smuggled from Israeli prison
The al-Asmar case is the latest example of a phenomenon in which Palestinian prisoners serving lengthy sentences have, according to Palestinian reports, smuggled sperm out of Israeli prisons in an effort to have children while incarcerated.
Al-Asmar’s family said his sperm was smuggled out about two years ago and subsequently frozen.
An Israeli security official said the smuggling referred to in the reports occurred before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
According to the official, Israel Prison Service policies have since changed, and the types of meetings that previously allowed Palestinian prisoners to transfer materials or have private visits with their spouses are no longer permitted.

Pro-government Adilet party sweeps Kazakhstan election, exit polls show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
21:26:39 UTC
06:26:39 KST

A newly formed pro-government party has won a large majority in Kazakhstan's snap parliamentary election, three exit polls showed, in a result set to cement President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's power over the major energy and minerals exporter.
The exit polls, published by Kazakh state media, showed the Adilet party winning between 70 percent and 72 percent of the vote, with turnout above 74 percent.
Four small opposition parties also won seats, according to the polls.
Adilet was formed earlier this year by the president's top aides and swiftly absorbed the previously long-ruling Amanat party.
Sunday's election was triggered by the adoption of a new constitution earlier this year, which streamlines parliament from two chambers into one.
A former Soviet diplomat and top United Nations official, Tokayev has led Central Asia's largest economy since 2019, maintaining warm relations with the West, Russia and China.
One chamber
Kazakhstan's Supreme Court said last month that the new constitution allowed Tokayev to run for a fresh seven-year term.
Tokayev took office as the chosen successor of Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan's founding president, who ruled from 1991 to 2019.
He broke with Nazarbayev after unrest in 2022 that Tokayev has described as a coup attempt by Nazarbayev allies.
Voting in the capital, Astana, Tokayev told journalists it was too early to say whether he would seek another term.
He also said he would announce his choice of vice president, an office created under the new constitution, within the next seven to 10 days, adding that the nominee would be a "well-known" person.

The ministers in charge of urban planning, housing and territorial development, as well as the minister in charge of territorial administration and decentralization, accompanied by local authorities, visited the site to assess the extent of the damage and oversee rescue operations.
The landslide was reportedly caused by the collapse of a large mass of household rubbish that had accumulated at the site over several years.
The Guinean government has not yet released an official death toll.
According to local media reports, the authorities had planned to close the Dar-es-Salam rubbish dump on Sunday, the same day the disaster occurred. ■

China Focus: Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
05:26:07 CST
06:26:07 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a visit aimed at renewing a friendship with the Chinese people that first took root more than two decades ago.
The 69-year-old will spend part of his stay planting trees alongside his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades.
Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification.
At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life.
The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees.
In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed.
On May 18, the two finally connected over a video call. Yin, who had been practicing over and over, greeted him in her slightly broken English: "You are brother!"
Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert.
Ahead of Sakolsky's arrival in Inner Mongolia on Sunday afternoon, Yin, no less excited, brought with her pepino melons freshly picked from her orchard.
"I went to pick some pepino melons for him, so he can taste the fruit from the desert the moment he steps off the plane," she said. "When I tell him I grew these in the desert, he won't believe it."
At the Ordos Ejin Horo Airport in Inner Mongolia, as soon as Yin spotted him coming down the escalator, she rushed to him. Overcome with emotion, the two hugged tightly, weeping with joy after more than two decades apart.
"This is a dream come true," said Sakolsky. "She made a promise 27 years ago and she kept her promise. I never thought I would see her again. It is a miracle, but it shows culture and people can still keep promises."
Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks.
The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said.
Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students.
Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. ■
