03:52:35 KST

Halis Sünnetci
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Dominik Szoboszlai converted a penalty in the ninth minute of stoppage time as Liverpool came from behind twice to earn a dramatic 2-2 draw against Newcastle United on Sunday.
Anthony Elanga gave Newcastle an early lead at St. James’ Park before Cody Gakpo equalized in the second half.
Substitute Joe Willock restored the hosts’ advantage less than three minutes later, but Szoboszlai’s late spot kick denied Newcastle victory in Matthias Jaissle’s first Premier League match in charge.
Newcastle opened the scoring through a counterattack in the fifth minute.
Liverpool left space in midfield, allowing William Osula to surge forward before playing Elanga through on goal. The Swedish winger finished calmly past Alisson Becker and into the bottom-left corner.
The goal ended Elanga’s run of 40 league appearances without scoring, dating back to April 2025.
Liverpool nearly equalized in the 18th minute. Rio Ngumoha’s cross was overhit, but the visitors regained possession and Milos Kerkez delivered another ball into the area.
After Newcastle failed to clear, Florian Wirtz fired toward the bottom corner, but debutant goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek produced a sharp save.
Newcastle threatened again in the 24th minute when Yoane Wissa played Osula into the area. Jeremy Jacquet applied pressure, while Alisson left his line quickly to smother the forward’s attempt.
The hosts maintained their advantage until halftime despite Liverpool controlling more possession and winning several corners.
Liverpool drew level in the 54th minute through Gakpo.
Ryan Gravenberch played a direct pass to his fellow Dutchman, who turned and advanced toward the penalty area before drilling a powerful shot into the bottom-left corner.
Newcastle responded almost immediately.
Wissa led a counterattack and released Joe Willock, who had entered the match moments earlier. The midfielder cut inside and curled a shot past Alisson from about 20 yards, with the ball striking the post before crossing the line in the 57th minute.
Wissa came close to extending Newcastle’s lead in the 68th minute but failed to connect with Lewis Hall’s low cross across the six-yard box.
Alisson then kept Liverpool in the match in the 86th minute, racing off his line and blocking Wissa’s low effort with his legs.
Liverpool were awarded a penalty deep into stoppage time after substitute Victor Munoz drove into the area and was brought down by Hall.
Szoboszlai stepped up and powered the penalty into the top-left corner in the 99th minute, giving Hornicek no chance.
The result gave Newcastle and Liverpool one point each from their opening match of the Premier League season.

WSJ: Russia holds mobilisation exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast
Russian military officials conducted an exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast in July to test procedures for mobilising local residents.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing Western intelligence officials
Details: Western intelligence officials told the WSJ that Russian military officers had flown from St Petersburg to Kaliningrad Oblast last month, where they oversaw readiness planning and mobilisation procedures for local residents, including arrangements for their accommodation, food and weapons.
The exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast was just one of many such drills being held across Russia in preparation for a possible mobilisation.
The sources said the Kremlin has not yet decided whether to launch such measures and is unlikely to do so before the parliamentary elections at the end of September. However, Russian leader Vladimir Putin's determination to seize the entire Donbas could push him to take such a step.
The WSJ said that Moscow has failed in recent months to recruit enough new troops to replace battlefield losses, while the growing use of Ukrainian drones has "reduced the average Russian soldier's lifespan on the front to a matter of minutes, days or weeks". These manpower problems may leave Putin with no choice but to announce a new wave of mobilisation, US and European officials said.
Western intelligence also believes that, in the event of a possible escalation with the West, Russia could seize part of the Suwałki Gap, a strip of land linking Kaliningrad with Belarus through neighbouring Poland and Lithuania.
The WSJ reported that rumours of a possible new mobilisation have caused concern inside Russia in recent weeks and months, with men searching online for ways to leave the country in an emergency. Some Russians have already identified places where they could stay for several months to wait out a possible mobilisation.
A mobilisation could help reinforce Russia's line of contact and accelerate its advance towards Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in Donetsk Oblast. However, if it were launched this late in the year, before fighting slows in winter, it is unclear what practical effect the move would have.
Background: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 11 August that Russia is preparing to carry out additional mobilisation in the autumn after its sham parliamentary elections.

23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
 Libya needs to strengthen cooperation with Iraq across various sectors, acting Foreign Minister Taher Al-Baour said Sunday.
Baour made the remarks at a joint news conference with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein in the capital Baghdad, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
“Our relationship with Iraq is longstanding, and the two countries share many common issues,” Al-Baour said.
He added that Libya seeks to become an effective state within the Arab region.
The Libyan minister stressed the need for cooperation and information-sharing with Iraq in several fields, including education, health and oil.
Hussein, for his part, said efforts were underway to develop relations with Libya and affirmed Baghdad’s support for a peaceful settlement among the Libyan parties.
He added that Baour’s visit would include the signing of a number of memorandums of understanding.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi also discussed with Al-Baour and his accompanying delegation ways to strengthen bilateral relations.
Zaidi received a written message from Libyan National Unity Government’s Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh emphasizing “the importance of consolidating and strengthening bilateral relations between Iraq and Libya,” according to a statement from his office.
The message also included an official invitation for the Iraqi prime minister to visit Libya “at the earliest possible opportunity” and stressed the importance of continued coordination and consultations to align positions at international forums regarding challenges facing the Arab region.
Zaidi said Iraq was “determined to build the best possible foreign relations with brothers and friends.”
He emphasized the importance Baghdad attaches to opportunities for cooperation and economic integration to “strengthen capabilities, support sustainable development and reinforce the foundations of a positive partnership.”
Baour arrived in Baghdad earlier Sunday for an official visit of an unspecified duration to participate in meetings of the Libyan-Iraqi Joint Committee on Sunday and Monday, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The committee is reconvening after a 25-year hiatus.
Upon his arrival, Baour held talks with Hussein on bilateral relations and ways to develop cooperation in various fields.
They also discussed regional and international issues of mutual concern and exchanged views on them, the ministry said.
The Libyan-Iraqi Joint Committee is a high-level institutional framework intended to strengthen bilateral relations and facilitate agreements covering economy, trade, investment, health, education and security.
The precise date of the committee’s establishment could not be confirmed, but sources told Anadolu that its first session was held in 2000, when the two countries agreed that it would convene annually.
Its second and most recent session was held in the Libyan capital Tripoli in 2001.
The committee’s meetings were subsequently suspended following the 2003 US invasion of Iraq and the fall of Saddam Hussein’s government, followed by the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s government in Libya in 2011.

Russian volunteers shoot down much-hyped Ukrainian missile with machine-gun (VIDEO)
A small Russian mobile air defense unit consisting of volunteers has successfully shot down a Ukrainian missile Kiev touted as its “most successful” weapon by firing at it with a machine gun, according to Kursk Region Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein.
The intercept occurred during a Ukrainian drone and missile attack overnight on Sunday. According to Khinshtein, the BARS-Kursk brigade, made up predominantly of residents of the border region, received an alert about an incoming strike. Minutes later, one of its mobile air defense units detected a “huge” missile traveling at 500 kilometers per hour at an altitude of less than 50 meters. The soldiers managed to hit the missile, forcing it to lose altitude and eventually fall into a wooded area.
A video of the intercept recorded by BARS-Kursk soldiers and published by Khinshtein shows the unit detecting the projectile flying at a low altitude and shooting at it. The missile is then shown crashing into the ground in a massive fiery blast. The second part of the video shows soldiers examining the wreckage at the crash site.
The Russian military was able to retrieve the missile’s mission input data from the wreckage and determine that the projectile, with a range of 3,000 kilometers and carrying a warhead with explosives equivalent to a ton of TNT, was aimed at a “strategic facility” in Tula Region in central Russia.
“Our volunteers did not just shoot down a missile. They prevented a catastrophe and saved human lives,” the governor said, vowing to recommend the air defense unit servicemen for a decoration. He also called it an example “of what a Russian solider is capable of.”
The Ukrainian military has routinely targeted civilian and energy infrastructure in drone and missile strikes deep into Russian territory. Moscow has condemned the Ukrainian strikes on civilian infrastructure and residential areas as terrorist attacks, adding that they are apparently intended to compensate for Kiev’s setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces continue their steady advance.
Russia has responded to the attacks by intensifying long-range missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Ukrainian forces.
Unveiled in 2025, the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile has been touted by Kiev as a state-of-the-art weapon. Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky described it last year as “by far the most successful missile in Ukraine’s arsenal.”
The missile is produced by Fire Point – a Ukrainian defense contractor personally promoted by Zelensky during his trips to Western nations.
The company was later revealed to be de facto owned by the Ukrainian leader’s longtime former business partner, Timur Mindich, known as “Zelensky’s wallet” in Kiev. The businessman fled Ukraine last year after a major corruption scandal in which he was named as one of the primary suspects.

Tusk’s stance on Nord Stream motivated by ‘economic expediency’ – Putin
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s position on the Nord Stream pipeline sabotage is motivated by the fact that Warsaw lost out economically on the project, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in an interview with Vesti published on Sunday.
The statement came just days after Tusk said that those responsible for the September 2022 blasts should not be ashamed, but rather those who built the pipelines. Warsaw had long opposed the pipelines’ construction over concerns about Europe’s dependence on Russian energy, he told reporters on Thursday.
According to Putin, the Polish prime minister’s “motives are very simple – economic expediency.”
The initial plan for the Nord Stream project envisioned one of the pipelines going through Poland, he said. However, the decision was ultimately made to “to run the second line along the bottom of the Baltic Sea in order to minimize risks,” he added.
Even back then, Warsaw was against this, Putin added.
“Partly because it would lose certain economic advantages for Poland as a transit country. Secondly, Poland would lose revenue from the transit of our hydrocarbons. This position is absolutely nothing new,” he said.
Tusk’s statement came a day after a Ukrainian national suspected of taking part in the bombing of the Nord Stream pipelines was arrested in Croatia on a European warrant.
German investigators maintain that the sabotage was carried out by a small group of Ukrainians who used counterfeit documents to rent a sailing yacht and transport military-grade explosives to waters off the Danish island of Bornholm. There, the group allegedly used commercial diving equipment to set the charges on the pipelines at a depth of around 100 meters.
Moscow has long dismissed the theory as fantasy, arguing that the operation could not have been carried out in NATO-controlled waters without state backing.
In a 2024 interview with American journalist Tucker Carlson, Putin hinted that the blasts were likely orchestrated by the CIA.

The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:45:00 UTC
03:45:00 KST

The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration
Lauren Edwards’ campaign is trying to restart a stalled process to legalized assisted dying in England and Wales — and she’s taking cues from her native Australia.
People gather outside the U.K. Parliament in London during the House of Lords' second reading of the assisted dying bill, on Sept. 12, 2025. | Peter Nicholls/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain is still lagging behind Australia when it comes to assisted dying. But one Labour MP who has seen the debate in both countries is hoping she can push forward a thwarted attempt at change in the U.K.
“If I had six months to live and I was facing a potentially very frightening, very painful, very uncomfortable death, I would want to be able to have the choice to choose to end my life surrounded by my family,” Lauren Edwards, who became an MP in 2024 — and hails from Melbourne, Australia, tells POLITICO in an interview.
Edwards’ support for assisted dying is shaped in part by the laws in Victoria, where she still has family. In 2017, it became the first Australian state to legalize assisted dying for people expected to die within six months, or 12 months for those with neurodegenerative diseases, and who face unacceptable suffering.
Advertisement
Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue.
It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand.
Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around.
It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live.
“When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.”
Sense-checking the legislation with family down under was “really important” when weighing up whether to support Leadbeater’s earlier proposals, she says.
Edwards has Australian friends who have settled in Britain too — and contrasts a friend able to attend his mother’s assisted death in Australia with British families currently worried about prosecution for helping relatives to die. U.K. law punishes the offense with up to 14 years in prison.
Lauren Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model. | House of Commons
“[The] status quo is not neutral. It is not benign,” Edwards argues. “It is a situation where, if we don’t make this legislative change, unfortunately, we will be allowing that pain, fear and isolation.”
In October 2024, an independent review of assisted dying in Victoria by the state Department of Health’s Centre for Evaluation and Research Evidence found the system to be safe and “operating as intended” with “no reports of ineligible individuals” accessing substances to end their lives.
However, access to assisted dying varies across the vast state — which is only slightly smaller than the entire U.K. — and just “a few practitioners” deliver the majority of care. Victoria has been urged to press the central Australian government for more funding.
Advertisement
Choice of priorities
Back in the U.K., the main political parties have agreed that the decision to legalize assisted dying should be a matter for parliament, rather than any one administration. MPs were not whipped to vote in any particular way on Leadbeater’s bill, and the issue is treated as a matter of conscience.
But there was tacit endorsement for the most recent attempted overhaul from the top of Keir Starmer’s government. Before entering No. 10, Starmer promised broadcaster Esther Rantzen — who has stage four lung cancer — that he’d make time for a vote in parliament.
Leadbeater’s bill also received technical support from civil servants in the Department for Health and Social Care and the Ministry of Justice to ensure its workability.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham appears to have other ideas. Burnham was not an MP when assisted dying passed the Commons last year and abstained in a 2015 vote during a previous stint in parliament.
More strikingly, when asked about his stance on the issue last month, Burnham said “the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care” needs to happen first — and argued it would be “very challenging” to introduce assisted dying without substantial progress on these two running policy sores.
Edwards remains bullish. She commends the PM’s commitment to sustainably funding social care — Burnham has kicked off cross-party talks on the issue and asked for a speedier inquiry — and she insists his professed skepticism hasn’t put her off.
Advertisement
“It’s really important that we consider them together,” Edwards says of social care and assisted dying. “I don’t think that there is a reason to delay” changing the law, she argues, highlighting £125 million provided by Starmer’s government for adult and children’s hospices. (A Public Accounts Committee report said this one-off funding did not directly pay for service delivery or solve financial problems facing the sector.)
Edwards’ bill has a four-year implementation period. That means if it becomes law next year, assisted dying wouldn’t be permitted until 2031. She believes the two systems can work on a “dual track” and that poor palliative care won’t incentivize people to access assisted dying.
“I don’t necessarily think that lack of care is a motivator for this option,” she argues. “I think it’s a last resort when physical suffering really can’t be relieved.”
Yvette Cooper speaks during a visit to a care home in London on July 29, 2026. | Pool photo by Kirsty Wigglesworth via WPA/Getty Images
From MPs to peers
A majority of Starmer’s Cabinet backed the bill last time, including Health Secretary Yvette Cooper and Justice Secretary Alex Norris — but only 12 MPs need to switch sides for the bill to fall, making the margins tight. Indeed, suspended Labour MP Karl Turner told POLITICO he’ll vote against the bill after abstaining last June.
“People’s views are largely what I expect them to be when we next vote on this,” Edwards argues. “We haven’t seen any significant moves away from people who were supportive of the bill.”
Then there is the substantive question of the House of Lords. Edwards condemns the “small minority” of peers she blames for filibustering the previous bill. She said she is happy to work with peers on good faith amendments in the “scrutiny process” this time around.
Advertisement
The pro-assisted dying camp will be relying on a little-used pair of laws — the Parliament Acts — which would, in narrow circumstances, allow a bill to be passed despite being deadlocked or defeated by peers in the House of Lords again. “I want to get it back to [peers] ASAP so that they will have the maximum amount of time to finish the job of scrutinizing,” Edwards says.
An impassioned opposition campaign last time around argued Leadbeater’s bill was not safe. The Royal College of Psychiatrists, while neutral on the principle of assisted dying, said it could not support her plans due to a lack of clarity about their profession’s role in the process and whether adequate resources are in place.
While Edwards may struggle to win over Burnham, she hopes to “sit down and have a conversation” with the prime minister before MPs return from recess in September.
One open question remains: how Starmer himself will vote. As prime minister, he voted for it, but didn’t explain his reasoning. Now freed from the constraints of government, Edwards hopes Starmer will make an intervention.
“He has a well-known legal background, is very considered and is obviously a really crucial voice,” she says. Starmer’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Erdogan once had Israeli friends: This is how the alliance with Turkey collapsed and what to worry about
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:42:22 UTC
03:42:22 KST

Israel and Turkey have been escalating both their activity and rhetoric against one another over their involvement in Syria, but the recent history of this relationship includes moments that are hard to imagine today: Israeli fighter pilots trained in Turkish skies; military and intelligence officers exchanged information; Israel’s defense industry upgraded Turkish fighter jets and tanks; Ankara served as a channel for messages between Jerusalem and Damascus; and leaders from both countries maintained close personal ties.
Today, and even more so after the strike on the base in Syria, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s “Don’t” warning to the Turks and the arrest warrant issued against him by Turkey, the situation is completely different. An Israeli security official, referring to the crisis with Turkey, said: “We’re not exactly rushing to end the crisis with Turkey. We’ve had enough. We tried the nice approach with them, but it didn’t work. Erdogan never stops inciting against us.”
He noted that U.S. President Donald Trump is not intervening for now: “He is keeping his distance, but that could change. He is letting the sides blow off steam. Everyone is concerned there could be a loss of control or a miscalculation. I think Erdogan is even more worried than we are.” 
The official added that “the entire Middle East knows that Israel is the strongest country in the region. Erdogan continues with the insults and the comparisons to Hitler, but he understands he cannot stretch this any further.”
In the past, by contrast, there also were more human moments. In the summer of 1999, when one of the deadliest earthquakes in Turkey’s history devastated large areas in the northwest of the country, Israel was among the first to arrive with aid. Hundreds of rescue and medical personnel set up field hospitals and worked in the disaster zone. In that event, 9-year-old Shiran Franco was rescued alive after about 100 hours under the rubble in intense heat, without food or water. Her father, twin brother, grandfather and grandmother did not survive.
The 1990s were the honeymoon period in Israel-Turkey relations. The Middle East peace process, the collapse of the Soviet Union and shared concerns over Syria, Iran and terrorist organizations created a strategic foundation for cooperation. In February 1996, the two countries signed a military cooperation agreement that included exchanges of information and experience, joint training and reciprocal access to ports. Just months later, Israeli F-16s were already training in Turkish airspace. Turkey had vast aerial training zones, while Israel had operational experience and technological know-how. Both sides benefited.
The defense alliance also took on an industrial dimension, including a deal worth about $650 million to upgrade 54 Turkish F-4 Phantom aircraft. Israel also participated in upgrading F-5s, while agreements were signed in parallel in the fields of missiles and armaments. There also were programs and deals involving Turkish M-60 tanks, unmanned aerial vehicles, warning systems and other technologies. Israel was not only Turkey’s ally, but a partner in modernizing its military.
In February 1999, Abdullah Ocalan, leader of the Kurdish rebel organization PKK, was captured in Kenya and handed over to Turkey. Western reports attributed a role to the Mossad in tracking him and even assisting in his capture. Israel officially denied the reports, but their very existence illustrated just how strategic and deep the relationship between the two countries was perceived to be.
Even Recep Tayyip Erdogan — an Islamist politician whose office displayed a picture of Al-Aqsa Mosque back in his days as mayor of Istanbul — did not rush to sever Turkey’s ties with Israel after his election in 2003. Two years later, he came on an official visit to Israel, and Israeli Foreign Ministry officials say diplomatic and economic cooperation between the countries strengthened afterward. It was a period in which personal and business ties were formed: Erdogan was considered a personal friend of brothers Yuli and Sami Ofer, and his son did business in Israel.
At the same time, cooperation in energy and infrastructure was being examined, including especially ambitious ideas for transporting Israeli gas to Turkey, which could have turned Turkey into an energy gateway to Europe. In March 2004, before Israel became the desalination powerhouse it is today, it signed an agreement to ship water by giant tankers from Antalya. The deal never materialized, but the broader picture and vision were clear: Israel would provide Turkey with technology, security and energy, while Turkey would provide strategic depth, expanded markets and a bridge to the region.
Trust between the countries was so well established that, during the Olmert government, after the strike on the nuclear reactor at Deir ez-Zor, Turkey tried to mediate between Israel and Syria. In 2008, four rounds of indirect talks between Israel and Syria were held with Turkish mediation, and Erdogan also tried to assist in returning the remains of Israeli spy Eli Cohen, as well as in contacts over the return of Gilad Shalit, who was being held by Hamas. Much water has flowed through the Bosphorus since then, and today Israel and Turkey are wary of each other’s military presence in Syria.
Four years ago, ynet reported that Erdogan had received medical advice from an Israeli doctor, Professor Yitzhak Shapira, who served as deputy director of Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv and was responsible, among other things, for medical tourism at the hospital. According to the report, Shapira and Erdogan met in the United States.
The Mavi Marmara crisis
The turning point came with the Second Lebanon War. Alongside anger over the destruction in southern Lebanon and Beirut, a perception grew in Turkey that Israel no longer treated it as a strategic partner and was acting in the region without taking Turkish interests into account. The crisis deepened around Operation Cast Lead, which began at the end of 2008. Erdogan, who until then had been one of the most prominent Muslim leaders to maintain an open channel with Israel, became one of its fiercest critics.
Then came the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2009. During a panel on the Gaza operation, Erdogan attacked Israeli President Shimon Peres and left the stage in protest after a heated exchange. Within hours, the incident became a symbol across the Arab and Turkish worlds. Erdogan returned home a hero. The model of cooperation with a Muslim state collapsed
The crisis reached another peak in May 2010, during a flotilla organized by a Turkish group to break the naval blockade of the Gaza Strip. IDF forces took control of the Mavi Marmara, which was part of the flotilla, and the incident ended with the deaths of 10 Turkish citizens and injuries to several IDF soldiers. For Turkey, it was a red line: diplomatic ties were sharply downgraded, the Turkish ambassador left Israel and the security relationship faded. The strategic alliance of the 1990s was over, aside from one small but significant event in which Turkey sent two firefighting aircraft to help during the Carmel wildfire in the fall of 2010.
Despite the deterioration in diplomatic ties, some security and intelligence cooperation remained. One example came in 2022, when Israel and Turkey thwarted — almost at the last moment — an Iranian attempt to attack or abduct Israelis in Istanbul. Israeli security officials said the Mossad and Turkish intelligence services worked together. It was a reminder that even amid a deep diplomatic crisis, another layer of relations can continue — ties between security services that understand that sometimes a common enemy matters more.
But suspicion existed in that sphere too. In 2013, reports in the United States claimed that then-Turkish intelligence chief Hakan Fidan, today Erdogan’s hard-line foreign minister, had passed information to Iran that enabled it to identify a network of sources working for Israel. The allegations were never proven, and Turkey denied the reports, but the mistrust was impossible to hide.
The October 7 rupture
A first reconciliation attempt took place under Barack Obama. At the end of the U.S. president’s visit to Israel in March 2013, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Erdogan and apologized for the deadly outcome of the Mavi Marmara raid. Three years later, the two countries signed an agreement under which Israel would pay $20 million in compensation to the families of those killed, while Turkey would remove legal measures against Israeli soldiers and commanders connected to the incident.
Diplomatic relations returned to ambassadorial level. As a Yedioth Ahronoth correspondent, I accompanied the late ambassador Eitan Na’eh to Erdogan’s 1,000-room palace in Ankara when he presented his credentials. At the time, there was hope for a new beginning. Even in Istanbul’s bazaar, merchants missed Israeli tourists. But relations remained fragile, and in 2018 they were downgraded again against the backdrop of clashes in Jerusalem and events along the Gaza border fence.
In 2022, there was another attempt to rehabilitate relations, with President Isaac Herzog visiting Erdogan and the appointment of a new ambassador, Irit Lillian. In February 2023, the earth shook again in Turkey, and once again Israel sent a large rescue delegation, which saved the lives of 19 Turkish citizens. Erdogan awarded a medal of appreciation to the commander of the Israeli delegation, Col. (res.) Golan Vach, and for a moment it seemed as though history was repeating itself. Then came the October 7 massacre.
After the war began, Erdogan adopted an especially harsh line against Israel and became one of its loudest critics on the international stage. While he views Hamas as a legitimate part of the Palestinian struggle, Israel found it increasingly difficult to continue turning a blind eye to Turkey allowing members of the organization to conduct political and logistical activity from its territory.
The rupture no longer remained solely diplomatic. In May 2024, Turkey announced a halt to all imports from and exports to Israel until a permanent ceasefire was reached in Gaza and humanitarian aid was guaranteed. Before that, trade between the countries was worth billions of dollars annually. It was a dramatic move because for years the economy had been one of the pillars that kept the relationship afloat even during crises.
The clash in Syria
Diplomatic relations between Israel and Turkey have not been formally severed, but they are at a deep low. The Israeli Embassy in Ankara is not operating at full capacity, and in practice there are no Israeli diplomats on Turkish soil; the embassy and consulate teams operate from a third country. In July 2026, it was reported that after Lillian stepped down the ambassador’s position remained vacant.
Still, the Turkish Foreign Ministry website lists the embassy in Tel Aviv as an active mission. The reason is simple: even when diplomatic ties collapse, security channels are still needed, and Syria is the best example. For years, Israel and Turkey were partners in efforts to curb Iranian and Syrian influence in the region. Today, the reality is the opposite.
After the fall of the Assad regime, Turkey deepened its involvement in Syria and supports the new government of jihadist, or perhaps former jihadist, al-Jolani. Israel is naturally concerned about the expansion of Turkey’s presence in its northern neighbor. Turkey currently controls 5% of Syrian territory, while Israel controls 0.1%.
Last week, the confrontation reached an unusual point when Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur base in Syria, saying there was a threat stemming from Turkish intentions there, which Turkey denied. The United States is now working to create a deconfliction mechanism, while Azerbaijan is also trying to mediate between the sides to ease tensions.
Azerbaijan also has hosted mediation talks between Israel and Turkey since April 2025. The Turkish delegation was headed by Ibrahim Kalin, the intelligence chief and a close Erdogan confidant, while the Israeli delegation was headed by Tzachi Hanegbi, then national security adviser. After several meetings in Baku, the sides agreed to establish a hotline between the IDF and the Turkish military to prevent friction in Syria, particularly between the air forces. The arrangement worked well for a period but gradually faded.
Relations have entered a sensitive period
The rift with Turkey also pushed Israel to seek other partners in the eastern Mediterranean. Strategic ties with Greece and Cyprus deepened. Cooperation developed in security, energy and infrastructure. Ankara viewed this to a large extent as an attempt to build a counterweight to Turkey. The idea of an Israel-Turkey gas pipeline, which could have turned Turkey into Israel’s energy gateway to Europe, also lost its political viability. A senior Israeli official acknowledged that the alliance with Greece and Cyprus was intended to create a “wall” against Turkey and signal that it would be unwise for the rivalry to turn into a military confrontation. The 1990s vision of Turkey as a bridge between Israel, Europe and the Muslim world collapsed.
Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Israel-Turkey story is that this is not a story of two countries that never got along. On the contrary. They got along very well. There were years when Israel saw Turkey as a central strategic partner. Israeli pilots trained on its territory. Turkish military systems were upgraded by Israel. Intelligence personnel worked side by side. There were economic, security and personal ties. Erdogan himself visited Israel. Israel tried to mediate with Syria through Ankara. Then, within less than a decade, that same Turkey became one of Israel’s fiercest critics.
In 1999, when relations were at their peak, Israelis crawled into the rubble in Turkey to save people they had never met. In 2023, after years of crises, they did it again. Between those two earthquakes came 24 years of history: a military alliance, intelligence cooperation, aircraft, tanks, Syria, Davos, the Mavi Marmara, reconciliation, Hamas, Iran and October 7. The countries changed. The leaders changed. The region changed. But the images of Israeli rescue teams beneath the rubble in Turkey remained almost identical. Perhaps because they are a reminder that relations between countries are not always only what their leaders say. Sometimes, beneath all the interests, alliances and hostility, there remains a history of deep human connection.
And the next chapter is no longer only about Gaza or Jerusalem. It runs through Syria — and there, for the first time in years, Israel and Turkey could find themselves not merely arguing with one another but operating in the same military arena, with conflicting interests and an urgent need for coordination channels to prevent a slide into direct confrontation.
Relations have now entered a highly sensitive period tied to Israel’s election campaign. Whatever Netanyahu does, he will be suspected of trying to inflame the front for political reasons. This is where the United States enters the picture. It must act as the responsible adult and immediately lower the flames. The key to whether the escalation continues lies in Washington’s hands.

Greece: Migrants clash with police at detention center
August 23, 2026
Migrants clashed with police at a detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the premises after cutting through a perimeter fence before police detained about half of them again, authorities said on Sunday.
Greece is a major point of entry for migrants to Europe, and the country's conservative prime minister has introduced tough rules to deport those who've been denied asylum in the country.
Greece, along with other European Union countries, for example, is in talks with African countries about establishing centers for failed asylum-seekers, a move that has drawn criticism from international rights groups.
Police deploy flashbangs during clashes
Police said they called for reinforcement to the detention center in Sintiki, a few kilometers from the Bulgarian border, after migrants threw rocks at police.
Authorities used flash-bang grenades against people during those clashes, which they said lasted until the early hours of Sunday morning.
At least five migrants were injured and taken to the hospital. Police recaptured 17 of those who escaped and the search continued for 18 others.
The temporary accommodation center houses about 450 people while their applications are processed, a protracted procedure that can take a long time.

Viral 'Cat in the Hat' TikTok trend sparks fun fake videos but also real fear

Viral 'Cat in the Hat' TikTok trend sparks fun fake videos but also real fear
- Published
"He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.
Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers.
The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake.
"I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."
A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.
One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.
The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.
Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.
Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.
In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.
That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults.
"I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.
Her mother was horrified by the prospect.
"You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.
There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.
In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.
There is also a fake Facebook post claiming to be from Yorkshire Police - no force with that name actually exists - and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.
In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."
As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.
In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer.
And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".
Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.
But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."
A post on X that appears to have accelerated the current viral phenomenon appears to have been made on 8 August, by DiscussingFilm, when the pop culture site posted that the original costume was being auctioned off by Propstore.
The post has 10 million views. , externalComments describe it as "nightmare fuel" and "genuinely haunting", suggesting it had been pulled from a 'cursed attic'.
The lot is scheduled to be sold, external on Wednesday as part of an auction of 1,400 pieces of film and TV memorabilia and is predicted to fetch a price of up to $24,000 (£17,500).
Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress.
"I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."
For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.
Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.
The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.

Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' —Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense

Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' —Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
Key developments on Aug. 22-23:
- 'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
- Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says
- Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
- Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
- Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system, with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.

 Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says 
Ukraine is preparing changes to its mobilization system, including potential revisions to the country's draft age, secretary of the parliamentary defense committee Roman Kostenko said on Aug. 22.
Kostenko said that financial incentives offered to encourage Ukrainians to sign military contracts have failed to significantly increase recruitment, prompting officials to consider other measures.
"There are already talks and, as far as I know, some things are changing in the draft age," Kostenko said, adding that the Defense Ministry or General Staff would provide further details. He declined to say whether the draft age could be lowered or raised.
The lawmaker noted that Ukraine does not plan to move away from compulsory mobilization in favor of an exclusively voluntary system.
Kostenko also denied reports that authorities are considering eliminating mobilization exemptions for parents with three or more children, saying there are no such legislative initiatives currently under consideration.
No changes are planned regarding the mobilization of women, Kostenko said, adding that military service for women will remain voluntary.
As the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine goes on, mobilization has become among the most contentious domestic issues in the country.
Ukraine's military faces a growing need to replenish fighting units, build reserves, and allow existing soldiers to rotate off the front line. As Ukraine steps up its mobilization efforts, draft offices are often accused of forced conscription without compliance with fundamental civil rights and ill-treatment of conscripts.
Under martial law, Ukrainian men aged 25 to 60 are currently subject to conscription and are forbidden from leaving the country except under a certain number of specific circumstances.
Meanwhile, Russia reportedly plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Aug. 23.

Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."

Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander says
Ukrainian drones have struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said on Aug. 23.
The two jets, a Su-33 and a Mig-29, as well as a large Orion strike drone, were hit at the Vityazevo airfield in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar Krai, Brovdi said.
The Orion is a large Russian unmanned aerial vehicle developed by Russia before the full-scale invasion and similar in class to the Turkish-made Bayraktar TB-2 operated by Ukraine.
On a battlefield dense with enemy air defense assets and interceptor drones on both sides, drones the Orion and TB-2 have been largely rendered useless.
Over 2026, Russia adapted the Orion for a new role: launching the cheap Banderol cruise missile, now regularly used against Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure.
All three strikes, videos of which were shared on Brovdi's Telegram channel, were carried out by the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, which specializes in long-range strikes.
Other targets included S-400, Pantsir, and Tor air defense systems, as well as eight high-value radars in Krasnodar Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Russian-occupied Crimea.

Yasin Güngör
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
American military casualties in the war with Iran have reached 774, including 18 fatalities, according to the latest figures from the Pentagon’s casualty reporting system.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) indicates that 756 service members have sustained injuries since the war commenced on Feb. 28.
The data is now divided into two distinct periods, reflecting a shift in the conflict’s diplomatic and military status.
The first phase, labeled Operation Epic Fury, accounts for 14 deaths and 417 wounded. Among these fatalities, seven were classified as hostile deaths, including those killed in action or who died of wounds. The remaining seven deaths in this category resulted from accidents or undetermined causes, primarily affecting the US Air Force and Navy.
A second category, titled Overseas Operations, tracks losses sustained since July 7, the period after the memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran was rendered virtually ineffective and one day before President Donald Trump officially declared the ceasefire "over." This phase has recorded four hostile deaths, all from the US Army, and 341 wounded personnel.
The US Army has borne the heaviest burden of the conflict, with 11 total fatalities and 589 injuries across both reporting segments.

Iraq's 20,000 illiterate electric ministry employees is indicator of larger dysfunction - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:29:27 UTC
03:29:27 KST

Iraq is trying to help by enrolling electricity ministry employees in a program to address adult illiteracy after a new report found that “nearly 20,000 Iraqi electricity ministry employees illiterate.”
But the challenge may be larger than the fact that so many are illiterate. The problem is they are working in a key energy infrastructure field in a country that is now at the center of the Iran conflict with the US and Israel. Iraq has suffered greatly from the chaos in the Strait of Hormuz.
In the last weeks, several key Islamic Republic officials journeyed to Iraq to pressure the country. Iran is offering a trade-off. Iraq may be allowed to export more oil via the Strait of Hormuz. However, Baghdad would likely have to shelve a plan to rein in Iranian-backed militias.
What do the 20,000 illiterate electric employees have to do with this? They are a symbol of a system in Iraq that has allowed corruption and infrastructure decay to grow over the last decades. This is in part due to Iranian influence. Iran has tried to control Iraq and make it dependent. Electricity and energy are some of the ways that Iran seeks to make Baghdad dependent.
Iran’s role in trying to harm Iraq’s electric grid is clear. For instance, the one part of Iraq that is partly free from Iranian influence is the autonomous Kurdistan Region. That region was recently able to solve many longstanding electrical problems via new energy investment and the Dana Gas project at the Khor Mor field.
This field helps supply gas to power plants in Erbil and other areas of the Kurdistan Region, accounting for around 75% of the region’s electricity capacity. Kurdistan went from a region where many people relied on generators to a place where there is electricity all day long.
Iran has used its militias to target the Khor Mor field. This has caused a suspension of gas and electricity flow. Now another dispute has arisen. Reports from Rudaw and other media note that Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum deny claims by the regional government that they supplied natural gas to the rest of Iraq.
Illiterate employees may be 'ghost' employees
The issue is that the illiterate employees of the electricity ministry may be “ghost” employees who don’t even work. It’s not clear how one would have so many illiterate employees in a key sector.
Rudaw says that “nearly 20,000 employees of Iraq’s electricity ministry are illiterate and have been enrolled in a government program to teach them reading and writing, an education ministry official said on Saturday, attributing the high number largely to the hiring of contract workers in recent years.”
“We have launched a joint program with the Iraqi Ministry of Electricity to teach 19,939 employees in Baghdad and other provinces,” Haitham Munther, director of media and communications at the Executive Agency for Literacy Eradication at the Iraqi education ministry, told Rudaw’s Gashaw Khalid.
And why has this happened?
“He attributed the large number of illiterate employees primarily to the widespread recruitment of contract workers in recent years,” Munther said. “In principle, it should be impossible for an employee to be illiterate. However, as you know, the issue of contract workers arose in recent years. Previously, the number of Ministry of Electricity staff was stable between 90,000 and 95,000, but in recent years, more than 100,000 people have been added solely through contracts.”
Illiteracy wider problem throughout the ministry
There are more problems of illiteracy across Iraq’s government. At the Interior Ministry, 11,000 members are learning to read.
“Iraq’s 2024 national census put the country’s illiteracy rate at 15.3%. While senior civil service positions generally require university or technical qualifications, illiteracy among government employees is concentrated largely among lower-ranking personnel, including members of security forces, local police, municipal services, and facility protection forces.”
It should be noted that Iraq’s electricity grid has long been one of the country’s strategic vulnerabilities. Despite possessing some of the world’s largest oil and natural gas reserves, Iraq continues to struggle to provide reliable electricity to its population.
The country’s modern electricity crisis has its roots in decades of conflict. The Iran-Iraq War, the 1991 Gulf War, years of sanctions during the 1990s, the 2003 US-led invasion, and later the war against ISIS have all damaged power plants.
There is also Iraq’s dependence on Iranian energy. Since 2017, Iraq has relied heavily on imports of Iranian natural gas to fuel power plants near Baghdad and Basra, while also importing electricity directly from Iran.
This illustrates how the illiterate employees are only the tip of the iceberg.

IDF begins construction of six new training bases incorporating lessons from Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:29:17 UTC
03:29:17 KST

Six training brigade bases will be built for the 7th, 188th, 401st, Kfir, Nahal, and Givati Brigades across Israel, incorporating lessons learned from October 7, a senior Defense Ministry official told Walla on Sunday.
The Defense Ministry views the project as an operational initiative because it directly affects the training and preparation of all IDF Ground Forces combat units for future challenges and extreme scenarios.
“The entire training and instruction environment will change following the establishment of the new training bases, and this will be reflected starting from the basic needs of soldiers, such as the type of beds and hot water in the living quarters, to training classrooms integrated with new technology and simulators,” the senior official explained.
He added, “A rapid access approach for tanks and Namer armored personnel carriers to the training areas has been incorporated in order to streamline the training process.”
According to the official, the 7th Brigade training base in northern Israel, covering 20,000 square meters, including a bus parking area, is in advanced stages of construction and will receive its first group of recruits in August 2028.
Where will the IDF's new training bases be?
The 188th Brigade training base in the Jordan Valley, at the site currently used by soldiers from the haredi Hasmonean Brigade who will move elsewhere, is also under construction and is expected to be delivered in August 2027.
The Kfir Brigade training base in the Jordan Valley is in advanced stages of construction, with its new sections expected to be delivered to the IDF in 2028.
The Nahal Brigade training base near Tel Arad is currently in the planning stage, with construction expected to begin in the coming months as part of a five-year project. The work will be carried out as part of a redevelopment and reconstruction process.
Next to the Shivta training base of the IDF Artillery Corps, the 401st Brigade training base will be established, with construction expected to begin in 2027.
The construction of the Givati Brigade training base, which has faced project delays for more than a decade and a half, is currently in the planning stage and is expected to be completed around 2031 to 2032.
Base planning includes a focus on the IDF's future
According to the senior Defense Ministry engineering official, the planning of all the new training bases includes a focus on future needs. For example, at the armored brigade bases, covered tank maintenance centers will be built adjacent to the living quarters, rather than several kilometers away as they were in the past.
Buses will be able to reach close to the living quarters in order to reduce the time soldiers spend entering and leaving the bases. Similar planning will apply to access routes to dining halls and living quarters, reducing time spent moving between different areas.
New urban warfare training facilities for tanks will also be built. In the medical field, specialist clinics will be established at all of the training bases, including physiotherapy clinics.
Additional emphasis was placed on tank simulators, which will allow training to be more precise and enable soldiers to practice even during periods of extreme heat in the field.
The official explained that the large scale of facilities at each training base will give commanders greater flexibility when planning daily schedules.
Company-level living quarters planned
The official also described the planned company-level living quarters.
“This is a two-story building that includes a kitchenette, a club, bathrooms and showers at the required capacity and not with the overcrowding of the past, with shading, a nearby company area, and nearby fitness facilities,” he said.
The dining hall complex, synagogue, and all other public buildings will be concentrated in a single area close to the company compounds.
“Recruits will not have to walk for hours and hours to the dining hall. Everything will be close to them,” the Defense Ministry official said.
“In the company building, they will have a washing machine, a lounge area, a refrigerator for meals and food and drinks when the dining halls are unavailable, open 24/7 and located inside the living quarters. There is also investment in the sleeping quarters, including outlets for the various mobile devices, shading, and accessible showers inside the building.”
The official also emphasized that thought was given to the location of the new training bases and their surrounding security components based on lessons learned from October 7 and Hamas’s breaches of IDF bases.
The planning includes infrastructure protection, the types of walls and barriers used, protected spaces, perimeter fencing, and measures designed to ensure operational continuity.

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:23:01 UTC
03:23:01 KST

North Dakota State has won at a record rate at the lower levels. The Bison are rumbling into the FBS
FARGO, N.D. (AP) — North Dakota State’s road to the highest level of college football was paved by an unprecedented run of success, with 10 national championships serving as sparkling souvenirs from a two-decade stay in the Championship Subdivision.
That exit sign for the Bowl Subdivision came into view through a rare and bitter taste of failure.
The Bison rumbled last year into the FCS playoffs with the top seed, a first-round bye and an unbeaten record. Then came Dec. 6 and the fateful game against Illinois State. The Redbirds, a conference rival, rallied three times from two-touchdown deficits for a one-point victory at the Fargodome. The 19,000-seat stadium was about half full for the thriller.
“That was the point in time for me when I said, ‘We’ve got to get this done,’” athletic director Matt Larsen recalled. “We were really close already. I remember thinking to myself, ‘If we don’t make this move, this might be the norm.’ I think our fan base is as passionate as they’ve always been, but they wanted a new challenge. This provides that new energy and new competition.”
The latest era for this powerhouse on the prairie starts on Saturday when North Dakota State hosts Jacksonville State in its first game as an FBS program. The Bison then make their Mountain West debut on Sept. 12 at Air Force, marking yet another turn on the sport’s carousel of conference realignment. Sacramento State is also moving up to the FBS this season.
“I always knew it could happen, but I never was really thinking about it,” linebacker Donovan Woolen said. “To play better games against better competition is going to be a lot more fun. To be able to test our abilities and see our fullest potential of what we can do as players and as a team, I think we’re ready for it.”
The Bison built a dominant program decades ago
After winning three national championships (1965, 1968, 1969) in what was then the NCAA’s College Division, the Bison won five more Division II titles (1983, 1985, 1986, 1988 and 1990) after the original lower tier was divided into two. The first big move came in 2004 to the FCS, where attention-grabbing wins over Big Ten and Big 12 opponents laid the groundwork for those record 10 championships over a stunning 14-year span that included four different head coaches.
The Bison went 9-5 against FBS foes, with four of those losses coming by a combined 12 points, and counted Iowa, Iowa State, Kansas, Kansas State and Minnesota — twice — as victims of their stampede. The program’s all-time record in playoff games is 86-20, including a jaw-dropping 51-7 in the FCS tournament.
“There’s been murmurs and all that for probably five years now, but to finally make that jump, it’s pretty cool to see and I’m excited for the guys back at Fargo,” said Seattle Seahawks left guard Grey Zabel, who was a first-round draft pick out of North Dakota State in 2025 and promptly got a Super Bowl ring out of his rookie season. “They’ve got the support staff. They’ve got the coaching staff. They’ve got the community, the fans, the players, the talent. It’s just a matter of putting in the hard work and having the right attitude, effort and mentality.”
Being ready to move up requires a lot more than national titles
Playing in the biggest city in a state without a pro team, the Bison have naturally become a regional draw boasting a proud network of supporters. Tom Blattner, a 1996 alumnus, gave in 2021 with his wife through their foundation a $15 million gift toward the $54 million indoor facility that also allows the soccer, baseball, softball and golf teams to practice in the dead of winter.
Fargo is a growing city of more than 125,000 people with a metropolitan area — including Moorhead, Minnesota — that’s about double that, but a midsize market has its financial limits. The university enrolled close to 12,000 students last fall, including about 9,700 undergraduates, more than only Wyoming and Air Force in the Mountain West.
NDSU’s $5 million reclassification fee to the NCAA and $12.5 million entry fee to the Mountain West were privately funded, so some donors will undoubtedly be tapped out for a while. The football program added 22 scholarships in the move to the FBS, and the increased travel and other competitive upgrades has roughly doubled the operating budget, Larsen said, from 2025 expenses of about $8 million.
As long as the College Football Playoff includes a spot for the Group of Six conferences that comprise the underbelly of the Power Four-driven FBS, the Bison will have a big prize to pursue even if their days of winning national championships with regularity are all but done.
“To be able to compete year in and year out for a conference championship, to me that’s a signifier that we’ve built a competitive program. If you’re doing well in the Mountain West, that means you’re doing well across the Group of Six as well,” Larsen said. “We don’t want to just go. We want to go compete right away.”
The buzz around the football facilities has been palpable this summer, perhaps no stronger than when players began to get their hands on the latest edition of the popular EA Sports video game, College Football, which for the first time includes North Dakota State. Now they can relax at home after practice and pick the Bison to control instead of Alabama or Ohio State.
“To play as yourself in a game, that’s something every little kid wants to do when they grow up,” Woolen said.
NDSU’s traditional rivals probably won’t be a prominent part of its future
North Dakota State was joined on its jump to the FCS by South Dakota State, which beat the Bison in the 2022 national championship game and won it all again in 2023. North Dakota and South Dakota eventually moved up from Division II as well.
The Bison are open to playing regional schools in the future, Larsen said, but that can’t be an annual event with a nonconference schedule that has room for only FCS game. North Dakota State fans seeking matchups with the neighbors to the north and south will probably have to settle for other sports.
Northern Illinois, another one of the three newcomers to Mountain West football this season, could become a rival as the only other Central Time Zone team in the league from a part of the country the Bison try to recruit hard. Wyoming, where current head coach Tim Polasek was recently the offensive coordinator under Craig Bohl, a former North Dakota State head coach, is another candidate to stoke the competitive fire.
For now, Bison fans have some fun road trips to look forward to, with two games in Northern California, one in Las Vegas and one in, yes, Honolulu.
“There’s a lot of excitement around the community for sure,” wide receiver and kick returner Jackson Williams said.
Winning never gets old to coaches or players, but all those blowouts of teams in the bottom half of the top-heavy Missouri Valley Football Conference weren’t doing much for the fan base. Plus, taking home that many trophies in such a short amount of time can create an anticlimactic feeling.
“I think it’s bittersweet, to sum it up, but I do think with where college football is headed there was no other decision to be made,” Polasek said. “We’re excited to be moving up, and the time was right. It’s just an opportunity we couldn’t pass up.”
___
AP Sports Writers Andrew Destin in Renton, Wash., and Steve Megargee in Green Bay, Wis., contributed to this report.

Fast-moving wildfire in Reno, Nevada, forces thousands to evacuate homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:22:15 UTC
03:22:15 KST

A fast-moving Nevada wildfire exploded to more than 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) on Sunday, pushing from the Sierra foothills toward the center of Reno and urging nearly 90,000 residents to evacuate as flames threatened neighborhoods and reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus.
The Hawk fire’s “GO NOW” evacuation zone had expanded to the edge of the university campus as strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation fueled the blaze, according to Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue in Reno. Of those urged to evacuate, 42,000 were under strict orders. An additional 45,000 people were in the evacuation warning zone, and encouraged to leave now and be prepared to stay away for several days to clear the roads for first-responders.
“If you have been told to evacuate, please don’t wait!” Hillary Schieve, Reno’s mayor, said in a statement posted on social media on Saturday night. “Structures have already been burned in this fire and your life is more important than a building. Evacuating before the fire arrives also allows our firefighters to focus their efforts on battling the blaze.”
Authorities confirmed three civilians and three first responders had been injured in the fire and several structures have been destroyed. Officials said the fire was human-caused but did not provide additional details on how the fire was started, saying it was under investigation.
Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe county and mobilized the Nevada national guard. Two helicopter crews were deployed to support aerial firefighting operations, while 60 troops were assigned to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. However winds were whipping the flames, complicating the fight.
“It was extremely confusing,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.
The fire had already proved to be a challenge on Saturday night, moving exceptionally fast, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hotspots while residents were trying to get out, Balaam said.
The fire was so small on Saturday morning that it wasn’t even a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.
“The wind really blew it up,” Duvall said.
“Approximately 400 personnel are currently working on the incident, with resources coming together from local, state and federal agencies, including ground crews and air resources,” the Truckee Meadows statement said.
The rapidly expanding fire was surrounded by neighborhoods, and nearly 10,000 homes and businesses in Washoe county were without power on Sunday. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed because of the fire.
Reno has a population of more than 280,000 residents.
David Barb returned from a weekend hunting trip to find the fire had leveled his taxidermy shop, but his house nearby appeared to have been spared thanks to workers with a landscaping company who cut a fire break, he said. His wife was home when the fire started on the other side of the mountain and later evacuated to a friend’s house.
“I’m kind of devastated, but thank God everyone’s safe,” he said on Sunday.
Washoe county emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said pets could not be brought there. Small and large animals were instead to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.
At least 20 road closures were in effect as of Sunday afternoon.
The University of Nevada’s Reno campus remained just outside the evacuation zone on Sunday morning. The university, which had an enrollment of about 24,000 students in fall 2025, said officials had established an emergency response plan should conditions change. The first day of classes at the university is 24 August. However, students who are new to the university were allowed to move in as early as 13 August.
The Reno-Tahoe international airport also remained outside the evacuation zone, and commercial flights were unaffected on Sunday. The smaller Reno-Stead airport was closed to general aviation traffic because of the Hawk fire but remained open to firefighting aircraft.
Authorities were also closely watching a county detention facility located several blocks from the outer edge of the evacuation warning area.
“We have those inmates in mind and we are making sure that we have plans in place in case we may have to evacuate the facility,” said Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff.
The Hawk fire comes just weeks after three wildfires fueled by dry and windy conditions north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes earlier this month, according to the Nevada national guard.
Associated Press contributed reporting
