Asus ROG Swift RGB Stripe OLED Review: Clarity King
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.
Top-notch contrast. Outstanding color performance. Crisp motion clarity. Absolutely loaded with extra features.
TIRED
Mirror-like display finish isn’t for everyone. Stand takes up a lot of space on the desk. Expensive at full price.
RGB Stripe OLED panels are the new hotness in 2026. The new OLED panel technology is designed to improve text clarity and color performance, which potentially give a monitor like the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM a broader appeal beyond just a typical gaming monitor.
That is, perhaps, why Asus takes the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach. At a glance, it might seem like a typical 4K OLED gaming monitor. It has a 26.5-inch tandem 4K RGB Stripe OLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and HDR support with VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certification. But it's also rounded out with tons of features, which helps make the higher price of $1,200 easier to swallow.
Super Glossy, Superior Contrast
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM has the company’s unique TrueBlack display finish, which is designed to deliver an ultrahigh-contrast experience in a wide variety of lighting conditions. It does so with a high-gloss coat that minimizes the impact of ambient light across the display.
It’s not just marketing drivel. The TrueBlack finish provides noticeably deeper black levels in a bright room. The matte OLED finish on Samsung’s OLEDs looks positively hazy by comparison. Glossy OLED monitors from competing brands also look less contrast-rich, though the difference is most noticeable in a very bright room—brighter, I suspect, than most PC gaming dens.
I also feel it comes across in how colors present. Technically, the monitor’s results are modest for an OLED monitor: It has a color gamut that spanned 94 percent of DCI-P3 and 89 percent of AdobeRGB. That’s a tad more narrow than top QD-OLED monitors, which can hit up to 98 percent and 95 percent, respectively. However, the ultra-clear, high-contrast look of the panel amplifies the sense of impact. I’m not saying it’s better than the best competitors, but the PG27UCWM’s overall image quality is in the upper tier. That's at least partially due to the fact that RGB Stripe OLED also improves “color volume," which is a display's ability to maintain color that gamut had max brightness.
Unfortunately, the vivid and contrast-rich image is paired with mirror-like reflections. I could likely use the monitor to shave. It’s not a problem in a dark room, but it’s noticeable when even modest ambient light is present.
This is an important, and divisive, point. Many OLED purists adore an ultra-gloss finish because it highlights the rich contrast and color the technology can provide. Others, myself included, prefer matte displays that reduce or eliminate discernible reflections.
There’s no right answer to this question, but you’ll need to decide your preference before you make a purchase.
Great for Sharpness, Great HDR
Beneath the PG27UCWM’s glossy coat you’ll find a tandem RGB Stripe OLED panel with a native resolution of 3840 x 2160. It’s crisp. Earlier OLED monitors have used an unusual sub-pixel arrangement that could hurt image clarity, but the PG27UCWM has a more conventional RGB sub-pixel layout that eliminates the issue. You'll sometimes see this marketed as “5th-Gen QD-OLED," and it initially launched in 34-inch monitors like the Alienware AW3426DW. But finally, the PG27UCWM is bringing it to the more standard 27-inch size.
Text clarity, in particular, has always been one of the chief issues about those shopping for OLED monitors, and I no longer have complaints in that regard. The resolution helps, too, providing a pixel density of about 165 pixels per inch across the 26.5-inch panel. The panel’s sharpness was excellent with the monitor connected to both my Windows 11 desktop and my MacBook Air M4.
HDR is where the PG27UCWM’s tandem OLED panel really begins to earn its keep. My testing found it can hit up to 800 nits of brightness. While that’s not a record-setting result, it’s in line with other premium OLED monitors, which typically offer 800 to 900 nits in my testing (the best barely clear 1,000 nits). The monitor also supports Dolby Vision HDR, which is rare.
The PG27UCWM’s brightness, contrast, and resolution combine to deliver real impact in HDR games. It’s so bright that it can at times feel overwhelming. Fortunately, Asus includes HDR brightness adjustment options that let you tone down the brightness if you’d prefer.
Asus’ PG27UCWM isn’t uniquely bright in HDR though. The Alienware AW3426DW, Acer Predator X27 X1, and MSI MPG 32URXW are among the monitors I’ve tested that deliver similar HDR brightness (and some of which are significantly cheaper). Still, the PG27UCWM performs much better than least expensive OLED monitors like the entry-level Alienware AW2726DM, which can only deliver roughly 400 nits in HDR.
Motion Clarity Checks the Boxes
The PG27UCWM can reach a refresh rate of up to 240 Hz at 4K resolution. That’s standard for a high-end 4K OLED in 2026. It also provides a dual-mode feature that can reduce the resolution to 1080p in exchange for a refresh rate of up to 480 Hz. That’s less common, though many OLED monitors now offer a similar feature.
I think the 1080p/480Hz mode will prove niche, as the monitor’s motion clarity is already excellent at 4K and 240 Hz. Motion blur is minimal and small objects are easy to make out. Though perhaps most useful in games, the monitor’s motion clarity is also noticeable on a Windows 11 or macOS desktop. Scrolling text is readable and OS animations look ultrasmooth.
Still, the 480 Hz mode has uses. It’s ideal for people who like to play competitively in esports titles, yet also want to enjoy maximum image quality in single-player games. The PG27UCWM can handle both without compromise.
The PG27UCWM lists compatibility with AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA Adaptive Sync. In practice, many monitors that list support for only one of these can work with all three, as they are based on the same core technology. However, I always prefer to see official support listed, so you don’t have to guess whether adaptive sync will work with your PC or game console.
Features Galore
The PG27UCWM is more than just excellent image quality though. Asus has packed it full with a treasure trove of features to sweeten the deal.
The monitor’s design is top-notch. It includes attractive transparent plastic elements on the rear of the display and an RGB-LED logo that can be synced to other RGB-LED devices with Asus’ Aura Sync. An ergonomic stand is included and offers the usual range of adjustment for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot; VESA mounting for third-party arms and stands is possible with a provided adapter.
There’s also an 1/4-inch screw mount on the top of the stand neck. This is a common type of mount for camera and streaming equipment. You can use the mount to place a webcam or ring light above the monitor. It’s an uncommon but useful feature.
I do have one nitpick with the stand, and that’s the stand base. Asus opts for a wide base that takes up a lot of desk space. It’s not the largest I’ve seen, but I prefer the more compact stand base found with competitors like the MSI MPG 272URX and Alienware AW2725Q. On the plus side, though, the stand is remarkably solid. Most monitor stands allow a hint of wobble if I purposefully jostle my desk, but the PG27UCWM is unbothered.
Image-quality purists will be happy to see the monitor is packed with adjustments. These include multiple color space presets, color temperature and gamma modes that target precise values, and six-axis color saturation adjustment.
The monitor even has a built-in sensor that can detect ambient light and the user’s presence. This is used primarily to enable the monitor’s OLED burn-in reduction features, which can turn off the monitor automatically when you step away (if it’s not on, it won’t burn in).
Connectivity is great, too. The monitor has two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and one USB-C port with DisplayPort input for a total of four video inputs. All of the inputs can reach 4K at 240 Hz, and the DisplayPort 2.1 port offers UHBR20 data rates of up to 80Gbps, which means it can hit the 4K/240 Hz target without display stream compression.
The USB-C port offers 90 watts of power delivery for charging a connected laptop or tablet. A USB-C hub is included, as well, and provides three downstream USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 ports. The USB-A ports are accessible through the USB-C input or a USB-B input. A KVM switch is present as well. As if that wasn't all, Asus even throws in a three-year warranty for good measure.
What’s the Catch?
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM is a great gaming monitor with a long list of features. It has a beautiful, sharp image, smooth-motion clarity, good HDR, lots of display inputs, and a USB hub. It even looks nice on a desk. The super-vivid, super-reflective TrueBlack coat won’t be to everyone’s taste, but it delivers on its promise to improve perceived contrast.
Which brings us to the only serious issue with the PG27UCWM: the price.
The monitor will set you back $1,200 at retail price. That’s a lot of clams for a 27-inch 4K OLED monitor. The PG27UCWM does a lot to justify a higher price, but I can’t broadly recommend the PG27UCWM over less expensive options like the PG27UCDM (currently $950) or MSI MPG 272URX (currently $800). Neither of those have the newer RGB Stripe OLED, of course, but that might not be enough for the average gamer to full appreciate given the hundreds of dollars of difference in price.
Still, the PG27UCWM is worth consideration if you want a flagship 27-inch 4K OLED monitor with the latest panel technology and a boatload of features when it becomes available in October. A 32-inch model will also be launched alongside it.

Emotions can destroy everything: astrological forecast for August 24–30

Emotions can destroy everything: astrological forecast for August 24–30
Kyiv • UNN
The eclipse may intensify emotions and tension. The astrologer advises checking information, nurturing relationships, and avoiding impulsive actions.
This week, we can expect a lunar eclipse, which will bring a surge of emotions. Professional astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko told UNN readers how to get through this challenging period and avoid doing anything foolish.
We are approaching the end of the eclipse corridor, with its main event being the lunar eclipse on August 28 at 7:13 a.m. Kyiv time.
"The week from August 24 to 30 may have a very serious impact on our consciousness, subconscious, and psycho-emotional state," the astrologer believes.
According to Bazylenko, this year's eclipse appears to be quite tense.
"A lunar eclipse always occurs during a full moon, when the Sun and Moon are in opposition. In astrology, the Moon is associated with our emotions, subconscious, home, family, habits, sense of security, and deep reactions.
Therefore, this week's main events may take place not only around us—there will be a great deal happening inside us as well," the astrologer explains.
Why the lunar eclipse will make us particularly emotional
In the eclipse horoscope, the Sun and Moon form a tense configuration with Uranus.
"Uranus is what adds an element of surprise, abruptness, and a desire to instantly break free from whatever is limiting us. Emotionality may be heightened. What we previously managed to restrain may suddenly come out. Old grievances, fears, family conflicts, and painful experiences may resurface," Bazylenko believes.
Therefore, we need to pay closer attention to our emotional state and relationships with those close to us, avoid harsh statements, refrain from making decisions while feeling hurt, and not suddenly rush to change everything.
"Not every strong emotion requires immediate action. And this is probably one of the main pieces of advice for the entire week," the astrologer is convinced.
Because of the features of this eclipse, we may feel confused—you may feel that something needs to be done but not see the full picture.
"Therefore, if circumstances allow, do not rush into decisions that cannot be easily reversed. Do not end important relationships because of one argument. Do not quit impulsively. Do not issue ultimatums. Do not abandon an important project simply because something has gone wrong now. Give yourself time—after the eclipse, the situation may look completely different," the astrologer emphasizes.
On the day of the lunar eclipse, it may be difficult to maintain a good mood. The astrologer notes that you do not need to force yourself to be happy—try to get through this day with greater kindness and care toward yourself and those around you.
"Do not take your inner tension out on your children, parents, or partner. Do not respond to someone else's aggression with aggression. Do not destroy relationships because of an emotion that may disappear by tomorrow," the astrologer emphasizes.
According to Bazylenko, after August 25, Mercury will move into Virgo, and our thinking will become more rational; we will pay greater attention to details and become more practical. However, the first half of the week remains difficult: we will perceive information too emotionally or one-sidedly.
The astrologer advises doing the following this week:
-  check important information;  
-  reread documents;  
-  do not spread unverified news;  
-  do not immediately respond to provocative messages;  
-  be more attentive while driving;  
-  do not make final decisions at the peak of emotion. 
Bazylenko emphasizes that not every piece of news will be true, and not every thought or emotion should be translated into action.
"This recommendation concerns not only personal life. In global politics, unexpected, sharp, or categorical statements and decisions are also possible. The struggle of ambitions and the desire to prove one's own right at any cost may prove especially dangerous," the astrologer emphasizes.
How to properly prepare for the eclipse
The lunar eclipse on August 28 may become a symbolic boundary between what we no longer want to carry with us and the life we are ready to create going forward.
"I would not advise meeting the eclipse with fear.
On the contrary, this is a good moment to clear away what is unnecessary—both literally and symbolically.
The day before, you can tidy up your home, get rid of things you no longer need, create a calm atmosphere, take a bath or shower, and get more rest.
You can light a candle and simply spend some time alone with yourself," says the astrologer.
She also advises taking a clean sheet of paper and writing down everything you would like to free yourself from: fears, resentments, feelings of guilt, worries, destructive attachments, conflicts, or habits that drain your energy.
"Read what you have written and think about what you truly no longer want to carry with you. After that, you can tear up the sheet or symbolically destroy it. If you use fire, do so only in a safe manner. This is not a magical way to change your life instantly. But as a psychological and symbolic point of closure, this practice can be very powerful. Especially now, when many of us are living under prolonged stress," Bazilenko believes.
According to the astrologer, the eclipse period itself is the time when one can get rid of harmful habits, change one's lifestyle or attachments, because in the astrological tradition, a lunar eclipse is associated with the completion of cycles.
"If you have long wanted to give up a harmful habit, you can symbolically choose the end of the eclipse as your starting point. You do not need to promise yourself that you will change forever in a single night. Start with a specific period—for example, the first 21 days of a new routine—and keep moving forward," the astrologer suggests.
But after the eclipse ends, it is worth changing direction.
"Before the eclipse, we let go. After the eclipse, we create. Think about what is missing from your own life. Perhaps it is time to start moving more, go to the gym, improve your diet, sleep, or daily routine. Some people need to learn how to rest properly. And some simply need to say kind words to their loved ones more often.
I often repeat one thought: our destiny is our character. And our character is largely made up of our habits," Bazilenko explains.
The weekend will bring relief
Throughout the week, we are supported by the harmonious interaction of Jupiter and Saturn, which, according to the astrologer, becomes particularly strong on August 29.
"This is an important stabilizing factor. Jupiter provides an opportunity to see the prospects, while Saturn helps structure life and maintain a sense of stability. Do not destroy—build. Instead of fuss, choose consistency; instead of an instant result, lay a foundation," Bazilenko explains.
But on the same day, Uranus's tense aspect to the Sun once again raises the themes of personal ambitions, independence, and the desire to act against the circumstances.
"And here, ego may become the main problem. Do not issue a challenge merely to prove your strength. Do not argue just to win. Do not force your way through where an agreement is possible. Do not allow your own ego to destroy what is important," the astrologer emphasizes.
A tense week for Ukraine
"In Ukraine's horoscope, the period of the lunar eclipse looks quite tense.
According to my astrological calculations, Mars forms a strong opposition to Uranus in the country's chart. This is an aspect of sudden, unpredictable events and heightened tension," says the astrologer.
According to her, people should be particularly vigilant on the night of August 23–24, as well as on August 26, 27, and 28.
"This does not mean that a specific dangerous event will necessarily occur on these exact dates. But from an astrological point of view, I consider them the most tense. Therefore, there can be only one recommendation here: do not ignore air-raid alerts and official warnings. Take care of yourselves and your loved ones," the astrologer explained.
Astrological forecast for all zodiac signs
Pisces, Virgo, and Gemini may feel the particularly strong influence of this eclipse. Pisces experience the eclipse itself, the Sun is in Virgo, and Gemini are involved in the tense configuration through Uranus.
But this week has its own scenario in store for every sign.
ARIES
This week, you especially need silence. What you have long been putting off "until later" may surface: fatigue, unexpressed emotions, old resentments, or inner fears.
Do not try to overcome your own emotions by force. On the contrary — give yourself the opportunity to rest, get enough sleep, and spend some time alone with yourself.
A very important inner realization may come to you: what it is time to give up forever. Do not rush to tell everyone about it. First, listen to yourself.
TAURUS
The eclipse may conduct a kind of audit of your social circle.
You may suddenly feel very clearly who is truly your person and which relationships are maintained merely out of habit. Emotional conversations with friends, changes in plans, or even the unexpected return of someone from the past are possible.
But do not rush to erase anyone from your life in a single evening. The main question of the week is: who do I want to move forward with?
GEMINI
One of the most important signs of this eclipse. Uranus in Gemini is involved in a tense configuration with the Sun and the Moon, so events may develop very unexpectedly. This may especially concern work, status, career, reputation, and major life decisions.
You may feel a strong desire to drop everything, abruptly change direction, or say what has been building up inside you for a long time. Do not take irreversible steps at the peak of your emotions. What seems like an ending now may, after some time, turn out to be the beginning of an entirely new professional chapter.
CANCER
For you, this eclipse may become a moment of a change in worldview. Sometimes we live for years with certain beliefs, and then one event makes us look at everything completely differently.
Issues involving education, documents, travel, relocation, or future plans may become more active.
But the most important changes will take place within: you may stop believing in what you once believed. Do not be afraid to change your mind. That, too, is a sign of growth.
LEO
Following the powerful solar eclipse in your sign, August continues to change your life. This time, money, shared finances, debts, loans, obligations, and issues of trust may come to the forefront.
Do not make major financial decisions under the influence of fear.
But there is also a deeper level: the eclipse may show you whom or what you are too strongly attached to. Sometimes freedom begins not when we receive something, but when we stop being afraid of losing it.
VIRGO
For you, this is one of the strongest eclipses of the year.
The Sun is in your sign, while the Moon during the eclipse is directly opposite, in Pisces. Therefore, relationships become the main theme. Marriage, partnership, love, conflicts, agreements — everything that has long been left unspoken may become obvious.
But do not rush to put an end to things. The eclipse may not destroy relationships, but show what exactly needs to change in them. For some, this will be an ending. For others, a very serious conversation. And for others still, on the contrary, a decision to move to a new level of intimacy.
LIBRA
Your body may simply say: "Enough." If lately you have been living in a state of constant haste, taking on too much, or ignoring your fatigue, this week you should reduce your workload.
The theme of the eclipse for you is habits, routine, work, and everyday life.
Think not about how to do even more, but about what you can stop doing.
For Libras in particular, this period is very well suited as a starting point for a new daily routine, sleep schedule, physical activity, and a more caring attitude toward yourself.
SCORPIO
For you, the eclipse may affect a very personal area — love, children, creativity, and your ability to enjoy life. Feelings may become much stronger.
An important event in a romantic relationship or a situation involving children is possible.
But there is another interesting theme: you may suddenly remember a talent, desire, or dream that you once set aside. Not everything that returns from the past needs to be welcomed back into your life. But some dreams truly deserve a second chance.
SAGITTARIUS
The eclipse touches on one of the deepest themes — home and family.
Long-standing family issues, relationships with parents, or situations that the family has preferred not to discuss for years may become more acute. For some, the question of housing, renovations, relocation, or changing their place of residence may arise.
But the main thing is not real estate. The main question of this eclipse for you is: Where is my true home, and who do I feel safe with? The answer may turn out to be unexpected.
CAPRICORN
Be very attentive to your words. One conversation this week may change much more than it initially seems. Unexpected messages may arrive, arrangements may change, and old topics may resurface. Do not respond immediately if you have been emotionally affected.
Be especially careful when checking documents and information. And this week, you may hear a very important truth. Perhaps not the one you wanted to hear, but precisely the one you have long needed to know.
AQUARIUS
Money and your sense of self-worth are in the spotlight. Changes in income, unexpected expenses, or the need to reconsider your financial priorities are possible. Do not buy something expensive merely to emotionally compensate for stress.
But the eclipse will put a much more interesting question before you: How much is my time really worth? Perhaps you have long been devoting too much energy to places where you are not valued enough. And right now, this will become obvious.
PISCES
The main sign of this lunar eclipse.
On August 28, the Moon will be in Pisces, so this period may feel especially personal for you.
Your attitude toward yourself, your appearance, relationships, and the future may change — even toward the role you are used to playing for others.
Your emotions may be very intense. Therefore, the main thing is not to mistake a temporary emotional state for the final truth about your life. Give yourself time.
For many Pisces, this eclipse may bring a major inner cycle to an end. You may feel that you no longer want to be the person you used to be. And this is not necessarily a crisis. Sometimes it is simply the moment when the old version of us has become too small.

The Israeli forces have arrested at least 14 Palestinians, including a child, during raids in the occupied West Bank, amid attacks by illegal settlers that included the burning of property and the destruction of agricultural land.
Illegal Israeli settlers burned a residential room belonging to a Palestinian in the northern part of the town of Osarin, south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, local sources told Anadolu on Sunday.
They also set fire to a vehicle, partially burning it, and spray-painted racist slogans at the site, the sources added.
In Bethlehem, Israeli illegal settlers attacked the Khala'il al-Louz area east of the city, damaging irrigation pipes used for crops, cutting down trees, and damaging Palestinian property and agricultural land.
Illegal settlers also uprooted olive and grape trees from Palestinian-owned land in the village of al-Minya, east of Bethlehem, according to the official Palestinian news agency Wafa.
In Nablus, Israeli forces raided the towns of Beita, Tell, and Beit Dajan, storming and searching several homes, Wafa added.
In Tulkarem, Israeli army and police vehicles raided the city, concentrating their presence in the city centre and market area, harassing Palestinians. Police issued traffic tickets to Palestinian vehicles, according to eyewitnesses.
The witnesses added that the army raised the Israeli flag on the minaret of a mosque in the Nur Shams refugee camp, east of Tulkarem.
International warnings
Meanwhile, two Palestinians, including a child, from the village of al-Rashaydeh in Bethlehem, were detained during an incursion.
In Qalqilya, the army arrested six Palestinians after raiding the city and searching homes in the Kafr Saba and al-Naqqar neighbourhoods, according to Wafa.
The army also rounded up five Palestinians from the city of Tulkarem and another from the town of Beita during its incursions.
In Ramallah, Israeli forces closed the western entrance to al-Mughayyir village, northeast of the city, preventing Palestinians from entering or leaving. They also subjected some Palestinians to field interrogations and fired tear gas towards vehicles.
Local sources told Anadolu that the western entrance is currently the village’s only access point after the Israeli army closed its eastern entrance on Oct. 7, 2023.
According to the same sources, illegal Israeli settlers burned a tent, equipment and animal feed belonging to a Palestinian farmer on the outskirts of Burqa village, east of Ramallah.
The occupied West Bank has witnessed a surge in illegal settler attacks and Israeli military raids since the outbreak of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, amid Palestinian and international warnings over the consequences of the continued escalation.

Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, sacked minister tells BBC
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:56:43 BST
21:56:43 KST

Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, sacked minister tells BBC
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked questions about corruption in his government, his sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has told the BBC.
Fedorov, a popular minister who modernised the military and pioneered drone warfare, was fired last month after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces.
He told the BBC a money laundering investigation announced last week meant Zelensky should be asked about his awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
But he said he had not himself seen the president engage in any corrupt activity.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity", Federov said.
The former minister also repeated his appeal for elections to be held in Ukraine, days after releasing a video where he called for a wartime vote.
"Democracy should not be the hostage of Putin", he said - but stopped short of declaring his own political ambitions.
There were angry protests over Fedorov's sacking but his support dwindled and demonstrations ended on Wednesday, after his replacement was confirmed. His call for a vote has been widely rejected.
Asked whether he missed his old job, the 35-year-old replied "No", citing the relentless stress of managing Ukraine's war with Russia while transforming its defence ministry.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections are suspended. Zelensky's five-year presidential term ended in May 2024.
But Fedorov said it was his "moral right" to start the conversation about elections.
"We should not be afraid of discussing it. That's what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?"
If elections were never held, he said, "then we are no longer a democracy".
- Sacked Ukrainian defence minister calls for presidential election 
  - Published4 days ago
In his earlier video statement Fedorov had argued that "people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made".
He shied away from criticising the president directly and declined to answer whether he backs Zelensky to win any election.
Zelensky said he believed wartime elections would currently be too dangerous for Ukraine in remarks released on Sunday.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk," he said. "Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine."
Experts have cited a number of obstacles to holding such a vote, including how soldiers, millions of Ukrainian refugees and people from occupied territories would vote, as well as disinformation threats from Russia.
Fedorov's video highlighting political corruption last week came the day before a money laundering investigation was announced into lawmakers and bankers.
Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office, alleged to be involved, was sacked.
Fedorov said there were questions about the president's awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions."
A spokesperson for the president had earlier told BBC News: "Since the former minister was part of every government since 2019, it's strange that he phrases it as though these were somehow different governments without him. As everyone remembers, we didn't hear any strong statements from him back then."
Fedorov claimed he had rooted out elements of corruption from defence procurement but warned it was still affecting Ukraine's frontline capacity.
The former minister said he'd had no contact with the president for "a couple of weeks", and had no evidence the president was personally corrupt.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity. So that's my personal experience with him."
As defence minister and previously digital transformation minister, Fedorov is credited with innovating to replace soldiers with an "army of drones", saving lives on the battlefield and enabling long-range Ukrainian strikes on Russian military targets, oil refineries and distribution warehouses - thousands of kilometres over the border.
He said he would continue to promote new ways to fight the war and confirmed a visit to the United States in the coming weeks, where he hopes to meet Elon Musk.
The billionaire businessman's Starlink satellite communications system has been key in Ukraine's success. Fedorov aims to convince Musk to extend the technology into Russian airspace to assist Ukrainian strikes, without the Kremlin benefiting from access.
"The best tech companies in the world are supporting us and they will be investing in our victory, in ending this war. And we need to stay in touch with them regardless of my position. I have a previous successful track record of working with them and I need to stay in touch with them for my country," he said.
Fedorov criticised bureaucracy in the UK and other countries supporting Ukraine for delays in supplying weapons.
The UK is a longstanding supporter of Ukraine, spending £16bn supplying weapons since the war began. It was confirmed last week that British-made drones have been used to attack Russian targets.
Fedorov said he was grateful for British support but blamed "bureaucracy and red tape" for delays in receiving promised equipment.
"Governments are lagging behind the realities on the ground. It's not only the issue for UK, but for other countries as well that announce some assistance and we are not getting it until the end of the year."
Fedorov urged direct funding of the latest Ukrainian drone production, in place of outdated skills and equipment from other nations: "We don't need repairs of tanks when we no longer use tanks."
He said timely deliveries would help save not just Ukrainian lives.
"Unfortunately, our losses, our blood, our military experience is beneficial to all of you guys. You can get this experience for all the assistance that you give us."
Fedorov denied having immediate political ambitions but didn't rule out a future run for president.
"It will all depend on how soon we'll be able to relaunch this democratic election process, [...] how much energy I would have, whether I will preserve my team, whether I will be able to respond to the question myself, whether I can handle this position of the president or not.
"What's more important, is whether people will tell me, yeah, we can trust you handling that position."
Correction 23 August: This article originally said Mykhailo Fedorov's video highlighting political corruption was released the same day a money laundering investigation was announced into lawmakers and bankers. It has been corrected to reflect that the video was released the day before the announcement.

Indonesian police arrest 72 people suspected of starting forest fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Indonesian police arrest 72 people suspected of starting forest fires
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesian police on Sunday arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the recent forest and peatland fires as huge blazes in central and western parts of the country triggered a harmful cloud known as a choking haze.
Indonesia has been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia, according to Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB.
Fires are a regular problem in the country and often strain relations with neighbors.
Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, said Mohammad Irhamni, director of special crimes at the National Police’s Criminal Investigation Agency.
The arson suspects were being investigated in connection with 89 forest and land fire cases across five provinces on the island of Borneo and four on Sumatra, Irhamni said.
He said most of the suspects were accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations at lower cost. Investigators were still tracing financial records to determine whether companies financed or ordered the land clearing, signaling the probe could expand beyond those arrested.
“We will not stop at the perpetrators on the ground,” Irhami said in a news conference Sunday in the capital, Jakarta. “We will determine who benefited from these activities and who was ultimately behind them.”
The suspects face charges that carry penalties ranging from hefty fines to prison terms of up to 15 years, he said.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto flew on Saturday to Central Kalimantan province, where more than 7,600 hectares (18,700 acres) have burned, to encourage authorities to get the haze cloud under control.
Prabowo promised government resources required to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps, and vowed to hold accountable any companies found to have contributed to the fires.
“I hope we can control this soon,” Prabowo said during the visit. “We have experienced worse forest and land fires in the past, and we were able to overcome them.”
Accompanying the president was Prasetyo Hadi, the head of State Secretariat. He said at least four companies in West Kalimantan province are under investigation for allegedly using fire to clear land. If they are proven to have intentionally set the fires, they could face sanctions, including the revocation of their operating permits, he added.
Smoke from the fires on Sunday blanketed parts of Borneo, the world’s third-largest island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Indonesia administers about three-quarters of the island, where the country’s Environment Ministry recorded more than 3,700 hot spots on Sunday.
BNPB chief Suharyanto said fire activity had increased in West, Central and South Kalimantan provinces on Borneo, where many blazes worsen due to peatlands, prolonging the dangerous haze in several areas.
Fires that appear “extinguished on the surface may still contain embers underneath, so sufficient rainfall is crucial to rewet the peat and fully suppress the fires,” said Suharyanto, who, like many Indonesians, uses a single name.
The western island of South Sumatra also battled fires, with more than 1,700 hot spots detected on Sunday, causing a choked haze cloud and reducing visibility to only 10 meters (33 feet) in some areas, the ministry said.
Cloud-seeding resumed over Kalimantan on Sunday, with 30 helicopters for water-bombing and aerial patrol missions, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Meanwhile, Malaysia has suffered severe smoke from the fires, with its eastern state of Sarawak among the hardest hit. One district recorded “very unhealthy” air quality on Friday, while eight others posted unhealthy readings, prompting the closure of nearly 600 schools and affecting about 200,000 students, the Sarawak government said.

“It was crazy with Gabi, I almost T-boned him,” Hülkenberg said over team radio.
The Dutch Grand Prix is dropping off the schedule after this season and the many orange-clad Dutch fans who turned up to support Verstappen instead saw Norris and his orange McLaren take the win.
Verstappen said he simply misjudged his speed on the damp track after pre-race rain.
Charles Leclerc was fifth on another disappointing day for Ferrari ahead of its home race in Italy in two weeks’ time. Hulkenberg was eighth for Audi, with Fernando Alonso ninth in the best result of an otherwise-disastrous 2026 for Aston Martin. Alpine’s Pierre Gasly rounded out the top ten.

A tiny pore identifies cyanobacteria toxins in lake water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:52:21 UTC
21:52:21 KST

EPFL researchers have developed a nanopore sensor that distinguishes seven toxins from cyanobacteria blooms, and can detect one common toxin at concentrations far below World Health Organization guidelines.
Cyanobacterial blooms, like the ones that occur in Lake Geneva are rapid, dense growths of photosynthetic bacteria in fresh and marine waters that can threaten the health of swimmers and their pets.
Blooms can release microcystins, a family of toxins that threaten drinking-water supplies, recreational waters and aquatic ecosystems. More than 300 microcystin variants, known as congeners, have been identified, and they can differ subtly in structure while producing different biological effects.
Detecting microcystins quickly and telling them apart is still difficult, as each of most common methods have limitations. ELISA immunoassay tests are relatively fast and sensitive, but they generally cannot identify individual microcystin congeners and may cross-react with related compounds. Liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), is far more selective, but requires expensive equipment, trained specialists and sample transport. Depending on the analysis, results may take from a day to several weeks.
Now, scientists in the groups of Matteo Dal Peraro and Tamar Kohn at EPFL have developed a nanopore sensor that detects microcystins one molecule at a time. The work, which was led by Alissa Agerova and Juan Francisco Bada Juarez, is published in ACS Nano.
Seven molecules distinguished
The sensor uses aerolysin, a protein that spontaneously forms a “nanopore” channel through a thin membrane, around ten nanometers long, with a narrowest point about one nanometer across.
When a voltage is applied, ions flowing through the channel generate an electrical current. As a microcystin molecule interacts with or passes through the pore, it briefly blocks part of that current. The depth and duration of the blockage provide a characteristic signal for the molecule.
Based on this readout, the team distinguished between seven individual microcystin congeners under controlled laboratory conditions. The signals remained sufficiently distinct for all seven populations to be separated even without more sophisticated data classification.
Testing cyanobacteria in Swiss lakes
The researchers then tested the system with natural lake-water samples, which they filtered to remove particles that could interfere with the nanopores
“Filtration is an obstacle in the sense that it implies more sample manipulation before analysis,” says Tamar Kohn. “In the future we would like to find a way to analyze the samples without the need for filtration, or at least automate this step to avoid lengthy sample manipulation.”
In water from Lake Geneva, they successfully separated two closely related microcystins that had been added at concentrations representative of strong blooms. The lake water did not prevent the pore from distinguishing the two toxins.
In a sample collected during a cyanobacterial bloom in Lake Lugano, the nanopore identified and quantified one of the best-studied microcystins, MC-LR. It measured a concentration of 12.7 nanomolar, closely matching the 13.1 nanomolar result obtained by LC-MS/MS.
By creating a salt-concentration gradient across the pore, the researchers also improved sensitivity and detected MC-LR at concentrations as low as 25 picomolar. This is 40 times below the provisional WHO guideline of 1 nanomolar for lifetime exposure to MC-LR in drinking water.
Field-use and startup
The technology is not yet mature to be used in the field, as the lake samples were filtered and adjusted to high salt concentrations before measurement. But because nanopores are compact and produce electrical signals in real time, the sensor could eventually be incorporated into portable systems for on-site, real-time water monitoring. Further engineering can help adapt the same principle to detect other cyanotoxins or small environmental pollutants.
Further developing, scaling, and commercializing the technology is the focus of a future startup, CYnANO, currently being planned by the paper’s first author, Alissa Agerova.

Restored Pomodoro sphere unveiled at Tehran museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:50:27 UTC
21:50:27 KST

Pomodoro’s masterpiece gets new lease of life in Tehran museum
TEHRAN – A monumental bronze sphere by late Italian sculptor Arnaldo Pomodoro has been unveiled at Tehran’s Time Museum following months of conservation and restoration project, marking the centenary of the artist’s birth.
The unveiling ceremony was attended by Hamidreza Soleimani, CEO of the Dafineh Museums of the Mostazafan Foundation; Ahmad Mohit-Tabatabaei, head of the Iranian Museums Association; Emmanuel Marchi, cultural attaché of the Italian Embassy in Tehran; Amir Qassemi, head of Tehran Municipality’s Tourism Headquarters; and representatives of Iran’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
The 3,000-kilogram bronze sculpture, known as Sfera di Pomodoro, was created in 1974 and brought to Iran in 1978. It had previously been installed at Tehran’s Eram Park before being transferred to the courtyard of the Time Museum in northern Tehran.
Soleimani said the study, treatment, restoration and reconstruction of the sculpture took about two years, with the restoration of the sphere itself requiring around 18 months.
Given the sculpture’s unique characteristics and its metal construction, preliminary studies alone took six to seven months, he said.
The restoration team established contact with the Pomodoro Foundation in Italy and obtained its conservation and treatment protocols, Soleimani said. The foundation remained involved throughout the project, receiving progress reports, monitoring the condition of the work and, at certain stages, supervising the restoration process online.
Soleimani said the restoration was carried out by an experienced team of cultural heritage specialists led by Manijeh Hadian Dehkordi. Mitra Etezadi and her colleagues later joined the project, with the final conservation methodology developed through consultations among the specialists involved.
“This project was not the result of the decision or work of a single person,” Soleimani said, emphasizing the role of the multidisciplinary team throughout the restoration.
Also, Marchi, for his part, welcomed the completion of the restoration on the occasion of Pomodoro’s centenary and thanked Iranian conservators for their efforts to preserve the Italian artist’s work.
The giant masterpiece had suffered various forms of environmental and surface damage during its years at Eram Park, according to Iranian heritage experts.
Pomodoro, who was born in 1926, is internationally known for his polished bronze sculptures characterized by ruptures and openings that reveal complex internal structures. His Sphere within Sphere series explores the contrast between apparently perfect external forms and their intricate interiors.
Large-scale works from the series are displayed at prominent locations including the United Nations Headquarters in New York, UNESCO headquarters in Paris and St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City.

Telling Central Synagogue members, “I stand with you,” New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch on Friday called last week’s attack at the Midtown house of worship, for which a man was charged with federal hate crimes, part of a “broader pattern” of bias attacks against Jews in New York City and around the world.
Tisch spoke during the Shabbat service at the Manhattan synagogue, where one week earlier Larry Montes, 46, was accused of striking a 63-year-old woman and yelling “F*** you, n****r!” at a 65-year-old Black security guard before spitting in his face and headbutting him.
She emphasized the disparity in the number of crimes targeting Jews, who make up only 10% of the city’s population, but who are targeted in roughly half of all hate crimes in New York City.
“Those numbers are staggering, but sometimes the data can be just that, numbers on a page, abstract, at a distance,” she told the congregation. “What happened here last Friday brought that hatred inside the doors of this synagogue.”
The commissioner said the NYPD has been tracking attacks targeting Jewish victims across the globe ever since Hamas and terrorist groups attacked Israel on October 7, 2023.
“Since October 7, hate has ricocheted across the globe, and the Jewish community has been targeted again and again,” Tisch said. “We have watched rhetoric shift from slogans to direct calls for violence.”
She said violence against Jews abroad may inspire attacks closer to home.
“Every high-profile attack raises the risk of another. Individuals already on the edge do not always need instructions. Sometimes, all they need is a spark,” the top cop said. “That is why we take threats seriously, and why we work aggressively to intervene before hatred becomes violence.”
NYPD doing everything it can to thwart antisemitic attacks
The commissioner sought to reassure the congregation that the NYPD was doing everything in its power to safeguard Jewish New Yorkers and thwart antisemitic attacks.
“Across New York City, our precinct commanders and community affairs officers are in contact with synagogues and yeshivas, doing everything we can to ensure their safety,” Tisch said. “Our Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau acts aggressively against potential threats and directs resources where they are needed.”
“As a proud Jew and a lifelong member of this congregation, you have my word that I stand with you in these uncertain, precarious times,” Tisch pledged.
“And as Police commissioner, you have my word that behind that commitment stand 35,000 members of the NYPD willing to risk their own lives for people they have never met, supported by the most robust municipal counterterrorism capacity in the world and a Hate Crimes Task Force that is second to none.”
After she finished her remarks, the Central Synagogue members all rose to their feet and gave Tisch a sustained standing ovation, before the service ended with music and the traditional sharing of challah bread.
'Yasher Koach Madame Commissioner'
Worshipers watching the service on the house of worship’s Facebook livestream were heartened by Tisch’s steady presence and reassuring words.
“Yasher Koach [good job] Madame Commissioner,” one posted, meaning “good job” in Yiddish.
“If Commissioner Tisch is this good every day as she is from the bima, I feel hopeful for New York,” another wrote, referring to the rabbis’ platform at the front of the temple.
The bizarre attack, part of which was caught on a livestream of the previous week’s Shabbat service, outraged Jewish leaders and public officials, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said he was “horrified” by the hateful incident.
“Our administration will always stand against bigotry in all its forms,” he said. “We will use every tool at our disposal to confront antisemitism and keep Jewish New Yorkers, and all New Yorkers, safe.”
Montes called congregants at Central Synagogue “swine” and himself God, before attacking congregant Michele Anaberg-Poma, 63, and the security guard while screaming a racist slur at him, cops said. He also grabbed and threw two $10,000 candle holders to the ground, breaking them, and screamed at the congregation, according to prosecutors. Police said he also spewed, “F***k the Jews.”
Ananberg-Poma posted on Instagram the night of the attack, remaining defiant despite Montes’ berserk outburst.
“You will not punch out our Jewish light. You will not stand and cause harm to our eternal light,” Ananberg-Poma wrote. “We will continue to sing our prayers of peace, love, and joy while protecting the voices that lead us each week.”
Montes was charged with two counts of committing hate crimes and one count of damage to religious property resulting in bodily injury for last Friday’s attack, according to the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office. He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted on the top charge.
His relatives called Montes a troubled man whose struggles have worsened since the recent death of his grandmother, who raised him.

Azerbaijan, CNN, and the question Israel should ask itself - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:47:13 UTC
21:47:13 KST

Last week, Azerbaijan filed a lawsuit against CNN in a US federal court over what it describes as false and defamatory reporting about its role in the 2026 Iran conflict. CNN alleged that Israel had deployed military and intelligence personnel to Azerbaijan and used Azerbaijani territory for operations against Iran.
Baku has categorically rejected those claims as false, stressing that Azerbaijan does not permit its territory to be used by any state for military operations against a neighboring or third country.
This is not simply a dispute about reputation.
The allegations carry potentially serious security consequences. The IRGC had separately warned that states hosting forces used in attacks against Iran could face retaliation. In March 2026, drones Azerbaijan said had been launched from Iran entered Azerbaijani airspace and struck near Nakhchivan airport and a school, injuring civilians. Tehran denied responsibility.
Against that background, a report portraying Azerbaijan as a participant in military operations against Iran rather than as a neighboring state seeking to remain outside the conflict is not an abstract matter. It can affect diplomacy, security calculations, and, potentially, civilian lives.
Azerbaijan also argues that CNN relied heavily on anonymous sources despite receiving an official denial before publication.
The use of unnamed sources deserves particular scrutiny in this case. A source described simply as someone “familiar with the matter” may be exceptionally well placed. But in the Iranian information environment, one cannot exclude the possibility that such a source could also be linked to an actor, including within the IRGC, with an interest in shaping the narrative.
The public has no way of knowing the source’s institutional affiliation, proximity to the alleged operation, or possible agenda.
The fact that even Iranian officials later rejected elements of the account only underscores how unstable and contested the narrative was. Yet by that stage, the CNN report was already being recycled in the region as something approaching established fact.
How CNN was used to reinforce Iran’s narrative
That is where the problem becomes larger than CNN or Azerbaijan.
Regardless of whether CNN’s account was exaggerated, incomplete, or based on information unavailable to the public, its publication gave Iran a valuable instrument with which to reinforce one of its longstanding regional narratives: that Azerbaijan serves as a platform for Israeli military and intelligence operations against the Islamic Republic.
The report was especially consequential because its account closely resembled Iranian claims that Azerbaijan had hosted Israeli military facilities used to support operations against Iran, including during Operations Rising Lion and Roaring Lion. Iranian outlets, including Tabnak, Mashregh, and ILNA, subsequently cited CNN as evidence of an Israeli military presence in Azerbaijan.
This is how information warfare works.
It does not depend solely on fabrication. It operates through selective quotation, the removal of qualifications, repetition, and the conversion of allegations into apparent facts.
A report that begins with anonymous sources, carefully worded claims, and unresolved questions can gradually be repackaged as confirmation of what Tehran had previously asserted without persuasive public evidence.
The CNN attribution is especially valuable for Iranian messaging because claims made directly by Iranian officials about Israeli bases or covert activity in Azerbaijan are likely to be dismissed by many international audiences as propaganda.
Once a prominent American news organization reports similar allegations, however, Iranian outlets can invoke a source with global credibility.
The message is no longer merely an Iranian accusation.
It becomes something that “even CNN” has supposedly confirmed.
This is why I see Azerbaijan’s lawsuit as more than a legal dispute. It is an attempt to impose a cost on the circulation of claims Baku regards as dangerous disinformation.
Whether the lawsuit ultimately succeeds is for the US court to decide. But Azerbaijan’s decision to pursue the matter is itself significant.
Baku did not simply issue a denial and wait for the news cycle to move on. It decided that allegations it considered harmful to its reputation and potentially dangerous to its national security should be challenged through institutional and, where appropriate, legal means.
Accusations against Israel are piling up - but its response is fragmented
The contrast with Israel is striking. For years, Israel has faced hostile reporting, grave accusations in international institutions, and campaigns by anti-Israel activists and advocacy networks. Claims are repeated by activists, journalists, and international officials until disputed allegations can gradually acquire the appearance of accepted fact.
Yet Israel’s response is often fragmented. Private Jewish organizations, researchers, lawyers, and individuals are frequently left to confront these narratives, while the state itself rarely pursues a sustained legal or institutional strategy.
One recent example is the effort by members of Raphael Lemkin’s family and the European Jewish Association to challenge the US-based Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention over what they describe as a distortion of Lemkin’s legacy and the use of his name to advance false genocide accusations against Israel. More than 100 letters were sent to Pennsylvania and federal officials, including Gov. Josh Shapiro and Attorney General Dave Sunday, asking authorities to examine the institute’s use of Lemkin’s name and likeness. The episode illustrates a broader problem: in the absence of a coherent state-led strategy, private organizations and individuals are often left to confront institutions whose claims can shape international perceptions of Israel.
Israel does not need to sue every critic, journalist, or organization that publishes something it regards as unfair. Nor should legal action become a substitute for legitimate debate or a weapon against serious journalism.
But there is a difference between criticism and factual claims capable of causing substantial diplomatic, legal, or security damage.
When such claims are demonstrably false, or when contested allegations are repeatedly presented as established facts, a state should have the capacity to respond systematically. That can include rapid factual rebuttals, demands for corrections, engagement with relevant institutions, and, in exceptional cases, legal action.
Azerbaijan’s global reach may be more limited than Israel’s, but Baku has shown a willingness to use the tools available to it when it believes a dangerous narrative threatens its interests.
That instinct deserves Israel’s attention.
In modern information warfare, silence does not necessarily make an allegation disappear. It can give it time to accumulate citations, credibility, and authority until the original uncertainty surrounding it is forgotten.
Azerbaijan has decided that serious claims affecting its reputation and security should not simply be allowed to circulate unanswered. They should be challenged and, where appropriate, tested in court.
Israel should ask itself why it so often leaves that task to others.
The author is an Iran expert at the Jerusalem Institute of Strategy and Security.

KINSHASA, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the March 23 Movement (M23) rebel group have agreed on a roadmap for peace negotiations, setting out sequenced steps and timelines for further talks, according to a joint statement issued on Saturday.
The two sides said that, during meetings held from Aug. 17 to 21 in Switzerland, they assessed progress and challenges in the Doha peace process while discussing the implementation of existing commitments and the way forward for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement.
Following the assessment, the two sides developed a roadmap outlining the sequence and timetable for future negotiations. They also agreed to establish a mechanism to review progress and address challenges in implementing obligations and commitments under the framework agreement.

They also stressed the importance of adopting a standardized method for reporting alleged ceasefire violations and reaffirmed their commitment to pursuing negotiations toward comprehensive peace and conflict resolution.
Since January 2025, the M23 has intensified offensives in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu, seizing several key cities.
In July 2025, under Qatari mediation, the DRC government and the M23 signed a declaration of principles in Doha. In November, the two sides signed a framework agreement, pledging to build trust through dialogue, advance stabilization in stages and address the root causes of the conflict. ■

Ex-diplomat Navdeep Suri flags 'trouble establishing citizenship' during Punjab SIR
Edited by: Rohitashwa Ranjan / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 23, 2026, 19:31 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small

NEW DELHI: Former diplomat Navdeep Suri on Sunday said he was facing "trouble establishing his citizenship" during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Punjab, despite having represented India in three countries.In a post on X, Suri shared his experience with the voter roll revision and said he was asked to provide "unspecified documents" to establish that he was an Indian citizen."Sharing my experience with #SIR in Punjab. Went to BLO, submitted Voter ID and Aadhaar card, was assured that everything is in order. Got a message today from a volunteer saying some details don’t match with SIR in 2003!" Suri said.
He said that after speaking to the booth-level officer (BLO), he was asked to collect a notice and return with documents proving his citizenship."Spoke with BLO, was told that I should come and collect the notice. And then come again with unspecified documents that show I am an Indian citizen. Replied that I was not in India in 2003, so they’ve asked for passport as proof," he added.Suri said he had documents apart from his voter ID and Aadhaar, but questioned what the process would mean for ordinary citizens."I happen to have documents other than voter ID and Aadhaar card.
But can’t help asking: If I have trouble establishing my citizenship after representing India in three countries, what’s the fate of the common citizen? Ease of Living, I presume!" he said.Former ambassador Navdeep Suri has served as India's high commissioner to Australia and ambassador to UAE and Egypt.The SIR was first launched in Bihar in June 2025. Following the exercise, more than 60 lakh names, including those of deceased voters, were removed from the electoral rolls. In West Bengal, around 90 lakh voters were deleted from the rolls ahead of the assembly elections.Under the SIR process, voters who were not included in the 2002 or 2003 electoral rolls are required to submit documents linking them to people included in those legacy rolls. The Election Commission of India (ECI) had initially listed 11 acceptable documents, excluding Aadhaar.
Following proceedings in the Supreme Court, the poll panel expanded the list to include Aadhaar as an acceptable document.The Supreme Court has also made observations on the broader constitutional implications of the exercise, stressing that while the ECI has the power to revise electoral rolls, those powers cannot be "untrammelled" and must comply with principles of transparency and natural justice.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Mexican governor accused by U.S. of drug trafficking abruptly resigns a day after returning to office

Sinaloa Gov. Ruben Rocha Moya said in a social media post on Friday that he was resuming leadership of the northwestern state, a role he stepped away from in May to face an investigation by Mexican prosecutors. On Saturday, less than a day later, he shared a document on X asking the state congress to authorize "a temporary leave of absence of indefinite duration, exceeding 30 days."
Rocha Moya's announcement on Friday drew criticism from President Claudia Sheinbaum, the leader of his party, who said Saturday that "no personal interest can ever be placed above the interests of the people" and of Mexico, without explicitly naming anyone in her X post.
"Power without principles becomes arrogance; power without limits, abuse."
When journalists questioned her about Rocha, the leftist leader referred them to her post.
"I found out through his tweet," Sheinbaum told reporters of his return to his job. "I just put out a post on X; that's all I have to say."
The U.S. Justice Department charged Rocha and nine other officials of the ruling Morena party in April. It demanded their extradition for allegedly colluding with the infamous Sinaloa Cartel to distribute drugs inside the U.S. It was the first time the U.S. had publicly charged a sitting Mexican politician.
Rocha on Friday insisted he had "committed no crime" and was returning to office "with a clear conscience and head held high."
The 77-year-old is an ally of Sheinbaum and very close to her mentor, former President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador. He has been governor of the northwestern state of Sinaloa since 2021.
The governor was embroiled in a scandal in 2023 involving the Sinaloa cartel, in which his name was published in a letter written by a then-Sinaloa cartel capo whom leaders of a rival faction of the cartel had kidnapped. The cartel capo was handed off to law enforcement in the U.S. The capo said in the letter that when he was kidnapped, he believed he was on his way to meet with Rocha Moya.
Rocha Moya faces federal charges, including narcotics importation conspiracy and possession of machine guns and destructive devices, along with another conspiracy count. If convicted, he could face life in prison or a mandatory minimum of 40 years behind bars.
Using the threat of tariffs, U.S. President Trump is demanding that Mexico redouble its efforts in the war on drugs.
The Republican frequently claims Mexico is governed by politicians linked to drug trafficking and has offered military support to Sheinbaum, who has rejected any such intervention.
The Sinaloa cartel is one of six Mexican narcotrafficking groups designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the Trump administration.

The German government plans to invest approximately €12 billion ($14 billion) to develop a new arsenal of long-range weapons aimed at deterring Russia, Politico reported.
The initiative, described in the documents as a key priority for both Germany and NATO, aims to equip the German armed forces with the ability to strike targets hundreds or thousands of kilometers behind enemy lines.

The conventional, “below the nuclear threshold” capabilities would be used to target command posts, airfields, missile launchers, and supply hubs.
The ministry’s strategy consists of a four-part plan. The first phase involves deploying a new, low-cost cruise missile starting in 2027. The second phase focuses on the United States, with an internal goal to achieve initial operational readiness of US Typhon launchers armed with Tomahawk missiles by the end of the decade, providing Berlin with a proven interim weapon.
The final two phases of the plan involve the joint development of highly advanced weapon systems with the United Kingdom, slated for introduction by the middle of the next decade.
According to the internal documents, the capacity building will require “nearly €12 billion” in state funds. The funding has not yet been approved but was submitted as part of the state budget planning process.
A spokesperson for the German Defense Ministry declined to comment to Politico on the specific figures or individual programs, stating that the ministry will only comment after parliamentary review.

Russian hybrid threats in Germany
The military buildup comes as Germany weighs taking diplomatic action against Moscow over mounting hybrid security threats.
The German government is currently reviewing the international legal basis for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and has not ruled out terminating a 2011 bilateral agreement that allows it to operate. Germany’s next opportunity to terminate the agreement takes effect in June 2027, requiring Berlin to notify Moscow by Dec. 6, 2026.
The Foreign Ministry cited “Russia’s increasing hybrid activities” as the primary reason for the review. The Russian House, operated by the sanctioned Russian state agency Rossotrudnichestvo, has traditionally hosted cultural events but is now facing heightened scrutiny.

The U.S. Navy has awarded two contracts under its CHAOS program. The project is believed to involve CoAspire’s RAACM-ER cruise missiles and Zone 5 Technologies’ Rusty Dagger.
According to DVIDS, the CHAOS program is focused on developing low-cost, scalable strike weapons. Its main goal is to provide the U.S. Navy and its allies with affordable, precision-guided systems capable of engaging both surface and land targets.
The new missiles are expected to help address the shortage of anti-ship weapons and replace aging systems.
According to available information, CoAspire’s RAACM-ER missile has a range of more than 1,800 km, while Zone 5’s AGM-188A Rusty Dagger, weighing around 225 kg, has a range of more than 930 km.
The first stage involves developing a ground-based launcher, with mass production expected to begin by 2028. The system will later be adapted for launch from ships and, if needed, from aircraft.
The U.S. Air Force has conducted drop tests of the Rusty Dagger cruise missile, developed for Ukraine under the ERAM program, from an F-16 fighter aircraft.
The integration test campaign comprised a series of captive-carry and separation tests, including assessments of weapons-system compatibility, proper loading procedures, and aerodynamic/flight compatibility with the F-16.

Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap
August 23, 2026
After days of negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, representatives from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23 have agreed to a shared roadmap designed to facilitate peace in the DRC after years of brutal war.
The US State Department, which was involved in mediating talks alongside the African Union (AU), Switzerland and Qatar, released a statement describing the situation on Saturday evening.
The State Department said the agreement builds on a US-brokered deal signed last November in Doha, Qatar, adding that Congo and the rebels had "developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement."
Despite a ceasefire being in place since November 15, the shift to peace has been slow, though prisoners, for instance, were recently exchanged.
The newly agreed roadmap made clear that an observer mission monitoring the ceasefire will receive support from UN MONUSCO peacekeeping forces and that further negotiations designed to bring about lasting peace will take place soon.
Hundreds of civilians have been killed and millions displaced by fighting between the two sides since early 2022, when M23 — with backing from neighboring Rwanda — began its quest for control of resource-rich eastern Congo and its gold, cassiterite, coltan and diamonds.
M23, which is accused of committing brutal wartime atrocities, has controlled large swaths of the North and South Kivu provinces since 2025.
The State Department statement released on Saturday said both sides had thanked mediators "for their steadfast support in advancing peace and stability in eastern DRC and the broader Great Lakes region."

Stating that the National Iranian South Oil Company, as the largest crude oil producer in the country, has been a pioneer in developing private sector participation in the upstream oil industry, he added: In the second half of last year, the trend of signing investment contracts grew significantly, and these contracts are focused on three main axes: collecting associated gases and extinguishing flares, crude oil processing, and providing onshore drilling rigs.
The Director of Investment and Business Development of the National Iranian Oil Company said: In the field of collecting associated gases and flare gases, 23 contracts have been signed with the private and non-governmental sectors, the implementation of which will provide the basis for extinguishing 57 flares in Khuzestan province.
Moghiseh added: The implementation of these contracts has not stopped, and it is predicted that by the end of this year, about 400 million cubic feet of associated gas will be collected. Also, during Government Week, 40 million cubic feet of flare gas in the Khuzestan area will be collected and prevented from being burned.
Increasing processing capacity by 380,000 barrels
He cited contracts for purchasing crude oil processing services using skid-mounted rapid-installation equipment as the second axis of cooperation with the private sector and said: In this sector, seven contracts have been signed for seven oil fields, the implementation of which will add 380,000 barrels per day to the country's oil processing capacity.
The Director of Investment and Business Development of the National Iranian Oil Company continued: This capacity is equivalent to about 11 to 12 percent of the country's oil processing capacity, which will be created with the participation of the private and non-governmental sectors.
Moghiseh, referring to the progress of some projects in line with or ahead of the schedule, added: With the continuation of support and cooperation of investors, it is possible to bring some of these projects into operation earlier than the scheduled date.
Providing services for 18 onshore drilling rigs
He cited the provision of onshore drilling rig services as the third axis of investments and said: Providing these services is one of the prerequisites for development, increase, and maintenance of production in the country's onshore oil fields.
The Director of Investment and Business Development of the National Iranian Oil Company added: The National Company of South Oil-Rich Regions, within the framework of public-private partnership contracts, has assigned the provision of services for 18 onshore drilling rigs to the private and non-governmental sectors.
Moghiseh, referring to the first onshore rig supplied under the guaranteed purchase scheme for onshore drilling rig services, said: This rig was supplied and brought into the country with private sector investment and is currently being set up, and will soon begin drilling operations in the Ab-Teymour field.
Emphasizing the support of the National Iranian Oil Company for the presence of the private sector in the upstream oil industry, he stated: Utilizing the capacity of the private sector in upstream projects can pave the way for increasing production and strengthening the capacities of the oil industry in the next 5 to 10 years.
The Director of Investment and Business Development of the National Iranian Oil Company added: The investments made in this field, in addition to increasing production, can have positive effects in terms of employment, development of operational capacities, and increasing the country's foreign exchange earnings.
Moghiseh said: Based on the plan presented by investors, it is predicted that in the next two to three months, a significant number of additional rigs will be supplied and brought into operational areas.

Iran-Turkey agreement document for rail connection exchanged
