Double jeopardy? Luigi Mangione state case unlikely to proceed, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:32 UTC
21:00:32 KST

After Luigi Mangione admitted in Manhattan federal court that he killed UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, most experts believe that the state murder case against is highly unlikely to proceed – though some still see a slim possibility that it may yet happen.
Mangione, who pleaded guilty on 14 August to two federal stalking counts, was scheduled for a New York state trial on 8 September for murder and weapons charges in the December 2024 killing. In the wake of Mangione’s surprise plea, legal experts said New York’s state-level double jeopardy law – which means someone cannot be tried twice for the same crime – could derail his local prosecution.
Mangione’s defense team, seizing on this law, quickly filed a motion to dismiss his state case. Judge Gregory Carro, who is overseeing the state case, decided on Monday to postpone Mangione’s trial, scheduling a proceeding for 10 December and giving both sides deadlines to file their legal arguments about dismissal.
It was a remarkable turnaround for a case that been eagerly anticipated in the wake of Thompson’s killing on the streets of Manhattan in 2024. It had also become a flashpoint in a discourse about American’s struggles with the for-profit US healthcare industry, and launched Mangione himself to near folk-hero status among a hard core of supporters.
Now Mangione’s possible punishment in the wake of his plea potentially lifts the veil on his lawyers’ legal gambit, but points to risks associated with this strategy. Prosecutors disclosed in court that a sentencing range under federal guidelines would span from 292 to 365 months, though they vowed to seek a life sentence. And, there remain potential legal avenues for the survival of Mangione’s state case albeit very small, experts said.
Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor who now practices white-collar defense at the firm Dykema, said: “At this point, it seems like his goal is to try to get out of prison sometime in his 50s, but even that path is narrowing as we speak.”
“He’s trying to do the best with the hand that he has, and it’s a difficult hand,” he added.
The defense might be betting that a federal judge would be more lenient about sentencing than Carro, who could impose a maximum 25 years-to-life sentence if Mangione were convicted in state court.
The legal community has described Carro as “fairly tough on crime, fairly sympathetic to victims”, Chutkow said – so Mangione’s defense might have factored this track record into estimating a possible state sentence versus federal one.
Joseph McNally, a former federal prosecutor who now directs emerging litigation at McNicholas & McNicholas, said he expects Mangione will receive a life sentence – or something close. Even though this would be a possible outcome in a state trial, Mangione’s defense would still see resolving this case federally as more desirable.
“Serving out long-term imprisonment, including life imprisonment, it’s typically better and safer for an inmate to be in federal prison than state prison,” McNally said.
Although federal prison is no “country club”, with Mangione facing the strictest of prisons, “if you ask somebody: would you rather serve your time in state custody or federal custody? An inmate would say that they’d rather serve their sentence in federal custody.”
Jeffrey Greco, a former prosecutor who now helms defense firm Greco Neyland, said: “At the end of the day, there is a very good chance Mangione is still doing life in prison. The only difference: is he doing it in a federal lockup, or is it a state facility upstate?”
Though legal experts generally believe Mangione’s state case is all but done, prosecutors are likely poised to explore nuances in the law to argue that it should persist.
The Manhattan district attorney’s office certainly says it is going to continue fighting the case, remarking in a post-plea statement: “While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan DA’s office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr Thompson and his family.”
Jeremy Saland, a defense attorney who worked as a prosecutor in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, explained that state and federal authorities are typically allowed to pursue parallel cases. New York has its own double jeopardy law, however, stipulating that a person cannot be prosecuted for the same thing in state court if it stems from “the same underlying criminal transaction”.
“But, there are some exceptions,” Saland said. Are the elements of the crime different? What harm is the legislature trying to protect against with state laws?
“If they’re different and there’s different elements, then is there a window to say you know what, this would be the exception to the double jeopardy,” Saland said.
“We understand and we know that he pleaded guilty to a stalking charge, and we also know that in the state case, he’s facing a ‘murder two’ charge.”
Salad said he believes that the Manhattan district attorney’s office will focus on the distinction between the elements of these crimes and intended harm.
“You have one that is an intentional murder, meaning: ‘I intentionally sought to kill you. This was my purpose and goal.’ And that would be the state. Whereas on the federal level, it’s different. You’re stalking someone and as a result, that causes death, but it was not your intent, as per the statute, to murder that person.”
“It could put them in fear of their life for sure, but that’s very different. You may have killed that person for sure,” he continued, noting that while Mangione admitted to killing Thompson, “he did not say, nor was it required by the statute, that he intentionally killed Brian Thompson.”
Maurice Johnson, a former prosecutor with the Manhattan district attorney and federal prosecutor in south Florida, now a partner at Lewis Brisbois Bisgaard & Smith, voiced similar sentiments about a possible prosecution strategy.
“I think what the prosecution is going to argue is: your honor, this defendant pled guilty to stalking in the federal system. We are charging him with second-degree murder and other charges.”
He said of state prosecutors’ potential argument: “These are separate elements so technically, these are not the same offense. It may be stalking there, but it’s murder here.”
Johnson believes that Mangione will likely be able to avoid state charges. While Mangione admitted to killing Thompson, this admission overlaps with the state murder charge, in his view.
In Chutkow’s view, the Manhattan DA’s office has already been laying the groundwork to make this argument, pointing to a July letter filed amid rumors of plea talks.
In that letter, Manhattan state prosecutors said any guilty pleas “must account for the seriousness of defendant’s offenses, the loss of an innocent life, the impact of those crimes on the victim’s family, and the other state interests that are implicated, including the sanctity of life principle that underpins the state homicide charges”.
“I do think that the state does have a pretty good argument here, but this is relatively untested,” Chutkow said, noting that there is not an abundance of state appeals court decisions that would readily settle this issue.
“There hasn’t been a lot of case law, and so I think the Mangione team is, in essence, throwing up a Hail Mary to see if they can’t land that touchdown by getting the state prosecution barred.”

====================================================================================================

How to make the perfect zaru soba, or cold soba noodles – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:32 UTC
21:00:32 KST

Although every culture craves something different in hot weather – chilled beetroot soup in Lithuania, cooling buttermilk drinks in India, gazpacho in Spain – what many of these dishes have in common is a certain soothing silkiness as they slide down the throat, plus a decent helping of salt. Japan’s zaru soba, which Namiko Hirasawa Chen of Just One Cookbook describes as her family’s “go-to meal when the summer heat and humidity soar”, is no exception. Cold, slippery noodles paired with a savoury dipping sauce, it’s a simple, satisfying dish that’s ready in 15 minutes, and can be accessorised with crunchy salads, sweet seafood or creamy tofu sides for something more substantial. Traditionally served on a bamboo mat, or zaru, to allow the noodles to drain, you can get away without one at home (though lose the seaweed and you can call it mori soba instead), this is definitely one to stick in your summer repertoire alongside the chilled soups, watermelon salads and cucumber sandwiches.
The noodles
Zaru soba isn’t the only chilled noodle dish that Japan slurps in summer – Emiko Davies favours her mother’s somen (delicate wheat-flour strands), while Shota Nakajima makes a case for hiyashi chuka, a Chinese-inspired ramen salad. Sadly, though, spindly somen and fresh ramen are trickier to source in the UK than buckwheat soba, which can be found in many larger supermarkets.
In fact, Yumiko Maehashi of RecipeTin Japan reckons that these noodles’ nutty flavour is best enjoyed cold: “I read in a Japanese soba article that some soba fanatics would not consider the soba in hot soup as ‘soba’.” Not all, however, are created equal, as Maehashi goes on to explain: “Some soba brands indicate the ratio of buckwheat and wheat flours mixed in the soba noodles. The more buckwheat flour, the more flavour and the more expensive … It is really your preference as to what sort of soba noodles are the best, but, in general, the more expensive dried soba noodles cook to al dente better.” If you’d like to keep this dish gluten-free, you’ll need to look for 100% buckwheat noodles (and a gluten-free Japanese soy sauce – Kikkoman makes one), but, otherwise, it’s up to you. Buckwheat can, after all, be an acquired taste, especially in such a simple dish.
The noodles are cooked without salt, I suspect to facilitate the contrast with the dipping sauce. Swirling them around the pan for the first 15 or so seconds, as Maehashi suggests, is a helpful tip to ensure that the strands don’t clump together. It’s also vital to rinse them well afterwards, to quickly cool down the noodles before they overcook, and to wash off some of the starch that will otherwise turn those lovely, silky noodles into a sticky bird’s nest (trust me on this). Chen dunks hers in iced water, too, but I don’t find that this step makes much of a difference texture-wise. Then again, neither do I notice that doing so causes the “noodles to ‘tighten’ up too quickly, losing their texture and flavour”, as Lisa Kitahara at Okonomi Kitchen claims, but I’ll concede I’m no soba expert.
Once cooled, the soba are best consumed immediately, but if you find they’ve started to tangle, give them a rinse under cold water to separate the strands, then drain them well again afterwards. Traditionally, soba are served on a flat bamboo straining mat called a zaru, but as long as you toss them well, a less picturesque plate or bowl is fine.
The sauce
The proper way to eat zaru soba, according to Maehashi, is to “pick up a few strands of noodles and dip only the bottom half of them into the dipping sauce by simply lowering the chopsticks. Many people drop all the noodles they just picked up into the dipping sauce,” she adds, “but this is not a real gourmet way of eating buckwheat noodles. By dipping only part of the soba noodles in, you can taste the flavour of the noodles and enjoy it better.” So that’s you told.
As only a little of the accompanying mentsuyu sauce gilds each helping of noodles, it has to be intense in flavour, hence the principal ingredients: salty soy sauce, mirin (a sweet rice wine; alcohol-free alternatives are available), umami-rich seaweed and dried, smoked tuna flakes. Maehashi points out that you can substitute ready-made dashi stock, easily found in any Japanese specialist store, for the kombu and katsuobushi element of things; indeed, you can even buy mentsuyu in bottles, if you prefer, but it’s so easy to make that it won’t save you much time.
Chen, and chef Aya Nishimura in her book, Japanese Food Made Easy, both add sake as well, which, though not mandatory, does give their sauces an interesting complexity that proves very popular with my testers (save yourself some money and go for a cooking sake, unless you’re planning to drink the rest of the bottle). We also enjoy the brown sugar that Nishimura and chef Maori Murota include, the latter in her book Tokyo Cult Recipes. Feel free to leave it out if you prefer; you can always stir some in at the end if you decide the sauce needs some sweetness. (Equally, Chen explains, if the sauce is too salty for your taste, you can dilute it with iced water.) Nishimura sticks in a couple of shiitake mushrooms too; I find them a bit overwhelming, but it does strike me that if you don’t eat fish, you might like to substitute these for the tuna flakes.
The only small faff with this recipe is thinking ahead to ensure the sauce is cold before you eat, which is why it’s worth making several batches of it in hot weather; once strained, it keeps well in the fridge. I’d recommend keeping the kombu and tuna in for a few hours, as Murota seems to suggest, to extract as much flavour as possible. And don’t discard them once you separate the two, either; they can be saved and used to make furikake rice seasoning.
Chef Masaki Sugisaki of Dinings SW3 in London, meanwhile, advises that, “once you have finished the noodles, heat the reserved noodle cooking water and add it to the dipping sauce. It is traditional to drink this as a soup, because the water contains nourishing minerals.”
The accompaniments
Zaru soba becomes nori soba with the addition of some shredded nori, those roasted laver seaweed sheets used to wrap some sushi rolls. This, along with fiery wasabi and spring onions, are the most common accompaniments in the recipes I try. Murota recommends daikon and garlic chive or the white part of a leek, rather than spring onions, and she and Nishimura include grated ginger too. All of these, along with the ground toasted sesame seeds that add an interesting additional texture to Nishimura’s dish, are possibilities. In fact, in the privacy of your own home, add whatever you want, but do bear in mind that the pleasure of this dish is its simplicity – silky noodles and salty broth – so try to avoid the temptation to load it up like a salad before you’ve even tried it.
Perfect zaru soba
Prep 10 min
 Cook 10 min
Infuse 30 min
Chill 2 hr+
Serves 2
2 x 75g bunches of soba noodles
  1 piece nori (optional)
2 spring onions, or garlic chive leaves
Wasabi, fresh or paste
For the sauce 
5cm x 5cm strip kombu
4 tbsp Japanese soy sauce
  4 tbsp mirin 
  2 tbsp sake (optional; if not using, add 2 tbsp extra water)
1 tsp brown sugar 
  5g katsuobushi (bonito) flakes
Put the kombu and 150ml cold water in a small saucepan and leave to sit for half an hour.
Add all the remaining sauce ingredients, bar the katsuobushi.
Slowly bring to a boil, then turn off the heat, add the katsuobushi, leave to cool, then chill for a few hours, and preferably overnight.
Bring a wide pan of unsalted water to a boil. Add the noodles and stir for a few seconds to ensure they don’t clump together.
Cook according to the packet instructions (usually about five minutes) until very slightly al dente.
Scoop the noodles into a sieve (save the cooking water) and rinse under cold water to cool completely, tossing them with your fingers to separate the strands. Shake the sieve a few times to remove as much water as possible.
Strain the sauce (you can save the kombu and katsuobushi to make furikake). Cut the nori into thin strips, finely chop the spring onion and grate the wasabi, if necessary.
Serve the sauce in individual bowls with the noodles (on bamboo mats, if you have them) and accompaniments on the side for dipping. Once the noodles are finished, add cooking water to the remaining sauce to taste, to make a broth, and drink.
- 
  Zaru soba: when did you discover this deliciously cooling noodle dish, where can you find the best, and what do you like to serve it with?

The African firms adopting Chinese AI as US-China rivalry intensifies
Lower costs, downloadable models and greater language flexibility are helping Chinese AI models gain ground across the continent
The United States may want the world to choose sides in the AI race with China, but in Africa, many businesses are pursuing a more pragmatic strategy: using Chinese models where they offer better value or flexibility, while keeping their options open.
For example, when African insurtech platform Curacel expanded the range of artificial intelligence (AI) models powering its internal infrastructure, it did not look only to Silicon Valley.
Henry Mascot, chief executive and co-founder of Curacel, said Chinese models delivered comparable results at lower cost on high-volume tasks such as coding, data extraction, classification and customer support, although Western systems remained stronger on the most demanding reasoning and reliability-sensitive work.
“In our experience, the leading Chinese models have closed much of the performance gap,” Mascot said.
He said Curacel’s multi-model set-up allowed it to use GLM-5.3 selectively.
“We can route suitable workloads to it based on quality and cost without moving the entire stack or locking ourselves into one vendor,” Mascot said. “We have also used lower-cost [Chinese] models within client deployments.”

Psychological models suggest female libido disparities stem from early behavioral conditioning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:02 UTC
21:00:02 KST

We are in the midst of a sex recession. Young people today are having half as much sex as previous generations did, roughly the same amount as seniors.
Solutions to this decline tend to place the burden on women. Go online and you’ll find endless advice urging women to get their sex drive back. Self-help books, herbal supplements and pharmaceutical ads promise to reignite female libido, as if women’s desire is something that mysteriously breaks and needs to be repaired.
For decades, women’s lower sexual desire has been treated as biological fact — the product of evolution or hormonal destiny.
But the experiences that shape desire tell a different story: The libido gap begins long before adulthood, in the earliest experiences that teach young women what sex is like and who is entitled to enjoy it.
Early experiences of sex
Adolescence is a window of opportunity for learning how to have healthy, enjoyable sex. The adolescent brain is especially attuned to reward and peer social connection, so early experiences with closeness, communication and pleasure can leave lasting marks.
And yet it is during this window — when interest in sex comes online and the brain is primed to learn from experience — that most young women get the worst sex of their lives.
Across studies in North America and Europe, adolescent girls’ first sexual encounters, especially with boys, are more painful, less pleasurable and more ambivalent than boys’ first experiences. Fewer than one in 10 young women report orgasm during their first sexual experiences.
The “orgasm gap” at this milestone is rarely discussed and is roughly three times larger than the one that later makes headlines among adults.
These differences reflect the unequal conditions under which sexual learning unfolds. At precisely the developmental moment when experience teaches the body and mind what intimacy feels like, adolescent girls are most likely to learn that sex is something to endure rather than enjoy.
That learning accumulates over time.
Fixing the wrong problem
Adolescence is when desire itself is shaped, as the brain wires connections between pleasure and motivation. Unequal experiences during this period can have lasting effects on sexual comfort, confidence and interest. What begins as differences in experience can come to look like differences in biology.
But that can change when early experiences are more equal. When young people approach sex as mutual exploration and feel safe enough to express what feels good, the pleasure gap shrinks — and so does the desire gap.
Same-gender encounters, for instance, tend to involve more mutual stimulation and higher satisfaction for women, a reminder that what shapes sexual pleasure is not who one’s partner is, but whether pleasure is treated as mutual.
We continue, however, to focus on the symptoms of low desire instead of the the bigger picture. We treat women’s low sexual desire as a problem to be fixed. We prescribe pills, sell devices and urge women to change their mindset. These fixes that promise to help women reclaim their desire are trying to recover something that was never lost and override lessons learned when the brain was most sensitive to experience.
Desire is shaped by learning that sex can be safe, reciprocal and pleasurable — lessons not everyone has the privilege to learn.
Women’s pleasure has never been evenly valued, and it is especially overlooked when it comes to adolescent girls. From the start, they receive mixed messages about sex: be desirable but not desiring, participate but don’t ask for too much, endure discomfort quietly.
These early lessons matter.
These unequal experiences also teach boys what sex is supposed to be like. Many young men grow up learning that sex should be consensual but not necessarily mutual, often ending when the man “finishes.”
Desire was never lost
Is it any surprise, then, that half of adult women report ongoing difficulties with sexual desire?
Treating this as a personal or medical defect, however, misses the mark. Women don’t lose their desire for sex; they simply learn earlier in their lives whether sex is likely to be enjoyable and equitable. Their bodies and minds adapt wisely letting them know whether their pleasure will be prioritized, treated as secondary or ignored altogether.
This doesn’t mean women are doomed to low libido as adults. Desire continues to be shaped by experience throughout adulthood, although learning later in life often requires more conscious effort than the automatic imprinting that happens in adolescence.
Recognizing that desire was learned — not broken — can itself be freeing. But helping women adapt as adults sidesteps the real issue: women are taught as girls that their pleasure comes second.
And although we can’t change the past, we can still change the conditions under which sexual learning is happening now in relationships, in cultural messaging and in the spaces where young people learn about intimacy. If women want to desire sex and experience it as fulfilling, that is.

After 10 years at United, CEO Scott Kirby is thinking big about the future of his airline from JFK to AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

NEWARK, New Jersey — Scott Kirby says he doesn't believe in revenge.
"Everyone thinks I do, but no, I don't," said the United Airlines CEO, whom American Airlines fired 10 years ago, when he was president of that carrier. "I compete aggressively."
United announced it had hired him as president on Aug. 29, 2016, a blink after American disclosed his departure. Now, Kirby is running the second-most profitable U.S. airline after Delta Air Lines. And his former employer, American, is a distant third of the big, more-than-century-old, U.S. carriers, though it's working to ramp up revenue through a host of upgrades, including bringing back seatback screens.
Kirby floated the idea of megamergers with both Delta and American in the past year, combinations that would bring together some of the biggest airlines in the world. He's so far been rebuffed, and antitrust experts were skeptical about the possibility.
He's thinking bigger than he has before as the industry faces ever-higher costs, limited airport infrastructure and a population that's ready to shell out more to fly — often in the expensive seats — to the next "it" destination.
Eyeing JFK from EWR
CNBC rode with Kirby from the west side of Midtown Manhattan to United's hub at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey earlier this month, where the 59-year-old executive outlined his vision for the carrier before his flight.
Kirby said he wants to expand United's footprint at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport after his airline returns to the congested airport through a partnership with American's former partner, JetBlue Airways, as early as next year.
"We got a bunch of irons in the fire to try to find ways to do it," he said, adding that United could at some point acquire slots from carriers that aren't flying profitable routes out of the airport.
And while United already holds the crown among U.S. airlines for international flights, which are in high demand among U.S. tourists, he wants to expand the carrier's footprint abroad even more. This week, United is set to announce a host of new international routes, the carrier's annual splash that has previously included new dots on the map like Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia and Bilbao, Spain.
United has been touting its international expansion for years, saying its vast network acts as a driver for customer loyalty and sign-ups for lucrative travel rewards credit cards. Its route announcements typically come with much fanfare.
Kirby, a three-decade airline executive, is the United States' most outspoken airline CEO. His team knows this, and they've stopped telling him well in advance what will be on tap for the next batch of Instagram-friendly routes.
"They no longer tell me in advance because they're afraid I'll spill the beans, which is fair," he said.
While Delta has still had a lead on profits, CEO Ed Bastian doesn't want to give up ground to United. It is starting to expand flights over the Pacific, a United stronghold.
"People say, 'Well, when is it someone else's turn?' Well, I'm never going to let that be someone else's turn. It's always our turn," Bastian told students at Columbia Business School in April 2024. "We always get a chance to prove it every single day. ... Yesterday really doesn't matter. It's only today and tomorrow that you can think about."
1 minute break
It's been a decade since Kirby started at United. He joined the airline in August 2016 after he was let go by American when he was president and didn't have a path to eventually becoming CEO.
United dropped a securities filing just after American disclosed Kirby's departure, saying he would be taking the president role at the Chicago airline. American promoted then-Chief Operating Officer Robert Isom to president that day, Kirby's old role. Isom was named American's next CEO in late 2021.
"I joke that most people take a few weeks, a couple months between jobs. I took 60 seconds," Kirby said.
United promoted Kirby to CEO from president in May 2020, while the industry was reeling from Covid, its worst-ever crisis.
The executive ranks at the tops of United and American trace their roots back to America West and other airlines, before a wave of mergers over the past two decades left four carriers holding more than three-quarters of U.S. flight capacity.
"One of the things also I learned at American: There's only so much change you can make as the No. 2," he said. "You can push too hard and you get fired."
United was in the midst of upgrading its cabins when Kirby joined in 2016, including with its highest-end Polaris pod seats for long-haul business class. But he said his first order of business was going through money-losing routes with a highlighter to figure out what was working and what wasn't.
The company considered closing its bases at Los Angeles International Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport in Virginia. Kirby said he stopped that idea, and both stayed open.
The airports are critical for United. LAX is one of the airline's most important hubs, though no carrier has a handle on that airport like they do others. And Kirby took a day trip from his son's soccer camp in Brazil last month to fly up to meet with President Donald Trump to unveil a $22.5 billion revamp of Dulles in the Oval Office.
AI, mergers and the future of travel
Stock analysts and legal experts were highly skeptical about a merger between United and one of the other U.S. giants.
People familiar with the matter said Kirby approached Delta but was turned down, as The Wall Street Journal first reported last month. The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the talks. Delta declined to comment. The carrier's president, Peter Carter, told CNBC at an industry conference in June that he doesn't see a merger or acquisition in Delta's future.
American, meanwhile, publicly rejected a merger offer from United this spring.
"At the end of the day, we spend time looking at things that have a chance of happening. We don't spend a lot of time pursuing impossibilities," Isom told CNBC in an interview in late June.
Kirby told CNBC that he hasn't changed his stance and he's not interested in acquiring a smaller airline, like JetBlue. "That's still the case," he said.
"Everything I say would require a willing partner," Kirby said.
When asked about antitrust concerns and likely pushback from state attorneys general, he said, "All of the objections are ... based on a premise that the airline industry is a commodity."
And Kirby said the industry has since evolved and that Delta and United have differentiated themselves, with their routes, onboard cabins and other products.
He said he wants United to grow in South America and in the Southeast U.S., but there's a lack of places to build out new hubs that make sense.
"Those are two places that are holes for United that are hard to fix on a stand-alone basis," Kirby said.
The best place for serving South America is Miami International Airport, he added. American had a more than 60% share of passenger enplanements in the 2025 fiscal year, according to airport data.
Putting mergers aside, Kirby said artificial intelligence tools for both employees and customers will make traveling easier and improve reliability, a tall order for any airline that is susceptible to weather, constrained airports and a host of other daily surprises from mechanical problems.
He wants delays expressed in clear English to customers.
"I firmly believe in no excuses, and so we don't make excuses," he said.
Even still, in the first half of the year, United ranked behind Delta and Alaska Airlines, which recently merged with Hawaiian Airlines, for on-time arrivals, according to the Transportation Department.
Kirby said outside factors or outright crises will always challenge the industry and said he is focused on the long-term future of the airline.
"Our employees often ask me like, 'What keeps you awake at night,' and I tell them, 'nothing,'" he said. "My job is to set the company up so none of you ever have to have a sleepless night worrying about your jobs."
He said his goal is to never have another furlough at the airline.
When asked if he would retire eventually, Kirby said, "I hope I will know when to retire and do it gracefully with a great transition with great people."

United's next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

In August 2018, the then-president and now CEO of United Airlines Scott Kirby told a room of reporters at an aviation conference in Denver about the airline's big plans for the new Boeing 737 Max 10: lie-flat, premium seats and a host of profitable, transcontinental routes.
The plane was supposed to start flying in 2020.
Hundreds of those seats have been in storage because its certification — which was expected more than six years ago — is far behind schedule. Now, Boeing and many of its customers expect the company to win federal approval for the plane, the largest in the bestselling 737 Max family, soon, so United has to decide what to do with all those seats.
"We got a bunch of lie-flat seats that we don't know what to do with," Kirby told CNBC during an interview earlier this month at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey. "They don't fit on other airplanes."
United hasn't disclosed the layout it will use on the planes, or where it will fly them. The airline set its earlier plans for the Boeing 737 Max 10 before it even offered a premium economy section.
The delays for both the newly approved Boeing 737 Max 7, the smallest model, and the yet-to-be-certified Max 10 came after the manufacturer had to redesign an anti-icing system. Boeing was also dealing with increased scrutiny after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing won approval for the 737 Max 7 earlier this month, with big customer Southwest Airlines expecting to fly them sometime in the first half of 2027.
United pivoted because of the Boeing delays and recently outfitted a subfleet of its Airbus A321neo narrow-body aircraft with 20 of the newly designed Polaris suites, premium economy options and other new seats as part of the industry's race to add high-yielding seating on its planes. It's dubbed the subfleet the "Coastliner" for transcontinental routes.
But the dimensions and requirements aren't the same on both planes, leaving United with a decision on what its interiors will look like.
It expects to get the first Boeing Max 10s in summer 2027. It has 167 of the aircraft on order, according to its most recent quarterly filing.

“As for production localization, the major companies that are ready to supply us with aircraft are ready to localize production in Ukraine. They are ready to help us, but, as you understand, this can only be done under appropriate security conditions,” he said.

From Middle East to e-sports: Macron hosts Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:55:20 UTC
20:55:20 KST

Long ostracised on the international stage after the murder of Saudi journalist and dissident Jamal Khashoggi, "MBS" has in recent years regained status as a valued strategic partner.
French president Emmanuel Macron is on Sunday hosting Saudi Arabia's crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, for a two-day visit whose agenda ranges from e-sports to the war in the Middle East.
Several agreements covering health, transport and energy are to be signed on Monday, the second day of the visit, according to an official at the French presidency, underscoring the strength of relations between Paris and Riyadh. The leaders are expected to address the "major economic and strategic issues that underpin the Franco-Saudi partnership", the Élysée said, notably in energy, aerospace and defence.
According to the Élysée, the visit "reflects the vitality of the dialogue between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and France, and will help to strengthen the strategic partnership that binds our two countries. To that end, the President of the Republic and the crown prince will for the first time hold a meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council".
The visit will, however, get under way on a different note on Sunday evening: Emmanuel Macron will receive Saudi Arabia's strongman - known as MBS from his initials - at the closing ceremony of the e-sports World Cup being held in Paris.
Still according to the presidency, "Organised for the first time outside Saudi Arabia since it was created, the staging of this global championship in Paris testifies to France's renewed appeal as a host for major international sporting events" and "also illustrates the shared ambition of France and Saudi Arabia to make sport and culture drivers of their rapprochement".
The event, which brings together the elite of e-sports - from video games to chess - and enjoys MBS's active backing, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time.
The Élysée official declined to say whether the agreements might cover the large "Dragon Ball" theme-park project, backed by a Saudi fund and under consideration in Val-d'Oise, in the Paris region.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host a series of major global events, including the World Expo in 2030 and, above all, the 2034 football World Cup.
Will human rights be on the agenda?
Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States and historically at odds with Iran, is also closely following developments within the Islamic Republic in the wake of the US-Israeli conflict.
On Monday afternoon, MBS and Emmanuel Macron will chair the first meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council.
The two leaders "will exchange views on the main regional issues, in a context that calls for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners in favour of stability and peace in the Near and Middle East", to quote once again the Élysée's wording.
It remains to be seen whether human rights will feature prominently on the agenda, some eight years after the murder and dismemberment of Saudi dissident journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018.
A United Nations investigation described Jamal Khashoggi's death as an "extrajudicial execution for which Saudi Arabia is responsible". US intelligence services concluded that MBS had "approved" the operation that led to Khashoggi's killing. Riyadh denies these accusations, blaming them on agents who acted on their own initiative.
In December 2021, Emmanuel Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet MBS in Saudi Arabia after Khashoggi's killing. In July 2022 it was bin Salman who came to Paris - and that visit sparked fierce criticism on the left, Le Parisien (source in French) reported at the time. "On the dinner menu between Emmanuel Macron and 'MBS', the dismembered body of journalist [Jamal] Khashoggi ? (…) No ! Oil and arms !", the Green politician Yannick Jadot protested at the time. Julien Bayou, then national secretary of Europe Écologie-Les Verts, said in turn that "France is not a doormat for dictators in search of rehabilitation on the international stage".
Since then, the Saudi crown prince has made several trips to France: Saudi Arabia is too important economically and regionally for France to allow the relationship to deteriorate for long.
Ultimately, the oil factor - Riyadh is the world's leading crude exporter - especially against the backdrop of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Europe's determination to wean itself off Kremlin fuels, has only served to seal this return to favour.

Pete Buttigieg returns to South Carolina as he weighs another White House run
ORANGEBURG, S.C. (AP) — The last time Pete Buttigieg was giving a political speech in South Carolina, it was to mark a distant finish in the state’s primary that effectively ended his campaign for president.
Returning this weekend as he mulls a second run for the White House, Buttigieg set out to reintroduce himself to the state and the Black voters he struggled to win in 2020. The results were encouraging.
There was a standing ovation in a Black church in South Carolina when Buttigieg was credited for helping bring millions of federal dollars to the area for a project as President Joe Biden’s transportation secretary. A second ovation came as Buttigieg gave a speech warning of a country in “big trouble” while laying out his own vision for what should come next.
“There is no such thing as again in real life. The only way out is through,” Buttigieg told the crowd of more than 200 people at an NAACP Freedom Fund Dinner. “If we recognize and embrace a future that is different from the past, we will do better.”
The warm applause was a markedly different reception than six years ago, when a fourth-place showing in South Carolina helped derail Buttigieg’s presidential campaign while exposing his failure to connect with Black voters. The state is likely to have an even greater say in his political future as the first contest in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028.
Starting the election calendar in South Carolina is intended in part to give Black voters a greater voice at the outset of the nominating process. For Buttigieg and other potential contenders, winning the support of this group that makes up a majority of South Carolina’s Democratic electorate is essential.
“You need to demonstrate that you can win Black voters,” said Jaime Harrison, a former Democratic National Committee chair and South Carolina Democratic Party chairman. “If you can’t win Black voters, you can’t be the nominee of our party.”
The 2028 campaign is already coming to South Carolina
Buttigieg insists he has made no final decision about whether to run for president again.
“Right now, I’m totally focused on 2026,” he told reporters Saturday.
But his South Carolina trip — a week after visiting another early-voting state, Nevada — had all the trappings of a potential presidential bid.
He raised money Friday in Charleston with Nancy Lacore, a U.S. House candidate trying to flip a Republican-held seat. On Saturday morning, he spoke at a policy conference before traveling to Claflin University, a historically Black university in Orangeburg.
Davina Perry, a third-year student at Claflin, said she came away from Buttigieg’s visit thinking he would be a “good candidate” if he ran.
“Secretary Pete has definitely put himself on my radar for 2028 now, for sure,” Perry said. But, she added, “I do want to see more representation from people who look like me.”
That evening, Buttigieg attended a dinner at a church in Orangeburg, a nearly three-quarters Black city with a deep history in the Civil Rights Movement. The crowd included local NAACP leaders, ministers and elected officials. Buttigieg worked the room, giving hugs and taking photos.
“He is responsible for the Railroad Corner,” said Orangeburg Mayor Michael Butler, referencing a project aimed at revitalizing the city’s downtown that received a $22.7 million federal grant. “Do I need to say any more? We need to stand and welcome the former secretary.”
Buttigieg used the speech that followed to make a broader case about the direction of the country, arguing that Democrats cannot separate Americans’ economic frustrations from a political system he described as increasingly broken.
“I have come to believe that the kitchen table cannot be improved unless we are also reforming the institutional and political floor on which that kitchen table sits.”
Black voters will have the first say for Democrats in 2028
For Buttigieg, the weekend offered signs of how much has changed since he came to South Carolina in 2020 as a 38-year-old Indiana mayor asking voters to take a chance on him. He points to what he delivered during four years in Biden’s Cabinet, including specific projects in the state.
But Buttigieg said he also came to South Carolina “to propose something” about the country’s future. Butler, Orangeburg’s mayor, liked what he heard.
“His speech was what you talk about at the kitchen table. How America is going to survive all of this?” Butler said. “He brought hope to us.”
South Carolina Democratic leaders say the close, personal engagement with candidates is exactly what they hoped for. Those involved in the push to make South Carolina first envisioned the living-room conversations and retail politics long associated with Iowa and New Hampshire.
“You got to go listen. You got to go all over the place,” Harrison said. “You have to make meaningful investments. That’s how you win South Carolina.”
Buttigieg is hardly alone in his early trip to the state.
Other potential 2028 contenders, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California and U.S. Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey have made trips to the state as what is expected to be a large Democratic field begins to take shape. Former Vice President Kamala Harris already has deep ties in the state.
The electorate they will encounter has changed from 2020, when Biden’s victory in the state resurrected his presidential campaign and put him on a path to ousting Republican President Donald Trump.
Four years later, Trump defeated Harris and returned to the White House, which Black leaders say has significantly hurt their community. Earlier this year, a Supreme Court decision weakened a core provision of the Voting Rights Act, threatening Black political representation across the South.
“We must start our process where democracy must still be fought for, in the full view of the nation,” former interim DNC chair Donna Brazile said in a speech this year advocating for South Carolina to go first.
Buttigieg addressed that anxiety directly Saturday night, describing efforts to weaken the Voting Rights Act as the culmination of a “multidecade effort.” He warned of a broader push “to demolish African American political power.”
Harrison said Buttigieg’s trip this weekend was a “good start,” but that Buttigieg and all the other potential 2028 candidates have a long road ahead to prove themselves to the state’s voters.
“It has to be a good start and then you got to continue,” Harrison said. “It can’t just be, ‘Oh, pop in and then I’m going to pop back out.’”

Powerful storm hits Baltic countries, killing 2 and leaving hundreds of thousands without power

Powerful storm hits Baltic countries, killing 2 and leaving hundreds of thousands without power
WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Two people died and around half a million people were left without electricity across Latvia and Lithuania after a powerful cyclone, bringing rain and strong winds, hit the region on Saturday and into Sunday morning.
“This seems to be the most severe storm in Latvia since 2005 in terms of its overall impact,” Andris Viksna, from the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Center, told the AP.
One person died in Jelgava, central Latvia, when part of a building collapsed on Saturday, and others were injured across the country. Wind speed exceeded 67 mph on Saturday in the capital, Riga. At many stations, half of the average monthly rainfall was recorded on Saturday.
More than a quarter-million people were left without electricity and mobile services were disrupted.
Rail and other public transport services were affected by trees and other objects falling on infrastructure. The Riga airport said on Sunday morning that flights could be delayed or rerouted because of the severe storm overnight.
One person also died in neighboring Lithuania after being hit by a falling tree. Others were injured and over 200,000 residents were without electricity on Sunday morning.
Strong winds also battered Estonia, with the western and northern parts and its islands most affected. Ferry services to islands were disrupted and trains arriving from Latvia and Lithuania delayed.
Northeastern Poland was affected by the storm, too, with over 100,000 people losing power.
The contribution of climate change cannot be properly assessed yet, said Viksna from the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Center, but “it is plausible that human-caused climate change may have intensified the rainfall associated with the cyclone.”
The situation was expected to improve on Sunday and certainly by Monday.

Odesa Takes Center Stage in Fiction Abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:51:00 UTC
20:51:00 KST

Odesa has confirmed its status as the Ukrainian city that inspires the greatest number of novels and thrillers in foreign literature, particularly in English and Italian. The city provides an ideal setting for both espionage stories, thanks to memories of the Cold War, and crime fiction, given its long-established reputation as the capital of the Ukrainian mafia – although it would be more accurate to describe it as a city where several criminal gangs operate.
Even when a plot has nothing to do with crime or espionage, simply including the name Odesa in the title can make a book more appealing. One example is Frederick Forsyth’s bestselling The Odessa File, which has no connection whatsoever with the Ukrainian city.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Here are the most recent titles published outside Ukraine.
Frederick Forsyth and Tony Kent
This is the sequel to the famous 1972 bestselling thriller The Odessa File. Once again, “Odessa” is an acronym for a clandestine neo-Nazi organization and does not refer to the city.
Fifty years after uncovering the secrets of Odessa – the underground organization of former Nazis that sought to regain power – the now elderly and retired journalist Peter Miller suspects that someone on his long list of enemies may be behind the deaths of his son and daughter-in-law in a tragic car accident.
By 2025, Odessa has been replaced by Medusa, which has attained a degree of covert power greater than anything Odessa ever possessed. The rise of the far right in German politics, the surge in violence and terrorism against Germany’s immigrant population, and the angry response of its citizens are all symptoms of a hidden danger, deliberately created by someone who must be stopped at all costs. Odessa’s heirs are playing for the ultimate prize: control of the White House.
Russia Strikes Ukraine-Moldova Border Crossing for Second Night in a Row
                                                                                                                                                                         
Leonardo Gori
This is the latest Italian novel in the series featuring Carabinieri Captain Bruno Arcieri, set in Italy during the Fascist period and extending into the post-war years. It is a spy story set in Odesa after the Second World War, during the Cold War.
In the spring of 1948, Colonel Bruno Arcieri, an officer in the Italian intelligence services, is assigned a particularly dangerous mission. He must be parachuted beyond the Iron Curtain, near a city in Eastern Europe, to track down an undercover agent possessing important information about the Soviet Union.
In 1948, the city that Mussolini called “Stalingrad by the sea” becomes a Cold War battleground. The war has been over for three years, Odesa is a Soviet city and Stalin is in power. The city is an important Black Sea trading hub for the transport of grain and for Jewish emigration to Israel – the State of Israel was established that very year. Furthermore, the Black Sea marks the frontier between NATO and the USSR, while Odesa serves as a naval base for the Soviet fleet.
The setting bears similarities to the present day: the figures in power have changed, with Putin replacing Stalin, but the locations featured in the novel recall those of the war in Ukraine.
The story is rich in evocative settings, from Istanbul at sunset to the yellow hues of sunflowers in the Ukrainian countryside – an image that calls to mind Van Gogh’s famous Sunflowers paintings and the popular 1970 film Sunflower, starring Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Julian Evans
An elegant love letter to the Ukrainian port by an author who lived in the city and traces its transformation from an exotic haunt of criminal gangs into a symbol of freedom, now under attack amid the violence of Russia’s war.
Julian Evans explores Odesa’s rich heritage, its multi-ethnic soul and its new Ukrainian identity. He transports us in imagination to the shores of the Black Sea and to Odesa, one of Eastern Europe’s most beautiful cities – a place of multiple identities that refuses to be confined to any single definition. It is Italian, French, Jewish, Greek, Moldovan, German, Ukrainian, Crimean Tatar and much more besides.
Both the Russian and Soviet empires attempted to flatten this diversity into a single imperial identity. They failed. Today, in an act of retaliation, Russia is attempting to destroy Odesa, launching missiles and drones at its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Yet Odesa is also searching for a new identity. This remains a work in progress and is not yet entirely complete, making the city extraordinarily vibrant and, in many respects, still misunderstood by foreigners and Ukrainians alike.
Gabrielle Sher
Gabrielle Sher’s book is a historical horror novel following a Jewish family living in a shtetl in Odesa, the port city that was then part of the Russian Empire and is now in Ukraine. It is an original blend of Jewish folk tales and folk horror, featuring numerous references to the Kabbalah, golems and dybbuks, all set against a historical background.
In an imagined Russia during the era of the pogroms, a grief-stricken family turns to ancient magic to bring their bright and spirited teenage daughter, Yetta, back to life. Fear has engulfed their shtetl. Jewish people are mysteriously disappearing, and everyone is expecting an imminent attack. When violence descends upon them, Yetta is killed.
Overcome with grief, her father Mordechai draws upon his still-limited knowledge of ancient texts and ancestral magic to restore her to life. Miraculously, Yetta returns – but although she looks the same, she is no longer the girl she once was. She senses that her family is hiding a horrible secret from her. It is a story of familial love set against a climate of looming violence and systemic oppression.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Marco Cardetta
Odesa, Ukraine: a city belonging to everyone and no one; mother of geniuses, poets, refugees, convicts, revolutionaries, exiles, prostitutes, mystics and musicians. A city built, destroyed and rebuilt over the centuries by Italians, Greeks, French, Germans, Jews, Tatars, Circassians, Georgians, Poles, Romanians, Moldovans, Albanians, Armenians, Azerbaijanis, Bulgarians, Russians, Ukrainians and Roma.
Italian writer Marco Cardetta’s book is a poem in 22 cantos that, through the voices of numerous original characters, form a fully fledged novel in verse. It creates a visionary portrait of the encounter between the self and the world, between the West and its forgotten margins, and between memory and oblivion. Odesa is not a city to be described: it is a place of the mind.
The author’s language is a deliberate and highly original blend of archaisms, Russianisms, Ukrainianisms, Yiddish and Ancient Greek – a polyphony reflecting the very nature of Odesa. The style moves between ballad, fable and dramatic monologue.
Conceived and written before 2022, the work has nothing to do with the Russo-Ukrainian War. It is a portrait by someone who had already imagined Odesa as a universal archetype, long before the world turned it into a symbol of war.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Michael P. Kleiman
A detective story that leads to Odesa. Jean Paul “JP” Beauregard, a detective with the New Orleans Police Department, sees his world collapse when his wife, Yvette, is brutally murdered during a war between criminal gangs. When the conventional justice system becomes mired in bureaucracy, JP decides to retire and search on his own for the man who ordered his wife’s murder: Alexey Krutikov, the kingpin of Brooklyn’s ruthless Bandera crime syndicate.
JP crosses the Atlantic to infiltrate Odesa’s underworld in the midst of the war in Ukraine. Posing as an independent operative, he enters a shadowy world of deep-rooted corruption, maritime terminals after dark and dangerous criminal groups.
It is a gripping account of one man’s relentless quest for revenge, unfolding from the sweltering, jazz-filled streets of New Orleans’ French Quarter to the mysterious streets of Odesa.

Antarctic ice sheet sees temporary mass gain: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:50:22 CST
20:50:22 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- A new international study shows that Antarctica's ice sheet gained 695 billion metric tonnes of mass between 2021 and 2023, slowing down its long-term ice loss against the backdrop of climate warming.
Researchers from China, the United States, Hungary and Japan found that the ice gain was the largest recorded in nearly two decades of satellite observations. They believe an atmospheric phenomenon thousands of kilometers away drove the gain, with warm tropical oceans promoting heavy snowfall on the world's southernmost continent and counterbalancing ice lost to melting.
The Antarctic ice sheet is one of the main sources of uncertainty for global sea level rise. Between 2003 and 2024, the continent lost about 140.5 billion metric tonnes of ice per year on average.
First author Wang Yunhe, an associate researcher at the Institute of Oceanology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the unusual ice gain was driven by warming in the tropical western Pacific Warm Pool, one of the world's warmest ocean regions and one of the strongest sources of heat release to the atmosphere. From 2021 to 2023, sea temperatures in the region warmed unusually and persistently, ultimately reshaping atmospheric circulation.
"Water vapor from the mid-latitude Indian Ocean was transported to East Antarctica, bringing heavy snowfall there and causing the ice sheet mass to increase," Wang said.
However, the study, published in the journal Nature, noted that similar warming events occur roughly once a decade, suggesting the ice gain is temporary and cannot reverse the long-term trend of ice loss.
West Antarctica continues to lose ice, and ocean warming threatens some outlet glaciers in East Antarctica by melting ice shelves from beneath and accelerating ice flow, Wang added.
In a companion commentary also published in Nature, Jonathan Wille, a researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research, wrote that researchers must account for tropical climate variability to understand Antarctica's future and that of the rest of the planet. ■

Can Iran retaliate against countries that join US ‘economic war’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:50:22 UTC
20:50:22 KST

Can Iran retaliate against countries that join US ‘economic war’?
Iran warns that countries backing US economic sanctions will be considered an enemy of Tehran.
Iran has threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the United States’ “economic war” against it, as diplomatic efforts to end the months-long war have stalled and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has drastically decreased.
The warning from Iran’s top security official on Saturday came as the US plans to announce new sanctions on Monday that could further strain the struggling Iranian economy.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iranian president says time to end war with US from ‘position of strength’
- list 2 of 3Iran says new US sanctions violate sovereignty of other states
- list 3 of 3What did war with the US reveal about Iran’s weapons capabilities?
So, how can Tehran retaliate?
Here’s what we know:
What has Iran said?
On Saturday, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the IRIB state broadcaster that Iran was appealing to all countries around the world, including its neighbours, not to join the US’s “economic war”.
“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said, warning of “seismic” retaliation.
Rezaei also warned Iran’s neighbours that if they participated in Trump’s economic warfare, “not even a drop of oil” would leave the Gulf region, including by alternative export routes away from the Hormuz chokepoint through which a fifth of global oil and gas exports pass in peacetime.
Iran has attacked US military installations and civilian locations since the war began on February 28 , on the pretext that Tehran was on the verge of having nuclear bombs. That claim was debunked by the US intelligence agency, as well as the UN’s IAEA nuclear watchdog.
The US operates military facilities in more than a dozen locations across the Middle East and North Africa, including in Gulf nations, such as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Thousands of US soldiers are also stationed across the region, including in Jordan.
Rezaei’s remarks came days after US President Donald Trump announced that his government would undertake the “most crushing economic operation” yet against Iran. He also pledged “tremendous economic consequences” for any country that gives Iran “any type of lifeline”.
The US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, echoed his threats the following day, saying, “You’re either with us or against us”. He also urged cooperation from China, which buys more than 80 percent of Iran’s oil shipments.
On Sunday, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said: Iran is “in a full-scale economic, military and security war” with the US. He said Washington falsely predicted before the war that it would fall amid US aggression and become like Venezuela.
“The enemy had assessed that if Iran falls, it will become Venezuela,” he said in a televised speech.
“Not only did it not happen, but it became a power that amazed the world with its resistance, solidarity and cohesion.”
How can Iran retaliate?
Rezaei described Iran’s strategy as a three-stage sequence, starting with talks with countries cooperating with the US to de-escalate tensions.
“Of course, we will first negotiate with them. We will hold talks and tell them to step aside and distance themselves from the United States.”
“But if they do not act, we will strike. We will target that country’s interests,” he added.
Rezaei’s warning that alternative export routes outside Hormuz could be targeted, probably points to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait gateway to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has used it to export its oil following the blockade of Hormuz. Tehran imposed a blockade on Hormuz in response to the US war and has since used it as leverage in negotiations with Washington to end the war. The US has put Iranian ports under a naval blockade, impacting Tehran’s international trade.
Hamidreza Azizi, a researcher on Iran at the Clingendael Institute, said in a post on X on Saturday: “Tehran appears to be trying to establish deterrence at an earlier stage, by signalling that even preparations for an attack could trigger an Iranian response.”
Azizi said two elements in the new “offensive doctrine” are emerging: preemption, which is aimed at preventing a perceived threat from materialising; and disproportionate retaliation, which is aimed at raising the cost of any attack that does occur.
Iran’s warning to Gulf states joining Trump’s economic war is “essentially an ultimatum” to the Gulf states, he said, adding that Iran’s military-security establishment “is increasingly preparing for another round of escalation”.
Will Iran’s neighbours join the US in its economic warfare?
Gulf countries, which are Iran’s neighbours and also US allies, have increasingly been finding themselves caught in the middle of the war. So it is unclear if they will join Washington in economically threatening Iran further.
Iran’s attacks on Gulf nations have impacted their economies, which use Hormuz for most of their exports, including oil and gas.
While Gulf nations have condemned Iranian attacks on their territories, analysts say Gulf states closely aligned with Washington recognise that a functioning political relationship with Iran is necessary due to its close proximity.
The UAE restored diplomatic relations with Iran in 2022 but imposed a trade embargo last week after accusing Tehran of a missile attack. Iran denies responsibility.
Saudi Arabia and Iran agreed to normalise ties in 2023 under a deal brokered by China, both likely a calculation that engagement with Iran was safer than permanent confrontation.
While the Iranian attacks on Gulf states have tested this idea, they have not necessarily shattered it.
“Ultimately, Gulf countries can’t change geography. They have to live and work alongside Iran,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University told Al Jazeera in an interview last month. “They don’t want the instability that would come from the fall of the Islamic Republic. I think some Gulf states have pushed for harder strikes – not to precipitate its collapse, but to weaken the more hardline elements of the IRGC.”
Also last month, Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Al Jazeera that confidence in diplomacy to end the crisis remains low but, at the same time, no nation in the region “can afford another long war”.
As a result, that “will keep them away from a completely uncontrolled level of escalation”, and depleted global oil inventories will make a prolonged confrontation between the US and Iran unattractive.
“All inventories have not been able to be replenished” during the ceasefire, Parsi added. “We are at a much lower level globally.”
What we know about international sanctions against Iran over previous decades?
Since 1979, Iran has faced sanctions from the US and other nations in the West. The United Nations has also imposed sanctions on Tehran.
The US first imposed sanctions after the 1979 Islamic Revolution that toppled the pro-Western ruler Reza Shah Pahlavi. Washington said that was in response to Iranian students taking Americans hostage at the US embassy in Tehran.
Washington also halted oil imports from Iran and froze $12bn in Iranian assets following the revolution. Iranian products were banned from import into the US, apart from small gifts, informational material, foodstuffs and some carpets.
In 1995, President Bill Clinton issued executive orders preventing US companies from investing in Iranian oil and gas and trading with Iran. He banned US trade with Iran and investment. A year later, the US Congress passed a law requiring the US government to impose sanctions on foreign firms investing more than $20m a year in Iran’s energy sector.
Then in December 2006, the United Nations Security Council, whose members include China, Russia, the UK and France, imposed sanctions on Iran’s trade in nuclear-energy-related materials and technology and froze the assets of individuals and companies involved in related activities.
The sanctions were mainly an effort to curtail Iran’s growing nuclear capacity, but while programmes to enrich uranium were stopped in 2002, they restarted in late 2005. In subsequent years, the UN toughened the sanctions and imposed more. The European Union also followed suit.
In 2015, Iran signed a nuclear deal – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) – with the US, EU, China, France, Germany, Russia and the United Kingdom. The deal put a cap on Iran’s nuclear programme in return for the complete lifting of sanctions.
However, in 2018, during his first term, Trump announced the US withdrawal from the nuclear treaty and reimposed all sanctions on Iran that were lifted under the treaty as part of his “maximum pressure” campaign against Tehran.
In 2019, the Trump administration designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) a ‘Foreign Terrorist Organisation’. Additionally, he imposed sanctions targeting petrochemicals, metals (steel, aluminium, copper) and senior Iranian officials.
During Trump’s first term, Qassem Soleimani, the head of the IRGC’s elite Quds Force, was assassinated in a drone strike in Baghdad in 2020. The US also imposed additional sanctions on Iran.
The Biden administration, in power from 2021 to 2025, kept in place most US sanctions.
Last September, UN sanctions were reimposed due to Iran’s nuclear programme when the UNSC voted against permanently lifting economic sanctions.

On the edge of the Gobi Desert lies Dunhuang, an ancient oasis city that once stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road. Here, the Mogao Grottoes preserve one of the world's greatest collections of Buddhist art, including exquisite centuries-old murals and sculptures.

By combining traditional craftsmanship with modern technology, they are helping this thousand-year-old legacy endure for generations to come.

Feature: Four decades on, Baidui Cup continues to fuel Beijing's youth football
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:50:16 CST
20:50:16 KST

by sportswriter Li Chunyu
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Returning to the Baidui Cup for the first time as head coach of China's men's national football team, Shao Jiayi found the same passion and desire from young players as he had during his own childhood.
"I competed in the Baidui Cup decades ago, and much of my happiness at that time came from creating exciting moments with my teammates in summer," the 46-year-old said during this year's Baidui Cup, one of Beijing's biggest youth football tournaments.
This year marks the first time that the tournament has two separate groups - recreational and competitive.
The recreational group is open to young football enthusiasts, while the competitive group caters to club youth teams and youth training academies. According to organizers, more than 1,400 teams and over 15,000 players participated in the Baidui Cup this year.
"What touched me most was the fearlessness of the young players," Shao said. "Football demands and encourages physical contact. I saw these kids were willing to go into challenges. Our young talents are really brave and fully enjoy the stage to show themselves."
For Fu Ming, a Chinese referee who returned from FIFA World Cup duty last month, the Baidui Cup is a festival not only for children, but also for referees and officials.
Even with his busy schedule, Fu, 43, has long wanted to officiate the Baidui Cup, viewing it as a valuable opportunity to communicate with young referees and players.
"The World Cup and Baidui Cup differ a lot in intensity, but my attitude towards each game remains the same," Fu said. "My movement and decision-making on the pitch have become second nature. I naturally brought all my habits to the Baidui Cup. Young referees can observe how I position myself and move around the field."
In a competitive U15 match officiated by Fu, referee Chen Xueyang watched on from the sidelines.
"I graduated from Capital University of Physical Education and Sports where Fu instructed me at a football referee training camp," recalled Chen, 25. "After I became a referee, I sometimes sent him video clips of controversial or challenging calls for advice, and he would give me a call right away. He asked for my opinion first and then shared his own perspective."
"Fu gave me tremendous support. He sets an example for our young referees to learn from," Chen added.
Player Niu Yuhao spoke after his team won the match 2-0. "Fu is a world-class referee and controlled the game pace well," he said. "I have been playing football for eight years since primary school. I hope to enjoy football and build up my physical fitness."
After the final whistle, the young players took a group photo with Fu, who also gave many of them his autograph.
"Without joy, there will be no motivation," Fu said. "A football match serves as an excellent lesson for children, through which they can learn to win honorably and accept defeat gracefully. Even though they are opponents on the pitch, they should still help when others are in need."
While the inaugural Baidui Cup in 1984 attracted 112 teams, that number has expanded to over 1,000 in recent years.
"The large number of young football participants in Beijing lays a solid foundation for cultivating more talents in the future. Football fueled by passion will always accompany them on their journey of growth," said Hu Jianping, president of the Beijing Football Association. ■

Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:50:12 UTC
20:50:12 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.
The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time to a demand made by the sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.
“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.
Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.
That shifted when Fedorov, a popular minister who had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.
It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.
Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”
Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.
Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.
“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors in 2027--28.
The US could help by supplying “some small percentage” of its stockpiles – about 5% to 10%, he added. Ukraine was willing to pay and it would mean the country “could get through the winter”, he said, calling on the US to make what would be “a very significant difference both in protecting lives and diplomatically”.
Following a conversation with Zelenskyy on Saturday, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had agreed to strengthen French support for Ukraine, including through the delivery of interceptor missiles, without giving further details.
Ukraine’s allies in the so-called coalition of the willing – an initiative led by France and Britain – will meet on Monday to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.
Russia is seeking to build up forces for a renewed effort to capture the rest of the eastern Donetsk province it does not control by the end of the year, though Zelenskyy said he was confident Moscow would fail to capture the area, comprising principally the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The president said he believed Russia would try to conscript a further 300,000 soldiers after the Russian parliamentary elections in September. It would be a “peripheral mobilisation” conducted away from Moscow, St Petersburg and other main cities in an effort to regain momentum in the almost deadlocked frontline, he said.

The 24 solar terms, consisting of 12 major solar terms and 12 minor solar terms, were created thousands of years ago by the ancient Chinese to guide agricultural production.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:49:38 CST
20:49:38 KST

NAIROBI, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Four suspects have been arrested following the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem, and authorities are hunting for more suspects, a government official has said.
Rebecca Miano, cabinet secretary in the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife, said in a statement issued on Saturday that 15 of the deaths were recorded between June 24 and July 24, while three more were reported last week.
Miano said the ongoing investigations were yet to establish criminal culpability, adding that the government would allow the investigative and judicial processes to run their course and prosecute anyone found to have unlawfully killed, poisoned or harmed wildlife.
She said the Kenya Wildlife Service, in collaboration with security, investigative and scientific agencies, has intensified its inquiries into the cause of the deaths, noting that comprehensive field investigations, laboratory analysis and environmental sampling have already been undertaken.
According to Miano, preliminary laboratory results point to the probable involvement of a toxic substance, with earlier indications suggesting that cyanide poisoning may have resulted from the ingestion of pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from farms adjacent to wildlife habitats.
However, Miano noted that these findings remain subject to further scientific verification before the investigation is deemed complete.
The official emphasized that the government will enhance monitoring of risks arising from the misuse, illegal application, trafficking or careless handling of hazardous substances that may endanger wildlife, people and ecosystems. ■
