60 years ago NASA took the first ever photo of Earth from the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:11:39 UTC
20:11:39 KST

In April, as the intrepid crew of Artemis II shot around the moon, NASA astronaut Christina Koch snapped a photograph of the distant Earth setting behind the lunar surface. It was an image with a 60-year-old legacy—one that often has been eclipsed by another famous photograph.
Koch’s picture drew instant comparison to the latter iconic image, “Earthrise,” a photograph shot by NASA astronaut Bill Anders during the Apollo 8 mission in December 1968. Like Artemis II, the Apollo 8 spaceflight looped around the moon—a crucial step on the road to NASA’s 1969 moon landing. But in truth, Koch’s image had an even earlier inspiration.
August 23 marks the anniversary of the first time Earth was photographed from the vicinity of the moon. The picture was taken on that date in 1966 by NASA’s Lunar Orbiter 1, the first U.S. spacecraft to ever orbit the moon.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Launched on August 10, Lunar Orbiter 1 was tasked with taking close-up pictures of the moon, in particular, nine possible landing sites for the upcoming Apollo missions. Over several days, it took hundreds of pictures covering more than five million square kilometers (two million square miles) of the lunar surface. Among those photos was a grainy black-and-white shot: in the foreground, it showed the rough terrain of the moon, pockmarked by craters, while in the background, it captured a semicircle of Earth, stark white against the inky black backdrop of space.
Without Lunar Orbiter 1, Anders might never have taken his iconic "Earthrise," seen below. Anders shot the picture on Christmas Eve in 1968.
Lunar Orbiter 1 was initially supposed to orbit the moon for a year, but that was not to be. After just months into its mission, NASA engineers determined the spacecraft’s condition had deteriorated beyond repair. In order to prevent any possible interference with the then upcoming Lunar Orbiter 2, NASA commanded it to crash into the farside of the moon during the vessel’s 577th orbit on October 29.
Still, looking at “Earthrise” and Koch’s “Earthset,” it is clear that Lunar Orbiter 1’s legacy lives on. While the missions get more elaborate, the sense of wonder at seeing our planet in space from our natural satellite hasn’t changed, despite the passing of 60 years.

How “thunderquakes” could help reveal hidden structures inside the Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:11:01 UTC
20:11:01 KST

When lightning strikes, it superheats the air around it and creates a shock wave that we hear as thunder. But thunder doesn’t just travel through the atmosphere to our ears.
When that energy reaches the ground, some of it is converted into seismic waves that ripple through the soil and rock beneath. The resulting vibrations are known as “thunderquakes.”
Until now, scientists haven’t understood these signals well enough to make practical use of them. Our team’s research shows that thunderquakes can be used to map the structure beneath the Earth’s subsurface—such as groundwater movement, environmental contamination, sinkholes, or for evaluating building sites and foundations—just like X-rays image inside the human body.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
We discovered this by listening to thunder with something found in communities around the world but unusual as a seismic measuring instrument: fiber-optic cable.
Turning fiber optics into vibration sensors
Using a technique called distributed acoustic sensing, we turned an ordinary fiber-optic cable, the kind used for internet or phone service, into a string of thousands of vibration sensors.
A laser-pulsing computer, called an interrogator, sends light through the cable and measures tiny changes caused by vibrations along its length. In our experiment, part of the Penn State FORESEE project, we used a cable that is over 2 miles (more than 4 kilometers) long. That gave us more than 2,100 sensors, spaced only a few feet apart, all listening to the ground at once.
Over two years, we used an old telecom fiber to record and identify 458 clear, high-quality thunderquakes.
The enormous amount of detail captured by this process has allowed us to see something that had been difficult to observe before: specific types of seismic waves produced when sound from the atmosphere interacts with the ground.
The most important of these seismic waves are what we call air-coupled Rayleigh waves. They are measurable at the surface but can be used to study the subsurface far below, even down 300 feet (around 100 meters).
How a thunderquake ‘X-rays’ the ground below
The trick to this technique is known as seismic dispersion: Waves of different frequencies travel at different depths. By measuring how the thunderquake’s wave speeds changed with frequency, we could reconstruct the seismic wave speed at different depths, which allows us to interpret the properties of the ground beneath the fiber.
The result was the equivalent of an X-ray of the subsurface extending roughly 300 feet underground, without drilling a single hole.
Imaging the subsurface typically requires specialized equipment, such as truck-mounted vibration sources or arrays of sensors that have to be installed for surveys. These approaches can be expensive and difficult to deploy over large areas.
Thunderstorms offer a naturally occurring source of seismic energy that is already spread across the landscape. And fiber-optic cables are buried beneath cities and towns around the world.
Instead of bringing a seismic source to the ground, we can listen to the storms passing overhead. That could eventually make it possible to monitor the shallow subsurface continuously, using infrastructure that is already in the ground and seismic energy that is already coming from the sky.
What we found at our test site
In State College, Pennsylvania, where we conducted the tests, the geology is mostly limestone and dolomite, rocks that can slowly dissolve as groundwater moves through them. Over time, this process creates fractures, caves and sinkholes.
Our thunderquake study revealed four distinct areas where seismic waves traveled much more slowly than through the surrounding rock. These “weak zones” could be caused by fractured or weathered rock or the presence of water or air. Two of them coincide with areas where satellite radar shows that the ground is actively subsiding. The depths of all four are consistent with fractures and voids documented at nearby sites.
These results matter because karst landscapes like the one beneath State College are widespread. They cover roughly 20 percent of the world’s continental land area and affect nearly a quarter of the global population. Sinkholes, groundwater contamination and other hazards associated with these landscapes can threaten buildings, infrastructure and public safety. Knowing where these hazards are allows for better construction and planning.
Not just for thunder, and not just on Earth
Our results demonstrate a fundamental process: Sound waves in the atmosphere can be converted into useful seismic waves in the solid Earth. But thunder is only one example.
Sonic booms, volcanic eruptions and meteor airbursts can produce similar atmospheric shock waves, potentially creating other natural seismic sources.
The idea may even extend beyond Earth. Earth-like tectonic earthquakes are not expected to be common on some other planets and moons, but atmospheric disturbances may still be present.
Titan, Saturn’s largest moon and the destination of NASA’s upcoming Dragonfly mission, is one intriguing possibility. If lightning and thunder occur there as models predict, atmospheric energy could potentially provide another way to investigate its subsurface.
Back on Earth, the atmosphere is constantly interacting with the ground beneath our feet. Our work suggests that this interaction could be a source of information about the hidden world below us.

"The FSB is blackmailing me": how Russian secret services tried to recruit a volunteer through his son, and why he decided to go to Moscow to save him
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:10:00 EEST
20:10:00 KST

"The FSB is blackmailing me": how Russian secret services tried to recruit a volunteer through his son, and why he decided to go to Moscow to save him
Mykhailo Puryshev, a volunteer who is well known in Ukraine for repeatedly travelling to besieged Mariupol to evacuate families, flew to Moscow of his own accord on 17 August 2026. He says he did so because he was being blackmailed: Russia's Federal Security Service, the FSB, had threatened to conscript his son into the Russian army and send him to fight against Ukraine unless Puryshev agreed to cooperate.
Shortly before his departure, Ukrainska Pravda managed to speak to some of Mykhailo's friends, and to Mykhailo himself. The volunteer was already outside Ukraine, in Poland, when our conversation took place. Here we tell his story in his own words.
It was the middle of summer 2026. The paperwork was almost complete. Mykhailo Puryshev, a serviceman who was close to being discharged, was doing household chores at his home on the outskirts of Kyiv. A year of military service was behind him, as were his health problems, although he was still feeling the effects of the two heart attacks he'd suffered. Just a few more documents to get hold of, and he could go back to volunteering.
Suddenly a call came through on Telegram. It was his son Oleksandr. Mykhailo hadn't seen him for more than four years. He was an adult now – 18. Mykhailo would probably have struggled to recognise him if they met. Oleksandr sounded anxious.
His son's frightened voice came down the phone. "Dad, there are some people here and they want to talk to you."
Mykhailo ended the call and rushed to find a second phone. Another call came through from his son's number. Mykhailo started recording. A man's voice came down the phone, speaking in Russian.
"Good afternoon, Mikhail [Mykhailo in Russian – ed.]. You understand who you're talking to. The equivalent of your 'security service'. Let's be friends, Mikhail. If you don't want to be friends… you help the military, don't you? How would you feel if your son were on the other side, up against those people? Who matters more to you, Mikhail?"
At first Mykhailo didn't know what to do. If they'd called from an unknown number, he could have sworn at them and hung up. But they were calling from his own son's number. That meant these people were with him and had him under their control. He had to figure out how to save him. How to save his son from the FSB.
Family in Russia and blackmail using his son
Mykhailo had divorced long before the full-scale invasion. His ex-wife took their two children – a son and a daughter – and moved to Russia. She had lived in Pskov since 2016. From time to time, his son would visit him in Mariupol. Father and son travelled around the country, ate hot dogs at petrol stations, stayed in good hotels and went to amusement parks. Oleksandr was interested in programming and computer games and dreamed of studying abroad. Russia's invasion changed everything.
Father and son began to talk less often. Mykhailo didn't want to put Oleksandr at risk unnecessarily because of his volunteer work. So Oleksandr was usually the one who called. He told his dad that the other kids at school didn't talk very nicely about Ukraine or Ukrainians. It seemed the invasion was forcing him to grow up too fast.
It was obvious that the Russians would draft his son into the army as soon as he turned 18. Mykhailo tried several times to get him out of Russia. First he attempted to enlist the help of his ex-wife: he tried to persuade her to sign some documents so that their son could fly to see Mykhailo's brother in Canada. But she refused. Then he tried to do it secretly, through acquaintances and friends. The plan almost worked, but at the last moment Oleksandr said he couldn't go through with it: if he fled to Canada, his mother would be very upset.
Then, on 16 July 2026, came the call mentioned at the start of this article.
The man from the "equivalent of the security service" who had suggested that they "be friends" was in fact issuing a direct ultimatum: either Mykhailo helped the Russians or his son would be sent to the front lines. Mykhailo was warned that if he tried to tell anyone about the conversation or attempted to get Oleksandr out of Russia with the help of relatives, the threats would quickly be carried out. But if their "friendship" worked out, they assured him they would help arrange Oleksandr's studies, possibly even abroad. They even promised to provide money for his education.
The Russian asked whether Mykhailo was in contact with his ex-wife and why their relationship was so strained. We do not know the details of Mykhailo's family life, but the man from the "equivalent of the security service" guaranteed that he could sort that out too. He promised that the next call would come from his ex-wife's number. They also said they wouldn't bother him too often: twice a month max.
"I felt dirty," Mykhailo recalled. "All sorts of ideas kept running through my head about how to sort this out. I cried. I wondered what to do. I was worried about my son, afraid they might have locked him up somewhere. He was frightened. Those people who'd come to see him weren't friends; they'd come to scare him. I think he was terrified."
The second time the Russians called, it was via Telegram from an unknown number, and they were excessively polite. Even when Mykhailo became emotional, they said calmly: "We're speaking to you politely, aren't we? And I know a lot about you. I respect you. And I'm speaking to you respectfully."
The unknown caller told Mykhailo to buy another phone and a new SIM card and to find a good hiding place for them. When the time came, he was to make contact.
The subsequent conversations, if they can be called that, became more specific: the Russians explained what they expected from the cooperation they were proposing. They wanted information about foreign military personnel serving in Ukraine's defence forces and the locations of various units. They were particularly interested in Azov.
"Has something happened to you? Why are you so sad? Why are you off social media? Why aren't you posting anything?" asked the unidentified caller who wanted to "be friends".
Mykhailo didn't know what to say. He couldn't swear at him. Nor could he directly refuse to cooperate. After all, the Russians were holding his son hostage. Mykhailo didn't know what had happened to him, where he was, or what conditions he was being held in. He didn't even know whether his son was free. The Russians desperately needed Mykhailo to go back to his volunteering and his social media as though nothing had happened.
"I've just gone through the military medical board and I'm waiting for the paperwork. I'm being discharged," Mykhailo explained. "And technically, I'm supposed to be at my permanent duty station. So just to avoid any questions, I'm staying at home, not really going anywhere, and I won't be posting anything until I have the documents."
The Russian kept asking when Mykhailo would be able to return to volunteering, because it was "very, very necessary" that he do so. This time, however, the conversation was more friendly than businesslike: the man from the "equivalent of the security service" seemed to have changed tactics and was trying to act more casually, asking about the weather, Mykhailo's health, relationships, women. And, almost in passing, he asked where Mykhailo's unit was currently stationed.
Mykhailo gave a vague answer: "Somewhere in the east."
There were five calls in total. It was becoming clear that the Russians were losing patience and were no longer prepared to believe that the military medical board bureaucracy could take so long. They demanded that Mykhailo go back to his volunteering and finally begin cooperating with them.
The last conversation took place on 3 August. After that, they communicated only by text. Mykhailo even deleted the text messages to make it look as if he really was interested in cooperating with the Russians.
The decision
Meanwhile, a plan was taking shape in his mind. Mykhailo spoke to various people who suggested different ways of resolving the situation, including physically getting Oleksandr out of Russia.
But putting other people's lives at risk was unacceptable to the volunteer, as was forcing his son to take such a risk. Mykhailo decided to fly to Moscow and sort it out once and for all.
"Everyone's worried about whether I'll be all right. But if someone else got my son out, wouldn't they have a family too? Of course they would. This is my problem. I've tried to solve it. There is no option in which no one suffers. This is my child – I can take responsibility for him myself. I believe this is the best option there is," Mykhailo explained.
All this time he kept on trying to contact his son, but there was no answer. Then, around the beginning of August, his ex-wife called relatives and repeatedly urged them to tell Mykhailo not to try to contact Oleksandr.
The unknown Russian man who had "wanted to be friends" kept promising to arrange a conversation with Mykhailo's son. At one point he even suggested meeting in person, saying that Mykhailo could travel to Russia via a third country such as Kazakhstan. To convince him that he had the necessary connections, the man even promised to make sure that no stamp showing that Mykhailo had crossed into Russia would be put in his passport. But Mykhailo never once got to hear his son's voice.
"It was difficult," he said. "I considered different ways of solving the problem. Some of them wouldn't have been ideal for me. How long can someone who's had two heart attacks survive in captivity? Not long, I don't think. But there is hope that perhaps things will turn out differently.
I always say that wherever I've been and whatever I've done, I've always put my faith in God. Because there was no logic to any of it. Let them do whatever they want. My son will stop being of interest to them. There'll be no one left to blackmail me with, and nothing to blackmail me over. There will be no reason to waste resources."
Eventually Mykhailo travelled to Poland and on to Türkiye. On the Turkish coast, he bought a plane ticket to Sheremetyevo airport in Moscow. His plan was to arrive at the airport and be detained at passport control.
"I've left a video explaining everything. I wanted people to understand me. Parents will understand why I did this. If they're decent, proper parents, borders won't matter to them. Parents will go and get their children, whatever the cost," Mykhailo said.
He said that just before the flight, he'd finally felt a sense of relief. Suddenly he remembered how much he'd loved swimming in the river as a child. He used to jump in off a dam. It was incredibly scary. But once you'd taken that step, there was no way back. All you could do was plunge into the water and swim...
From entrepreneur to volunteer
We can't know exactly what Mykhailo was feeling at that moment. But he certainly knew who he would be dealing with and what those people are capable of. After all, he had first-hand experience of dealing with Russian occupying forces in Mariupol in 2022.
The Russians were interested in Mykhailo Puryshev for a reason. He was one of the few volunteers who had managed to get into Mariupol during the occupation and evacuate people. He later continued helping civilians evacuate from frontline cities, including Kherson.
Before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mykhailo did not consider himself a volunteer. He lived in the city and ran several businesses, including an IT company and a nightclub. On 24 February 2022, he took his family and relatives to safety in Ukraine's west, bought a red Mercedes minibus, painted "Volunteer" all over it and drove back to Mariupol. He managed to get into the city on 8 March. He was lucky: at the time, he didn't understand the immensity of the risks he was about to face.
Mykhailo made six trips to Mariupol in all. He brought aid into the city in his red minibus, and on the return journey he took families with children out. There were no humanitarian corridors, so attacks would be going on during the evacuations.
On subsequent trips, other people Mykhailo knew also went with him in their own vehicles, which meant they could rescue more people. By his estimate, around a thousand Mariupol residents were rescued during the spring of 2022. The volunteer's trips were reported on by Ukrainian and international media outlets, including Euronews, Fox News, CNN, the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne, 1+1, NV and local outlet Mrpl.city.
Getting through the Russian checkpoints wasn't easy. The Russian occupying forces thought Mykhailo was either insane or a spy. They would search his vehicle thoroughly. Eventually they began to recognise him. They thought he would either be killed by Russian artillery or accidentally shot by his own side. During one of his trips, a shell landed near his minibus, damaging the bonnet and blowing out one of the side doors.
His final trip to Mariupol was in May. Mykhailo had learned that there might be children inside the Azovstal steelworks, so he decided to try to rescue them. He took two megaphones in addition to his usual humanitarian supplies. He planned to drive around the plant and broadcast a recorded message offering evacuation. Mykhailo hoped that by doing this, he would be able to locate civilians who were sheltering from the constant bombardment alongside the Ukrainian troops.
This time, however, he failed to reach the city. During his previous trip he had been threatened by so-called militants from the "DPR" (the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic) at one of the checkpoints. They said that if they saw his Mercedes again, they would put him in a basement and either keep him prisoner or shoot him.
Mykhailo was detained at a checkpoint near Mariupol. His vehicle was confiscated and he was taken away for interrogation. There were a lot of people in the building where he was held. They were all taken away to be interrogated. They were tortured too. Electric shock was the main method.
There was one incident that Mykhailo is unlikely ever to forget. One of the prisoners was tortured so brutally that he could literally no longer walk. He was dragged bodily into the room.
"The guy had left the room on his own two feet, but when he came back, they had to drag him in," Mykhailo recalls. "People immediately started looking for ways to help him, searching for painkillers. The stench of burnt skin was overwhelming – they'd subjected him to such severe electric shocks. It felt as though human life meant absolutely nothing there."
But the collaborators were the most brutal. At times they were even more vicious than the Russians. In their eagerness to prove themselves useful to the Russian occupying forces, they could torture prisoners in an attempt to extract information that did not even exist.
The Russians laughed at Mykhailo's determination to reach Azovstal. When they realised that he was completely serious, they asked him how he could possibly imagine doing it. Eventually, during one of the interrogations, Mykhailo was released. The Russians even returned the red minibus he'd arrived in. On the way to Zaporizhzhia, he managed to evacuate two more families with children. He called the other volunteers and advised them not to travel to the city any more: it was becoming too dangerous.
But that wasn't the end of his volunteer work. Mykhailo spent some time delivering humanitarian aid to Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts after they had been liberated. During one of his trips to Kramatorsk, he came up with the idea of setting up invincibility centres – heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist people facing hardships due to power cuts – for both military personnel and civilians. Water was a major problem in frontline cities: people had been unable to wash properly for months.
The first invincibility centre was established in Bakhmut. A well was drilled in a basement, and a filtration system enabled up to 1,000 litres of water an hour to be pumped through it. People started coming to the pink basement – Mykhailo and the other volunteers painted the centres pink – to wash themselves, do their laundry, or pick up toys that the volunteers had left there for the children.
This was also how they found families with children who were reluctant to leave. Mykhailo and his friends would keep track of them and try to persuade them to evacuate. Sometimes they succeeded. Similar invincibility centres were later established in Avdiivka, Vuhledar, Kupiansk, Druzhkivka, Kostiantynivka, Kherson and Huliaipole. The most expensive one cost just over half a million hryvnias (about US$11,100). Eventually the Russians began bombing the centres. They claimed on Russian television that the volunteers were "helping the Nazis".
The volunteers suspected that local collaborators were helping the Russians locate the basements equipped for washing and doing laundry, as they would enter the premises and film them. They managed to catch one of these "helpers" red-handed, and several others were caught later.
Mykhailo officially registered his volunteer organisation, naming it Unity of People. Some members of the team decided to enlist in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and he joined them. He wanted to keep an eye on his friends.
But after suffering two heart attacks and related health issues, Mykhailo was deemed unfit for military service – he was having to take four different medications every day to keep his condition under control. He returned to his home near Kyiv, where he was finishing up the paperwork and planning his next volunteer projects, when on 16 July, he received that phone call from the FSB.
***
Mykhailo Puryshev landed at Sheremetyevo on the morning of 17 August. He has not been in contact with anyone since. His friends have no information about what has happened to him.
Videos continue to appear on Mykhailo's social media accounts, but he said that his team would handle all communication from then on.
- -
P.S. Ukrainska Pravda has contacted human rights advocates who are aware of Puryshev's situation and are trying to find ways to help him.
UP also requested comment from the Security Service of Ukraine, but had not received a response at the time this article was posted.
P.P.S. During our conversations with Mykhailo and his friends, we expressed concern about his decision and warned him about the possible risks. However, it was clear from our conversations that unfortunately, Mykhailo was not going to change his plans.

US court reverses Trump’s 75-country visa ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:06:44 UTC
20:06:44 KST

US court reverses Trump’s 75-country visa ban
A US court has overturned a Trump administration rule that suspended the issuing of immigrant visas to people from 75 countries.
The State Department announced the restrictions in Janurary, which did not apply to tourist or student visas, saying they were needed to prevent the entry of those who would “take welfare and public benefits.” Russia, Brazil, Colombia, Albania, Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, and Pakistan were among the nations covered by the policy.
Judge Jeannette Vargas of Manhattan said in her ruling on Friday that US consular staff had been ordered to reject visas for all applicants from the blacklisted countries even if they were able to support themselves.
Under American laws, an immigrant’s application can only be turned down if the person is determined likely to become a “public charge” by a review of their finances, health, and skills.
“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” the judge stated.
Vargas, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, also found that Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not have the authority to impose the visa ban.
The ruling came in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups, along with applicants for immigrant visas and American citizens whose relatives had been denied visas to the country. The Trump administration can still appeal.
Responding to NPR, a State Department spokesperson would not comment on ongoing litigation. The Trump administration is “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants,” the spokesperson insisted.
A sweeping clampdown on immigration, which the White House says is needed to improve domestic security, led to nationwide protests after the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal agents in Minnesota in January.
Besides imposing visa restrictions, the US government has stepped up deportation of illegal aliens, with Guatemalan President Bernardo Arevalo saying earlier this week that some 2,300 Mexican nationals had been flown to his country from the US since the start of year, despite objections by Mexico.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) also faces scrutiny over conditions in its detention centers. At least 52 people died in the agency’s custody during the first 500 days of Trump’s second term, according to a report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.

British diplomat returns to Istanbul with Turkish language in tow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:06:10 UTC
20:06:10 KST

British Consul General in Istanbul David Reed, who took up his post four months ago, shares that he waited 15 years to return to Türkiye, where his diplomatic career first took shape during an early posting in Greek Cyprus and where he has now resumed speaking Turkish.
His connection with Türkiye began around two decades ago, when he was assigned to Cyprus and needed to learn Turkish. During language training in London, he spent time in Turkish cafes before living with families for six weeks each in Istanbul and İzmir.
“I wanted to be able to use Turkish again and had to wait 15 years to return to Istanbul,” Reed said in an interview with the daily Hürriyet. To refresh his language skills, he watched Turkish television series, as well as films by acclaimed director Nuri Bilge Ceylan, and read Turkish newspaper articles.
Born in Portsmouth in 1978, Reed developed an interest in history and current affairs. He studied law at Cambridge University before joining the U.K. Foreign Office in 2003 after three years at a commercial law firm.
His first overseas posting was in Greek Cyprus in 2005, at a time when the Annan Plan dominated the political agenda. He recalled efforts to encourage dialogue between the two communities through negotiations, economic ties and sporting events.
“Diplomacy is a matter of patience,” he said, stressing the importance of understanding history, listening to different perspectives and finding common ground.
Reed sees artificial intelligence and climate change among the world’s biggest challenges, describing AI as a transformation on the scale of the Industrial Revolution. He also highlights cooperation with Türkiye ahead of COP31, which will be held in Antalya in November.
He describes U.K.-Türkiye ties as being on an upward trajectory, with bilateral trade reaching £28 billion ($38 billion) by the end of the first quarter of 2026 and 4.4 million British visitors traveling to Türkiye. Defense cooperation, including the planned sale of Eurofighter Typhoon jets, is another major element of the partnership.
For Reed, however, diplomacy remains rooted in a principle as old as the relationship itself: building influence through relationships and partnerships. “The classic diplomacy of William Harborne is still valid,” he said, referring to the first official English ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, appointed by Queen Elizabeth I in 1581.

Iran’s president wants to revive MoU to end stalled US war
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended a recent memorandum of understanding as the best way for the country to move beyond what he described as a situation of "neither war nor peace".
In a speech published by state-run IRNA early on Sunday, he said members of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council believed the memorandum represented the best possible agreement based on what he described as dignity, wisdom and the national interest.
"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."
The deal memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war with Iran and reaching an accord on its nuclear program. That period ended last week, but the two sides remain far apart, with no signs of compromise on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global shipping.
Pezeshkian also linked the agreement to Iran’s economic prospects, saying the country could not attract investment in this stalled phase.
"Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk," he said. "We have to remove this risk from the country."
Nearly six months into the war with the United States and Israel, the Iranian economy is suffering under sanctions and a naval blockade.
Meanwhile, the hard-line new leader of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council warned Tehran’s neighbours against joining the new US effort to strangle Iran’s economy.
"If [Trump] wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner," Mohsen Rezaei said in an interview with the state broadcaster that aired Saturday.

Switzerland plans mandatory reporting of organised crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:05:01 UTC
20:05:01 KST

Switzerland plans mandatory reporting of organised crime
The federal government and the cantons are planning to introduce a mandatory reporting requirement for any indications of organised crime.
An employee at a land registry office who notices suspicious real estate purchases, or a food inspector who finds evidence of money laundering during an inspection at a bar: In the future, they may be required to inform law enforcement authorities if they encounter evidence of organised crime. This was confirmed by Eva Wildi-Cortés, director of the Federal Office of Police (Fedpol), on Swiss public television, SRF.
The reporting requirement would apply to all cantonal and municipal employees. The cantons themselves proposed this as part of a consultation process that has just concluded, says Wildi-Cortés.
Employees of land registry offices, food inspectors, and labor market inspectors are very close to the action. “They have insight into business operations. They notice irregularities that they can report. We rely on that,” said the Fedpol director.
Originally, the federal government had planned only a right to report. Government employees would thus have been free to decide whether or not to file a report – but if they did report something, they would not have been liable to prosecution.
Preventing infiltration
Fedpol hopes that, thanks to reports from municipalities and cantons, the federal government and the cantons will be better able to uncover the covert activities of drug rings, human trafficking gangs, or cybercriminals. The goal is to prevent the infiltration of the economy and society.
The federal government and the cantons intend to finalise the new reporting requirement by the end of the year as part of a national action plan to combat organised crime. The cantons themselves will then be responsible for implementing it.
More
Switzerland to adopt a national strategy to combat organised crime
Some cantons already have a mandatory reporting requirement in place, while others only grant government employees the right to report. In still other cantons, employees currently have no leeway. Under certain circumstances, they may even face criminal charges if they breach official secrecy by reporting their observations.
Federal employees are already subject to a reporting requirement.
Fedpol exposure
For years, Fedpol has been warning that criminal groups are infiltrating the economy, society, and even government agencies. It provided proof of this itself at the end of April, when a Fedpol officer was exposed.
He is alleged to have sold investigative information to the drug mafia. Director Wildi-Cortés says she did not know the Fedpol Federal Security Service employee personally. Her federal agency has over 1,000 employees.
Wildi-Cortés emphasises that her staff uncovered the mole on their own. Following the arrest, they checked whether all regulations – for example, regarding access rights to police data – had been followed: “At first glance, no mistakes were made.”
However, a more in-depth analysis is currently underway. It is possible that further measures will be taken, such as stricter screening procedures for new hires.

Russia’s New Banderol Missile Ends Up in Belarus After Veering Away From Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category

Russia’s New Banderol Missile Ends Up in Belarus After Veering Away From Ukraine
Several Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missiles crossed into Belarus during Moscow’s massive attack on Ukraine, with at least one reportedly flying around 75 miles into Belarusian territory before running out of fuel and crashing into a field, according to OSINT community Oko Gora on August 22.
Ukrainian monitoring channels tracked multiple Banderol weapons entering Belarus beginning at around 4 am, while a Belarusian military aircraft was scrambled from Baranovichi airfield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Separate reports indicated that a Su-30 fighter was sent up as one of the weapons moved deeper into the country.
According to Ukrainian monitoring resource Monitor, one Banderol traveled approximately 120 kilometers, or 75 miles, inside Belarus without being brought down by Belarusian Su-30s. It eventually exhausted its fuel supply and fell into a field. The circumstances could not be independently verified.
Other monitoring reports indicated that at least 12 Russian Banderol missile-drones entered Belarusian airspace during the attack. It remains unclear whether any were destroyed or disrupted using electronic warfare.
The incursion came during another large-scale Russian aerial attack on Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Air Force said its defenses destroyed or suppressed 191 aerial targets between the evening of August 21 and the morning of August 22, including three Kh-31P/Kh-59 missiles, six Banderol munitions and 182 drones. Russian strikes were recorded at 41 locations, while debris from intercepted weapons fell at another 12 sites.
Russia also launched 217 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones and decoys. More than 50 were jet-powered, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.
The S8000 Banderol is a relatively new Russian weapon combining characteristics of a cruise missile and long-range attack drone. Developed by Russia’s Kronstadt company, it has an estimated range of roughly 500 kilometers, or 310 miles.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence says Russia can produce up to 80 Banderol missiles per month. The weapon reportedly cruises at 520-560 kilometers per hour and can reach maximum speeds of 620-650 kilometers per hour.
Earlier, a Russian “Banderol” missile crossed from the Odesa region into Moldova on August 17, Ukraine’s Air Force reported, before an unidentified aircraft crashed near the village of Tălmaza in the country’s Ștefan Vodă district.

Netanyahu vows to block Palestinian state as polls put his bloc short of majority

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state in Gaza or the occupied West Bank for as long as he remains in office.
His remarks came in response to Mansour Abbas, leader of the United Arab List, who said Palestine already exists as a state and is recognized by most of the world.
Abbas urged Israel and the U.S. to recognize Palestine as well.
“As long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state controlled by Iran, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria,” Netanyahu said, using the biblical term for the occupied territory.
Speaking at his party’s general conference in the Arab city of Tayibe earlier on Aug. 22, Abbas said his party was seeking peace between Israel and Palestine.
“The State of Palestine exists, and the world recognizes it,” Abbas said, calling on Washington and Tel Aviv to recognize it as well.
Netanyahu’s remarks came ahead of Knesset elections scheduled for Oct. 27, with opinion polls showing his Likud party and its coalition partners falling short of the 61 seats required to form a government.
Likud, which currently holds 32 seats, has fallen sharply in recent surveys, with a poll on Aug. 21 putting it at 20 seats.
A Channel 13 poll published Aug. 19 projected Netanyahu’s Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies at a combined 51 seats, 10 short of a parliamentary majority.

Iran Unleashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
11:01:56 UTC
20:01:56 KST

Iran Unleashed
The dominant power in the Middle East from now on will not be the U.S. or Israel but Iran.
For years, Iran confronted a balance of power in the Middle East that tilted against it. The region was dominated by a hostile American superpower, a nuclear-armed and militarily superior Israel, and significant local actors—Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates—that were strategically and economically aligned with the United States.
Today finds Iran in entirely new circumstances. It has gone head-to-head with the superpower and Israel, withstood a pounding from their most advanced weapons, and more than survived. As a result, Iran has, with American help, completely reconfigured the power structure of the Middle East and the Persian Gulf. The dominant power in the region going forward will be Iran, not the U.S. or Israel. Neighboring countries are already making their adjustments to this new reality. More distant powers will too. For years, the world has been dealing with an Iran constrained. It will now discover what Iran unleashed looks like.
Iran doesn’t need a deal with the United States. The common assumption that a weak and impoverished Iran would eventually have to make some accommodation to American power, open the Strait of Hormuz, and set about tending to its badly damaged economy has proved mistaken. The Islamic Republic has rarely appeared weaker or more vulnerable than it has over the past two years. Last February, President Trump renewed his “maximum pressure” campaign of international sanctions, which severely damaged Iran’s already-weak economy and cut billions of dollars in state revenues. Israel and the United States then launched the 12-day war that June to destroy Iranian nuclear facilities. The war significantly damaged Iran’s program and revealed just how vulnerable the country was to Israeli and American strikes. Then, in February, the United States and Israel launched the most recent war with the killing of the regime’s supreme leader and the great majority of its senior officials, followed by more than five weeks of unremitting attacks on Iranian military capabilities.
Yet through all of this, the regime has survived and made no concessions. On the contrary, Iran exposed America’s Achilles’ heel: the vulnerability of Iran’s neighbors. A major turning point came in mid-March, when Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field, and Iran retaliated against Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex, the world’s largest liquefied-natural-gas facility. The attack showed that although Iran obviously could not defeat the United States in an air war, Iranian missiles and drones could inflict enough damage on the oil-and-gas infrastructure of the Gulf to plunge the world into a prolonged economic crisis. The Gulf States understood this immediately, and so did Trump. He halted attacks on Iranian energy targets, ordered a reluctant Israel to do the same, and soon brought the larger campaign to a stop without extracting a single Iranian concession. Ever since, and despite many threats, Trump has not once ordered another strike against Iranian energy infrastructure.
This alone was enough to alter the balance of leverage between Iran and the United States. From April through last month, Trump repeatedly threatened to launch another massive attack against Iran. Each time, Iran threatened retaliation, Gulf States warned of the consequences, and Trump backed off. By his third or fourth bluff, Tehran had reason to conclude that the United States was no longer prepared to follow Iran up the ladder of escalation. Trump made this clear when he noted in mid-June that continuing the war would lead to “economic catastrophe,” possibly even a “depression,” and that he did not want to become President Herbert Hoover. Ever since, Trump has been trying, with notable desperation, to end the conflict.
The memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran adopted in June reflected this reality. Although phrased to save face for the United States as much as possible, the MOU was a clear Iranian victory. It declared that the Islamic Republic of Iran, and no other nation, would “make arrangements” for the “safe passage of commercial vessels” through the Strait of Hormuz. In dialogue with Oman, without intermediaries or other participants, Iran would determine the strait’s administration “in line with the applicable international law and the sovereign rights of coastal states.”
The MOU did not call for a return to the prewar status quo. Neither did it provide the United States any say over future administration of the strait. Rather, it designated Iran as the only actor other than the weak Oman, and it even allowed Iran to charge nations for safe passage after 60 days. The MOU thus codified the defeat that the United States had suffered back in March, when Trump apparently realized that he either could not or would not risk further attacks on energy facilities in the region.
In retrospect, Iran’s leaders do not seem to have believed that they needed the MOU. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei reportedly had to be persuaded by President Masoud Pezeshkian to sign it. Tehran’s relative indifference was understandable: The American concessions reflected such desperation to end the war that the Iranians could well have expected that the U.S. would eventually retreat, with or without a deal.
Iranian leaders certainly did not hesitate to blow up the cease-fire almost immediately when the U.S. Navy began shepherding tankers through the Omani side of the strait. Trump may or may not have understood the full extent of the concessions his negotiators had made regarding control of the strait, but from the Iranian point of view, the Omani route was an attempt to recapture what the U.S. had given away. For a while, the United States and Iran engaged in tit-for-tat strikes, culminating in intense American attacks in mid-July. When these had no effect, Trump warned on July 15 that the United States was “going to knock out all their power plants” and “all their bridges” unless Iran negotiated. Yet again, no attack followed.
Then the world, and the Iranians, learned one of the main reasons: Revelations that American stocks of crucial munitions were dangerously low, and that no less than the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff himself was looking for an “off-ramp,” sent a clear signal about the future course of American strategy. A major assault on Iran would threaten American interests elsewhere by weakening the United States in the possible event of a Chinese move on Taiwan or a Russian onslaught against a NATO member.
Missile shortages would also increase the hazards involved in a massive attack on Iranian infrastructure. The U.S. would be forced to send more manned aircraft within range of Iranian air defenses, and it would have relatively few interceptors on hand to protect the Gulf States and its own regional bases. The risk of American casualties would be high, as would the danger to the region’s energy infrastructure. And nothing would guarantee that such an assault would be any more effective than the five-plus weeks of bombings were earlier this year.
American actions have made plain that Washington fears escalation more than Iran does—not just for now, but for the future. This places limits on what the United States can do even at low levels of conflict. Because any military action against Iran risks stepping onto an escalation ladder that the U.S. does not want to ascend, even tit-for-tat strikes seem no longer to be part of American strategy. The president has reportedly told his advisers that he does not want to order more strikes. The Iranians have struck at several UAE ships this month and even fired ballistic missiles at the country, but the United States has not responded since July—a fact undoubtedly noted by the UAE and Iran’s other neighbors.
Given the evident American reluctance to fight another major campaign, Iran has reason to wonder what it can get from a deal that it will not get anyway without one. Senior Iranian officials are now calling for the withdrawal of American forces, the lifting of the American naval blockade and all sanctions, the freeing of Iran’s frozen assets, and the payment of war reparations. The conventional wisdom is that Iran’s leaders know that these demands are nonstarters for Washington and that they are therefore either rubbing Trump’s nose in defeat, angling for a better deal, or overplaying their hand. Many observers still assume that control of the strait is a bargaining chip to squeeze more concessions out of the United States or get Trump back to the MOU. But we are well past all that. A victor does not have to go back to the bargaining table except to set the terms of surrender.
Iran has now laid out those terms. They may appear maximalist and excessive, but Tehran must hardly believe that it has reason to ask for less. Iran has made clear for months that control of the strait is not negotiable. The notion, constantly floated by the Trump administration and the media, that the Iranians can’t make up their minds and that they keep shifting their positions is nonsense. As far back as April, Mojtaba declared that Iran would implement “new legal frameworks and management” of the strait and that “foreigners who come from thousands of kilometers away” had no place in the Gulf, “except at the bottom of its waters.” On a day commemorating Iran’s defeat of Portugal in the strait in 1622, he declared that “by the will and power of God, the bright future of the Persian Gulf region will be a future without America.”
The idea that, having survived both military strikes and sanctions, Iran will now succumb to sanctions alone is deluded. Mojtaba has overhauled Iran’s national-security leadership and installed veterans of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in top positions. Former IRGC Commander Mohsen Rezaei now heads the Supreme National Security Council, and other hard-line security officials have been elevated. The regime emerging from the war is being reorganized by men who believe that Iran survived an American-Israeli attempt to destroy it and that defiance, not compromise, produced victory.
But this is not just triumphalism. For Iran, control of the strait is neither a luxury nor a bargaining chip. Given the likelihood that, at some future point, Israel or the United States will attack again, deal or no deal, the strait provides Iran’s strongest and surest deterrent. It is also the key to unlocking many of the shackles that a U.S.-dominated world order placed on Iran over the course of decades, and to undoing a regional and global economic system designed to exclude and impoverish it. Some so-called moderates within the Iranian establishment may well regard the strait as a bargaining chip, but they are not winning the argument, for reasons that are not hard to understand. An IRGC spokesperson stated the regime’s perspective plainly: “For us, the Strait of Hormuz is not merely an economic waterway, but rather a key component of our geopolitical and strategic power.”
Iran has been establishing the mechanisms of control for months and instructing shipowners and nations as to how the system will operate. It created the Persian Gulf Strait Authority and demanded that shipping companies register with it, obtain permits, follow Iran-designated routes, and pay for Iran-provided insurance and security.
Neither is Iran claiming merely the right to collect money. It is also claiming the right to decide who may pass. It has proposed excluding vessels associated with governments it deems hostile, such as the U.S. and Israel, and it has demanded compensation from nations that participated in attacks against it. Iran is establishing the principle that passage through the strait will henceforth be a privilege that Tehran can grant, condition, delay, or deny. Other nations have already begun acquiescing to the new arrangement. India, Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, China, and others have sought to come to terms.
Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz is a more useful instrument of power than a nuclear weapon would be. A nuclear weapon might deter an attack, but control of the strait gives Iran leverage every day, over dozens of countries. With it, Iran can reward friends, punish enemies, extract revenue, force the loosening of sanctions, and make governments think twice before opposing Iranian policies. It can do all of this without firing a shot, and while preserving the ability to threaten violence when necessary.
The sanctions strategy that for decades served to isolate Iran rested on international cooperation. Nations that depend on access to the strait—Japan and South Korea, for example—will have to choose between access to a reliable energy supply and participation in American-backed sanctions. Will they choose solidarity with Washington—this Washington—over their economic interests? In the new order that Iran is creating, a global sanctions regime is likely to be unsustainable.
Iran will probably sustain its control over energy flows for at least a couple of years. The most optimistic projections suggest that establishing alternative pipelines and export routes that circumvent the Strait of Hormuz will take this long. But one wonders whether these will even come to fruition. New pipelines, ports, and energy facilities will be just as vulnerable to Iranian missiles and drones as the old ones were. Will Iran simply stand by while neighboring states construct the means to escape its control? The small states that must build and protect such routes are going to be wary of incurring Iran’s wrath, and American protection has proved inadequate. Iran is already trying to draw Iraq away from developing alternative oil-export corridors, in part by offering safe passage for Iraqi tankers on Iranian terms.
The regional adjustment has begun. Gulf rulers who once counted on an American security guarantee must now make their peace with the power that proved capable of defeating their protector. Saudi Arabia’s rejection of the U.S.- and Israel-backed Abraham Accords in favor of a strategic compact with Pakistan and Turkey hints at the shape of the future. The Abraham Accords represented the consolidation of Israeli power and influence in the region and the further containment of Iran. The Mecca pact is something else entirely. Neither Pakistan nor Turkey regards Iran as a major threat; Pakistan, like Iran, has close relations with China; Israel regards Turkey as a regional threat second only to Iran. Instead of an American-Israeli order, this will be an alignment less implacably hostile to Iran, less friendly to Israel, and more independent of the United States. The signatories also have nuclear weapons in common: Pakistan has them, and the Turks and Saudis want them.
Meanwhile, Iran will be free to resume its own nuclear-weapons program without fear of another major attack. This fact in itself will transform the regional balance. Last year, Israel and the United States bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities for 12 days without facing serious Iranian retaliation. Now Iran has been emboldened to use its control of the strait, and threats against neighboring states and their energy infrastructure, to deter any such strikes for the foreseeable future. American missile and interceptor stocks will take a long time to replenish, and may well be needed in other parts of the world in years to come; Iran will all the while be rearming with Russian and Chinese help, potentially leaving the U.S. in a worse position a year from now than it is in today.
The effects will extend far beyond the Middle East. American allies in Asia and Europe can see that a relatively brief war against a second-rank power has consumed much of America’s supply of the weapons needed for missile defense. They can see that the United States began a war it could not finish, exposed its partners to retaliation, and then stopped when the costs became too great. Beijing’s conclusions about Taiwan, and Moscow’s conclusions about Europe, may be impossible to know. But America’s allies will inevitably be asking whether Washington has the weapons, stamina, and political will to sustain another major conflict. In fact, they already are.
That the Iranian regime could fall is, of course, possible. It is corrupt, repressive, economically incompetent, and widely hated by its people. But it had all of these weaknesses before the war. What it did not have was control of the world’s most important energy choke point, the prospect of growing revenues and influence, the demonstrated ability to deter the United States, and the prestige of an impossible victory.
A regime that survived what much of the world believed would destroy it, and then forced the world’s dominant power to retreat, will likely emerge strengthened, at least for a time. Such success tends to breed confidence, and perhaps overconfidence. But it is not likely to make Iran’s leaders less ambitious or less committed to the faith that saw them through this miraculous triumph. Recently, senior Iranian officials began talking publicly about adopting a “fully offensive” posture, and reports have emerged of Iranian plans to expand its targets to include European countries hosting American bases. To see stories in The New York Times asking, “Who will blink first?” is amusing, given that the Iranians until now have never once blinked, while the Trump administration has done nothing but blink. Iran may even start fighting again to force the U.S. to lift the naval blockade. Given the American administration’s proven fear of escalation, the hope is not unreasonable. The world has spent decades worrying about what Iran might do if it acquired a nuclear weapon. It should now worry about something even more consequential: an Iran that has defeated the United States, no longer fears American attack, and controls access to the Persian Gulf. Nuclear weapons alone could never have given Iran this kind of power. The failed U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has.

Feature: When a Chinese mythic world travels without translation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:01:53 CST
20:01:53 KST

Chen Aijun works in an optical shop in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Youyi)
CHENGDU, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The video came with almost no instructions.
There was no narration explaining the mythology behind palaces rising above an ocean of clouds in the video, nor subtitles identifying the heavenly gates, cranes or tiny figures moving beneath them.
Yet viewers outside China quickly began naming the world for themselves.
Some called it "paradise." Others saw a "Celestial Palace" or an "Immortal Realm" familiar from Chinese fantasy games and television dramas. One user wrote, "Waiting on Wukong to show up," invoking the Monkey King from the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West," or the hit game "Black Myth: Wukong."
The interpretations differed, but viewers did not seem to need the same cultural knowledge to enter the conversation.
Earlier this month, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning shared the 33-second AI-generated video on social media with a question: "What does the Chinese heaven look like?"
It opened up a hermeneutic discussion, with responses overseas suggesting a cultural image does not necessarily need to elicit exactly the same interpretation for everyone in order for it to be viewed meaningfully.
"The right to interpret ultimately lies with the audience," said Zhang Zheng, deputy dean of Tsinghua University's School of Journalism and Communication.
People encountering unfamiliar cultures inevitably draw on what they already know, Zhang said. Rather than fully grasping every cultural reference, what matters is whether audiences can encounter the work, understand it and respond to it emotionally.
Before strangers abroad could interpret this particular world, however, it first had to get out of one man's head.
Chen Aijun, 34, is an optometrist in Chengdu, capital of southwest China's Sichuan Province.
By day, Chen leads a quiet, down-to-earth life in a neighborhood optical shop. Inside, he worked among eyeglass frames and optometry equipment. On his computer was another landscape entirely: cloud seas, immense palaces, flying cranes and figures in ancient robes.
Chen's heaven did not come from any single ancient text.
Growing up in the 1990s, he watched "Journey to the West" and later encountered "The Investiture of the Gods," xianxia (immortal heroes) novels and fantasy games. Those stories mixed over time with images of Chinese architecture and landscapes he saw online.
He has never visited nearby Mount Emei, and most of what he knows of Mount Huangshan's famous sea of clouds comes from videos.
What appeared on his screen was therefore not a reconstruction of one fixed mythological scene, but a world shaped by traditional stories already filtered through television, novels, games, the internet and his own memory.
For years, Chen had no way to make that world visible.
He never studied painting, design, photography or 3D modeling. After high school, he joined his parents' optical business and eventually took over the shop.
Generative AI changed the gap between imagining an image and possessing the technical skills to show it to someone else.
More than a year ago, Chen began teaching himself through free online tutorials. In September 2025, he started regularly posting AI videos, and a month later began experimenting with palaces floating above clouds. He has since published more than 200 videos.
The process, however, involves far more than entering a few prompts. The technology lowered the technical threshold, but it did not make the choices for him.
When creating Nantianmen, the mythical heavenly gate, Chen first defines the spatial rhythm and tonal hierarchy, pairing towering architecture and cloud seas with deliberately miniature figures to amplify the celestial realm's grand scale.
If the result does not match the picture in his mind, he tries again. He often generates over 1,000 images a day, revising a single scene repeatedly before moving on to animation, editing, color grading and music.
The machine can generate a thousand possible heavens. Chen still has to decide which one is his.
"AI-produced images can be soulless, and it takes human inspiration and aesthetic sensibility to endow works with warmth and vitality," he said.
Zhang believes Chen's experience reflects a broader shift brought about by generative AI. He said AI is giving people without conventional artistic training access to forms of expression that once required specialized skills. But what they create still depends on what they bring to the tool.
"A person's existing knowledge inevitably shapes how they use AI," Zhang said.
Chen brought his memories to the machine. Viewers abroad, in turn, brought theirs to the image.
"Everyone brings their own associations to these scenes," he said.
If his imagined world had to be reduced to three elements, he would keep clouds, architecture and people. The first two should feel immense, he said, while the last should remain small.
The details are culturally specific, but the visual effect is more immediate: tiny human figures dwarfed by vast clouds and monumental architecture. The responses suggest that viewers did not need to understand every cultural reference to find a way into the image.
Chen has no overseas social media accounts and learned that the video was attracting attention abroad only when friends sent him screenshots.
His life at the optical shop has changed little. He still checks eyesight and fits glasses when customers come in, then returns to his computer when the shop grows quiet.
He now hopes to make longer AI videos with fuller stories. He also wants to visit Mount Emei and, one day, Mount Huangshan.
For years, images of distant mountains and clouds reached Chen through screens. His imagined landscapes later traveled through screens to people he had never met.
Now he wants to see the real mountains and clouds for himself. ■
Chen Aijun makes AI videos in an optical shop in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Youyi)

Divorcing devices: how digital detox helps Hongkongers ‘carve out moments’

For Robert Broad, stepping away from electronic devices has become part of a self-care routine he developed after the Covid-19 pandemic.
The 56-year-old recalled how spending long hours in front of screens while working remotely affected his physical and mental health and reduced the time he spent with family and friends.

Determined to restore a sense of balance, Broad began with small, manageable steps that could develop into lasting habits.
When he returns home from work, he puts his mobile phone in a drawer. He has disabled news alerts and keeps notifications on only for his parents and anyone who may need to reach him in an emergency.
He has also switched his phone to greyscale to make it less appealing and checks his emails in batches rather than as they arrive. He stops checking them at 8.30pm each day.

Explainer: Why the latest round of Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
19:01:22 CST
20:01:22 KST

OTTAWA, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Canada will impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of American goods from Sept. 8 in retaliation for Washington's latest duties, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday.
The 50-percent U.S. tariffs, covering an equivalent value of Canadian goods, took effect just after midnight Saturday following the collapse of trade talks on Friday, further straining relations between the longtime allies.
LAST-MINUTE BREAKDOWN
Carney said he suspended the talks because Washington introduced last-minute changes that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," even though the two sides had appeared close to a mutually beneficial agreement earlier in the week.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed three proclamations on July 20 to impose additional 50-percent tariffs on certain goods from Canada, citing Ottawa's "discriminatory treatment of American products."
On Tuesday, Trump announced a three-day pause of the tariffs, which were scheduled to take effect on Wednesday, saying the two sides had reached a deal pending the finalization of formal documents.
Carney said on Saturday that Canada had been prepared to remove its remaining retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum and automobiles if Washington substantially reduced its corresponding duties, and was also willing to encourage Canadian provinces to return U.S. alcoholic beverages to store shelves.
"They asked too much and offered too little," he said.
According to Carney, the U.S. proposals restricted Canada's ability to pursue trade arrangements with other countries, and undermined its protections for the French language, culture and national sovereignty. He did not disclose the details of those demands.
Washington, however, blamed the breakdown largely on late demands from Canada, with U.S. tariff rates on heavy-duty trucks emerging as a key sticking point, Politico reported, citing people familiar with the talks.
"They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News, adding that no further trade talks are scheduled with Canada.
A UNITED RESPONSE
In his televised address, Carney announced retaliatory tariffs targeting U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, and promised to release the details in the coming days.
"You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked," Carney said when asked whether Canada was in a trade war with the United States.
Carney's tough position has drawn broad support across party and provincial lines.
Pierre Poilievre, leader of the main opposition Conservative Party, called on Canadians to stay united against "unfair attacks."
"Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal," he said.
Several provincial premiers also backed Carney's decision.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the prime minister had his "full support" for a strong response "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," urging provincial leaders to remain united as "Team Canada."
British Columbia Premier David Eby noted that U.S. demands that Canada cut or reduce its trade with other countries would turn it into "the economic equivalent of the 51st state," which he described as "never acceptable" to Canadians.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said in a statement that while the U.S. tariffs will hurt, Carney made the right decision to reject an "unfair and unreliable" deal.
A recent Leger poll found that 56 percent of Canadians wanted the government to take a hard line and make no further concessions in talks with the United States, and more than 70 percent supported stronger retaliatory trade measures.
A BROADER SHIFT IN ECONOMIC TIES
In his address, Carney argued that the decades-long expansion of economic integration between Canada and the United States was over.
He accused Washington of using economic integration as a weapon.
"We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship," Carney said.
He also criticized the shifting U.S. justifications for tariffs, ranging from fentanyl and a television advertisement quoting former U.S. President Ronald Reagan to bridge tolls and wildfire smoke, as lacking seriousness and severely damaging foundational trust.
Since taking office in 2025, Carney's government has accelerated efforts to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States and diversify its trade relationships.
Ottawa has sought to expand trade with markets in Europe and Asia, develop ports and energy corridors, remove internal trade barriers and double Canadian exports to non-U.S. markets over the next decade, Carney said in his address.
The collapse of talks has also added uncertainty to the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The pact remains in force, but the latest U.S. tariffs apply even to Canadian goods that comply with its rules, unlike many earlier U.S. duties.
The scope for a rapid shift, however, remains limited. The United States still accounts for roughly three-quarters of Canada's merchandise exports, while cross-border supply chains in sectors such as automobiles and energy remain deeply integrated.
Meanwhile, Carney underscored the importance of Canadian energy to the United States, noting that Canada supplies 99 percent of U.S. natural gas imports, 85 percent of its electricity imports and 60 percent of its crude oil imports.
"I don't think they want us to stop sending it," he said. ■
