TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A startup showcase that has grown from six teams to 16 will be one of the expanded features at SEMICON Taiwan 2026, alongside programs connecting chip developers with investors.
The event is expected to reach a new record size, with 4,300 booths and participation by more than 1,300 companies. It opens Sept. 2 at Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, per CNA.
Investment will play a larger role in this year’s startup program, which is adding venture capital firms, corporate investors, and accelerators. More than 40 semiconductor startups will take part, with AI computing accounting for the largest technology category, per NextApple.
Nearly 40 talks are planned for the new Silicon Startups Stage over the three-day exhibition. Topics will range from AI chip design and advanced packaging to silicon photonics, quantum technology, smart manufacturing, and sustainability, according to NextApple.
The startup lineup reflects a push beyond conventional chip development into optical and quantum computing. Projects include silicon-based quantum systems built with standard CMOS processes, optical hardware for AI inference, and technologies designed to increase data-transfer capacity in large AI systems, per the reports.
An invitation-only Venture Day on Sept. 4 will feature pitches from 10 to 12 startups seeking investment and strategic partnerships. The broader exhibition will also feature Lumentum, Foxconn, MediaTek, AMD, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google.

Zelenskyy speaks about Ukraine's Patriot missile needs and agreements with Germany
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:38:00 EEST
19:38:00 KST

Zelenskyy speaks about Ukraine's Patriot missile needs and agreements with Germany
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs up to 360 missiles for Patriot air defence systems this winter, and stressed that Germany has agreed to supply several hundred PAC-2 missiles in 2027-2028.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists on 23 August, as cited by Interfax-Ukraine and reported by European Pravda
Details: According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine needs 300-360 missiles for Patriot air defence systems, while a total of 600 such missiles are produced per year.
Quote: "I wanted to find 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our Air Force is 360. But when only 600 are produced a year, 360 is not easy to come by. We're working with countries on additional options. And I'd really like to believe we can find a way to get some small percentage of US stocks – say, 5% or 10%. And we're ready to pay for that supply. That way, America could replenish its stockpile, and we could get through the winter. Such a political decision by America regarding the supply of missiles could change a great deal, both in terms of protecting lives and diplomatically."
Details: Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said he had agreed with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on the supply of 600 PAC-2 missiles for 2027-2028.
"PAC-2 can also shoot down ballistic missiles, you just need more of them," the president noted.
Zelenskyy also spoke about talks with the American side.
Quote: "The Americans are seriously increasing production in the second half of 2027 and beyond. But that takes time, unfortunately. So we keep talking to them now about the volumes we need – the volumes are actually there."
Details: The president said Ukraine received 675 missiles throughout the whole of 2023, while in 2025 it received 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased over that period. In 2026, deliveries of 264 PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles are planned.
Quote: "PAC-3 is what we receive from the US through the PURL programme. All our partners – both the Americans and the Europeans – understand exactly how much money they're transferring and exactly how many missiles they're giving us. There are also some separate bilateral agreements with individual European countries and Middle Eastern countries. But you can see there's unfortunately a downward trend, and that depends primarily on the American side."
Background:
- The same day, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine will receive new radars for its air defence systems, following a call with French President Emmanuel Macron.
- According to the Financial Times, US President Donald Trump turned down Zelenskyy's request for hundreds of additional Patriot interceptor missiles, citing America's own needs in the Middle East.
- Trump has also backtracked after earlier positive signals that he might grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot missiles, saying he has not yet made a final decision.

Russia withdraws ambassador to UK as Kremlin ratchets pressure over Ukraine support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:37:39 UTC
19:37:39 KST

Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, it has emerged, as the Kremlin continues to try to put pressure on Britain over its support for Ukraine.
Andrey Kelin left last month after seven years in the diplomatic post, according to the Russian embassy in London.
Tensions have since ratcheted up, with a warning by the embassy last week of “consequences” after it emerged Britain was supplying attack drones to Kyiv.
Russia’s online list of “senior diplomatic staff” in the UK now includes only Vasily A Tsyganov, chargé d’affaires at the embassy.
A gap between ambassadors was not unprecedented, said John Foreman, a former British defence attache in Moscow and Kyiv. But he said in a post on X: “The embassy’s strident ‘consequences’ statement this week and the huge deterioration of bilateral relations since 2018 and especially since the start of the war make me wonder if Moscow will permanently downgrade the relationship this time, by default by not replacing him.”
A spokesperson for the embassy said the Kremlin had concluded Kelin’s diplomatic mission on 21 July. “As for the state of Russia-UK relations across all areas, they have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative,” they added.
A spokesperson told the Sunday Times Kelin had made efforts to preserve channels of communication with the UK and accused the government of choosing a “path of confrontation” with Russia.
“He left Britain in the hope that a more constructive and respectful dialogue could eventually be restored, should the UK reconsider its policies towards our country,” they said, adding that the Kremlin had not yet put forward a replacement candidate.
The embassy later issued a statement saying there was nothing in the comments to imply that Russia intended to downgrade diplomatic relations with the UK.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “This is a matter for the Russian ministry of foreign affairs. We have an ambassador and embassy in Moscow to engage and raise concerns with the Russian government.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, which has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal and unprovoked invasion.”
Shaun Pinner, a former British soldier who later fought alongside Ukrainian marines before he was captured and held for a time by Russian forces, said there would be arguments that Kelin’s exit had been a “dangerous erosion” of communication between Britain and Russia but he added that this had not been the case for some time in reality.
He said: “If Moscow refuses to meaningfully engage, rebuffs attempts at communication and uses its diplomatic presence primarily to repeat Kremlin narratives, then we shouldn’t pretend we’re witnessing some functioning diplomatic relationship.”
Kelin has repeated Kremlin narratives in interviews to British media in recent years. In one on Sky News in June, he said that Russia “cannot lose” the war in Ukraine. He joined the Soviet diplomatic service in 1979.
Russia stepped up its rhetoric towards the UK last week after Ministry of Defence sources indicated a report that two drones made by British companies had been used by Ukraine’s military to attack targets inside Russia was true.
The Russian embassy, seeking to maximise the impact of its remarks, added in a widely reported statement on Telegram: “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer.”

Unknown

Norway to maintain Ukraine aid at around $9 billion in 2027, PM says
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre made the announcement during his speech at a ceremony to raise Ukraine’s National Flag, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
The Norwegian Prime Minister said that when speaking about the resilience of Ukrainians, its cost should not be forgotten. He noted that air raid sirens, nights spent in shelters, funerals, and separated families have become a tragic daily reality for millions of Ukrainians.
“Norway's support will continue. Backed by all parties in Parliament. In 2027 we will maintain support at the same level as this year, approximately 9 billion USD. The support is broad: military, humanitarian and financial. It will follow Ukrainian priorities,” Støre said.
He stressed that supporting and rebuilding Ukraine is not simply aid, but an investment in Europe’s own security.
“Later today, Norway and Ukraine will sign a declaration of strategic partnership. It puts our cooperation on a long-term footing. It is a partnership of mutual benefit,” the Prime Minister emphasized.
As reported, under the Nansen Support Programme, Norway is providing Ukraine with $9 billion in military and civilian assistance this year.
On Sunday, August 23, Ukraine is celebrating National Flag Day. In addition to Norway’s Prime Minister, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, President of Lithuania Gitanas Nausėda, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs arrived in Kyiv.

Zelenskyy rejects elections during war, warns of division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:33:44 UTC
19:33:44 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected calls to hold elections during the ongoing war with Russia, saying on Saturday that a vote under current conditions would be too dangerous.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in remarks made public on Sunday.
Ukraine has suspended elections under martial law, a measure that remains widely supported as the country continues to fight against Russia since 2022.
Zelenskyy made the comments during a briefing with journalists on Saturday, his first in several months amid a series of political crises.
Former minister calls for elections
The debate intensified after former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called this week for a way to organise elections, without proposing a specific roadmap.
Fedorov’s call came after Zelenskyy dismissed him, prompting thousands of people to take to the streets and some of the former minister’s supporters to distance themselves from him.
Experts have cited several obstacles to holding elections, including how soldiers, millions of Ukrainian refugees and residents of occupied territories would vote, as well as the risk of Russian disinformation.
Only 15 percent of Ukrainians believe elections should be held before the end of hostilities, according to a poll by the Kiev Institute of Sociology.
Zelenskyy criticised Fedorov during the briefing, saying he believed the former minister was moving towards “wrong things”.
Zelenskyy warns against division
The election debate comes as Ukraine and Russia exchange missile and drone attacks daily.
Zelenskyy said people had the right to protest but warned against what he called “disrespectful” attitudes towards members of the armed forces.
“Since when has marketing started to outweigh the people who are giving their lives?” he said.
He said society and the military must remain united and warned of the risk of “dangerous developments” if divisions deepen.
“We must acknowledge that there is this risk — that there may be movement in that direction, toward dangerous developments,” Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine Through the Eyes of the World: Artists Carry War, Memory, Home Across Borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Today, in a small coastal city of Pula, Croatia’s largest Ukrainian flag – stretching 35 meters – found its way to the city’s old-town square, marking 35 years since Ukraine declared its independence in 1991.
Three years have passed since Ukrainians displaced by the war first gathered to mark their country’s independence. The Cultural and Artistic Society of Ukrainians in Istria, Vatra, has organized the annual celebration ever since.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year’s event marks the fourth consecutive commemoration in Pula, led by Olesia Rusinova.
The celebration of that same identity now stands in sharp juxtaposition with the country well into its fifth year of defending itself against Russia’s aggression.
For Ukrainians in exile, the public commemoration reflects a deeper, private reality; though they now live in Croatia, they remain tied to Ukraine by an invisible thread, its tension palpable in their work, memories and everyday lives – further shaping what remains of their sense of home.
Olesia, an Odesa-born professional artist and performer, and Valeriia Pohrebniak Bednaić, a Kyiv-born ceramic and art teacher with a master’s degree in fine arts, spoke with Kyiv Post about displacement, identity and the effort – at times a struggle – to keep Ukraine visible and alive abroad.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Fedorov Says Corruption Prevents Ukraine’s Victory
“I feel like a bridge between Ukraine and Croatia,” Olesia said.
“You must learn the language, customs and traditions of the country where you arrive. Only then can you bring something of your own. Otherwise, what makes you any different from the occupier?”
Knocking on all doors
Before coming to Croatia, Olesia had already built a life rooted in Ukrainian culture.
She worked at the Odesa Academic Theater of Young Spectators and later earned a master’s degree in performing arts from the Luhansk State Academy of Culture and Arts in Kyiv.
Her connection with Ukrainian tradition began early. At 16, she had already released a video for a traditional Ukrainian song and helped coordinate an Independence Day festival in Odesa. Her first job was in a shop selling traditional Ukrainian clothing.
She left Ukraine for a holiday on Feb. 21; three days later, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
“People tell me that it is good that I am outside Ukraine – this way, I can be a voice for Ukrainian people.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Having arrived by car during the night, she said she went knocking on the doors of local communities and cultural centers the following day. “This is just who I am. I knock. Some doors open, some don’t,” Olesia said.
Within two weeks, she staged “Ukrainian Season,” a performance about Ukraine and its culture at the Dr. Inat Theater. Within five months, she had learned Croatian by ear and was talking on local radio.
Her later performances included “How Are You?” about emotions people conceal, and “(Un)plugged,” which examined propaganda and manipulation.
“People can no longer distinguish what is true from what is not,” Olesia said. “They often believe what is a lie, which we could see clearly from this war. That is propaganda for me – a system that suffocates you and closes your eyes.”
Carrying Ukraine
Olesia wears Ukraine openly. Traditional jewelry accompanies even her simplest clothes: rings, bracelets in national colors and handmade floral wreaths.
Pointing to her rings, she describes a dragon breathing fire and protecting Ukraine, while her bracelet bears the country’s national emblem.
“I carry Ukraine every day through jewelry,” she said. “For me, identity is not only the songs, folklore, traditional dress and jewelry. It is what you feel inside.”
In many ways, Olesia’s work has entered Istria’s cultural record. Now held by the Ethnographic Museum of Istria in Pazin, she created a Ukrainian traditional-style wreath placing her art within an institution dedicated to preserving the region’s cultural heritage.
The wreath reflects the role she has taken on in Pula – not simply preserving Ukrainian tradition abroad, but also allowing it to enter into the dialogue with the culture of the place she now calls a second home.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Local media first called her “a Ukrainian in Pula,” then “a Ukrainian with a Pula address.” Eventually, she became known as “the Pula Ukrainian” – Pulska Ukrajinka in Croatian – a label she accepted wholeheartedly as an expression of her belonging to both places.
Her cultural work reflects that dual identity. In 2024, Olesia released her first album, blending traditional Ukrainian music with original lyrics in a genre she describes as folktronica. Her 2025 mini-album, “Kolo,” brought Ukrainian and Balkan folklore into the same musical space.
Separately, she hosts a program called “Cultural Bridge [Kulturni Most]” as part of the European Solidarity Corps (ESC) program at Radio Rojc.
“I feel like a crossing between two cultures – someone who can help Ukrainians who have just arrived and connect Croatians with them,” Olesia said.
Valeriia, too, carries Ukraine through her art, but in quieter, tactile forms. In the first two years after the full-scale invasion, she marked every ceramic piece with a small blue-and-yellow heart – a sign of identity and solidarity embedded in the objects leaving her studio.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Valeriia’s business, “Sea of Cups,” continues to present itself as a space for Ukrainian and Croatian art. Its website tells the story of its founders and their connection to Ukraine, while a donation board for Ukraine’s military in the space directs visitors toward supporting Ukraine.
A life between homes
Valeriia’s connection to Istria began more than a decade ago, after her parents bought a small apartment there. Her father had initially considered buying property in Crimea, but Russia occupied the peninsula shortly after.
After February 2022, the journey to Croatia became one of escape. A trip that would normally have taken around a day lasted seven days amid long lines of cars leaving Ukraine.
Through her Instagram account, “Valerie Creating Things,” she began posting about the war alongside her art. She recalled posting from a shelter when the first explosions were heard.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“I was very afraid [to relocate to another country], of course. But the page helped me,” she said. “People started sharing my posts, and I found connections in Croatia that helped me find a job in a gallery.”
She later met and moved in with her husband, a Croatian national, and opened a business. Learning Croatian regulations and navigating bureaucracy were difficult for both. “I don’t think I would have opened the business without my husband,” she said.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Her child will go to kindergarten and school in Croatia, she said, and she does not plan to leave. Yet Kyiv remains her true home. Her parents still live there: though her father is now retired, her mother still works at a Ukrainian university.
“I live a double life,” Valeriia said. “My day starts with reading the news.”
She says she has not yet found a real community in Croatia. The war, she said, can feel like an invisible barrier between her and the people around her.
“I feel a big wall between myself and the people I speak to, as if the war is a wall,” she said. “No one wants to ask questions or talk about it. When I mention the war, people feel uncomfortable. There is no real connection – only small talk.”
“Still, I do not plan on leaving Croatia,” she added.
Country seen only through Russia
For both women, the war did not begin in 2022.
It began in 2014, with Russia’s occupation of Crimea and the outbreak of war in eastern Ukraine – a period often eclipsed abroad by the full-scale invasion eight years later.
“People did not know about the beginning of the war. They did not know about Crimea,” Valeriia said. “We expected a big war to happen. But then nothing happened. No one stepped in to protect Ukraine; our land was simply taken.”
She recalled repeatedly having to explain where Ukraine was to people she met abroad.
“Even in Europe, people rarely knew anything about Ukraine,” Valeriia said. “Before the war, I had to tell people it was near Russia.”
Language was also part of that erasure. Both women said that before the full-scale invasion, people often treated Ukrainian as interchangeable with Russian or were surprised to hear it spoken.
Both Valeriia and Olesia switched entirely to Ukrainian language in 2014, after Russia’s occupation of Crimea. It was a personal act of protest.
It is worth noting that Ukrainian and Croatian languages share more similarities than Ukrainian and Russian do. While Russians cannot understand Ukrainians, they said, Ukrainian and Croatians share between 60 and 80 percent linguistic similarities.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“I was born in 2000, and the Orange Revolution was in 2004,” Olesia said with a laugh. “My whole life has been revolutions.”
“Before, when we were not so present in public space, Ukraine was recognized through famous people,” Olesia said. “Now that we are everywhere, people recognize Ukraine through those they know personally and through what they do.”
Olesia confirmed Ukraine’s previous invisibility, saying that many people thought Ukraine was “something in Russia,” rather than a country with its own language, culture and political history.
She also recalled how distant the war in Donbas could feel even within Ukraine. At university, she had friends from Donetsk, but she said many of their fellow students did not grasp what they had escaped.
“You knew they had fled, but you did not know exactly what from,” she said. “It was like watching a movie. I think it’s the same for Europeans now. They don’t understand what people were really living through.”
For Olesia, the first images from the Bucha massacre after the Russian occupation were a moment of unbearable rupture.
“I wanted to scream and show it to the whole world,” she said. “But everyone’s life simply continued.”
Visibility with a cost
The full-scale invasion made Ukraine significantly more visible to the world. But both women say that visibility has weakened as the war has continued.
“In 2022, there was more compassion,” Valeriia said. “People shared content about the war, spoke to me and wanted to help. Now, people are more unhappy about it.”
“Sometimes I feel that the fact I am Ukrainian works against me,” she continued.
She does not, however, conceal her identity. Her work continues to blend Ukrainian and Croatian art together. 
                                                                                                                                                                         
Olesia also sees a growing anxiety around public visibility. Under online announcements for Ukrainian events, she has read hostile comments telling Ukrainians to “go back to Putin.”
Yet she believes silence is not an answer.
“People ask, ‘Why should we be loud again? Why should we disturb others?’” Olesia said. “But it’s not disturbing people. It’s informing them about what’s happening in Ukraine.”
War beyond the front line
Memories of Yugoslavia’s violent breakup remain deeply felt across the Balkans, even after decades have passed. A shared nation, once framed around “brotherhood and unity,” dissolved into wars marked by ethnic cleansing, mass displacement, war crimes and genocide.
That experience, including Croatia’s own war of independence fought throughout 1991-95, has helped shape the empathy most Ukrainians encounter in Pula.
Olesia recalls cultural workers providing space, equipment and support without charge because of this. She also learned one of her first Croatian words: polako.
“What I learned most from Croatians is to live slowly,” she said. But the war does not slow down for those whose families remain in Ukraine.
Olesia says Ukrainians have learned to work, laugh and perform while carrying the knowledge that their cities are under attack. “If a Ukrainian is smiling, it does not mean they are fine,” she said. “It means they have made every effort to smile.”
Through art, language, grief, work and ordinary routines, Ukraine remains – carried by the people who have rebuilt their lives abroad without ever fully leaving home behind.

Macron hosts Saudi's MBS for visit ranging from esports to Mideast
French President Emmanuel Macron welcomes Saudi crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman on Sunday for a two-day visit set to range from esports to the war in the Middle East.
Several agreements on health, transport and energy will be signed on the second day of the visit on Monday, according to a French presidential official, underlining the strength of the Paris-Riyadh relationship.
But the visit will kick off in a different style on Sunday evening from 1800 GMT with Macron hosting the Saudi strongman - known as MBS - at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup hosted by Paris.
The event, which brings together the leading performers in esports ranging from computer games to chess and has been eagerly backed by MBS, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time.
The French presidential official declined to comment on whether the agreements could touch on a vast theme park known as Dragons Ball, backed by a Saudi fund, which is mooted for the Val-d'Oise region outside Paris.
Saudi Arabia is also set to host a string of key global events, notably the Expo 2030 and above all the football World Cup in 2034.
Rights on agenda?
Saudi Arabia, a close US ally which has a history of tensions with Iran, is also closely watching developments in the Islamic republic in the wake of the US-Israeli war.
On Monday afternoon, MBS and Macron are to chair the first meeting of the Saudi-French strategic partnership council.
Macron and MBS "will discuss key regional issues, in a context calling for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners to foster stability and peace" in the Middle East, according to Macron's office.
It remains unclear if rights will feature high on the agenda, some eight years after dissident Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi was killed and dismembered inside Riyadh's Istanbul consulate in 2018.
A United Nations investigation described Khashoggi's death as an "extrajudicial killing for which Saudi Arabia is responsible".
US intelligence agencies determined that MBS had "approved" the operation that led to Khashoggi's killing. Riyadh denies this, blaming rogue operatives.
In December 2021, Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet MBS in Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Khashoggi killing. The Saudi crown prince has made multiple visits to France since then.

Elena Teslova
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
The most realistic window for a diplomatic settlement to end Russia's war with Ukraine is late 2026 through summer 2027, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
Speaking at a ceremony marking National Flag Day in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said the two sides remained divided over the issue of Ukraine’s withdrawal from Donbas as part of efforts to reach a settlement.
"We believe that this is the most active stage at which diplomacy can lead to the end of the war. It's the end of this year and the end of summer 2027," he said.
One cease-fire option being discussed with the US and Europe involves the reciprocal withdrawal of forces and the creation of a buffer “free economic zone” administered by a third party, he said.
Ukraine is ready to discuss a mutual halt to strikes on energy and agricultural infrastructure, he added.
Leaders of the Scandinavian countries and the Baltic States took part in Sunday's event.
Defense budget shortfall
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine faces a $27 billion shortfall in its defense budget, with $8 billion to $10 billion needed in advance to cover the beginning of 2027.
Nearly $20 billion more is required for military salaries, payments to families of service members killed on the frontlines, and other expenses, he said.
The Ukrainian president said Kyiv has not yet reached mass production of its own ballistic missiles due to technical issues, adding that two companies are working on the program.
“When there is mass production, then we will be able to deliver painful strikes against the enemy in response to their terror,” he said.
According to him, Ukraine could begin producing missiles for Patriot air defense systems jointly with Raytheon.
He said the US company had already held an initial technical meeting with Ukrainian officials, while Ukrainian defense company Fire Point was selected as a project partner.
Zelenskyy noted that Kyiv expects an assessment in the coming weeks on the project's timeline and feasibility.
He also announced deliveries of French air defense radars and a SAMP/T system in the fall, adding that agreements on additional Aster 30 missiles are expected to be signed in September.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had reached an agreement with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on the delivery of 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027-2028, noting that PAC-2 missiles can also intercept ballistic missiles, although more interceptors are required for such engagements.
According to him, Ukraine needs about 360 Patriot missiles for the winter period, while global annual production is about 600.
Rules out election during war
Zelenskyy also said SpaceX founder Elon Musk had rejected Ukraine's request to use Starlink satellite communications over Russian territory for defense-related purposes.
At the same time, Zelensky said that Ukraine is now receiving more encouraging signals from Musk's team and continues to seek a resolution.
He also confirmed that Ukraine has been deliberately targeting the warehouses of Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer.
"Why do we hit Wildberries in particular? Because this is both the supply of military goods and a lot of money," he said.
On domestic politics, Zelenskyy described holding elections during the war as a “tsunami for the state” that could divide Ukraine.
He also said anti-corruption agencies should operate independently.
Commenting on an investigation involving senior officials in the presidential office, Zelenskyy said there had been sufficient grounds to dismiss presidential office deputy head Iryna Mudra immediately after searches were conducted at her premises.

Experimental compound helps burn fat without muscle loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:24:17 UTC
19:24:17 KST

Experimental compound helps burn fat without muscle loss
Scientists found a compound that made mice burn more energy and lose fat without significant muscle loss.
- Date:
- August 23, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- A decades-old compound may point to a new way of treating obesity by making the body burn more energy rather than simply reducing appetite. In mice, TOFA increased energy use by as much as 18%, reduced body fat without significant muscle loss, and improved blood sugar, triglycerides, and fatty liver disease. It also produced stronger results when combined with GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound.
- Share:
GLP-1 medications have transformed the treatment of obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease over the past several years. Drugs sold as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound can produce substantial weight loss while helping patients control blood sugar.
But these medications can also cause problems. Some patients experience nausea and other gastrointestinal side effects. Because GLP-1 drugs reduce appetite and food intake, they may also contribute to nutritional deficiencies and loss of muscle, potentially increasing the risk of frailty and other long-term health issues.
Researchers at UC Berkeley are now investigating a very different strategy for treating obesity and diabetes. Instead of reducing the amount of energy a person consumes, their approach is designed to increase the amount of energy the body uses by raising metabolic activity.
A Different Way to Target Weight Loss
In a study published August 21 in Science Advances, the team reports that a molecular compound called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA) can interfere with the production of lipids such as cholesterol and triglycerides. At the same time, it activates genes that encourage cells to use fat for fuel and produce more energy.
In experiments with mice, TOFA improved insulin sensitivity and glucose control, reduced triglyceride levels, and improved signs of fatty liver disease. Obese mice treated with the compound lost fat while showing no significant reduction in lean muscle mass.
"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second."
Reviving a Compound First Discovered Decades Ago
TOFA was initially discovered in the 1970s and belongs to a group of compounds known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds reduce the body's production of lipids.
Several ACC inhibitors have advanced into mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic disease. One important obstacle is that many of these compounds can increase triglyceride levels, which may raise cardiovascular risk.
The UC Berkeley team found that TOFA behaves differently. In addition to acting as an ACC inhibitor, it activates PPARα and PPARδ, cellular receptors that switch on genes involved in taking up fat and burning it for energy.
In mice, this effect increased energy use by as much as 18% without causing the animals to become more physically active or increasing their body temperature. The researchers also found that TOFA did not produce the rise in triglycerides seen with some other ACC inhibitors, possibly because of its combined effects on lipid production and energy metabolism.
"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," said study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively."
One Compound Outperformed a Two-Drug Approach
The researchers also tested whether they could reproduce TOFA's effects with two separate compounds. They gave mice one compound designed to suppress lipid production and another intended to increase energy expenditure.
That combination did not improve overall metabolic health as effectively as TOFA by itself, suggesting that TOFA's particular combination of actions may be important to its effects.
The team then examined whether TOFA could be paired with existing GLP-1 medications. These included semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic or Wegovy, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound.
In mice, combining TOFA with these GLP-1 drugs produced larger improvements in body weight, glucose control, insulin levels, and triglycerides than either treatment produced on its own.
"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.
Human Testing Is Still Needed
Despite the promising results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA has so far been studied only in animals. Its safety and effectiveness in humans remain unknown and will need to be evaluated in future studies.
With support from Berkeley's life sciences entrepreneurship ecosystem, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck, the researchers have created a company called ReRx Therapeutics to help move the research toward potential use in patients.
The research was funded through discretionary funds from UC Berkeley, with additional assistance from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.
Additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

A multi-functional oral small molecule targeting energy and lipid metabolism to treat obesity and related metabolic disorders. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (34) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3119

Ukraine: Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections
August 23, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that holding elections in his country amid the full-scale Russian invasion would be highly dangerous, in remarks made in response to a call from the former defense minister to organize a vote.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks released on Sunday.
Under martial law, elections are currently suspended in the country as it fights the invading Russian forces. The measure has wide public support.
What did Zelenskyy say about the proposed election?
"If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war," Zelenskyy said in the firm rejection of the proposal by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov made the call a month after being fired by Zelenskyy as defense minister.
Fedorov enjoys significant support among younger Ukrainians, thousands of whom have been calling for his reinstatement, with some saying he could seek to challenge Zelenskyy if an election did take place.
However, a recent poll showed that Zelenskyy would still be more popular as a presidential candidate.
Zelenskyy was critical of Fedorov in his remarks, saying: "I believe he is going himself — or is being pushed — toward wrong things."
Russia planning mass mobilization — Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy also said that Kyiv believed Russia was planning to mobilize 300,000 more troops for its invasion after parliamentary elections take place in September.
He added that Moscow might draft hundreds of thousands more in 2027 as it seeks to capture the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, one of its main strategic goals.
Agreement on missile interceptors from Germany
As Ukraine continues to come under intense missile attacks from its neighbor, Zelenskyy also spoke of having struck an agreement with Germany on the supply of 600 Patriot PAC-2 missile interceptors for 2027-28.
The announcement comes after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Ukraine on Saturday.
The US Patriots are the only weapon in Kyiv's arsenal that can take on Russia's Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic missiles, but ammunition for the system is running short.
France on Saturday also promised to deliver new interceptor missiles.
As Europe seeks to fill the gap left by a US that, under Donald Trump, has shown ever more reluctance to help Ukraine, Norway has also said it plans to give another 85 billion Norwegian crowns ($9.2 billion; €7.8 billion) in financial support to Kyiv in the 2027 fiscal year.

Stubb pledges continued support for Ukraine during Kyiv visit
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:19:08 EEST
19:19:08 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb pledged continued support for Ukraine during a visit to Kyiv on Sunday, as Nordic and Baltic leaders gathered for talks on defence, security and further assistance to the country.
Stubb attended Ukraine’s National Flag Day ceremony with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders from Denmark, Norway, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
He drew a parallel between Ukraine’s war with Russia and Finland’s experience during the Second World War.
“We lost Karelia, but we did not lose our freedom and independence,” Stubb said during the ceremony, referring to territory Finland ceded to the Soviet Union.
Stubb said Finland would continue supporting Ukraine for as long as required. He also described Ukraine’s defence as part of Europe’s own security.
“Ukraine is the greatest security guarantee for all of us,” Stubb said. He said European support rested both on the defence of democracy, freedom and the rule of law and on European security interests.
Zelenskyy told those attending the ceremony that Russia would not subjugate Ukraine. He said the blue and yellow colours of the Ukrainian flag represented resistance after periods in which Ukrainian national symbols faced suppression.
The ceremony took place at the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War, near the Mother Ukraine monument in Kyiv.
Stubb travelled to Ukraine with his wife, Suzanne Innes-Stubb.
The delegation also includes Finnish Defence Forces commander Janne Jaakkola and representatives of Finnish companies. Stubb last visited Ukraine in February 2026.
The visit comes as Ukraine prepares to mark 35 years since declaring independence from the Soviet Union on Monday.
Security concerns remain central to the meetings. Russia has carried out repeated missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Ukrainian officials have warned that the country faces shortages of air defence missiles as Russia continues its aerial campaign.
France has agreed to accelerate deliveries of air defence equipment and missiles following talks between Zelenskyy and French President Emmanuel Macron.
Norway also plans to provide 85 billion Norwegian kroner, about €7.8 billion, in financial support to Ukraine over the next year, according to a Norwegian government statement. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine faces a budget shortfall of about €23 billion this year.
The talks in Kyiv also take place amid a renewed debate over elections in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy rejected calls on Sunday to hold elections while the country remains under martial law. He said a wartime vote would risk dividing the country and creating conditions that Russia would seek to exploit.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now would be a tsunami that would divide Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said, according to AFP.
Former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a way to hold elections before the war ends. Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing unnamed sources, that Fedorov has considered running for president or taking another role in a future election campaign.
Ukrainian law blocks national elections while martial law remains in force. Questions also remain over voting arrangements for soldiers, millions of Ukrainians living abroad and people in Russian-occupied territories.
The diplomatic meetings follow another period of strikes by both sides. Russia has attacked Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine has expanded long-range drone strikes against oil facilities and logistics sites inside Russia.
Stubb used his Kyiv address to link Finland’s own history with Ukraine’s current defence.
“You will win, you have won, and we will continue to support you,” he told the Ukrainian audience.

Zelenskyy sought to cast himself as a rampart against division.

Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:16:33 UTC
19:16:33 KST

Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."

Ukraine moves to practical work on ballistic missile defense - Zelenskyy spoke about two key projects
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:14:13 EEST
19:14:13 KST

Ukraine moves to practical work on ballistic missile defense - Zelenskyy spoke about two key projects
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is moving from political agreements to practical work on ballistic missile defense. Kyiv is simultaneously developing the pan-European Freyja shield project and producing its own analogues of the missile used by Patriot systems.
Ukraine is moving from political agreements to practical work on its own anti-ballistic capabilities, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Work is underway in two directions at once - the pan-European Freyja anti-ballistic shield and the production of a Ukrainian analogue of missiles for Patriot, reports UNN.
Details
Our anti-ballistic capabilities have several directions. The European direction is our joint Freyja project with Europe, and we are counting heavily on this program. The other direction is Raytheon. We are talking about the possibility of building a Ukrainian missile for the Patriot system. They view this idea positively. They selected a company that can do this - Fire Point. I met with Raytheon in the United States, and we agreed to move forward with this project. After that, they held their first technical meeting with the Ukrainian side regarding the details. Now we will wait for their response. I think we will receive it in the coming weeks. We will get an answer regarding the timeline and an understanding of whether it will succeed or not
In addition, the Freyja project is already moving from political agreements to practical work. European companies are beginning to join the technical implementation of the program directly.
The project has now moved from the leaders' positive reaction and willingness to work to the technical level. Companies are beginning to work in this direction in earnest
Earlier, Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh told UNN that Freyja is at the stage of integrating key components into a single system—radars, a launcher, a command center, and the interceptor missile itself. Testing of individual system components is ongoing.
Russia plans to produce 1,300 ballistic missiles per year
Creating two options at once for Ukraine's anti-ballistic protection, which can be integrated into the European security system, is critically important. After all, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Moscow seeks to reach a ballistic missile production rate of "100 per month," or approximately 1,300 per year. Ukraine has information that Russia currently has accumulated 600–630 ballistic missiles.
Russia could have up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year. They currently have 600–630. We have an approximate understanding of the level they expect to reach from today through the end of winter. They could have approximately 100 ballistic missiles per month. They do not have that capability yet. We are working to weaken their military industry; there are relevant tasks involving strikes on military targets and other anti-ballistic sanctions
Thus, the third track of anti-ballistic protection for Ukraine is finding 300 missiles for the Patriot system. Obviously, Russia plans to use all those accumulated missiles to strike civilian populations and Ukrainian businesses.
I wanted to find 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our Air Force is 360. But when 600 are produced per year, 360 is not easy. We are working with countries on additional possibilities. And I would very much like to believe that we will be able to find a way to obtain some small percentage of the U.S. stockpiles, say 5% or 10%. We are ready to pay for these supplies. In other words, America could replenish its stockpile, and we could get through the winter
We remind you
Fire Point is simultaneously expanding its own production base for missile programs. As the company's CEO Iryna Terekh previously said, at the end of 2027 the company plans to launch a solid rocket fuel plant in Denmark with a total area of more than 120,000 square meters.
The facility will be built in several stages. It is intended to supply fuel for FP-7 missiles, FP-7.x interceptors, and boosters for Flamingo. According to Terekh, locating part of the production capabilities in Denmark makes it possible to create a predictable base protected from Russian strikes for scaling up production.
According to Fire Point's estimate, once it reaches its planned capacity, the plant will be able to produce solid propellant each year for more than 4,100 FP-7 ballistic missiles or FP-7.x ballistic interceptors. During martial law, the company's products are primarily planned to be directed toward Ukraine's needs, while subsequently its production capabilities may also serve the European security system.

U.S. Army tests self-driving truck with drone-killing turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:12:44 UTC
19:12:44 KST

- The U.S. Army tested a self-driving Ford F-250 fitted with an Edda counter-drone turret during a Project Sandhills 2.0 live-fire exercise at Fort Bragg on August 18, 2026.
- The vehicle combines Forterra's AutoDrive autonomy system with a 9 Mothers-built turret designed to shoot down fast-moving drones at 10 to 100 meters.
A Ford F-250 that can drive itself carried a shotgun-armed drone-killing turret onto a live-fire range at Fort Bragg on August 18, 2026, the latest test in a U.S. Army program built to get engineers out of the blast radius during breaching operations.
The vehicle, tested at Range 63 as part of Project Sandhills 2.0, runs on the Forterra AutoDrive autonomy stack and carries an Edda counter-unmanned aircraft system turret built by Austin-based 9 Mothers. The Army described the vehicle as carrying modular systems to support automated obstacle reduction while limiting soldiers’ exposure to direct enemy fire.
Obstacle reduction is engineer-speak for clearing lanes through minefields, wire, and other barriers so troops and vehicles can move forward. It is dangerous, deliberate work, and it is exactly the kind of task the Army wants a machine doing instead of a soldier.
The Edda turret weighs about 23 kg (50 pounds) and detects drones acoustically, listening for the sound signature of small rotors rather than relying on radar or radio-frequency sensors that a drone can detect in return. Once it picks up a target, an onboard visual tracking system takes over and the turret engages with a shotgun effector, built to hit fast-moving drones roughly 7 inches across at ranges of 10 to 100 m (33 to 328 feet). Because the system stays passive until it fires, it does not broadcast a signal an adversary could use to locate the vehicle first.
Sandhills 2.0 grew out of an earlier Army effort known simply as the Sandhills Project, run by the 20th Engineer Brigade under the XVIII Airborne Corps. That first phase produced the Lancer, an unmanned ground vehicle built on a Polaris Ranger chassis, which the United States later sent to Ukraine. Sandhills 2.0 is meant to move that work from prototype demonstrations to systems the Army can actually field.
Forterra secured the prime contract for Sandhills 2.0’s autonomous breaching and terrain-shaping work on July 31, 2026, after taking part in earlier Army integration exercises. Under that contract, the company is delivering autonomous mission systems built on Ford F-250 trucks, intended to handle zone-clearing and line-charge deployment without a soldier in the vehicle.
The Army’s interest in pairing autonomous breaching vehicles with counter-drone defenses traces directly to Ukraine. First-person-view drones have proliferated on that battlefield, and the United States donated its own breaching vehicles there in 2025. Army officials have said publicly that FPV drones could jeopardize a breaching operation in a future conflict if the vehicles doing that work have no way to defend themselves while they work.
The August 18 test folded the Edda turret onto the autonomous F-250 platform to see whether a single vehicle can clear obstacles and defend itself against drones at the same time, rather than requiring a separate escort or a second vehicle carrying only counter-drone equipment.

China Focus: Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
18:04:52 CST
19:04:52 KST

Ronald Sakolsky (C), Yin Yuzhen (R) and Yin's husband Bai Wanxiang pose for photos at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Ordos on Sunday and was reunited with his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades. Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification. The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen)
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a visit aimed at renewing a friendship with the Chinese people that first took root more than two decades ago.
The 69-year-old will spend part of his stay planting trees alongside his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades.
Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification.
At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life.
The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees.
In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed.
Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert.
Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks.
The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said.
Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students.
Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. ■

Hamas in talks with former Fatah rival Mohammed Dahlan ahead of Palestinian elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:04:06 UTC
19:04:06 KST

Hamas is exploring potential alliances with figures and factions once considered to be on the opposite end of the Palestinian political spectrum, including former Fatah figure Mohammed Dahlan and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), ahead of the Palestinian Legislative Council elections, the terror group and other factions confirmed.
The election, set to be held on November 28, 2026, will be the first Palestinian legislative election in two decades, following Hamas’s takeover of the Gaza Strip a year after the previous election in 2006.
Dahlan met with Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt on Monday to discuss “unity of the national position,” the Democratic Reform Bloc, a breakaway faction of Fatah led by Dahlan, confirmed in a statement.
Hamas chief discussed roadmap for second phase of ceasefire with Dahlan
Imad Mohsen, spokesperson for the Democratic Reform Bloc, said Dahlan and Hayya “discussed in depth and with responsibility all issues concerning our Palestinian arena, foremost among them the efforts to protect our people and strengthen the national position… within the framework of the efforts of the leadership of the movement and the national forces to ensure the unity of the national position and the developments in the negotiation process that led to the approval of the roadmap for implementing the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.”
Dahlan rose to prominence in Palestinian politics as the first head of the Preventive Security Service (PSS). He oversaw the internal intelligence and paramilitary organization until he resigned in 2002 in protest at delayed political reforms.
During that period, Dahlan established himself as a powerful security figure within the Palestinian Authority (PA) and a prominent voice in internal political and security affairs.
Notably, Dahlan has accused both Fatah and Hamas of corruption and was reportedly behind a US-backed plot to unseat Hamas in 2007. Despite this, he began thawing ties with the group in 2017, appearing at public online events with officials from Hamas.
A Hamas official also confirmed to The National news site that the group is forming a “political alliance” with multiple factions, though the official said the matter remained “under study.” Abdel Fattah Dawla, the spokesperson of Fatah, denied that Hamas’s new political alliance held any legitimacy.
Fatah spokesperson denies Hamas alliance is legitimate
“On what political and national basis is this alliance being formed? What are its objectives and what are its points of reference?”
Harel Chorev, a senior researcher at the Moshe Dayan Center specializing in the social and political history of the Palestinians, commented to The Jerusalem Post that Dahlan’s likely temporary connection with Hamas should be seen more as a strategic play by the bloc than a true alliance.
“Dahlan wants to maintain his influence in the Gaza Strip, which he does with the money he brings in. He has no desire to be in second place. So, if an opportunity arises that allows him to take over, he will take over,” Chorev explained.
“In the meantime, he’s keeping all the cards very close to his chest and cooperating for the sake of the people, the civilians, and so on and so forth. But at the end of the day, he has no desire, as I said, to remain instrumental to Hamas’ purposes and not his own.”
On Hamas’s motivation, Chorev theorized that it was likely being pushed along by the more pragmatic figures in the group.
Support for Hamas fell from 35% 10 months ago (32% in the West Bank and 41% in Gaza) to 24% (18% in the West Bank and 33% in Gaza), bringing it level with support for Fatah, according to a survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research published earlier this month.
Asked who they would prefer to succeed Abbas, 16% named Hayya and 15% chose Dahlan.

Gal De Paz cast as Shoshana Damari in new musical about Israeli icon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:03:45 UTC
19:03:45 KST

Singer Gal De Paz, runner-up on this year’s season of Rising Star, has been cast as Israeli musical icon Shoshana Damari in a new biographical musical.
The production, titled Shoshana, marks De Paz’s theatrical acting debut.
The musical is written and directed by Gadi Tzedaka, the artistic director of the Hebrew Theater, where the show is scheduled to premiere in late October.
Shoshana will trace the singer’s cinematic life story through major formative milestones.
The narrative follows her arduous immigration to Israel, early integration struggles, departure from her parental home, marriage, and her lengthy journey toward becoming the “Queen of Hebrew Music.”
Shoshana Damari’s greatest songs return in new stage production
The production features a live orchestra conducted by Yonatan Perlman, soundtracked by Damari’s timeless catalog of anthems, including: “Kalaniyot” (“Anemones”), “Shnei Shoshanim” (“Two Roses”), “Hayu Zmanim” (“There Were Times”), and “Or” (“Light”).
“When they approached me, my immediate thought was the immense weight of responsibility,” De Paz shared regarding the casting.
“Shoshana Damari is part of Israel’s DNA. Coming from music rather than acting, I felt an opportunity to inhabit the character through the medium I know best – voice, body, stage, and emotion.”
Tzedaka cited De Paz’s specific performance qualities as crucial for the role, noting shared personality traits such as “humor, sensuality, boldness, and professional perfectionism.”
He added that rehearsals have uncovered a deep emotional capability and an extraordinary stage presence that revitalizes the legendary figure.
From Rising Star to the stage: De Paz’s musical journey
The 39-year-old De Paz brings a seasoned musical resume to the stage, despite her rookie status in acting.
Born in Eilat, she has been an active recording and touring artist for 25 years.
She is widely recognized as the frontwoman for The De Paz Band and a member of the collective Lucille Crew, boasting a discography of 11 independent and collaborative albums.
Her industry accolades include opening for Aerosmith at Tel Aviv’s Park HaYarkon in 2017 and collaborating with veteran rockers like Shalom Hanoch and Dudu Tassa.
Her mainstream breakthrough came earlier this year on Rising Star, where she secured second place behind winner Noam Bettan.
The production will officially launch its run in Or Akiva, followed by performances in Kfar Saba, Rishon Lezion, and Petah Tikva.

US military paper 'Stars and Stripes' warns about threat to independence after Pentagon fires staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:03:39 UTC
19:03:39 KST

The chair of the Stars and Stripes Publisher Advisory Board warned Friday that the Pentagon’s firing of senior staff threatens the US military newspaper’s editorial independence after its publisher, editor-in-chief, and a reporter received separation notices.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
“The Publisher Advisory Board is deeply concerned that these actions further threaten to interrupt the editorial independence that is essential to Stars and Stripes’ credibility and its ability to serve the military community with trusted, independent journalism,” Chair Rufus Friday said.
“We hope that the House Armed Services and Senate Armed Services Committees seek explanations to these actions,” he added.
Publisher Max Lederer, who announced his retirement this week, received a separation notice from the Defense Department and told employees in a farewell memo that he disagreed with the decision.
Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte also received notices Friday. Slavin said he and Korte were fired for participating in an interview with CBS News in which he argued that censorship of Stars and Stripes would be unacceptable.
“I am working for Stars and Stripes. Not for the Pentagon,” Korte told CBS’s Sunday Morning. “Not for any administration. Not for any policymaker. I am here to cover the military community.”
“I stand by the principle that Stars and Stripes should remain independent for service members,” Slavin told The Washington Post on Friday.
The Pentagon confirmed the firings and said the three employees have five days to appeal. Neither Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth nor the Pentagon commented further on the dismissals. The Trump administration has criticized the publication over alleged ideological bias.
US Defense Department aiming to eliminate 'woke distractions'
The Defense Department announced plans in January to overhaul Stars and Stripes and eliminate what it called “woke distractions.” Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the publication would be returned to its “original mission” of reporting for US service members. The Pentagon fired the publication’s congressionally mandated ombudsman in April. She sued the government on First Amendment grounds in June.
This month, the Pentagon installed active-duty Navy Capt. William Urban. Senate Democrats opposed the move in a letter to Hegseth, arguing it could further compromise the newspaper’s independence.
Stars and Stripes was first published during the Civil War and has continuously covered the US military community since World War II.

Six crimes vs. 1,246: inside Israel’s safest and most dangerous neighborhoods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
10:02:06 UTC
19:02:06 KST

They represent two extremes of the same Israeli reality. South Rothschild in Tel Aviv is a bustling nightlife and commercial district that ynet’s crime index ranks as the most dangerous neighborhood in Israel. At the opposite end is Complex 200 in Hod Hasharon, a quiet residential enclave ranked as the country’s safest.
What makes the comparison especially striking is their size. South Rothschild has 2,704 residents, while Complex 200 has 2,657. But that is where the similarities end.
In 2025, South Rothschild recorded 1,246 criminal offenses, compared with just six in Complex 200. A visit to both neighborhoods reveals how dramatically different urban environments can shape everyday perceptions of safety.
‘We don’t walk around here at night’
South Rothschild has undergone a striking transformation in recent years. Once a gray industrial area, it has become a fashionable urban district filled with boutiques, furniture and ceramics studios, bars, restaurants, wine venues and music.
Alongside that revival, however, is a very different reality.
According to ynet’s crime index, based on police data analyzed by Israeli real estate information company Madlan, South Rothschild was Israel’s most dangerous neighborhood in 2025. Its 1,246 recorded offenses amounted to 460.8 crimes per 1,000 residents, despite representing a roughly 10% decline from the previous year.
Among neighborhoods with more than 2,500 residents, it ranked 779th and last for safety.
People who live and work in the neighborhood describe a place where trendy businesses and urban neglect, nightlife and fear can exist only meters apart.
Alona, who works at a hummus restaurant on Levontin Street and has lived in the neighborhood for two years, said encounters with homeless people have become part of everyday life.
One night, while walking her dog near Allenby and Levontin streets, she said a woman began shouting abuse at her without apparent reason. Alona initially ignored her, but the woman followed her, shouted, cursed and spat in her direction before eventually throwing what appeared to be yogurt and another drink at her.
Two young men nearby eventually intervened.
Businesses have also adapted to conditions on the street. Nati, who works at a local printing business, described thefts and attempts to enter the premises, as well as vehicle break-ins nearby.
He said he does not feel afraid during the daytime, but the situation changes after dark.
“We don’t walk around here at night,” he said, adding that employees finish work at 4 p.m.
‘The girls can go out without us worrying’
About 15 miles northeast, life in Complex 200 in Hod Hasharon looks very different.
Ranked Israel’s safest neighborhood for 2025, the residential area recorded only six offenses during the entire year, equivalent to 2.3 crimes per 1,000 residents.
The neighborhood occupies roughly 47 acres between Weizmann, Zalman Shazar, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi and Hankin streets. Once agricultural land filled with citrus orchards, construction began there in 1990.
Today it contains about 1,000 homes, combining houses and apartment buildings surrounded by trees, pedestrian areas and traffic-calmed streets. At its center is the Children’s Path, dedicated to the 1.5 million Jewish children murdered in the Holocaust.
Residents say the physical design contributes directly to their sense of security.
“It’s really enjoyable living here,” resident Shir Gilad told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. “There’s a sense of security for children who can go downstairs and play without problems because there are no roads inside the complex.”
Resident Noa Levy also described the neighborhood as exceptionally safe, although she noted that housing prices are high.
“There’s investment in everything around us,” she said. “There’s an internal path, everything is well maintained and everything is close.”
Her sister, who grew up in the neighborhood from the early 2000s, said familiarity between residents also contributes to the atmosphere.
“Even when you take the dog out, there’s no fear because everyone already knows each other,” she said.
Noa Hirsch moved to the neighborhood from Herzliya with her family in 2019 and said its layout was one of the main attractions.
“As a mother, it’s a relief that when my daughters go to friends in the neighborhood, I don’t have to worry because they don’t need to cross a road,” she said. “I know they’re inside the community.”
South Rothschild and Complex 200 have almost identical numbers of residents. Yet one recorded more than 200 times as many crimes as the other in 2025.
The contrast illustrates how profoundly the character of an urban environment can shape daily life: in one neighborhood, workers organize their routines around when they feel comfortable being outside; in the other, parents describe allowing their children to move around the community with almost no concern.
