Congress MP Jairam Ramesh questions delay in formal closure of Monsoon Session
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Sunday questioned the “abnormal” delay in proroguing the Monsoon Session of Parliament, noting that the time gap between adjournment and prorogation is generally two to four days, but the Monsoon Session is yet to be prorogued after being adjourned on August 13.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh questioned whether the delay was because Union Home Minister Amit Shah was still looking for a two-thirds majority to get the delimitation-linked Constitutional amendment bill passed in a special session.The government, for its part, has denied any plans to convene a special session."The time gap between the adjournment of the Lok Sabha sine die and its prorogation is generally two to four days - although there are many instances when adjournment and prorogation have taken place on the very same day. Ten days have gone by since this Lok Sabha was adjourned sine die but still there is no information on its prorogation," Ramesh posted on X.
He acknowledged that the Monsoon Session in 2015 was prorogued 28 days after adjournment and the gap in 2021 was 20 days. However, there were no "diabolical moves afoot then," the Congress Rajya Sabha MP added.Ramesh linked the delay to the possibility of the Centre calling a special session to pass a major legislation, possibly the Delimitation Bill.
"What explains the abnormal delay now? Is the Union Home Minister still in search of his बहुकलंकित 2/3rd majority to get the Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation passed in a Special Session?" he asked.The Monsoon Session of Parliament began on July 20 and was adjourned sine die on August 13, its scheduled last day. It was largely washed out amid an impasse between the government and the Opposition over issues including the alleged Delhi Police brutality against students during their march to Parliament on the first day of the session and the alleged theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.
Monsoon Session awaits formal closure
Ramesh's post comes as the prorogation notification for the Monsoon Session had not been issued as of Sunday morning, meaning it is yet to formally end.According to constitutional provisions, the President convenes and prorogues Parliament sessions on the recommendation of the government.
Speculation over the Centre's next move on the delimitation-linked Women's Reservation Bill has continued after Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay raised the issue at the August 21 Southern Zonal Council meeting in Mahabalipuram, chaired by Shah.“I urge the Union government to provide a clear legislative assurance that no state will suffer a reduction in its percentage of representation in Parliament on account of its success in population stabilisation,” Vijay said.His remarks indicated a shift from the categorical opposition to delimitation expressed through the resolution he moved in the Tamil Nadu Assembly on August 12.However, Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar, who also attended the Mahabalipuram meeting, demanded that the central government retain the existing number of Lok Sabha seats — 543 — for the next 25 years.

Australia records 1st case of bird flu in mammal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:10:22 UTC
16:10:22 KST

Aamir Latif
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Australia on Sunday confirmed its first case of bird flu in a mammal after a long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia tested positive for the virus, local media reported.
Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins told reporters that the seal was found at Beachport, 300 kilometers south of the state capital Adelaide, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins said.
The infection was likely caused by exposure to infected wild birds or their shared environment, she said, adding that the detection did not appear to be associated with any other sick or dead marine mammals.
There have now been 298 positive H5 bird flu cases recorded in Australia since the outbreak, with 194 of those in South Australia.
"At this stage there is no evidence of infection in our poultry or agriculture systems," Collins said.
South Australia Environment Minister Emily Bourke said there were "devastating numbers" of detections in the state, with the fur seal case "something we always knew would be coming."
She said there is "no cure" or ability to stop bird flu, but the government is working very closely with the federal government on its national vaccination program.
She urged pet owners to keep their dogs on leads and cats indoors.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said in comments published on Saturday that Kyiv had opened “Pandora's box” with its strikes on Russian economic targets, saying that Russia would hit back at Ukraine's “most sensitive economic sectors.”
Ukraine has this summer escalated a campaign of drone strikes targeting Russian economic infrastructure, including oil refineries and online retailers' warehouses, seeking to destroy infrastructure it says is central to Russia's war effort.
Russia has responded with strikes against Ukrainian economic infrastructure, including Ukrainian grain exports via the Black Sea.
“The Kyiv regime set out to damage our economy. What did it do? It opened this Pandora’s box itself. Well then, expect a response targeting your most sensitive economic sectors,” Putin said in comments to a Russian state television journalist.

“We do face challenges regarding the shipment of our goods, but we will resolve these issues. Consequently, there will be no shortage on the global market,” Putin said.
Russia and Ukraine had previously adhered to a Turkish-brokered deal to protect grain exports on the Black Sea. But Russia exited the deal in 2023.
The Russian leader also restated his position that Moscow is open to peace talks, but only on the basis of “realities on the ground,” rather than what he called “exotic” proposals that he said had been made by Ukraine via intermediaries.

Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
The plan is likely to prompt Tehran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf in a bid to push up oil prices and force Trump to retreat
President Donald Trump is betting new sanctions, a naval blockade and ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can accomplish what thousands of bombs and missiles could not: force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war on US terms.
But like other US efforts to force Iran into capitulation, there is one main problem: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has claimed control of the vital Strait of Hormuz and sent volleys of attack drones across the Gulf, may be impervious to such pressure – and has plenty of ways to retaliate.
A major part of the US effort will come on Monday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to unveil details of a plan designed to shift the conflict from tit-for-tat strikes across the Middle East to full-blown economic isolation – a campaign that could touch nations ranging from China and India to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
Yet significant new economic pressure is likely to prompt Iran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf, including against energy infrastructure, in an attempt to push up oil prices and raise the cost of the US effort, forcing Trump to shift his approach once again.
“If this is actually effective, at some point, Iran will lash out again – they just will have no alternative,” said Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who worked on Iran issues at the State Department and White House National Security Council until last year. “Trump may see this as a different phase of the war, but I don’t think Iran does.”
Since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has repeatedly shown the ability to endure air strikes on thousands of targets, layers of sanctions and a US navy blockade – yet still retain the ability to hit back.

‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

On top of fears about extreme heat and possible jet fuel shortages, Britons planning summer holidays in the EU this year had another thing to worry about – long queues and waiting times caused by the bloc’s new border checks.
The EU digital entry and exit system (EES), which requires non-EU citizens to register and be photographed and fingerprinted on arrival and departure from the Schengen zone, has been technically in full force since April after launching last autumn, but has been beset by teething problems.
Despite reports of passengers facing three-hour delays and missed connections, Brussels rejected calls by airports and airlines to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. However, border police have been allowed to relax requirements if queues become unmanageable under an opt-out that expires next month.
Those who shared with the Guardian their experiences of the system since its introduction highlighted a range of problems and snags.
‘We checked in to Europe, but the EES says we haven’t checked out’
One of the main purposes of the system is to track whether non-EU citizens have spent more than their permitted 90 days in the bloc in a rolling 180-day period.
However, Martin Farrall, a retired university professor, says his EES record failed to record his exit from the Schengen zone and he had to chase the authorities to update it.
In May, the 67-year-old and his wife arrived by ferry at Hoek van Holland at the start of their camping trip in Denmark, both with a full residency allowance.
Martin says the Dutch border police enrolled them into EES “But no entry stamp was made on our passports,” he adds.
“On 30 June, 55 days after entry, we returned to the UK on the Dunkerque-Dover ferry. The French border police asked us where and when we entered Schengen, and we were handed back our passports without an exit stamp.”
Once home, Martin checked his residency tally and found that instead of having 35 days left it was rapidly diminishing.
“It appeared that EES had not been updated to show I’d left the Schengen area,” says Martin, who lives in Warwickshire. He was concerned that he would be registered as an “overstayer” at risk of refusal of entry in future.
He reported the error to the Directorate General for Foreign Nationals in France on 13 July but says he has not received a response..
When Martin checked on his day allowance again on 7 August, the EES website said he had zero days left, but when he looked on 17 August it had updated.
“The EES website now claims I have 34 days left to travel in the 180 window! When I checked my wife’s passport she apparently has 90 days left despite us both having the same travel to Schengen history. So God only knows what’s going on.
“I wonder how many other people who were waved through because of the hold-ups may also be in the same position.”
‘The system obviously wasn’t ready – it’s pretty shambolic’
Nadia, from Greater Manchester, thinks the system is not “communicating with other member states”. She made two trips to Schengen areas this summer with very contrasting experiences.
A trip to Tenerife in June was “quite straightforward”, but her experience in July at Frankfurt airport where she was picking up a connecting flight home, was much less so.
“The queue there was ridiculously long, and there was very limited information,” she says. “People were wandering around trying to work out where they needed to go.
“I’m very well travelled and pretty confident, but even I was slightly unsure and was thinking, is there some other queue I should be joining? There was no one nearby to check with without losing your place.”
Eventually, her passport was checked. “He didn’t actually take fingerprints then,” says Nadia, who is a solicitor. “I think the queue was so long they decided to dispense with that.
“It’s the efficiency of the system I question and the fact that individual member states’ systems do not talk to one another. They shouldn’t need to get information again if you have already gone through.
“It’s pretty shambolic, and I think people missing their flights because of it is just not acceptable, especially when there’s no recourse; it’s not your fault.”
Nadia is also unhappy about having to give her fingerprints repeatedly. “I’ve done it in a few countries now, but it’s something I feel very strongly opposed to,” she says.
“This is not in keeping with the intention of the scheme, which suggests that once registered, you should not have to keep re-entering your biometric data. You also wonder where the information is going – who’s seeing it, who else has access to it?”
‘There should be clearer signage about exemptions’
Evie, originally from Manchester but studying in Munich, says her student visa has caused EES confusion.
“In Munich airport, there are TV screens which explain the function of EES as a system to register ‘visitors’. As I hold an extended-stay visa for the purpose of studying, I would not describe myself as a ‘visitor’ as I can stay in Germany for up to 12 months,” the 23-year-old says.
She says that upon seeing she had a British passport, she was often directed toward the EES queue and had to explain her visa situation, after which she “was normally allowed to stand in the queue with everyone else”.
Evie says this has happened “virtually every time” she has flown in and out of Germany – in December, January, February and April – and believes there should be better signposting to avoid mix-ups, especially given unreliable airport wifi makes accessing online information difficult.
‘You could see people getting anxious’
Kevin and his wife, Christine, travelled to Lanzarote in June but struggled to get the machine to register their details.
“The arrivals hall was packed, but there were loads of machines,” the 75-year-old says. “Some were not working. I noticed people getting angry when their fingerprints would not enter. People started holding their fingers in different positions, and when that didn’t work, they would hit the glass harder.”
He says there was “not much assistance to be found” and when all attempts failed, people queued up to “have it done manually at the kiosk”.
“You could see people getting anxious,” says Kevin, who lives with Christine, 73, in Merseyside. He says the machines eventually registered them both.
The couple’s next trip is to Palma for a cruise, and they are bracing themselves for there to be issues. “We’ll be visiting different countries on the cruise,” Kevin says. “What happens then?”
‘The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me’
Martin, 68, a retired IT worker, said he and his wife struggled to operate the screen to register at Schiphol airport in the Netherlands.
“The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me,” says Martin of their trip at the end of April. “My wife had similar issues with her 71-year-old hands. Older people with drier fingers have trouble with touch screens.”
Eventually, Martin, who lives in Stockport, was sent to manual entry “where they forgot to stamp my passport”.
“When exiting Dusseldorf, the Germans got a bit excited about that and asked how we got into Europe,” he adds. “I just said the Dutch didn’t stamp our passports, and they accepted that.
“The interface is poorly laid out and will confuse the less technical I have an IT background, and it feels like the system was not walked through enough times. It’s a mess. It also hasn’t been properly tested for older people.”
‘My wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look’
Ed Griffiths, 67, a retired IT specialist, says his wife has impaired vision and could not work the machine at Prague airport as they passed through last September as she was unable to read the instructions.
“The photo/fingerprint machine failed for both of us, and we spent one hour 15 minutes standing in a slow queue of confused people waiting for staff to retry it, but my wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look, so they skipped the photo and she was waved through,” says Ed, who lives in Buckinghamshire. The delay meant their prebooked taxi nearly left without them.
Then the couple were in Milan in March and Ed had to re-register despite already having done so in Prague.
“The machine ignored my previous registration, my fingerprint was asked for and failed, I waited an hour in a queue for manual assistance retry,” he says. His wife, also 67, however, did manage registration and was waved through.
More recently, in Vienna in May an officer supervised the booths for photos and fingerprints. Again, the system ignored his previous registration, but the couple got through in five minutes.
“Twice we have been registered already, and it made no discernible difference,” Ed says. “We have not found assistance at machines, but at booths there has been some help.”

====================================================================================================

London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

Ten years ago, Alastair Harper was an advocate for young people’s health sitting in a stuffy meeting room in London planning an air pollution campaign. “My phone started buzzing,” he said. “I took the call, and then told the room I needed to leave immediately.
“I had to get to UCLH [one of London’s major hospitals]. My own child was headed there in a blue-lit ambulance because she was struggling to breathe London’s toxic air.”
Hundreds of thousands of parents across the UK capital had similar experiences in those years. Between about 6,000 and 8,000 people were dying prematurely each year in London in the late 2010s. In 2020, an inquest found that the death of Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah in 2013 had been a direct result of air pollution, the first time it had been listed as a cause of death in the UK.
This week, a study from Queen Mary University London (QMUL) showed a significant reversal. Children’s lungs had grown bigger and stronger since the most polluting vehicles have been restricted on the capital’s roads, scientists found. The ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – introduced by London’s mayor Sadiq Khan in 2019 and expanded in 2021 and 2023 – charges £12.50 a day for more polluting vehicles that do not meet stringent standards. It has drastically cut levels of nitrogen dioxide, a harmful pollutant.
To Harper, who later worked for Khan as an environmental adviser, and now works independently, relief at his own child’s recovery has been supplemented by the satisfaction of knowing that far fewer parents will experience such dread. “To know now that same air is so much safer for the kids that breathe it because of the political choice of one man makes me feel proud of this city,” he said.
Nick Hopkinson, a professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London, said the QMUL study was not a surprise. “There is an absolute wealth of evidence that air pollution is a major cause of ill health and premature death across the planet,” he said. Air pollution kills 7 million people a year globally, according to the World Health Organization.
Poor air not only causes respiratory difficulties and the stunting of children’s lungs, but also heart disease and stroke. It is associated with some forms of cancer, dementia, autism and cognitive difficulties in children too. New studies are adding to our knowledge, but we have known for decades of the basic dangers of dirty air. So why is there so much opposition to curbs on air pollution, which are clearly sound public health measures?
This opposition, culture war even, is central for all cities hoping to follow Khan’s lead. The leading causes of air pollution vary around the world – coal use in power stations in China and India, agricultural burning in south-east Asia, waste burning in many of the poorest countries and dust and local industry in others – but road traffic is a constant.
The technology to cut all of these types of air pollution already exists, says a former social development minister of Ecuador and now executive director of the Breathe Cities initiative, whose supporters include the Clean Air Fund and C40, a global coalition of mayors and leaders of nearly 100 major cities. “We know that we have the means to make a difference, and we are sharing knowledge and success stories so they can be replicated with impactful policies,” she said.
In the case of coal, the alternatives are renewable energy. Halting the burning of forests and peatlands would also combat the climate crisis. The alternatives to polluting traffic are public transport, electric vehicles, the redesign of cities and encouragement of active transport – walking and cycling. Trees are also important everywhere.
Paris and Barcelona have shown what is possible within a few years when mayors embrace the joys of cycling, following the lead long ago taken in Denmark and the Netherlands. New York’s Zohran Mamdani, now wearing a cycle helmet, hopes to do the same. But elsewhere in car-dominated America, infamously poor public transport provision, an intractable SUV culture and a president in Donald Trump intent on rolling back environmental protections mean widespread change is unlikely.
Other cities are working to make a difference. Bogotá is about to embark on its second Zuma, a clean air zone that involves expanding cycle lanes and footpaths, paving roads to suppress dust and planting trees. The Colombian capital won last year’s global Earthshot prize for its first Zuma. The city’s environment secretary, Adriana Soto, said: “Residents helped shape the design, particularly how the works would maintain access to their homes and respond to local mobility needs.” Hundreds of cities around the world now have clean air zones of varying sizes.
Another is Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, which passed an air quality act in 2022 that requires harmful emissions to be halved by 2035 and has installed a network of 50 low-cost monitoring stations as a first step. Imports of vehicles more than eight years old are banned, and the city is consulting on establishing clean air zones. The lead for the C40 Breathe Cities project in Nairobi, Victor Indasi, said: “More remains to be done, but Nairobi is firmly on the right trajectory.”
Bulgaria’s capital, Sofia, is saddled with old-fashioned heating systems dependent on coal and wood burning. These are being phased out and replaced with cleaner heat pumps, subsidised for those on low incomes, as part of a city-wide introduction – the first in south-east Europe – of low-emissions zones for transport and heating. Recent results show a 22% reduction in the average concentration of PM10 particulate matter, and a halving of days that exceed air quality guidance levels. Poland is also cutting its reliance on solid fuels.
In Australia, Melbourne’s mayor was inspired by a speech Khan gave last year before Brazil’s Cop30 climate summit. The first step was discovering that state-level monitoring was telling the city little about the real quality of its air at a neighbourhood level. “It was surprising to us that this wasn’t being measured,” a spokesperson said. With the new monitoring data coming in, the mayor has yet to decide what actions will be taken, whether a clean air zone or other restrictions, or carrots in the form of scrappage schemes and improved public transport. “We are still at the beginning of this journey,” the spokesperson said.
London’s low emission zone might not have happened if Khan had not staked his reputation on it. When he launched the scheme in 2019, he faced fierce opposition from political opponents and large groups of voters, and even his own party. The plan was challenged in the courts, businesses complained of the supposedly crippling costs, and Khan received personal threats and shouts of “Nazi” at public appearances. One survey found 60% of Londoners who replied to a consultation were against it.
In 2023, the resurgent Labour party under its new leader Keir Starmer faced an important byelection in Uxbridge, on the outer edge of London. The Ulez was a key issue for voters and Labour lost by a small margin, leading Starmer’s advisers to blame the zone and demand row-backs in London and elsewhere. Andy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, who took over from Starmer as prime minister this summer, abandoned plans for a Ulez after Uxbridge.
In all of these cities there is a sense of caution, even hesitancy, and none are moving fast enough. In London, the successes of the Ulez are threatened by the ballooning number of wood-burning stoves, a fashion accessory rather than a necessity for most of their urban owners. These are now a bigger source of particle pollution than traffic. More than 110,000 children were admitted to hospital with breathing difficulties in London in 2024.
Monitoring is a vital first step, but what is done with the data is what counts. That will involve tough measures. “There is always a price. You have to change people’s behaviour, you have to change the transport, the heating, the energy generation,” said Hopkinson. “The way things are in cities is the way they have developed over long periods, and changing all that is difficult.”
The pollution is often invisible. As Vaca Jones put it: “Air is not a tangible public good that people can feel and see. That means it is not a priority on the political agenda.”
Vested interests also intervene. Though studies show that air pollution takes an economic as well as a physical toll, businesses often complain – with little evidence – that curbs on driving will hurt them.
There is also the fact that the people driving the cars and operating the polluting factories are often not the same people whose children are being admitted to hospital. “Those who are suffering are those who have done least to cause the pollution,” said Chris Griffiths, a professor of primary care at Oxford University.
When Khan embarked on London’s Ulez, hysterical misinformation quickly spread online, suggesting the mayor intended to shut down London for his own ends. His deputy, Mete Coban, recalls the shock. “The personal abuse Sadiq got on the back of it was incredible,” he said. “I think it’s this, the misinformation, that is the number one thing that puts off other countries from doing this.”
Hopkinson said: “There is a kind of madness about it. “Disinformation, which is lying to people, is confusing them. They are trying to persuade people that air pollution is not bad for them, and climate change is not real.
“They are spreading wild conspiracy theories [for instance that 15-minute cities, where all amenities can be accessed within a small area, are devices of government control] and the far right are exploiting this and generating grievance.”
With the latest study adding to a growing pool of evidence of the Ulez’s success, proponents of cleaner urban air hope to be able to cut through the madness with facts that speak loudly to parents and responsible people everywhere.
As Hopkinson put it: “The question for pro-pollution campaigners is ‘why do you hate children?’”

‘So much still needs to be done’: Italian town marks 10 years since devastating earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

As people gather in Amatrice on Monday for a mass to mark the 10th anniversary of the earthquake that struck the hilltop town and several neighbouring communities, killing 303 and leaving thousands homeless, politicians and other public figures will pay tribute.
But for many, their words will offer little comfort: 10 years on, much of Amatrice, whose historic centre was wiped out by the 6.0 magnitude quake, is still being rebuilt and more than half of its roughly 2,100 residents continue to live in temporary housing.
“They will make a good show of it, bow their heads and say: ‘We did a lot,’” said Sonia Santarelli, the president of Comitato Civico 3e36, a grassroots initiative established soon after the disaster. “But nobody will put their neck on the line. They will say the reconstruction is going well … but how can that be when so many are in homes that are uninhabitable?”
A report published last week by ActionAid Italy highlighted severe delays in rebuilding Amatrice and other areas damaged by the earthquake. According to the findings, as of April 2026, construction on roughly two-thirds of the planned public projects had yet to begin, rising to seven in 10 in the hardest-hit areas. Some €4.85bn (£4.15bn) has been earmarked for the works, the report said.
The earthquake struck in the early hours on 24 August 2016, its tremors felt as far as Rome. Santarelli, who owns an agriturismo, or farm stay, in the hamlet of Torrita close to Amatrice, recalled being woken by a loud blast and the sound of buildings collapsing. There was virtually nothing left of the hamlet, she said, but fortunately nobody there died.
Santarelli counts her blessings that she was not made homeless either. Comitato Civico 3e36, whose name references the precise time – 3.36am – the earthquake hit, was founded to defend the communities affected and to ensure citizens have a voice in the reconstruction process.
Prefabricated housing villages were set up in 41 sites across the affected areas. The wooden homes are cramped and especially stifling in the heat. “The heat and humidity squelch you,” said Santarelli.
Furthermore, they are undignified places in which to die, she claimed, owing to limited space restricting the easy movement of coffins. Residents have also complained that the rooms are too small for traditional wakes.
Some of those displaced are still paying mortgages on homes that don’t exist any more. “You cannot make people live in these conditions for so long,” said Santarelli. “So much work still needs to be done.”
Projects that have been completed in Amatrice include a school and a handful of buildings in the historic centre. Construction of a new hospital is nearing completion and could open in 2027, provided it is fully equipped and staffed.
There are many explanations for the sluggish reconstruction. Matteo Renzi, the prime minister at the time of the quake, had pledged to rebuild the towns as they were. Renzi resigned at the end of 2016 after a referendum defeat and since then Italy has had five different governments, each appointing commissioners for the rebuild.
As with previous major earthquakes, such as the one that hit L’Aquila in 2009, reconstruction has been mired by bureaucracy, legal disputes and the general complexity of rebuilding historic centres in mountainous areas.
Much of the pressure falls on the mayor. Elected in 2021, Giorgio Cortellesi said reconstruction efforts were hampered by the Covid pandemic and then by a government eco-renovation scheme, which was intended to revive the post-pandemic economy but instead pushed up the cost of building materials and lured construction workers away to more profitable jobs in other parts of Italy.
Cortellesi, an engineer who was determined to contribute to Amatrice’s revival after miraculously finding his two sons alive during a desperate search through the rubble in the dark, said the reconstruction has gathered pace over the past couple of years.
However, there is “a significant housing emergency”, he acknowledged, exacerbated by construction firms renting out homes for their staff, in turn driving up rents for people who live there. He said the council is working to reclaim some of those properties.
As for the prefabricated villages, which are nearing the end of their 10-year warranty, they will need to be dismantled and their residents moved into their rebuilt homes. “They will return to their homes, which will be the safest in Italy and the most energy efficient,” Cortellesi said, but without offering a timeline for completion.
Amatrice’s population has declined over the past decade, with many choosing to move elsewhere for better prospects. But there is also a resilience among those who have stayed.
Sergio Pirozzi, who was mayor at the time of the calamity, is one of them. Within minutes of the earthquake striking, he captured the devastation in a few stark words: “Half of the town is gone.”
A football coach, Pirozzi had been at a dinner marking the 50th anniversary of the local team a few hours before. “Of those who I was with that night, 36 died and there were others who lost their wives and children. It is not something I will ever overcome,” he said.
And yet, despite also having to live with the delays and frustrations of rebuilding, Pirozzi’s attachment to Amatrice is undiminished: “For me, even today, this is the most beautiful place in the world.”

First Bus bans under-16s in Stoke-on-Trent travelling alone after 6pm after disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

For some, it is a quotidian nuisance that inevitably occurs when you are in the vicinity of teenagers. For others, it is an expression of modern-day lawlessness among young people.
Whatever view you take, antisocial behaviour on public transport has become a hot debate – and with the introduction of free bus travel for kids aged 5 to 15 across England during August, matters have come to a head in Staffordshire.
On Friday, the bus company First Bus banned all passengers aged 15 and under travelling without an adult after 6pm in Stoke-on-Trent until further notice.
The company said multiple incidents of antisocial behaviour had occurred since the government’s “cost of living-busting” flagship free travel scheme was introduced on 1 August, including one involving more than 100 young people acting in an “intimidating and aggressive way” at Hanley bus station in the city centre.
“Police had to be called,” local First Bus regional director Simon Mathieson told a journalist on BBC Radio Stoke. “Lots of my drivers, who want to do a good job, [were] feeling very unsafe; lots of passengers, trying to get home, [were] feeling very unsafe.”
He revealed the company had seen a large uptake of the free travel offer by children in the area, describing it as a brilliant scheme to get people using buses. But he added that one driver had since reported children had been swinging on strap handles on the handrails of his bus and running up and down the vehicle while it was in motion.
“That’s not really helping people feel like they can travel in safety and comfort,” Mathieson said. “Unfortunately – and very regretfully – because of the antisocial behaviour … We’ve made the decision to protect staff and other customers on the buses.”
Last year, the Liberal Democrats called for tougher action to be taken to tackle “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on buses and trains, including fines of up to £1,000.
The Scottish government is planning to bring in legislation that will allow it to force people who benefit from its free bus travel scheme – including young people aged 5 to 21 – to abide by a forthcoming code of conduct, or have their right to concessionary travel withdrawn or suspended.
But others say policies to prevent antisocial behaviour in public places are already disproportionate and can result in hefty fines.
For example, one passenger at Waterloo station who put a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a “completely full” bin was recently fined £500 by a Lambeth council enforcement officer who had been standing at a distance, watching the bin.
An 86-year-old pensioner was fined £250 in Skegness, Lincolnshire, last year for spitting out a leaf after it blew into his mouth.
Cllr Finlay Gordon-McCusker, the cabinet minister for transport at Stoke-on-Trent council, said it was disappointing that First Bus had decided to ban all unaccompanied under-16s in the evenings. “Sadly, the children paying the price are overwhelmingly the ones who did nothing wrong.”
He said that during his discussions with the company, he had questioned why more transport safety officers could not have been deployed to monitor the routes that were affected instead. “It’s a real shame that First Bus felt that this was their only option … It’s certainly not the option I would have liked to see put in place.”
He and his fellow councillors had welcomed the government’s free bus travel scheme in August, he said. “But clearly it’s presented an opportunity for some kids to travel across the city and cause trouble, which is what they’ve done in this situation.”
That doesn’t mean there is anything wrong with the policy, he added. “Teenagers with nothing to do in August isn’t a new phenomenon. The scheme didn’t create the behaviour. It changed its geography.”
He added: “What the free travel did, possibly, was move it [the antisocial behaviour] from the estates where it’s dispersed and largely unreported to the bus station where it’s concentrated, it’s visible and it lands in an incident log.”
He disagrees that banning unaccompanied children from buses in evenings is the right way to tackle antisocial behaviour in Stoke-on-Trent. A better solution might have been greater police presence at the bus station, he said, so that young people could have continued to benefit from the freedom of having unlimited free bus travel during the summer holidays.
“It’s certainly not fair,” he said. “I think it’s a crying shame that that freedom [to travel] has been taken away because of the unacceptable behaviour of a very small minority of young people.”
First Bus declined to be interviewed by the Guardian but said in a statement the decision had been approved by the Department for Transport (DfT) and has the full support of the council.
Drivers will continue to be able to exercise their discretion to provide free travel for unaccompanied children and young people if they are vulnerable or to ensure their safety.
A government spokesperson said: “Our Great British Summer Savings scheme allows kids under 15 to travel for free on participating services, to give families room to breathe and enjoy days out throughout August.
 
 “The scheme rightly offers all local operators flexibilities to deal with issues like anti-social behaviour, such as the right to refuse travel or localised time restrictions.”

Ministers have commissioned a pair of in-depth reports into how franchising businesses are policed in the UK, as the government considers introducing new laws after high-profile allegations about conduct in the sector.
The action follows a Guardian investigation last December, which revealed claims that Adrian Howe, a former Vodafone employee who had agreed to start a franchise in 2018, had taken his own life after pressure from the FTSE 100 telecoms group.
The Department for Business and Trade is understood to be working with the British Franchise Association on a study of the domestic market, while it has also engaged the Centre for Economic Policy Research to analyse different models in operation internationally.
Both studies will feed into the government’s assessment of the legal framework required to “ensure franchisees are properly protected, while avoiding unnecessary burdens on small businesses”.
The developments come as the department said that Lord Leong, who was named in July as minister for small business and enterprise, has been handed franchising as part of his portfolio.
His appointment follows a pledge in January by Keir Starmer to review laws governing franchising agreements, as part of the official response to the Howe case. The former Vodafone store manager was found drowned days before his new franchise was due to open its doors when his relatives said he had become convinced his deal with the multinational company would prove financially disastrous.
December’s Guardian investigation also spoke to two former Vodafone franchisees who recounted that commission cuts by the company in 2020 had caused their franchising companies to run up huge debts, which they each said contributed to them making attempts on their own lives.
They were among a group of 62 former Vodafone franchisees who brought a high court claim in 2024, alleging the company “unjustly enriched” itself and which MPs have compared to the Post Office Horizon IT scandal.
In July, Vodafone settled the 19-month-old court claim via a confidential agreement “without any admission of liability”. Howe was not included in that claim, which was launched after his death, but his family has since said they will continue to press the government to introduce an “Adrian’s law” to incorporate new regulations to govern the franchising sector.
Campaigners have argued that franchisees are uniquely exposed under the current UK system as the law treats their small companies as equals to huge corporations – even though there are often large imbalances in power formalised within the franchise agreements that govern the relationship between both parties.
During an adjournment debate on franchising in July 2025, the former Conservative minister John Hayes told MPs: “Franchising can be used as a method to exaggerate the power of the business at the heart of the franchise and to weaken the position of franchisees. My assertion is that is common and is particular in the case of Vodafone.”
A Vodafone UK spokesperson said: “While we are sorry if any partners have had a difficult experience, we reject any suggestion that our franchisees were put under undue pressure.
“We continue to run a successful franchise operation of over 350 stores, and many of our existing franchisees have expanded their business with us by taking on additional stores. We encourage everyone to raise issues, and we will always seek to resolve them.”
The company said last year it “wholly rejects” any suggestion that it had “knowingly or recklessly or negligently” put anybody involved with its franchise stores under unreasonable pressure.
Mental health experts emphasise that suicide is usually complex and can often involve many triggers.
The company has added that comparisons to the Post Office scandal are “wholly inappropriate”.

The South Asian cricketers bringing their sport to Lithuania one park meadow at a time

16:00:00 KST

On weekend mornings in Vingis Park, Vilnius' largest green space, walkers and joggers sometimes stop to watch something they've never seen before: cricket.
It takes a group of men about an hour just to set the pitch up – stretching a mat across the grass and pinning it down – and even then, the uneven ground sends the ball bouncing at odd angles. But for the South Asians who gather here a few times a month, it's worth it.
Cricket is one of the world's most widely followed sports, with a particular grip on the Indian subcontinent. The 2025 Champions Trophy final between India and New Zealand drew around 230 million viewers in India alone.
In countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, it is less a game than a piece of national identity – something most people grow up playing before they can properly explain the rules.
Lithuania, a country of fewer than three million people in northeastern Europe, is not among them. But a small and growing community of South Asian expats is trying to change that.
Finding something familiar
Taufeeq Shaik moved from India to Lithuania four years ago for work. Shortly after arriving in Vilnius, he found a Facebook group of people playing cricket in the city and went along.
"I realised people were playing seriously. That increased my interest – not just to play cricket, but to grow the community, to bring this game to Lithuania," he said.
Playing in an open public space means fielding a lot of curious questions. Passers-by stop to ask what's going on, and the players have learned to explain the basics – and sometimes to hand someone a bat and let them try. A few have come back.
The rules, admittedly, take some explaining. Cricket evolved in England over four centuries and spread worldwide during the British Empire; today it is sometimes described as a cross between baseball and chess, owing to the tactical complexity that sits beneath its unhurried surface.
The basic idea is simple enough: one team bats, scoring runs by hitting the ball and running between two sets of stumps; the other bowls and fields, trying to get the batters out. Matches range from three-hour Twenty20 games to traditional five-day Test matches.
A community of 60
Lithuania currently has four cricket clubs: Vilnius Cricket Club, Aquila Cricket Club, Kaunas Cricket Club, and Falcon Cricket Club, with around 60 active players – most of them South Asian expats working or studying in Lithuania.
Matches between the Vilnius and Kaunas clubs, players say, carry a competitive edge not unlike the fierce basketball rivalry between Vilnius' Rytas and Kaunas' Žalgiris clubs – though the tension evaporates the moment the game ends.
"I'm from one region of India, my teammates are from other regions. When we come together to play, we become like a family. Most of the people I play cricket with here are close friends," said Shaik.
The pitch problem
The community's biggest obstacle is practical: there are no proper cricket pitches in Lithuania.
Professional cricket requires a specially prepared surface, and the makeshift mat laid out in Vingis Park is a poor substitute – audibly so, as the ball skids unpredictably off the uneven ground beneath it.
As a result, official competitive matches are usually played across the border in Latvia or Estonia, which both have proper facilities.
"The first challenge is the playing surface," Shaik said. "If we want the player base to grow, if we want to host matches against clubs from other countries, this pitch isn't suitable for that."
The community has been in contact with the Lithuanian sports ministry, trying to make the case for investment in proper facilities – though cricket remains far enough from the mainstream that progress is slow. "We're happy with what we have for now. But we know it's not enough."
ICC-certified coaches and school visits
There are grounds for optimism, though. Several Lithuanian schools have begun showing interest in introducing cricket to pupils, and the community has a handful of coaches certified by the International Cricket Council – the sport's global governing body – who are able to visit classrooms and sports lessons.
One of them is Vinayagasundaram Subramani, who goes by Vinay, and who has lived in Lithuania for eight years, learning Lithuanian while working in a supermarket.
"Cricket has given me so much here. I got my ICC certificate, I can travel to schools to teach children. It's given me friendships I wouldn't otherwise have," he said.
When he and his teammates tell curious Lithuanians that they compete in matches representing Lithuania, he says, the reaction is invariably warm. "I've never seen anyone come and shout at us that we're taking their space. That simply doesn't happen here. Lithuanians are very welcoming, very kind. We feel like we belong."
What he misses most, playing cricket in a park far from home, is simple: "The only thing missing is friends and family cheering for you from the boundary. That's the only thing. But here we have teammates who support each other. Sometimes we even livestream matches when we travel to play in other European countries."

Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23

Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal
August 23, 2026
Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal on Sunday, after it found the deadly virus in a long-nosed fur seal.
Authorities in the state of South Australia said they found the virus in the seal in the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 kilometers (192 miles) from the state capital, Adelaide.
Austrialia has been combating the highly pathogenic influenza after it arrived in the country in June. Earlier this month it reported its first mass seabird deaths, marking an escalation.
What did authorities have to say?
There are an estimated 100,000 long-nosed fur seals in the state's waters. The infected individual was found dead with no signs of injury, authorities said.
Its death "does not appear to be associated with other sick or dead marine mammals," Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in televised remarks.
"Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins added.
"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins was quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation as saying.
The virus has not spread to Australia's poultry or agriculture, according to the government, which counted 297 confirmed cases as of Friday.
Earlier in August, the government said it would begin a bird vaccination program based on the species' vulnerability to the virus and conservation impact.

Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," Carney said.
US President Donald Trump hit back at Canada on Sunday, saying, "Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!"
"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" Trump added in a post on Truth Social.
New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries and take effect on September 8. More details would come next week, Carney said.
Trump had previously said Washington "should be able to have a deal with Canada", citing his "good relationship" with Carney.
But on Saturday, Canada's prime minister said Trump set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable even though earlier talks had been positive.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked."
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the New York Times on Saturday that the US had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos, as well as eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber.

Kazakhstan votes in parliamentary election expected to strengthen president’s grip on power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
06:53:01 UTC
15:53:01 KST

Kazakhstan votes in a parliamentary election expected to strengthen president’s grip on power
TALLINN, Estonia (AP) — Kazakhstan voted on Sunday in a parliamentary election that is expected to further strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s grip on power in Central Asia’s largest nation.
The pro-presidential Adilet party is widely predicted to win an overwhelming majority, with several smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also anticipated to enter parliament. The vote was the country’s first election to a new, single-chamber parliament called the Kurultai.
The 73-year-old Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who previously worked at the United Nations, has been in office since 2019.
Sunday’s vote was the culmination of a constitutional overhaul that Tokayev initiated in March, when 87% of voters supported a referendum to merge the two chambers of parliament into one and grant the president authority to appoint key officials, subject to parliamentary approval, including reestablishing the vice presidency.
Tokayev, who has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over the war in Ukraine, has justified the changes by citing the need for rapid decision-making in a fast-changing world.
Last month, Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Court ruled that the amendments effectively reset the clock on Tokayev’s previous terms in office, opening the door for him to run for another seven-year term.
The election comes at a difficult economic moment for Kazakhstan: inflation hit 10.2% in February, and tax hikes have fueled public discontent.
Analysts say the economic strain has made authorities wary of a repeat of the unrest of January 2022, when fuel price protests spiraled into violence that left dozens of protesters and police officers dead — a scenario Tokayev is seeking to guard against by concentrating power in his own hands.
Ahead of the election, Tokayev said it promised to be a “truly historic event.”
“Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country’s history,” Tokayev said on Friday. “Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state.”
The vote also took place against a backdrop of intensifying crackdowns on media freedom. Media organizations have urged Tokayev to drop criminal charges against several journalists under house arrest and to revise the country’s legislation to ensure media freedom. Authorities have opened roughly 10 criminal cases against independent journalists and popular bloggers.
The most recent case involves Lukpan Akhmedyarov, an independent journalist who hosts the YouTube project “Prosto Zhurnalistika,” or “Simply Journalism.”
He told The Associated Press that a criminal case was opened against him in August on charges of “disseminating false information,” after he published a list of Kazakhstan’s citizens fighting in Ukraine. He faces up to seven years in prison.
“In the run-up to these parliamentary elections, repression has intensified sharply, with attacks on independent media, cyberattacks, and criminal cases launched against independent journalists and popular bloggers,” Akhmedyarov told the AP, speaking from Almaty, Kazakhstan’s largest city.
“It feels like the authorities want to silence all media outlets they don’t control — everyone they couldn’t reach an agreement with or couldn’t buy off,” he added.
Akhmedyarov said that the streets of Kazakhstan’s major cities are “flooded with advertisements and posters for the pro-presidential Adilet party.”
“It is not very difficult to predict the outcome of these elections,” he said.

The blaze, which broke out overnight, had spread to 82,000 square meters and was assigned a Level 4 fire severity rating, according to the St. Petersburg branch of Russia's Emergencies Ministry.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,476,580 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:46:18 UTC
15:46:18 KST

Russia has lost around 1,476,580 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 22.
The figure includes 1,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,292 tanks, 25,202 armored combat vehicles, 138,219 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,451 artillery systems, 2,054 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,584 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 474,641 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,352 unmanned ground systems, 5,052 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, and 4,569 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

15:44:01 KST

Kazakhstan has elected its new, unicameral parliament in a tightly controlled process following changes to the country's constitution, with genuine opposition groups excluded from the race.
Seven state-vetted parties contested the election, while opposition groups were denied the status of political parties under legislation used to exclude them.
The Central Election Commission said 72.15% of the more than 12.6 million voters on the electoral register had cast ballots by 6 p.m. local time. Preliminary results are expected on August 24.
President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev, whose reform agenda paved the way for the creation of the new unicameral parliament, cast his ballot at a polling station in Astana, calling the election an "important historic event" for Kazakhstan. He said the vote was only the beginning of a broader reform effort.
Asked at the polling station whether he plans to seek another presidential term, Toqaev said it was too early to discuss the issue. His comments come after constitutional changes that have opened a legal path for him to seek another seven-year term.
Toqaev also said there would be changes to the government following the election, without providing details.
Under Kazakhstan's new constitutional system, the formation of a new parliament is expected to be followed by the resignation and re-formation of the government.
The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media.
Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Police did not immediately comment on the allegation.
Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. Arterkhan has previously faced prosecution over statements critical of the authorities.
The restrictions extended to independent election monitoring.
Under the election-monitoring rules, domestic nongovernmental groups receiving direct or indirect foreign funding cannot observe inside polling stations.
This has left independent Kazakh watchdogs outside the official monitoring process.
The authorities say 777 foreign observers are accredited, many representing regional organizations including the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
The SCO said its observers had recorded no violations or complaints during the first half of voting on August 23. The SCO mission said it would issue its final assessment after polling, with a news conference scheduled for August 24.
The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), whose interim report noted the absence of genuine opposition parties and independent candidates and concerns over restrictions on political expression, is also observing the vote.
More than 70 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries were deployed as part of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly observation mission, its 13th election observation mission in Kazakhstan since 1994.
The OSCE has criticized all of the elections held in this period, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor as head of state, Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev.
The vote also took place amid pressure on independent media.
According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism.
The CEC is expected to release preliminary results on August 24, with final results due within seven days. Separately, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) will present its preliminary findings on August 24.
The vote follows constitutional changes approved in a March referendum that replaced the previous bicameral parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai.
The Adilet party, which absorbed the former ruling party’s political structures as a new vehicle for the post-Nazarbaev era, is expected to dominate the first Kurultai.
A nationwide poll by the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development put the party at 70.2 percent support, positioning it to further cement Toqaev's grip on power.

A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck eastern Japan early Sunday, injuring more than 20 people and disrupting transportation, local media reported, citing the country’s weather agency and local authorities.
No tsunami alert was issued after the quake, which originated in the southern part of Ibaraki prefecture at a depth of 68 kilometers (42 miles), Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported, quoting the Japan Meteorological Agency.
The tremor registered lower 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale of 7 in parts of the prefecture as well as in central Tokyo.
More than 20 people were injured, including a young man and a woman in her 70s in Saitama, north of Tokyo, as well as nine people in Kanagawa and four in Chiba prefectures.
Several train services were delayed following the quake, while some trains ran at reduced speeds.
Some express services operated by Tobu Railway remained halted.
An intensity of lower 5 was also recorded in parts of Saitama and Chiba prefectures and central Tokyo.
No abnormalities were detected at the Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plant in Ibaraki prefecture or the disaster-stricken Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant and the nearby Fukushima Daini plant in northeastern Japan.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi instructed officials to ascertain the extent of the damage from the quake and provide timely information to the public.
The weather agency urged the public to remain alert for an earthquake registering lower 5 on the seismic intensity scale over the next week, especially during the next two to three days.
The latest quake was felt across a wide swath of the country, including northeastern and central Japan.

Interview: China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:37:38 CST
15:37:38 KST

ROME, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed four global initiatives offer a new perspective on international governance and new opportunities for international cooperation amid geopolitical fragmentation and global instability, said an Italian business leader.
The initiatives represent China's efforts to provide coordinated responses to challenges that transcend national borders, Mario Boselli, chairman of the Italy China Council Foundation, said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
They also represent a deepening of China's international vision following more than a decade of the Belt and Road Initiative, extending the focus from economic and infrastructure cooperation to development, security, dialogue among civilizations and global governance, he said.
He believes that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) could offer opportunities to deepen cooperation between China and Europe, including Italy.
The GDI's focus on climate change, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digitalization and technological innovation could create opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy, photovoltaics and energy storage, among others, said Boselli.
Italy and China can also strengthen cooperation among universities and research institutions in biotechnology, healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, he added.
Noting that the GCI could promote cooperation in culture, heritage conservation, universities and youth exchanges, he said Italy, with its rich cultural heritage and the strong appeal of "Made in Italy" in China, is "one of the most natural European partners" for such initiatives.
Taken together, the four initiatives outline a vision of a multipolar world with greater participation by emerging economies and countries of the Global South, Boselli said.
With its tradition of dialogue with China and complementary economic strengths, Italy can play a bridging role between China and Europe, promoting practical cooperation in sustainable development, innovation, culture and global governance, he said.
China's initiatives may not provide an immediate solution to current international tensions, but can offer "a space for reflection and dialogue" to identify more inclusive, practical and long-term forms of cooperation, he added. ■

A lower 5 quake is defined by the agency as shaking that causes most people to be frightened and to hold on to something stable, while objects may fall from shelves.

Escalating tensions
Tensions between Russia and the UK have ratcheted up in recent days, with Moscow issuing a warning through its UK embassy, stating – without further definition – that there would be “consequences” after it emerged that Britain was supplying drone technology to Kyiv.
In a statement on Telegram on Aug 17, the Russian embassy in the UK accused Britain of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis” and that “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer.”
Kyiv has stepped up attacks on Moscow and other parts of Russia in recent weeks, with a military source confirming to the BBC that UK drones had been used in attacks on Russia that reportedly caused more than £35bn in economic damage.
John Foreman, a former British defence attaché in Moscow and Kyiv, views Kelin’s withdrawal as a signal of Moscow’s disinterest in maintaining bilateral relations with the UK. In a post on X, Foreman stated: “The embassy’s strident ‘consequences’ statement this week and the huge deterioration of bilateral relations since 2018 and especially since the start of the war make me wonder if Moscow will permanently downgrade the relationship this time, by default by not replacing him.”
Following The Sunday Times report, the Russian embassy released a broader public statement to other national outlets – including The Guardian and The Telegraph – to deny that it was formally downgrading diplomatic relations, while simultaneously blaming London for pushing a path of confrontation.
Incoming British Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently stated that the UK is “with Ukraine 100%” as President Volodymyr Zelensky became his first international visitor.
Speaking to reporters on Aug. 18 after Moscow threatened “consequences” over drone supplies, Burnham said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin... We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
Missile blueprints
The UK appears to remain unfazed by the diplomatic rift with Moscow, as Burnham makes Kyiv the destination of his first foreign trip on Monday – Ukraine’s Independence Day. He is set to announce that Britain has agreed to allow UK defense company MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French equivalent of the UK’s storm shadow.
The move follows the UK being the first to gift long-range strike weapons for defensive purposes to Ukraine in 2023 and will allow the French and Ukrainians to move forward with the Ukrainian assembly of the missile.
Burnham said: “On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes. I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.”

129,000 still without power as Lithuania cleans up after weekend storm

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:14:00 UTC
15:14:00 KST

Around 129,000 electricity consumers remained without power on Monday morning, three days after a powerful storm swept across Lithuania, said Grid operator Energijos Skirstymo Operatorius (ESO).
"We really did have an exceptional storm – when we compare it with previous ones, we see it was almost 35% more intense than the last major one, in 2024. And we're not basing that assessment on damage to our own grid, but on call-outs to the Fire and Rescue Department – how many calls they received from residents about fallen trees," Renaldas Radvila, head of grid operator Energijos Skirstymo Operatorius (ESO), told LRT Radio on Monday.
The scale of the disruption peaked on Saturday evening, when 268,000 consumers were left without electricity.
The worst-affected areas are the Kaunas, Utena, Panevėžys and Vilnius regions, where full restoration could take until Saturday, Radvila said. Power in Šiauliai and Klaipėda was expected to be back to normal by the end of Monday.
He said the scale of the storm, rather than any shortfall in resources, was the main obstacle to a faster recovery, with crews drawn from the railways, municipal energy services, the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union and forestry teams all mobilised to help clear fallen trees.
Following the 2024 storm, ESO purchased 200 additional generators, meaning municipalities can now request equipment directly from local officials, who notify ESO, with generators delivered to the site within two hours.
So far, 183 generators have been delivered to 16 municipalities.
The storm also disrupted rail services over the weekend, after fallen trees and branches landed on tracks and overhead lines, forcing speed restrictions and delays.
Around 3,500 passengers were affected, Lithuanian Railways said. All obstructions have since been cleared from the tracks, though some power disruptions remain in parts of the network, meaning delays of up to 30 minutes are still possible on Monday.

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. Participants in the 5th All-Russian Youth Environmental Forum-Festival "Arctic. The Ice Has Broken", which ran in Naryan-Mar on August 17-22, cleaned the Pechora River's coast, press service of the Clean Arctic public environmental project said.
"The cleanup mission was organized on the eve of the Pechora River Day, which traditionally is celebrated on the last Sunday in August. The river is playing a special role in life of the locals. It is a favorite place where they come to relax, plus the river is an important transport route, and a fishing center. Besides, it is along the Pechora that goods are transported to the region during the summer navigation period," the press service said.
The forum's participants had to remove mostly glass fragments which people had left on the sand. After the coastline was cleaned, the forum guests organized a friendly volleyball match on this site, and then launched kites into the sky.
"We've been looking for a location for a long time, because it's not so easy to find dirty beaches along the Pechora, there's almost no waste there. The beach is about one and a half kilometers long, and we wanted it to look even cleaner after we were there," the press service quoted the Clean Arctic project's leader Andrey Nagibin as saying.
The Nenets Autonomous Region has been participating actively in the Clean Arctic project's missions, he continued. Over five years of work, volunteers have restored more than 50 hectares of land and removed 1,000 tons of waste. Previously, cleanup missions were organized in the villages of Old Varandey and Idkateley.
The Clean Arctic Public Environmental Project has been cleaning the northern territories since 2021. The volunteers focus on objects, left since the USSR times. Waste removal is a complex technological work, where the movement teams work carefully minding the Arctic nature. Over all seasons, the project's almost 10,000 volunteers have collected 22,000 tons of waste and cleaned 1,100 hectares of land. The project's general partner is the Rosatom State Corporation, and TASS is the general information partner.
About the forum
The 5th All-Russian Youth Environmental Forum-Festival "Arctic. The Ice Has Broken" featured about 300 young scientists, researchers, and environmental volunteers aged between 18 to 35. The forum's purpose is to show the Far North's opportunities to young people and to shape ideas for the Nenets Autonomous Region's development program.
The Arctic. The Ice Has Broken was organized by the Federal Agency for Youth Affairs (Rosmolodezh), the Nenets Autonomous Region's administration, and the Clean Arctic public environmental project. TASS was the event's information partner.

Suspected insurgents set fire to government buildings, shops, cars and utility poles in more than 70 locations across four of Thailand's southernmost provinces over the weekend, injuring at least three people in a coordinated series of arson attacks, authorities said.
More than 7,800 people have been killed in provinces bordering Malaysia since 2004, when the latest round of a long-running insurgency led mainly by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional (BRN) flared.
Here are more details provided by Thai officials:
There were at least 78 incidents across four provinces: 40 in Narathiwat, 21 in Yala, 15 in Pattani and two in Songkhla. No group has claimed responsibility.
Most of the attacks took place on Saturday evening across Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat and parts of Songkhla, with some more on Sunday.
Ethnic tensions as Muslims, Malay seek independence via insurgency
A rail line was hit by explosives in Narathiwat, prompting the suspension of services in that section.
Authorities have imposed a curfew in Narathiwat, and at a meeting on Sunday, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul asked the security forces to ensure public safety.
Thailand's predominantly Muslim and ethnic Malay deep south has faced a decades-long insurgency seeking greater autonomy or independence.
The region was part of the independent Malay sultanate of Patani before its incorporation into Thailand was formalized in 1909.
Attacks come as Thailand attempts peace talks with separatist group
The attacks come as Thailand seeks to revive peace talks with the BRN, the main separatist group fighting in the region.
Chief negotiator Thanut Suvarnananda told Reuters this month that Bangkok wanted to move beyond trading concessions for reduced violence and address political grievances, including governance.
Malaysian-facilitated peace talks have repeatedly stalled since they began in 2013.
Lieutenant General Norathip Poinok, who commands the Thai army in the southern region, told local media on Monday that authorities had received intelligence nearly two months ago warning of attacks on government buildings, shops and power infrastructure.
Norathip described the attacks as retaliation for crackdowns on insurgents and illicit businesses, including drug and contraband trafficking, that fund militant groups.

Legendary Festigal producer Miki Peled dies at 87
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:42:21 UTC
15:42:21 KST

Miki Peled, the legendary producer and founder of the Festigal show, passed away at the age of 87, it was announced Monday morning.
Peled, considered one of the pillars of Israel’s entertainment industry, left behind a remarkable legacy that shaped the childhoods of generations across the country.
Peled was born in Romania in 1939 and immigrated to Israel with his family in 1948. In 1981, he founded and produced the first Festigal show in Haifa, which over the years became a leading cultural institution and an undisputed symbol of the Hanukkah holiday in Israel.
Alongside Festigal, he led dozens of major performances and cultural events throughout his decades of activity, working with many of Israel’s leading artists and creators, an effort that earned him a lifetime achievement award from ACUM, Israel’s music and copyright organization.
Friends, partners, and colleagues described him as a mentor and visionary with a big heart, who knew how to identify talent at the beginning of artists’ careers and provide them with a real platform and opportunity to break through.
'A person who knew how to dream'
Yaron Peled, his son and creative partner, said: “Miki was much more than a producer. He was a person who knew how to dream, identify talent, give people an opportunity, and above all make people believe they could.”
Peled is survived by his wife Tami, children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, alongside generations of artists and performers who viewed him as a guiding figure.
His funeral will take place Tuesday at 4:00 p.m. at Kiryat Shaul Cemetery in Tel Aviv, where family members, those who cherished his memory, and leading figures from Israel’s cultural world will gather to bid him farewell.
